And here’s where it cuts deep—
Because God actually answers him.
But not the way we expect.
God says:
“I am doing something.”
Pause.
You’d think that would comfort him.
But it doesn’t.
Because what God reveals next…
feels worse than silence.

God tells Habakkuk He’s raising up a violent nation—
a ruthless force—to judge His people.
Let that hit.
The answer to injustice…
looks like more injustice.
The solution…
feels like chaos.
And suddenly, Habakkuk’s problem isn’t just suffering.
It’s God’s method.
This is where many people quietly walk away.
Not from church.
But from trust.
Because we can handle pain…
if it makes sense.
We can endure hardship…
if we understand the purpose.
But when God’s ways feel confusing—
When His timing feels off—
When His plan feels unfair—
That’s where faith gets tested.
And if we’re honest?
That’s where pride gets exposed.
We don’t just want God to act.
We want Him to act our way.
We want control dressed up as faith.
We want obedience…
without surrender.
But God doesn’t submit to our understanding.
He invites us into His.
Habakkuk doesn’t run.
He doesn’t numb out.
He doesn’t fake peace.
He climbs.
“I will stand at my watch and station myself on the ramparts; I will look to see what He will say to me…” (Habakkuk 2:1)
This is the detail most people miss.
He positions himself to listen.
Even when he’s confused.
Even when he’s uncomfortable.
Even when he doesn’t like what he heard last time.
That’s not passive faith.
That’s war.
And then God speaks again:
“The righteous shall live by faith.” (Habakkuk 2:4)
Not by clarity.
Not by control.
Not by having all the answers.
But by faith.
Let that confront you.
Because faith isn’t just believing God can.
It’s trusting God when you don’t understand why He did.
Now here’s where the story turns.
And it’s not what you expect.
Habakkuk doesn’t get a new situation.
The injustice doesn’t instantly disappear.
The tension isn’t neatly resolved.
But something inside him shifts.
By chapter 3…
The man who questioned God—
is now singing.
Listen to this:
“Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines… yet I will rejoice in the Lord.” (Habakkuk 3:17–18)
No fruit.
No evidence.
No visible breakthrough.
Still—
Joy.
How?
How does a man go from questioning God…
to worshiping Him in lack?
Here’s the truth.
Don’t miss this.
Habakkuk didn’t get better circumstances.
He got a deeper revelation.
He realized:
God’s faithfulness is not measured by what I see…
but by who He is.
And this is where your story collides with his.
Because some of you are in that exact place right now.
You prayed—
and nothing changed.
You believed—
and things got worse.
You trusted—
and God’s answer didn’t make sense.
And quietly…
your heart started to pull back.
Not loud rebellion.
Just subtle distance.
Less prayer.
Less hunger.
Less expectation.
Because disappointment, when left unchecked…
turns into distance.
But let’s go deeper.
Because the real issue isn’t just confusion.
It’s pride.
Yes.
Pride.
The belief that God should run His universe…
in a way that makes sense to you.
That if you were in charge—
you’d do it better.
Cleaner.
Faster.
Fairer.
And we don’t say it out loud.
But we feel it.
That quiet frustration:
“God, I wouldn’t have done it like this.”
That’s the ancient temptation.
The same whisper from the garden:
“You can be like God.”
But here’s the confrontation:
If God were small enough for you to fully understand—
He wouldn’t be big enough to save you.
Let that sink in.
Now here’s the Gospel.
Clear. Undeniable. Unavoidable.
Because Habakkuk’s cry echoes into a greater moment.
A darker hill.
A deeper silence.
On the cross—
Jesus Christ cried out:
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Matthew 27:46)
The same tension.
The same question.
But this time—
God doesn’t answer.
Silence.
Why?
Because in that moment—
Jesus was carrying your sin.
Your pride.
Your rebellion.
Your demand to understand everything before you trust.
The justice Habakkuk questioned—
fell fully on Christ.
Not delayed.
Not softened.
Not explained away.
Executed.
For you.
So now—
when you question God—
you’re not speaking to a distant ruler.
You’re speaking to a Savior who has already entered your confusion…
and bled inside it.
This changes everything.
Because the cross proves:
God is not careless.
God is not cruel.
God is not absent.
He is committed.
To redeem.
To restore.
To save.
Even when you don’t understand Him.
Even when His ways feel hidden.
Even when your prayers seem unanswered.
So what do you do now?
You do what Habakkuk did.
You climb.
You take your questions—
your doubts—
your frustrations—
and instead of walking away…
you bring them closer.
You stand at the watchtower.
You wait.
Not because everything makes sense.
But because Jesus already proved He’s trustworthy.
This is faith.
Not blind optimism.
But anchored trust—
in a blood-stained cross…
and an empty tomb.
So here’s the invitation.
Personal.
Direct.
Unavoidable.
Stop demanding explanations…
and start surrendering control.
Stop measuring God by your circumstances…
and start seeing your circumstances through God.
Bring your questions.
But don’t leave His presence.
Because the same God you’re questioning—
is the One who died to save you.
Right now—
in this moment—
you have a choice.
Will you withdraw?
Or will you draw near?
Will you harden your heart?
Or will you surrender it?
If something in you is stirring—
if conviction is rising—
if you know God is calling you deeper—
don’t ignore it.
Say this, even if your voice shakes:

“Lord, I don’t understand…
but I trust You.”
That’s where transformation begins.
If this hit you—
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He was important enough to be written…
paragraphs:
He was important enough to be written…
but quiet enough to be forgotten.
Read that again.
Because that might be you.

A name in the background.
A life that doesn’t feel loud.
A calling that doesn’t feel seen.

And that tension?
It’s where this story begins.

Azariah.
Son of Zadok.
One line in 1 Kings 4:2.

No miracles recorded.
No speeches quoted.
No crowds chanting his name.
Just… listed.
And if we’re honest, that’s what scares us.

Because deep down, we don’t just want to be faithful—
we want to be noticed.

We say we’re serving God…
but part of us is still checking who’s watching.

We pray—but hope someone hears it.
We give—but hope someone sees it.
We obey—but secretly wish it gets recognized.
And when it doesn’t?
Something inside us starts to ache.

“Does this even matter?”
“Is God seeing this?”
“Am I wasting my life in something small?”
Let me ask you something.

What if your greatest obedience…
never gets applause?

What if your most faithful season…
is completely hidden?
Would you still stay?
Or would you slowly drift into silent compromise?
Because that’s where it starts.

Not with rebellion.
But with disappointment.

You didn’t get the platform.
You didn’t get the recognition.
You didn’t get the moment you thought obedience would earn.

So now you obey… but with less fire.
You serve… but with quiet resentment.
You stay… but your heart starts negotiating.
That’s the hidden struggle no one posts about.

Delayed obedience.
Half-hearted faithfulness.
A slow fade into “just enough for God.”
And here’s the piercing truth:
You can be physically present in God’s work… and emotionally absent from God Himself.
Azariah stands in that tension.
Because his father, Zadok, was not hidden.

Zadok stood firm when others compromised.
When kings shifted and loyalties cracked, Zadok stayed faithful—
and God honored that.
Then comes Azariah.

No spotlight.
No story arc.
Just placement.
Some scholars interpret his role in 1 Kings 4:2 as a high-ranking priestly or administrative position under Solomon. That means this wasn’t a small assignment.
It was trust.
But here’s the AHA moment:
God trusted him with influence… without giving him visibility.
Let that confront something in you.
Because we’ve been trained to believe that impact requires attention.
But heaven doesn’t operate on algorithms.
Jesus said in Matthew 6:4, “Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”

Not might see.
Not eventually notice.
Sees.
Right now.

Every unseen prayer.
Every quiet sacrifice.
Every moment you chose purity when no one would’ve known.
God saw it.
But we still wrestle.

Because we don’t just want God to see…
we want people to confirm that we matter.
And that’s where pride hides.
Not loud pride.
Subtle pride.
The kind that says, “I deserve more than this.”

The kind that stays obedient…
but questions God’s wisdom in the silence.
Here’s the spiritual mirror:

You don’t struggle with being unseen.
You struggle with not being affirmed.
And that’s deeper.
Because it reveals where your identity is leaning.

If your worth rises and falls based on visibility…
then your soul is anchored to people, not Christ.
And that’s dangerous.
Because people are inconsistent.
But Jesus?
Unchanging.
Listen carefully.

You were never called to be known by many.
You were called to be known by God.
And in Christ, you already are.
But let’s go deeper.
Because the issue isn’t just visibility.
It’s sin.
Yes, sin.

Because at the root of our need to be seen…
is a heart that wants glory.

Even in ministry.
Even in service.
Even in “doing things for God.”
Isaiah 64:6 reminds us that even our righteous acts can be like filthy rags apart from Him.

That means even your “good works” can be contaminated…
if they’re driven by self-exaltation instead of surrender.
That’s uncomfortable.
But necessary.

Because the Gospel doesn’t just clean your behavior—
it confronts your motives.
And here’s the turning point.

Jesus didn’t die so you could feel important.
He died because you were lost.
Romans 5:8 says, “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

Not when you were visible.
Not when you were impressive.

While you were broken.
Hidden in sin.
Unworthy of attention.
That’s when He came.
That’s when He chose you.
That’s when grace entered.
And that changes everything.

Because now your identity is not built on what you do…
but on what Christ has done.

You don’t serve to be seen.
You serve because you’ve been saved.

You don’t obey to earn worth.
You obey because you’ve been given it.

You don’t need a platform to matter.
You have a Savior who already settled your value on the cross.
And here’s the identity shift:

You are not overlooked.
You are positioned.

You are not hidden.
You are being formed.
Azariah didn’t need a story arc.
He had a place in God’s unfolding plan.
And so do you.
Even if no one claps.
Even if no one posts about it.
Even if your name is just a “line” in someone else’s story.
Because in the Kingdom?
Faithfulness is never small.
Luke 16:10 says, “Whoever is faithful in little is faithful in much.”
God measures differently.
He’s not impressed by your visibility.
He’s looking at your heart.
And here’s the conviction:

Some of us want God to expand our influence…
but we haven’t surrendered our need for attention.
That’s why the growth feels delayed.

Not because God forgot you.
But because He loves you too much to build your platform on an uncrucified ego.
Let that sit.
Because grace is not just comfort.
It’s transformation.
And transformation requires surrender.
So here’s the invitation.

Not to try harder.
Not to perform better.
But to repent.

To lay down the need to be seen.
To surrender the quiet pride.
To release the hidden disappointment.
And come back to Jesus.

Not as a performer.
But as a son.
As a daughter.
Because at the cross, everything changes.

Your past—covered.
Your sin—paid for.
Your worth—secured.
Through Jesus alone.

Not your ministry.
Not your effort.
Not your visibility.
Him.
If this is hitting something deep in you…
Don’t ignore it.
Sit with it.
Pray through it.
Real growth. Real surrender. Real intimacy with God.
Because this isn’t about a moment.
It’s about a life.
So here’s what I want you to do.
For the days you feel invisible.

And next time, we’re going deeper into the names you skipped…
but heaven didn’t.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You didn’t wake up with a hard heart.
paragraphs:
You didn’t wake up with a hard heart.
You built it… one ignored conviction at a time.
And the scariest part?
You didn’t even notice when it started happening.

At first, it felt small.
Almost harmless.

Just a little delay.
A quiet “later.”
A subtle “it’s not that serious.”

God whispered…
But you postponed.

God nudged…
But you resisted.

God convicted…
But you explained it away.
And now?

His voice feels quieter.
Not because He stopped speaking…
But because your heart stopped listening.
This is how it happens.

Not in one moment of rebellion.
But in a thousand moments of hesitation.

A slow drift.
A quiet hardening.
A dangerous numbness.

You still go to church.
You still say the right things.
You still look like you’re okay.
But deep inside?
Something has changed.

Conviction doesn’t hit the same anymore.
Sin doesn’t feel as heavy.
Disobedience doesn’t feel as urgent.
And that should terrify you.
Because a hardened heart doesn’t feel hard.
It feels normal.

It feels justified.
It feels reasonable.
It feels safe.
But it’s not.
There was a time when you couldn’t sin without feeling it.

You used to pause.
You used to wrestle.
You used to repent quickly.
Now?

You sit in it.
You manage it.
You excuse it.
And the silence is growing.
Hebrews 3:15 says:
"Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion."
Today.

Not tomorrow.
Not when it’s convenient.
Not when you feel ready.
Today.
Because delayed obedience is the birthplace of a hardened heart.

Some scholars interpret this passage as a warning rooted in Israel’s rebellion in the wilderness—when they repeatedly ignored God’s voice until their hearts became resistant, unbelieving, and spiritually blind.
And here’s the weight of that truth:

They didn’t lose God’s voice.
They lost their sensitivity to it.
That’s the danger.

God is still speaking.
But are you still responding?
Let’s be honest.
You know that area.
That thing God has been pressing on.

That compromise.
That hidden sin.
That habit you keep justifying.

That relationship you know isn’t right.
That bitterness you refuse to release.
That private life no one sees.
You felt it before.

That conviction.
That tightening in your spirit.
That moment where God said, “Stop.”
But you didn’t.
And now it’s easier not to.
This is how hearts grow cold.

Not because God abandons you…
But because you slowly stop agreeing with Him.
And here’s the truth most people don’t want to hear:
A hardened heart is not just about behavior.
It’s about resistance.

It’s about hearing God…
And choosing yourself anyway.
But here’s where grace steps in.
Because this is not the end of your story.

The fact that this is stirring something in you…
The fact that you feel this tension…
The fact that something inside you is saying, “This is me…”
That’s not condemnation.
That’s mercy.
Because a completely hardened heart feels nothing.

No conviction.
No stirring.
No urgency.
But you?
You’re still feeling something.
And that means God is still reaching.
Listen carefully:
Jesus did not come for people who had it all together.
He came for hearts that were broken… distracted… wandering… even hardened.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."

Not when you fixed yourself.
Not when you softened your heart.
While you were still in it.
And this is the Gospel:

You and I have sinned.
We have resisted God.
We have ignored His voice.
We have chosen our way over His.
That’s not a small issue.
That’s rebellion.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
All.

Not some.
Not just “worse people.”

You.
Me.
Everyone.
And sin does something dangerous.

It hardens.
It separates.
It blinds.
Isaiah 59:2 says:
"But your iniquities have separated you from your God; your sins have hidden His face from you."

That distance you feel?
That dullness in your spirit?
It’s not random.
It’s the effect of sin left unchecked.
But here’s the turning point.
You don’t fix a hardened heart by trying harder.
You fix it by surrendering deeper.
Because Jesus didn’t just die to forgive your sins.
He died to give you a new heart.
Ezekiel 36:26 says:
"I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh."

A soft heart.
A responsive heart.
A living heart.
That’s what Jesus offers.
Not behavior management.
Transformation.
Through His death on the cross, Jesus took the punishment for your sin.
Through His resurrection, He made a way for you to be restored.
Not partially.
Completely.
But there is a response.
And this is where everything changes.
Repentance.
Not just saying sorry.
Not just feeling bad.
But turning.

Turning from sin.
Turning from resistance.
Turning back to God.
Acts 3:19 says:
"Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out."
Blotted out.

Not minimized.
Not managed.
Erased.
And when you repent?
God doesn’t hesitate.
He doesn’t shame you.
He restores you.
That voice you’ve been ignoring?
He’s not speaking to condemn you.
He’s calling you back.
Right now.
Not later.
Not after you fix everything.
Right now.
So let me ask you directly:
What has God been asking you to surrender?
What conviction have you been ignoring?
What area of your life is slowly hardening your heart?
This is your moment.

You can keep delaying.
Keep justifying.
Keep drifting.
Or…
You can respond.
Right now, in this moment, you can pray:

“Jesus… I hear You.
I’ve been ignoring Your voice.
I’ve been resisting conviction.
But I don’t want a hard heart anymore.

Forgive me.
Cleanse me.
Change me.
Give me a soft heart again.
I surrender.”
He will meet you there.
Not with anger.
But with mercy.
Because the cross proves something powerful:

God would rather die for your restoration…
Than leave you in your rebellion.
This is your invitation.
Not to religion.
Not to performance.
But to Jesus.
A soft heart is not built by perfection.
It’s built by surrender.
So respond.
While you still hear His voice.
If this spoke to you…
Save this so you can come back when your heart starts drifting again.

From hardened to healed.
From distant to restored.
From resistance to surrender.
Because Jesus still softens hearts.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They laid Him where animals eat.
paragraphs: They laid Him where animals eat.

Not in gold.
Not in silk.
Not in safety.
A feeding trough.
Why?

Because something deeper was happening…
…and most people still miss it.
You’ve been trying to clean yourself up before coming to God.

Hiding parts of your life.
Managing your image.
Performing righteousness.
But inside?

Still hungry.
Still ashamed.
Still not enough.
And you wonder…
“Why do I still feel empty, even when I’m trying to be good?”
This is where everything shifts.
The manger is not a cute detail.
It is a confrontation.
It exposes the truth we avoid:
We are starving.

Not physically.
Spiritually.

Hungry for meaning.
Hungry for peace.
Hungry for righteousness we don’t have.
And instead of admitting it…
We pretend we’re full.

We scroll.
We consume.
We chase validation.
We build identities out of applause.
But when the noise fades…
The ache is still there.
Because sin does not just make you guilty.
It makes you empty.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23

Not some.
All.

The polished ones.
The hidden ones.
The religious ones.
The broken ones.
All.
And sin doesn’t just stain your record.
It separates you from God.
“But your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God…” — Isaiah 59:2
That distance?
You feel it.

In quiet moments.
In restless nights.
In the guilt you can’t shake.
So you try harder.

Be better.
Do better.
Look better.
But no matter how much you perform…
You cannot feed your own soul.
And this is where the manger speaks.
Loud.
Clear.
Uncomfortable.
God did not send a system.
He sent a Savior.
“She gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger…” — Luke 2:7
A feeding trough.
Why there?
Because Jesus was not just born…
He was being revealed.
“I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger…” — John 6:35
Do you see it now?
The Bread of Life…
Laid in a place of feeding.
This was not random.
This was mercy with a message.
You are hungry.
And He came to be your food.
But here’s the part that cuts deep.
We don’t just hunger.
We rebel.
We don’t just lack righteousness.
We reject God’s rule.
We choose sin.

We justify it.
Hide it.
Rename it.

Secret sin.
Private compromise.
Quiet addictions.
And we think:
“No one sees.”
But God does.
And the weight of that truth?
It crushes.
“Be sure your sin will find you out.” — Numbers 32:23
That’s where shame grows.

In the hidden.
In the dark.
In the silence.
Shame whispers:

“You’re too far gone.”
“You’ve messed up too much.”
“You can’t come back from this.”
So you stay away.

From God.
From truth.
From light.
But the manger interrupts that lie.
Violently.
Because God didn’t wait for you to get clean.
He came into the mess.
Right into it.
Jesus didn’t just come to feed you.
He came to save you.
And salvation is not soft.
It is costly.
The manger points to something brutal.
The cross.
“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” — Luke 19:10
Lost.
That’s us.

Not slightly off.
Not a little confused.
Lost.
Dead in sin.
“And you were dead in your trespasses and sins…” — Ephesians 2:1
Dead people don’t fix themselves.
They need resurrection.
They need intervention.
They need a Savior.
And Jesus came for that exact reason.
Not to inspire you.
To rescue you.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Did you catch that?
While.

Not after you changed.
Not after you improved.
While you were still in it.

Still sinning.
Still hiding.
Still broken.
He came.
And He didn’t stay in the manger.
He walked toward the cross.
Willingly.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree…” — 1 Peter 2:24

Every lie.
Every addiction.
Every secret.
Every shame.
Placed on Him.
The innocent for the guilty.
The pure for the corrupt.
The Son of God…
For you.
This is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement.
Substitution.
Jesus took your place.

Your sin.
Your punishment.
Your death.
So you could receive:

His righteousness.
His forgiveness.
His life.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
That is not religion.
That is rescue.
But here’s the turning point.
You don’t automatically receive this.
You must respond.
Not with performance.
With repentance.
“Repent and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out…” — Acts 3:19
Repentance is not just feeling bad.
It’s turning.

From sin.
From self-rule.
From hiding.
And turning to Jesus.
Fully.
Completely.

No filters.
No masks.
Just surrender.
“Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” — Romans 10:9
Saved.
Not improved.
Not upgraded.
Saved.
So let me ask you something real.
What are you hiding?
What sin have you normalized?
What part of your life have you kept off-limits to God?
That thing?
That’s where He wants to meet you.
Not after you fix it.
Now.
The manger proves it.
He comes low.
So you don’t have to climb.
He comes near.
So you don’t have to pretend.
He comes as bread.
So you don’t have to starve.
You are not too dirty.
You are not too broken.
You are not too far gone.
But you are responsible.
To respond.
To repent.
To come.
Jesus is not asking for your perfection.
He is calling for your surrender.
Right now.
If this is hitting your chest…
Don’t ignore it.
That’s not emotion.
That’s conviction.
And conviction is mercy knocking.
Open the door.
Say it.
Mean it.

“Jesus, I’m done running.
I’m done hiding.
I turn from my sin.
I trust You.
Save me.”
He will.
“He who comes to me I will never cast out.” — John 6:37
Never.

Not you.
Not your past.
Not your mess.
Never.
If you’re ready…
And don’t keep this to yourself.
Come back to it when the lies return.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You didn’t bow to a statue…
paragraphs:
You didn’t bow to a statue…
but something is sitting on God’s throne in your heart.
And the scariest part?
You might be calling it a blessing.

You can worship something…
and still sing in church.

You can idolize something…
and still say “God first.”

You can love something more than God…
and not even realize you’ve replaced Him.
Because idols don’t always look evil.
Sometimes they look like:

• The relationship you can’t lose
• The success you can’t surrender
• The image you have to maintain
• The comfort you refuse to let go of
And slowly… quietly… dangerously…
Your heart shifts.
Not all at once.
But little by little.
You still pray.
But your mind is somewhere else.
You still worship.
But your heart is attached to something else.
You still say “God is enough.”

But deep down…
you don’t believe it.
And here’s where it gets real:
You’re not just holding onto it.
You’re depending on it.
You check your phone more than you seek His presence.
You fear losing it more than grieving the Holy Spirit.
You protect it… even if it means disobeying God.
You justify it.
You defend it.
You hide it.
And now…
It’s no longer a blessing.
It’s a master.
This is how idolatry works.
Not loud.
Not obvious.
But subtle.
Personal.
Convincing.
The Bible says:
📖 “Those who cling to worthless idols turn away from God’s love for them.” — Jonah 2:8
Let that hit.
You don’t just add an idol to your life…
You trade God’s love for it.
And maybe you’re thinking:
“But it’s not a bad thing.”
That’s the deception.
Idols are rarely evil things.
They’re good things we’ve made ultimate things.
Your relationship.
Your dreams.
Your ministry.
Your money.
Your reputation.

Even your calling…
can become an idol if it replaces the Caller.
📖 “You shall have no other gods before Me.” — Exodus 20:3
God isn’t competing for second place.
He doesn’t share His throne.
Not because He’s insecure…
But because He knows what will destroy you if He’s not first.
Here’s the tension:
You don’t realize how much something owns you…
Until God asks you to surrender it.
And when He does…
You hesitate.
You negotiate.
You delay obedience.
Why?
Because your heart is tied to it.
📖 “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” — Matthew 6:21
Your heart follows what you value.

And what you refuse to release…
reveals what you truly worship.
Let’s get honest.
What are you afraid to lose?
What controls your emotions?
What defines your worth?
What do you run to when you’re empty?
That’s where your idol is hiding.
And here’s the danger no one talks about:
Idols don’t just take God’s place…
They slowly take your peace.
Your clarity.
Your identity.
Your intimacy with God.
Because no idol can carry what only God was meant to hold.
So you feel anxious…
Restless…
Empty…
Even when you have the thing you thought you needed.
Because your soul knows:
This isn’t God.
📖 “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on You.” — Isaiah 26:3
Peace isn’t found in having more.
It’s found in having Him.
But instead of running to God…
We run to the idol.
We scroll.
We chase.
We cling.
We control.
Hoping it will fix what only Jesus can heal.
And here’s the breaking point:
Eventually…
God will confront the idol.
Not to punish you.
But to free you.
Because He loves you too much…
To let something else own your heart.
📖 “If you love Me, keep My commandments.” — John 14:15
Love is proven by obedience.
Not words.
Not feelings.
Not appearances.
So when God says:
“Let it go.”
“Walk away.”
“Trust Me.”
What do you do?
Do you surrender?
Or do you hold tighter?
Because that moment…
Reveals everything.
And here’s the truth you can’t ignore:
Anything you put above God…
Will eventually break you.
But here’s the hope:

Jesus didn’t come just to expose your idols.
He came to set you free from them.
This is the Gospel.
Not behavior modification.
Not religious performance.
Not trying harder.
It’s this:
You and I have all sinned.
Not just in actions…
But in what we’ve loved more than God.
📖 “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
Idolatry is sin.
Because it replaces God.
But Jesus came.
Not to condemn you…
But to rescue you.
📖 “But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
While you were chasing idols…
Jesus was choosing the cross.
He took your sin.
Your misplaced love.
Your rebellion.
Your hidden idols.
And He paid for it.
In full.
📖 “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree…” — 1 Peter 2:24
That includes the idols you don’t even talk about.
The ones you justify.
The ones you protect.
He sees them.
And still…
He offers you grace.
Not cheap grace.
Transforming grace.
The kind that doesn’t just forgive you…
But changes what you love.
Because salvation isn’t just about escaping hell.
It’s about restoring your heart back to God.
📖 “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17
New desires.
New identity.
New direction.
So you don’t have to stay trapped.
You don’t have to keep pretending.
You don’t have to keep choosing the idol.
You can surrender.
Right now.
Not later.
Not when it’s easier.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.
Because the longer you hold onto the idol…
The harder it becomes to let go.
But the moment you release it…
You make room for God again.
And nothing compares to Him.
Nothing.
So here’s the question:
What are you holding onto…
That God is asking you to surrender?
Say it.
Name it.
Bring it into the light.
Because freedom starts with honesty.
And grace meets you there.
Prayer:
Lord…
Search my heart.
Reveal every hidden idol.
Every place where I’ve loved something more than You.
Give me the courage to surrender it.
Not halfway.
Not temporarily.
Fully.
You are worthy of my whole heart.
Not just parts of it.
Not just what’s convenient.
Everything.
In Jesus’ name.
Amen.
If this hit you deep…
From hidden idols to holy surrender — because Jesus restores what we misplaced.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He helped nail Jesus to the cross.
paragraphs: He helped nail Jesus to the cross.
Then he said… “He is righteous.”
Pause.
How does a man go from executioner… to witness… in a single moment?
Something broke inside that centurion.
Something holy.
Because what he saw on that cross didn’t match what he expected.
And maybe… that’s exactly where your story begins too.
You can stand close to Jesus… and still not see Him.
You can hear the crowd… follow the system… do your duty… and still miss the truth standing right in front of you.
That centurion had blood on his hands.
Literal blood.
He wasn’t confused about sin.
He enforced it.
He participated in it.
He normalized it.
Day after day… crucifixions were just another shift.
Another body.
Another scream.
Another man claiming innocence.
But this time…
Something was different.
No curses.
No threats.
No desperate bargaining.
Just silence… dignity… and words that didn’t make sense in a place like that:
“Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” (Luke 23:34)
Forgive… them?
Forgive the ones hammering the nails?
Forgive the ones mocking Him?
Forgive… him?
That centurion wasn’t just watching a death.
He was watching mercy bleed.
Let’s be honest.
We like to believe we would have stood on the “right side” of the cross.
We imagine ourselves as the loyal disciple.
The brave defender.
The one who wouldn’t walk away.
But Scripture strips that illusion bare.
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way…” (Isaiah 53:6)
Not some.
Not most.
Every one.
That includes the religious.
That includes the moral.
That includes the quiet sinner with the hidden life.
And yes… that includes you.
And me.
The centurion is not just a character in the story.
He is a mirror.
Because sin doesn’t always look like rebellion.
Sometimes it looks like routine.
Sometimes it looks like “just doing my job.”
Sometimes it looks like silence when truth is dying in front of you.
Sometimes it looks like pride that says, “I’m not that bad.”
But the cross exposes all of it.
Then came the darkness.
“And it was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour.” (Luke 23:44)
Midday… turned to midnight.
Creation itself responded.
This wasn’t just a man dying.
This was judgment falling.
Some scholars interpret this darkness as a sign of divine judgment—God’s righteous wrath against sin being poured out.
Not on the guilty.
On the innocent.
Let that sink in.
The sky went dark… because heaven was dealing with sin.
Your sin.
My sin.
The centurion stood there… watching the impossible.
A righteous man suffering like a criminal.
A holy man absorbing what sinners deserved.
And suddenly, the script flipped.
This wasn’t Rome’s power on display.
This was God’s plan unfolding.
Then Jesus cried out:
“Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46)
Not defeated.
Not broken.
Surrendered.
Intentional.
Authoritative.
And when He breathed His last…
Something happened inside that soldier.
“Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, ‘Certainly this man was innocent!’” (Luke 23:47)
Did you catch that?
He didn’t just acknowledge.
He praised God.
This wasn’t just observation.
This was awakening.
Here’s the turning point.
The centurion realized:
“I was wrong.”
“I participated in this.”
“I stood on the side of injustice.”
“I helped crucify a righteous man.”
That’s shame.
Heavy.
Unavoidable.
Undeniable.
And maybe that’s where you are.
Not with nails in your hands…
…but with choices you regret.
Words you can’t take back.
A secret life no one sees.
A pride that kept you from surrender.
A sin you’ve normalized for so long it feels like part of you.
You look back and think:
“How did I get here?”
And deeper still:
“Can I even come back from this?”
Listen carefully.
The centurion did not undo the crucifixion.
He could not reverse his actions.
He could not earn forgiveness.
But he recognized the truth.
And that recognition opened the door to grace.
This is the Gospel.
Clear.
Uncompromising.
Hope-filled.
“For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” (2 Corinthians 5:21)
Jesus was innocent.
Completely.
Perfectly.
Sinless.
And yet…
He was treated as guilty.
So that the guilty…
Could be treated as righteous.
That’s substitution.
That’s grace.
That’s salvation.
Not earned.
Not deserved.
Given.
Through Christ alone.
And here’s where everything shifts.
The centurion saw innocence.
But you are invited to see something deeper:
Redemption.
Because Jesus didn’t just die in front of sinners.
He died for sinners.
“God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Not after you fix yourself.
Not after you clean up your life.
Not after you become “worthy.”
While you were still in it.
Still broken.
Still running.
Still resisting.
So what do you do with this?
You don’t admire it from a distance.
You respond.
You repent.
You turn.
“Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out.” (Acts 3:19)
Repentance is not shame crushing you.
It’s truth freeing you.
It’s saying:
“I was wrong.”
“I need Jesus.”
“I surrender.”
Maybe you feel like that centurion.
You’ve been close to truth… but never surrendered to it.
You’ve seen enough… but never responded.
You’ve lived your life… but never truly given it.
This is your moment.
Not tomorrow.
Not someday.
Now.
Because the same cross that exposed your sin…
Is the same cross that offers your forgiveness.
Look again.
The innocent Man.
Hanging there.
For you.
Not to condemn you…
But to save you.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” (Romans 8:1)
No condemnation.
Not less condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
None.
If you are in Christ.
So come.
Bring the shame.
Bring the failure.
Bring the hidden sin.
Bring the pride.
Bring the weight you’ve been carrying.
Lay it at the cross.
Jesus is not shocked by your sin.
He already carried it.
If this is you…
Respond.
Say it.
Mean it.
And let this be the moment everything changes.
If someone came to your mind while reading this…
It might be their turning point too.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They judged his age…
paragraphs:
They judged his age…
but heaven had already called his name.
Read that again.
Because someone reading this right now knows exactly what it feels like to be underestimated.

Overlooked.
Dismissed.
Silenced before you even speak.
And here’s the tension you don’t say out loud:

You love God…
but you’re tired of feeling small.

You want to be used…
but the voices around you keep shrinking you.

You feel the fire…
but people only see your flaws.
And deep inside, there’s a whisper:
“Maybe they’re right about me.”
Because Timothy felt that too.

He wasn’t the loudest.
He wasn’t the oldest.
He wasn’t the most respected in the room.
He was young.
And in a culture that honored age, that was almost a disqualification.
Almost.

Because while men were measuring his years…
God was measuring his heart.
But here’s the part we often skip:
Timothy didn’t just struggle with people doubting him.
He struggled with himself.

Fear.
Timidity.
Insecurity.
Paul had to remind him:
“For God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.” (2 Timothy 1:7)
That means Timothy was shrinking.

Holding back.
Second-guessing his voice.
Afraid to step fully into what God was calling him to.
Sound familiar?
Let’s go deeper.
Because this isn’t just about youth.
This is about shame.
The quiet kind.
The kind that says:

“You’re not enough.”
“You’re not ready.”
“You’re not worthy.”
“Sit down.”
And if we’re honest…
Some of that shame isn’t just from people.
It’s from your past.

Mistakes you haven’t forgiven yourself for.
Moments you wish you could erase.
Failures that replay at night when everything gets quiet.
So even when God calls…
You hesitate.
Because shame makes you feel like a fraud in your own calling.
Now hear the Word of God—not opinion, not emotion, not culture:
“Let no one despise your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.” (1 Timothy 4:12)
Notice this.
Paul does NOT say:
“Convince them you’re worthy.”
He says:
“Be an example.”

Not louder.
Not more aggressive.
Not defensive.
Just… faithful.

In speech.
In conduct.
In love.
In faith.
In purity.
That’s not performance.
That’s transformation.
Some scholars interpret this passage as both a personal charge to Timothy and a public standard—meaning his life itself would silence criticism over time, not arguments or titles.
Let that sink in.
God’s strategy for your life is not proving people wrong.
It’s becoming someone different.
But wait.
We need to go even deeper.
Because here’s the truth nobody tells you:

You can try to “be an example”…
and still fail.

You can try to be pure…
and fall.

You can try to be bold…
and freeze.

You can try to be faithful…
and drift.
Because at the core…
You’re still human.

Still broken.
Still battling sin.
And this is where everything shifts.
The message of Timothy is NOT:
“Believe in yourself and you’ll rise.”
That’s not the Gospel.
The message is:
You cannot save yourself.

Not with discipline.
Not with passion.
Not with potential.
Because the real problem is not your age.
It’s your sin.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)

That includes Timothy.
That includes you.
And sin doesn’t just make you weak.
It separates you from God.

That’s the real weight.
That’s the real crisis.
But here comes the turn.
The holy interruption.
The scandal of grace.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

Not when you got better.
Not when you became worthy.
Not when you proved yourself.
While you were still a mess.
Christ stepped in.
Jesus lived the life you couldn’t live—perfect, holy, pure.
He took your sin—every hidden failure, every secret shame—and carried it to the cross.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree…” (1 Peter 2:24)
And He didn’t stay dead.
He rose.

Victorious.
Alive.
Reigning.
So now salvation is not about your strength.
It’s about His sacrifice.
Let’s make it personal.
You don’t overcome shame by pretending it doesn’t exist.
You overcome shame by bringing it to the cross.
You don’t earn your calling.
You receive it… after surrender.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)
Cleanse.

Not partially.
Not temporarily.
Completely.
That means the voice saying “you’re disqualified”…
is not from God.
Because the cross has already spoken.
So what does this mean for you?
It means your past does not own you.
It means your age does not limit you.
It means your weakness does not define you.
If you are in Christ…

you are forgiven.
you are restored.
you are called.
Not because you’re impressive.
But because Jesus is enough.
But don’t twist this.
Grace is not permission to stay the same.
Grace is power to change.
Paul didn’t tell Timothy:
“Relax. Do whatever you want.”
He said:
“Practice these things, immerse yourself in them…” (1 Timothy 4:15)
That’s discipline.
That’s growth.
That’s surrender lived out daily.
Because real faith doesn’t just feel something.
It becomes something.
So here’s the confrontation:

Are you hiding behind your youth…
or surrendering it?

Are you using your insecurity as an excuse…
or bringing it to Jesus?

Are you letting shame silence you…
or letting grace transform you?
Because God is not waiting for you to get older.
He’s waiting for you to get surrendered.
Right now.
Today.
This moment.
Maybe you’ve been holding back.
Maybe you’ve been shrinking.
Maybe you’ve been disqualifying yourself before anyone else could.
Hear me clearly:
Jesus did not die for a smaller version of you.
He died to make you new.
So come back.

Not to religion.
Not to performance.
Not to pretending.
Come back to Christ.
Repent.
Lay it down—the sin, the pride, the fear, the shame.
And receive what you cannot earn:
Grace.
And from that place…
Stand.
Speak.
Live.
Not to prove something…
but because something has already been done.
If this is you—if something in your heart is breaking, waking, shifting—
Don’t ignore it.
That’s not coincidence.
That’s God calling.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He looked holy.
paragraphs: He looked holy.
And still said no to Jesus.
You can do everything right…
…and still walk away from eternal life.
He ran to Jesus.
Knelt in public.
Spoke with respect.
Asked the right question.
“Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
But something was off.
And Jesus saw it immediately.
Not the surface.
The soul.
This is the part we don’t talk about enough.
You can look clean on the outside…
while something owns you on the inside.
You can master behavior…
and still be mastered by your heart.
You can say all the right things…
and still be standing one step away from surrender.
The Rich Young Ruler was not a villain.
That’s what makes this story terrifying.
He was disciplined.
Moral.
Religious.
Respected.
He didn’t cheat people.
He didn’t live wild.
He didn’t rebel openly.
He obeyed.
At least… externally.
But heaven does not open for polished lives.
It opens for surrendered hearts.
Jesus didn’t argue with him.
Didn’t shame him.
Didn’t expose him publicly.
The Bible says something that should shake you:
“Jesus, looking at him, loved him.” (Mark 10:21)
Let that sit.
Jesus saw everything—

the pride,
the hidden attachment,
the quiet idol—
and still loved him.
Not with soft approval…
but with truth sharp enough to cut chains.
“One thing you lack…”
That’s the sentence nobody wants.
Because we all hope we’re already enough.
We want affirmation…
not confrontation.
We want reassurance…
not revelation.
But Jesus doesn’t flatter idols.
He exposes them.
Because He loves you too much to leave you owned by something less than Him.
“Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor… and come, follow Me.” (Mark 10:21)
That was the moment.
The line drawn in the soul.
Not about money.
About lordship.
Some scholars interpret this command as a specific test tailored to this man’s heart, not a universal command for all believers to sell everything—but the principle is universal:
Whatever owns your heart… must bow to Jesus.
And that’s where everything broke.
The man didn’t argue.
Didn’t rebel loudly.
Didn’t insult Jesus.
He just…
walked away.
Quietly.
Sadly.
Holding on.
“And he was sad at this word, and went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions.” (Mark 10:22)
Read that again.
He walked away…
sad.
Not angry.
Not hostile.
Just unwilling.
This is the danger nobody preaches hard enough.
You don’t have to hate Jesus to reject Him.
You just have to love something else more.
Let’s get real.
This isn’t just his story.
This is ours.
You can be:
Faithful in church…
but addicted in secret.
Kind to people…
but proud before God.
Generous publicly…
but unwilling to surrender privately.
Disciplined in habits…
but distant from Jesus.
And the scariest part?
You can feel close…
and still walk away when He asks for everything.
Because here’s the truth:
Moral behavior can hide spiritual bondage.
You don’t need scandal to be lost.
You just need something you won’t let go of.
Maybe it’s not money for you.
Maybe it’s:
Your image.
Your relationship.
Your control.
Your dreams.
Your secret sin.
Your comfort.
Your identity without Christ.
That one thing.
That quiet thing.
That “don’t touch this, Lord” thing.
That’s the place where this story becomes personal.
Because Jesus still says the same words today:
“Follow Me.”
Not admire Me.
Not agree with Me.
Not visit Me occasionally.
Follow.
Surrender.
Die to self.
Live in Me.
And here’s where the Gospel cuts deeper than morality ever can:
You cannot earn eternal life.
Not by obedience.
Not by discipline.
Not by being “a good person.”
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
That includes the rebellious…
and the respectable.
The Rich Young Ruler thought he could do enough.
Jesus showed him he could not surrender enough.
And that’s where grace enters.
Because while this man walked away from Jesus…
Jesus did not walk away from sinners.
He walked toward the cross.
Carrying what we could never carry.
Paying what we could never pay.
Dying for both kinds of people:
The openly broken…
and the secretly proud.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.” (Ephesians 2:8–9)
Salvation is not a reward for the disciplined.
It is a gift for the surrendered.
And here’s the beauty:
Where the Rich Young Ruler failed…
Jesus succeeded.
Where we cling…
He releases.
Where we hide…
He heals.
But don’t miss this:
Grace does not ignore your idols.
It destroys their power.
You don’t come to Jesus holding everything.
You come empty.
Honest.
Broken if needed.
But surrendered.
Because Jesus is not just Savior.
He is Lord.
And Lordship demands everything.
But gives back something greater:
Life.
Freedom.
Peace.
Eternal joy.
So let me ask you—
not casually…
but urgently:
What is the one thing you would not give up if Jesus asked you today?
Pause.
Answer honestly.
Because that thing…
might be the very thing keeping you from Him.
And here’s the invitation.
Not condemnation.
Invitation.
Jesus still looks at you with love.
Not disgust.
Not rejection.
Love.
And He still says:
“Come.”
Come out of hiding.
Come out of control.
Come out of pretending.
Lay it down.
Whatever it is.
No matter how deep it runs.
Because what you gain in Christ…
will always be greater than what you lose for Him.
“Whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.” (Matthew 16:25)
You don’t have to walk away like he did.
You can step forward.
Today.
Right now.
This is your moment.
Not to perform.
Not to prove.
But to surrender.
Say it in your own words.
Or borrow this:
“Jesus… I give You everything. Even the thing I’ve been holding back. Be my Savior. Be my Lord.”
And watch what grace does with a surrendered heart.
🔥 If this pierced you, don’t ignore it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He held everything… but owned nothing.
paragraphs: He held everything… but owned nothing.

And somehow—
that’s where most of us would break.

You won’t find his name trending.
No spotlight.
No covenant stamped on his identity.
Just a servant.

Trusted with everything…
yet promised nothing.
And here’s the tension:

How do you stay faithful
when the blessing passes through your hands—
but never lands on your life?

How do you carry someone else’s promise
without secretly wishing it was yours?

How do you serve God…
when it feels like you’re always second?
This is where Eliezer lives.

And if we’re honest—
this is where many of us are.

You smile in public…
but wrestle in private.

You serve in church…
but envy in silence.

You clap for others…
while questioning God’s timing for you.

You say, “Lord, I trust You”…
but deep inside, there’s a whisper:
“What about me?”
Let’s tell the truth.
Not the polished version.
The real one.

There are moments
you’ve obeyed God outwardly…
…but inside, you’ve resented Him.
Moments you’ve served faithfully…
…but secretly compared your life to others.
Moments you’ve carried responsibility…
…but questioned God’s fairness.
That’s the battlefield no one posts about.
The quiet war between faithfulness and frustration.
Between surrender and subtle pride.
Between obedience and entitlement.
Because here’s the raw truth:
We don’t just struggle with sin.
We struggle with wanting God’s blessings more than God Himself.
Eliezer could have become bitter.
Think about it.
Genesis tells us:
“But Abram said, ‘O Lord God, what will You give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?’” — Genesis 15:2
That’s not a casual statement.
That’s Abraham saying:
“If I die right now… everything goes to him.”
Eliezer wasn’t just a servant.
He was next in line.
He had proximity.
Access.
Trust.
Then God speaks.
And everything changes.
“This man shall not be your heir; your very own son shall be your heir.” — Genesis 15:4
In one sentence—
Eliezer’s future disappears.
Imagine that.
Years of loyalty.
Years of service.
Years of carrying responsibility.
And suddenly—
the promise is redirected.
No complaint recorded.
No rebellion mentioned.
No bitterness documented.
Silence.
Faithful silence.
Some scholars interpret that Eliezer is the unnamed servant in Genesis 24—the one entrusted to find a wife for Isaac. The text doesn’t confirm it explicitly, but if it is him…
then the weight of this moment deepens.
Because now he’s not just losing the inheritance.
He’s protecting it.

He’s sent to secure a future
that will never include him.
Let that sink in.
He prays.
“O Lord, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success today…” — Genesis 24:12
He seeks God—not for himself—
but for someone else’s promise.
He obeys precisely.
He speaks carefully.
He moves with reverence.
No shortcuts.
No manipulation.
No “I deserve this” energy.
Just faithfulness.
And that exposes something in us.
Because many of us would have negotiated.
Delayed.
Compromised.
Maybe even sabotaged.
Why?
Because our hearts are not naturally surrendered.
They are naturally self-centered.
Scripture is clear:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way…” — Isaiah 53:6
Not some of us.
All of us.
We drift toward self.
We default to “mine.”
We measure life by what we receive—
not by who we are becoming.
And that’s where sin lives.
Not just in actions—
but in orientation.
A heart that says:

“I will serve…
as long as it benefits me.”
That’s not surrender.
That’s transaction.
And God doesn’t redeem transactions.
He redeems hearts.
This is where the story pivots.
Because Eliezer—faithful as he is—
is not the Savior.
He points to One greater.
Jesus Christ.
The true and better Servant.
“For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45
Think about that.
Jesus didn’t just carry someone else’s promise—
He carried your sin.
He didn’t just lose an inheritance—
He laid down His glory.
“Though He was in the form of God… He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant…” — Philippians 2:6–7
And He didn’t serve from a distance.
He stepped into your mess.
Your pride.
Your hidden resentment.
Your quiet jealousy.
Your spiritual pretending.
He saw it all—
and still chose the cross.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not when you got it right.
Not when you became faithful.
Not when your motives were pure.
While you were still broken.
Still divided.
Still wrestling with “what about me?”
That’s grace.
Not earned.
Not deserved.
Given.
Through blood.
Through sacrifice.

Through a Savior who stayed faithful
when we could not.
And here’s the invitation:
You don’t have to keep pretending.
You don’t have to keep performing.
You don’t have to keep carrying hidden frustration like it’s normal.
You can come clean.
Not to a system.
Not to religion.
But to Jesus.
Repentance is not punishment.
It’s freedom.
It’s the moment you stop saying:
“God, give me what I deserve…”
and start saying:
“Jesus, give me what You died to offer.”
Forgiveness.
New heart.
New desires.
New identity.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation…” — 2 Corinthians 5:17
That includes your motives.
Your perspective.
Your definition of success.
Suddenly—
faithfulness is no longer about what you gain.
It’s about Who you belong to.
And when that shift happens—
serving stops feeling like loss.
And starts looking like worship.
So let me ask you—
honestly.
Where has subtle pride crept in?
Where have you served with conditions?
Where have you smiled… but silently resisted God?
Sit in it.
Because God is not exposing you to shame you.
He’s exposing you to heal you.
Bring it to Jesus.
Name it.
Release it.
Surrender it.
Right now.
Not later.
Say:

“Lord, purify my heart.
Teach me to serve without entitlement.
Anchor me in Your grace.”
And watch what He does.
Because the same God who saw Eliezer’s quiet faithfulness—
sees you.
Not your performance.
Not your image.
You.
And in Christ—
your life is not overlooked.
It’s being shaped.
For eternity.
🔥 If this pierced your heart, don’t ignore it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He obeyed… but not completely.
paragraphs: He obeyed… but not completely.
And God said, that’s enough to stop you.

You can be called…
and still be in danger.

You can be chosen…
and still be out of alignment.

You can carry a destiny…
and still be hiding disobedience.
Moses had just encountered fire.
Not ordinary fire.
Holy fire.

A bush that burned but was not consumed.
A voice that shook the ground beneath his excuses.
A calling that would rewrite history.

“Go back to Egypt.”
“Set My people free.”
This wasn’t small.
This was God-level assignment.
And then…
On a quiet night.

No crowd.
No spotlight.
No applause.
God moved to kill him.
Why?

What could be so serious…
that the same God who called him…
would confront him like an enemy?
Here’s the part we don’t like to preach.
The part that hits too close.
Moses had unfinished obedience.
Hidden.
Private.
Delayed.
Let’s open the text.
“At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death.” — Exodus 4:24
No warning.
No build-up.
Just divine interruption.
But then—something happens.

Something raw.
Something desperate.
Something bloody.
“Then Zipporah took a flint knife and cut off her son’s foreskin and touched Moses’ feet with it and said, ‘Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!’ So He let him alone.” — Exodus 4:25–26
Pause.
Feel that tension.
The issue wasn’t random.
It was covenant.
God had already spoken generations before:
“Every male among you shall be circumcised… it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.” — Genesis 17:10–11
Moses knew this.
He wasn’t ignorant.
He was… delaying.
Compromising.
Negotiating obedience.
Some scholars interpret that Moses delayed circumcising his son because of cultural pressure from his Midianite surroundings… or tension in his household.
But Scripture is clear about one thing:
God had commanded it.
And Moses hadn’t done it.
Let that land.
The deliverer of Israel…
Was disobeying the God of Israel.
Not publicly.
Privately.
And God said:
“Not like this.”
This is where it gets personal.
Because we love big callings.
We love purpose.
We love destiny language.
We love saying, “God is using me.”
But we don’t always love full obedience.
We say:

“God, I’ll go…
just not there.”

“I’ll serve…
but don’t touch this.”

“I’ll follow…
but let me keep this part.”
Partial obedience feels safe.
Manageable.
Reasonable.
But in the kingdom of God?
Partial obedience is still disobedience.
And here’s the dangerous part:
God may let you move for a while…
But He will confront what you refuse to surrender.
Not because He hates you.
But because He loves you too much to let you lead in hypocrisy.
Moses was about to stand before Pharaoh.
Declare God’s authority.
Carry God’s name.
But behind closed doors?
He was ignoring God’s command.
And heaven said:
“Fix this first.”
Let’s bring it closer.
Not Egypt.
Not Pharaoh.
Not Moses.
You.
What is that thing?
That quiet area?
That delayed obedience?
That hidden compromise?
The one you justify.
The one you minimize.
The one you say, “It’s not that serious.”
But deep down…
You know.
Because the Holy Spirit has already whispered it.
Again.
And again.
And again.
And you’ve been saying:
“Later.”
Listen carefully.
Delayed obedience is not neutral.
It is resistance.
And resistance creates distance.
Not because God walks away—
But because we do.
Now here’s where the story turns.
And this is the part that will break you… and heal you.
Blood was shed.
And judgment stopped.
Zipporah stepped in.
A knife.
A covenant act.
Blood touching Moses.
And suddenly—
The wrath passes.
Do you see it?
This isn’t just a strange Old Testament moment.
It’s a shadow.
A preview.
A prophetic whisper of something greater.
Because one day…
Another Son would bleed.
Not because of His disobedience—
But because of ours.
“But He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities… and by His wounds we are healed.” — Isaiah 53:5
Jesus didn’t come with partial obedience.
He came with perfect obedience.
“He humbled Himself by becoming obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.” — Philippians 2:8
Where Moses almost died for his disobedience…
Jesus chose to die for yours.
Let that hit.
Every hidden compromise.
Every delayed surrender.
Every “not yet, Lord.”
Jesus saw it.
And still—
He went to the cross.
“For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” — Romans 6:23
The penalty didn’t disappear.
It was transferred.
From you…
To Him.
That’s grace.
Not tolerance of sin.
But payment for sin.
Which means this:
You don’t clean yourself up to come to God.
You come to God…
and He cleans you.
But make no mistake—
Grace is not permission to stay the same.
Grace is power to change.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
So here’s the moment.
Right now.
Not tomorrow.
Not next week.
Not when it’s convenient.
Now.
What is God asking you to surrender?
What have you delayed?
What have you kept hidden?
This is not about shame.
This is about alignment.
Because the same God who confronted Moses…
Is the same God who sent Jesus.
Not to destroy you.
But to restore you.
But restoration begins with honesty.
No more excuses.
No more delays.
No more partial yes.
Give Him everything.
Not because you’re afraid of punishment—
But because you’ve seen His love.
And His love is too real…
To keep living divided.
So here’s your step:
Repent.
Not emotionally.
Not temporarily.
Completely.
Turn from the thing.
Turn toward Jesus.
Trust His finished work.
Walk in obedience.
Because the calling on your life is real.
But so is God’s holiness.
And in Christ—
You don’t have to choose between them.
You get both.
Holiness…
and mercy.
Truth…
and grace.
Conviction…
and forgiveness.
Right now—
Pray this in your heart:

“Lord, no more partial obedience.
I surrender everything.
Cleanse me. Change me. Lead me.
I choose You—fully.”
If this hit you…
📌 Save this so you don’t forget what God showed you
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They hurt you… in the place that taught you about love.
paragraphs: They hurt you… in the place that taught you about love.
Let that sink in.
You expected healing.
You got whispers.
You expected family.
You got distance.
And now there’s a question you’re too afraid to say out loud:
“Was God even there… when they broke me?”
Here’s the tension.
The wound didn’t just come from people.
It came from people who knew Scripture.

People who lifted hands on Sunday…
but used their tongues like knives on Monday.
And now you’re left holding two things that don’t make sense together:
Your pain…
and your faith.
Somewhere deep inside, a lie started forming.
“If this is church… I don’t want God.”
Not loud.
Not dramatic.
Just quiet… and deadly.
Let’s tell the truth.
Church hurt doesn’t just bruise your emotions.
It attacks your view of God.
It makes you question His goodness… because His people failed to reflect Him.
But don’t confuse representation with identity.
God is not the worst version of the people who claim His name.
Let me say that again.
God is not the worst version of the people who claim His name.
The Bible doesn’t hide this tension.
In Psalm 55:12–14, David writes:

But it is you, a man like myself, my companion, my close friend.
With whom I once enjoyed sweet fellowship…”
This wasn’t betrayal from the outside.
This was inside.
Close.
Personal.
Spiritual.
Some scholars interpret this passage as David referring to a specific betrayal within his inner circle.
Others see it as a broader picture of relational betrayal among God’s people.
Either way…
The Bible is not naïve about church hurt.
It names it.
It exposes it.
It grieves it.
And here’s what will shake you:
Jesus experienced it too.
Not from strangers.
From His own.
Judas walked with Him.
Ate with Him.
Heard His teachings.
Saw miracles up close.
And still… betrayed Him.
Matthew 26:48–50 shows it clearly:

“Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: ‘The one I kiss is the man; arrest him.’
Going at once to Jesus, Judas said, ‘Greetings, Rabbi!’ and kissed him.
Jesus replied, ‘Do what you came for, friend.’”
Friend.
Jesus still called him friend.
Even in betrayal.
And Peter?
He didn’t sell Jesus.
He denied Him.
Luke 22:61 says:
“The Lord turned and looked straight at Peter…”
Imagine that moment.
Eye contact.
After denial.
After failure.
After fear won.
So if you’ve been wounded by people in the church…
You’re not outside the story.
You’re inside it.
But here’s where everything turns.
Because if you stop the story at betrayal…
You miss the Gospel.
Let’s go deeper.
Your pain is real.
But so is your sin.
Not just what they did to you…
But what lives in all of us.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Not some.
All.
That includes the ones who hurt you.
And…
That includes you.
This is the uncomfortable truth.
We don’t just suffer from sin.
We participate in it.
Different expressions.
Same root.
And this is why Jesus didn’t come to build a perfect social circle.
He came to save sinners.
Broken people.
Messy communities.
Imperfect churches.
Here’s the Gospel.
Clear.
Unfiltered.
Non-negotiable.
You and I are separated from God because of sin.
No amount of church attendance, service, or good behavior can fix that.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God—not by works, so that no one can boast.”
Grace.
Not performance.
Gift.
Not earning.
And that grace was purchased through blood.
Jesus Christ lived the life we failed to live.
Sinless.
Perfect.
Holy.
Then He died the death we deserved.
On a cross.
In our place.
For our sin.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:

“But He was pierced for our transgressions,
He was crushed for our iniquities;
the punishment that brought us peace was on Him,
and by His wounds we are healed.”
By His wounds.
Not theirs.
Let that land.
Your healing will never come from perfect people.
It comes from a pierced Savior.
And three days later…
He rose.
Not just to prove power.
But to offer new life.
Redemption.
Restoration.
A clean heart.
A new beginning.
So what do you do with church hurt?
You don’t deny it.
You don’t idolize it.
You don’t build your identity around it.
You bring it to Jesus.
Fully.
Honestly.
Without editing.
Because if you let people push you away from Christ…
The enemy wins twice.
They hurt you…
and then your distance from God keeps you wounded.
But if you bring your pain to Jesus…
That same place of betrayal becomes a doorway to deeper intimacy with Him.
This is the shift.
Church hurt is not proof that God failed you.
It’s proof that humanity still needs a Savior.
And here’s the invitation.
Not to go back to fake smiles.
Not to ignore what happened.
But to come back to Christ.
The real One.
The faithful One.
The One who will never gossip about you…
never abandon you…
never misuse your trust.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit.”
Close.
Not distant.
So let me ask you.
What are you going to do with your pain?
Will you let it harden you?
Or will you let it lead you… back to Jesus?
If you’re tired of carrying this alone…
If you’re done letting wounds define your faith…
If something in your spirit is saying, “I need Him again…”
Then respond.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Pray.
Even if it’s messy.
“Jesus… I’ve been hurt. But I don’t want to walk away from You. Heal me. Restore me. Teach me how to trust again.”
He hears that.
He honors that.
He meets you there.
And when you’re ready…
Find people who don’t pretend to be perfect—
but are serious about following Christ.
They exist.
Not flawless.
But faithful.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She said it without shouting.
paragraphs:
She said it without shouting.
But heaven heard it like a wound.
“Lord… if You had been here…”
And just like that—faith cracked.

Not gone.
Just… bleeding.

Because nothing exposes the heart like delay.
Not denial.
Delay.
And this is where shame creeps in.

Because you prayed.
You believed.
You waited.
And still… it died.

The relationship.
The purity.
The dream.
The version of you that used to feel close to God.

Now you’re standing where Mary stood—
in front of something you know didn’t have to end this way.
And the thought you don’t say out loud?
“If Jesus really loved me… He would’ve shown up sooner.”

That’s the tension.
That’s the open wound.

Because we’ve been taught to celebrate miracles—
but nobody prepared us for the silence before them.
Nobody told us that sometimes Jesus delays on purpose.

Not to harm you.
But to reveal something deeper than your expectation.

In John 11:5–6, the Bible says:
“Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when He heard that Lazarus was ill, He stayed two days longer in the place where He was.”
Did you catch that?

He loved them…
so He stayed.
That word will confront you if you let it.
Because we’ve built a version of love that rushes in, fixes everything, and prevents pain.

But Jesus…
lets it unfold.
Some scholars interpret this passage to mean that Jesus delayed intentionally so that the glory of God would be revealed in a greater way—not just healing sickness, but conquering death itself.
But that doesn’t remove the tension.

Because while theology was forming—
Mary was grieving.

While purpose was unfolding—
Martha was disappointed.
And here’s where it gets real:

Delay doesn’t just test your patience.
It exposes your heart.

Because when God doesn’t move the way you expect—
you start questioning things you thought were settled.

His love.
His power.
His presence.
And quietly… shame begins to whisper:
“Maybe it’s your fault.”
“Maybe you didn’t pray enough.”
“Maybe you’re not worthy of showing up for.”

So now, not only are you grieving what died—
you’re carrying guilt for why it died.
That’s a heavy place.
That’s where many people stop trusting God.

But not Mary.
Not Martha.

They ran toward Jesus…
even with broken expectations.

They didn’t hide their disappointment.
They brought it to Him.
And here’s the part that will undo you—
Jesus didn’t rebuke them.

He didn’t say, “Fix your attitude first.”
He didn’t say, “Have more faith.”

He stood there…
and received their pain.

John 11:35 —
“Jesus wept.”
Not because He didn’t know what He was about to do.
But because He felt what they were going through.
This is not a distant Savior.
This is not a God who watches suffering from afar.

This is Jesus—
stepping into your grief,
standing in your delay,
and weeping with you in the middle of it.
But He doesn’t stop there.
Because the story doesn’t end in tears.
It turns.
Hard.

Jesus walks to the tomb—
the place where everything felt final.
And He says something that sounds almost offensive to human logic:
“Take away the stone.” (John 11:39)

Martha resists.
Because now it’s been four days.
Translation?
“It’s too late.”
“It’s too far gone.”
“It’s already decaying.”

And if we’re honest—
that’s what many of us believe about parts of our lives.

“This addiction? Too deep.”
“This past? Too dirty.”
“This version of me? Too broken.”
But Jesus doesn’t consult your timeline.
He confronts your unbelief.

John 11:40 —
“Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”
Then He calls into the darkness:
“Lazarus, come out.” (John 11:43)
And the dead man walks.

Not healed.
Resurrected.
This is where the Gospel explodes into the story.
Because Lazarus is not just a man.
He is a mirror.

We were the ones dead in sin—
Ephesians 2:1 says, “You were dead in the trespasses and sins…”

Not struggling.
Not improving.
Dead.
And no amount of effort could reverse that.

No discipline.
No religion.
No self-fixing.
We needed a voice from outside the grave.
We needed Jesus.
And that’s exactly what He came to do.
He didn’t come just to arrive “on time.”
He came to conquer the very thing that makes everything feel too late.

Sin.
Death.
Separation from God.
At the cross, it looked like God was late again.

Jesus died.
Buried.
Silence.

But three days later—
the stone moved.
And this time, it wasn’t Lazarus walking out.
It was Jesus Himself.
Alive.
Victorious.
Final.
So now, delay has a different meaning.
It’s not abandonment.
It’s not absence.
It’s not punishment.
It’s preparation for resurrection.
And that thing you’re ashamed of?

That failure you keep replaying?
That hidden sin you think disqualified you?
Bring it to the tomb.
Because Jesus doesn’t just manage behavior.
He calls dead hearts to life.
But here’s the part many avoid:
You have to respond.

Lazarus had to come out.
The people had to remove the grave clothes (John 11:44).

Grace raises you—
but you must step into the freedom.

So let me ask you, not as a preacher—
but as someone who has stood in delay too:

What have you already declared dead…
that Jesus is still willing to resurrect?

What shame are you still carrying…
that He already paid for at the cross?

Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”

Not less condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
None.
But it’s only true in Christ.

Not in effort.
Not in performance.
In Him.
So come out.

Out of hiding.
Out of shame.
Out of the lie that it’s too late for you.
Because if Jesus can stand in front of a sealed tomb and call life out of decay—
He can call you too.
Right now.
Right here.
This is your invitation.

Repent.
Turn from sin.
Surrender what you’ve been holding.
Trust Jesus—not just as a helper, but as Savior and Lord.
Let Him rewrite what you thought was finished.
If this hit your heart, don’t keep it silent.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re not being punished…
paragraphs:
You’re not being punished…
You’re being pursued.
And that feeling you’ve been trying to ignore?
It’s not going away.

You keep distracting yourself.
Scrolling. Laughing. Numbing.
But the moment it gets quiet…
It comes back.

That weight.
That conviction.
That uncomfortable awareness that something is not right between you and God.
And you don’t want to face it.
But you also can’t escape it.
Because deep down… you know.

You know what you’ve been hiding.
You know what you’ve been excusing.
You know what you said you’d stop… but didn’t.
And now?
It doesn’t feel the same anymore.
That sin you used to enjoy…
Now it leaves a bitter aftertaste.
That compromise you once defended…
Now it convicts you before you even finish it.
That double life…
Is starting to collapse under its own weight.
Let’s be honest.
This isn’t just guilt.
This is God getting your attention.
You thought you were just “overthinking.”
But you’re not.
You thought it was anxiety.
But it’s deeper than that.
You thought it would pass.
But it hasn’t.
Because God loves you too much to let you stay numb.
“Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline. So be earnest and repent.” — Revelation 3:19
That conviction you feel?
That’s not rejection.
That’s love.
Some people sin and feel nothing.

No conviction.
No resistance.
No internal war.
But you?
You feel it.
Immediately.
Deeply.
Relentlessly.
Why?
Because God hasn’t let you go.
The discomfort is mercy.
The conviction is evidence.
The restlessness is a signal.
You’re not too far gone.
You’re too called to stay where you are.
But here’s the tension…
You’re stuck between two worlds.
You don’t fully enjoy sin anymore…
But you’re not fully surrendered either.
So you live in this exhausting middle.

Half in.
Half out.

Church on Sunday.
Compromise in private.

Worship with your lips…
War in your mind.
And it’s draining you.
Because you were never created to live divided.
“No one can serve two masters…” — Matthew 6:24
You feel the tension because your soul was made for truth.
Not mixture.
And now God is doing something uncomfortable…
He’s interrupting your normal.
Doors you wanted… are closing.
People you relied on… are shifting.
Things that once satisfied you… are losing their power.
And you’re confused.
Frustrated.
Maybe even a little angry.
But what if…
This isn’t loss?
What if this is rescue?
“The Lord directs the steps of the righteous.” — Proverbs 16:9
Even the closed doors.
Even the delays.
Even the disruptions.
God will shut down what’s slowly destroying you.
Even if you don’t understand it in the moment.
Because your comfort is not His priority.
Your soul is.
And then there’s that pull…
That quiet, persistent whisper:
“Come back.”
You feel it when you wake up.
You feel it late at night.
You feel it in random moments when everything else fades.
You suddenly want to pray again.
You think about reading the Bible again.
You feel drawn…
But you hesitate.
Because shame starts talking.

“After what you did?”
“You think God still wants you?”
“You’ve gone too far this time.”
And so instead of running to God…
You pull away.
But listen carefully.
That voice?
That’s not God.
“There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
God convicts.
The enemy condemns.

Conviction says:
“Come back.”

Condemnation says:
“Stay away.”
And some of you have been listening to the wrong voice.
Yes, you sinned.
Yes, you compromised.
Yes, you ignored God.
But that is not the end of your story.
Because this is where everything changes.
Not when you get your life together.
Not when you “fix yourself.”
Not when you feel worthy.
But when you turn.
This is the Gospel.
Not behavior modification.
Not self-improvement.
Resurrection.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
That includes you.
That includes me.
That includes every person who has ever lived.
Sin is not just mistakes.
It’s rebellion.
It’s choosing ourselves over God.
And sin has a cost.
“For the wages of sin is death…” — Romans 6:23
Not just physical death.
Spiritual separation.
Eternal distance from God.
That’s the reality.
That’s the weight.
That’s the problem.
But here’s the miracle.
“…but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” — Romans 6:23
Jesus didn’t come for the perfect.
He came for the broken.
“God demonstrates His own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not when you cleaned up.
Not when you got serious.
Not when you fixed your habits.
While you were still in it.
Jesus took your place.
Your sin.
Your shame.
Your punishment.
On the cross.
And then He rose.
Defeating sin.
Defeating death.
Defeating the very thing that’s been holding you captive.
So now…
The invitation stands.
Not: “Be perfect.”
But: “Repent and come home.”
“Repent, then, and turn to God, so that your sins may be wiped out…” — Acts 3:19
Repentance is not just saying sorry.
It’s turning.
Changing direction.
Surrendering.
And yes…
It costs something.
Your pride.
Your excuses.
Your secret life.
But what you gain?
Is everything.
Freedom.
Peace.
Identity.
Restoration.
You don’t have to keep living like this.
Divided.
Exhausted.
Convicted but unchanged.
God is not asking for perfection.
He’s asking for surrender.
Right now.
Not later.
Not “when you’re ready.”
Now.
Because the fact that you’re reading this?
The fact that you feel this?
The fact that something inside you is stirring?
That’s not random.
That’s God.
So here’s the question.
Not for the crowd.
Not for your friends.
For you.
Will you keep running?
Or will you finally respond?
You don’t need a perfect prayer.
You need an honest one.

“Lord… I’ve been running.
I’ve been hiding.
I’ve been choosing my way over Yours.
But today… I turn back.

Forgive me.
Change me.
Lead me.
I surrender my life to You.
In Jesus’ name… amen.”
If this is you…
This is your turning point.
From hiding to healing. From shame to salvation. Because Jesus still restores.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Stop.
paragraphs: Stop.

You’re not tired because life is heavy…
You’re tired because you’re trying to control what was never yours to carry.
And here’s the part you don’t say out loud:

You pray…
but still panic.

You trust God…
but still grip everything like it all depends on you.

You say “Lord, I surrender”—
but your hands are still clenched.
Something is off.
And deep down… you know it.
Because this isn’t just stress.

This is a quiet war between your need for control
and God’s call to trust.

You check your phone again.
You replay the conversation.
You overthink the future like you can out-strategize uncertainty.
And every time you do…
peace slips further away.
Let me say something that might shake you:

Worry is not just emotion.
It’s misplaced worship.

You’re giving your attention, your energy, your focus…
to things that cannot save you.

You’re bowing—not with your knees,
but with your thoughts.
And the result?

Exhaustion.
Fear.
A heart that never rests.
But listen.
Jesus didn’t stay silent about this.
He stepped right into your anxiety and said:
“Can any one of you by worrying add a single hour to your life?” — Matthew 6:27
Not one hour.
Not one second.
You think worrying gives you control.
But Jesus exposes it for what it really is:
Powerless.
And then He goes deeper.
“Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life…” — Matthew 6:25
