Because faith sometimes leads you to a moment where you must release what you love most.

Jochebed made a small basket out of papyrus reeds.
She sealed it with tar and pitch so the water could not seep in.
The Hebrew word used here is “tevah.”
It’s the same word used for Noah’s ark.
Not a coincidence.
Because when God saves, He builds arks.
Little vessels of mercy that float in the middle of judgment.
Imagine the scene.

The early morning mist rising from the Nile.
The quiet movement of reeds along the riverbank.
A mother kneeling in the mud with tears streaming down her face.

Inside the basket…
a sleeping baby.
She knew what that river was known for.

It swallowed lives.
It carried crocodiles.
It had already taken countless Hebrew boys.
And still… she placed her son into the current.
Not because she gave up.
But because she trusted God more than she trusted her own strength.
That basket was not abandonment.
It was surrender.
And what happened next is one of the most shocking reversals in the Bible.

The basket drifted…
right into the world of Pharaoh himself.

Pharaoh’s daughter came to bathe in the river.
She saw the basket among the reeds.
She opened it.
And the baby cried.
That cry changed history.
The princess looked at the child and felt compassion.

The very household that ordered Hebrew babies to die…
would now raise one.
Pharaoh’s palace became the training ground of the future deliverer.
And here’s the detail that almost feels too beautiful to be true.
The princess needed someone to nurse the baby.
So Moses’ sister stepped forward and asked if she should find a Hebrew woman.
Guess who came.
His own mother.
God didn’t just save Moses.

He allowed the woman who surrendered him to raise him…
while Pharaoh’s household paid the wages.
Only God writes stories like that.

The enemy planned genocide.
God prepared a deliverer.
The river meant for death became the road of rescue.
But this story is not just about Moses.
It whispers forward.
Centuries later another child would be born into danger.

A jealous ruler would again order children killed.
Families would again run in fear.
But this child would grow up to do what Moses never could.
His name is Jesus.
Moses would one day lead Israel through the waters of the Red Sea.
But Jesus would step into a deeper river.

The waters of judgment.
The weight of our sin.
The wrath our rebellion deserved.
On the cross, Christ entered the flood for us.
And three days later…
He rose.

The grave could not hold Him.
Death could not silence Him.
The enemy could not stop the rescue plan of God.
That means something powerful for you today.
Maybe you feel like you are standing at the edge of a river.
Something you love feels out of your control.

A dream.
A child.
A future.
A calling.

You’ve prayed.
You’ve fought.
You’ve held on as long as you could.
And now the current looks terrifying.
Listen carefully.
God still rules the river.
The waters that scare you are not stronger than His sovereignty.
The place that feels like loss may actually be the beginning of deliverance.
The basket may feel fragile.
But when something is placed in God’s hands, fragile becomes unstoppable.
Maybe today your step of faith looks like Jochebed’s.
Letting go.
Trusting.
Believing that the God who watches the rivers also watches you.
And if you have never trusted Jesus Christ before, this story is an invitation.
Because the greater Deliverer has already come.
He entered the waters for you.

He died for your sin.
He rose to give you new life.

Repent.
Turn to Him.
Trust the One who rescues what the world says cannot be saved.
Because the same God who carried Moses through the Nile…
is still carrying people through impossible waters today.
And the story of grace is not finished yet.
Someone standing at the edge of a river today needs to remember this truth.
What looked like abandonment… was actually providence.

📖 “But when she could hide him no longer, she got a papyrus basket for him and coated it with tar and pitch. Then she placed the child in it and put it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile.”
— Exodus 2:3
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Saul’s story is one of the most sobering warnings in Scripture.
paragraphs: Saul’s story is one of the most sobering warnings in Scripture.

Not because he began wicked.
But because he began humble.

When Saul first appears in the biblical story, he doesn’t look like a man hungry for power. In fact, he looks like the opposite. When the time came for Israel to recognize him as king, Saul was hiding among the baggage (1 Samuel 10:22).
That image alone is powerful.
The man God had chosen to lead a nation was literally hiding.
And when the prophet Samuel confronted Saul later in his life, he reminded him of something important:
“Though you were little in your own eyes, were you not made the head of the tribes of Israel?” (1 Samuel 15:17).
Saul began small in his own eyes.
He began with the kind of humility that many people admire. The kind that seems safe. The kind that feels like it could protect a person from pride.
But Saul’s story reveals a deeper truth:
A humble beginning does not guarantee a humble heart forever.
Something inside Saul slowly changed.
At first, the kingdom was new. The calling was heavy. Saul depended on God’s direction through Samuel. But over time, Saul began to shift from dependence to insecurity.
And insecurity is often more dangerous than open pride.
Because pride announces itself.
Insecurity hides… until it feels threatened.
The moment that revealed Saul’s heart came after one of Israel’s victories. The women of Israel sang a song that echoed through the streets:

“Saul has slain his thousands,
and David his tens of thousands.”
— 1 Samuel 18:7
It sounded like celebration.
But to Saul, it sounded like comparison.
Scripture says Saul was very angry and that the saying displeased him (1 Samuel 18:8).
And then Saul said something revealing:
“What more can he have but the kingdom?”
In that moment, jealousy was born.
But the truth is, jealousy didn’t begin that day.
The song only exposed what was already growing in Saul’s heart.
Jealousy is rarely about the other person.
It is usually about fear, identity, and insecurity colliding inside a heart that no longer feels secure in God’s calling.

Saul was still king.
He still had the throne.
He still had authority.
Yet someone else’s praise felt like personal loss.
That is one of the most dangerous places a person can reach spiritually:
When someone else’s blessing feels like your defeat.
From that point forward, Saul’s life slowly turned into a chase. Not a chase for God. A chase for David.
The man who once hid among baggage began throwing spears.
The king who was chosen to lead began being consumed by comparison and suspicion.
And the tragedy is that David was never Saul’s enemy.

David honored Saul.
David served Saul.
David even refused multiple opportunities to harm Saul when Saul was vulnerable (1 Samuel 24, 26).
But jealousy distorts vision.
When insecurity takes root, even loyal people begin to look like threats.
Saul’s downfall reminds us of something deeply important:
Your greatest enemy is not always the person rising near you.
Sometimes the real battle is the part of your heart that struggles to trust God when someone else is blessed.
Comparison has destroyed countless callings.

Not because people lacked gifting.
Not because they lacked opportunity.
But because they could not handle someone else being celebrated.
Saul could handle being chosen.
But he could not handle being outshined.
And that is a test many people fail without realizing it.
Can you celebrate someone else's victory when it happens near you?
Can you honor another person's success without feeling smaller?
Can you trust that God’s calling on your life is still secure even when someone else’s influence grows?
Saul never won that battle.
And the saddest part of Saul’s story is not just that he lost a kingdom.
It’s that he lost peace long before he lost the throne.

Jealousy robbed him of rest.
Suspicion robbed him of trust.
Fear robbed him of joy.
The man who once led Israel became tormented by the very insecurities he refused to surrender to God.
And this is the warning Saul leaves behind for every generation:
If you don’t surrender your insecurities to God, they will eventually rule you.
You can be anointed and still become insecure.
You can be called and still become jealous.
You can start humble… and still fall if humility is replaced with comparison.
But Saul’s story is not only a warning.
It is also an invitation.
An invitation to build our identity in something deeper than applause.
Because when your identity is rooted in God’s approval, someone else’s success does not threaten you.
It inspires you.
It reminds you that God is still working.
The safest heart is not the heart that started humble.
It is the heart that stays surrendered.
And the most powerful test of humility is not how low you bow when no one notices you…
It’s how pure your heart stays when someone else is rising beside you.
So the real question Saul’s story leaves us with is this:
When God begins to bless someone near you…
Will your heart celebrate?
Or will it compete?

“A heart at peace gives life to the body,
but envy rots the bones.”
— Proverbs 14:30
Let Saul’s story be a warning we take seriously.
Because sometimes the greatest spiritual battles are not fought on battlefields.
They are fought inside the human heart.
And the victory that matters most is the one that keeps jealousy from ever sitting on the throne.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She was thrown away… after she was used.
paragraphs: She was thrown away… after she was used.

No goodbye.
No protection.
Just a desert… and a dying child.
But here’s the question that should shake you:
What if the place you thought was your ending… is where God finally reveals Himself?
Hagar didn’t plan this life.

She didn’t choose the scandal.
She didn’t choose the pain.
She didn’t choose to be used by people with power and then discarded when it became inconvenient.
She was a servant… caught in someone else’s broken story.

And suddenly—
she’s pregnant, hated, mistreated, and running for her life into the wilderness.
Pause.
Because this is not just ancient history.
This is you.

The moment you gave your heart to something that didn’t honor God.
The moment you became “useful” to people… but never truly loved.
The moment you realized—too late—that you were part of something messy, sinful, and out of control.
Now you’re left carrying the consequences.
Alone.
Ashamed.
Confused.
Shame is loud in the desert.
It whispers:

“You should’ve known better.”
“You are the problem.”
“You are forgotten.”

And if you listen long enough…
you start to believe that God has moved on without you.
That your story is now defined by your worst moment.
That you are no longer worth redeeming.
But then something happens in Genesis 16 that breaks every lie.
“The angel of the Lord found her by a spring of water in the wilderness…” (Genesis 16:7)
Found her.

Not ignored.
Not avoided.
Not rejected.
Found.
Let that hit you.

God did not wait for Hagar to fix herself.
He did not say, “Come back when you’re clean.”
He went into the wilderness… and met her there.
And then He asked:
“Hagar… where have you come from and where are you going?” (Genesis 16:8)
God already knew the answer.
But He wanted her heart.
Because healing begins when honesty is spoken in the presence of God.
And Hagar does something radical.
She gives God a name.
“You are a God of seeing… Truly here I have seen Him who looks after me.” (Genesis 16:13)
El Roi.
The God who sees me.

Not the version I pretend to be.
Not the filtered version for people.
The real me.

Broken.
Messy.
Regretful.
Seen.
But the story doesn’t end there.
Because shame has a way of circling back.
Genesis 21.
She’s cast out again.

No shelter.
No security.
Just a bottle of water… and a child slowly dying under the desert sun.
“She sat down opposite him… for she said, ‘Let me not look on the death of the child.’ And as she sat opposite him, she lifted up her voice and wept.” (Genesis 21:16)
This is not polished faith.
This is raw despair.

This is the moment where your prayers don’t sound holy…
they sound like breaking.
And here’s the turning point.
“And God heard the voice of the boy… Fear not, for God has heard…” (Genesis 21:17)
Then this:
“Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water…” (Genesis 21:19)
Don’t miss this.
The well was already there.
She just couldn’t see it.
Some scholars interpret this as a supernatural provision appearing in that moment. Others see it as God revealing what was already present but hidden by despair.
Either way—the message is the same:
God provides… even when you feel abandoned.
And sometimes your biggest problem isn’t that God is absent.
It’s that pain has blinded you to His provision.
Let’s go deeper.
Hagar’s story is not just about survival.
It’s about the human condition.
Because every one of us has stepped into a story marked by sin.

Maybe not Hagar’s exact situation—
but the same root:

Disobedience.
Broken desires.
Self-reliance.
Compromise.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
And sin always leads somewhere.

A desert.
A drought.
A distance from God.
But here is where everything shifts.

Because the God who saw Hagar…
is the same God who sent Jesus.
And Jesus didn’t just walk into a desert.
He walked into our sin.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Catch that.

Not when you cleaned yourself up.
Not when you fixed your reputation.
While you were still in it.

Jesus took the shame.
The rejection.
The consequence of sin.

On the cross, He was treated like the outcast…
so you could be brought in.
Hagar found a well.
But Jesus said something greater:
“Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again.” (John 4:14)
This is not temporary relief.
This is eternal restoration.
Not just surviving your mistakes—
being redeemed from them.
So let me ask you, heart to heart:
Where are you right now?

Still running?
Still hiding?
Still carrying shame that Jesus already paid for?
You don’t have to stay in the desert.
But you do have to respond.

Repent—not just feeling bad, but turning back to God.
Release the pride that says you can fix yourself.
Receive the grace that was bought by Christ alone.
God sees you.
Not to condemn you—
but to call you back.
Not to expose you—
but to restore you.
This is your interruption.
This is your invitation.
Come back to Jesus.
Let Him open your eyes again.
Let Him show you the well you thought didn’t exist.
If this pierced your heart, don’t ignore it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You think you’re losing…
paragraphs:
You think you’re losing…
but what if God told you to stop fighting?

You came ready to attack.
God told you to walk.

You wanted progress.
God gave you repetition.

You expected breakthrough.
God gave you silence.
And now you’re asking the question nobody says out loud:
“Did I miss God… or is this just not working?”
Let me pull you into Jericho.

Dust in the air.
Walls towering like they’re mocking you.
Enemies watching from above.
And you?
Walking.

Day 1… nothing.
Day 2… still nothing.
Day 3… people are starting to whisper.
“Is this really God?”

Day 4… doubt gets louder.
Day 5… your faith starts negotiating.
Day 6… embarrassment sets in.
Because obedience that doesn’t produce visible results feels like failure.
Let’s be real.
Some of you are there right now.

You’ve been praying… but the addiction is still there.
You’ve been obeying… but the door is still closed.
You’ve been faithful… but the breakthrough hasn’t come.
And deep inside, a quiet voice whispers:
“This isn’t working.”
But here’s the truth Jericho reveals:
God is doing His deepest work when it looks like nothing is happening.
📖 SCRIPTURE ANCHOR
“By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after they had been encircled for seven days.” — Hebrews 11:30
And in the original account:
“The LORD said to Joshua, ‘See, I have given Jericho into your hand…’” — Joshua 6:2
Wait.
Did you catch that?
“I HAVE given…”
Past tense.

Before the march.
Before the shout.
Before the walls moved.
God declared victory before evidence existed.

Some scholars interpret this as a divine pattern:
God settles things in the spiritual realm before they manifest in the physical.
Which means…

Your silence season is not empty.
It’s loaded.
🔥 ESCALATION — THE REAL BATTLE
Jericho wasn’t just stone.

It was pride.
It was fear.
It was the illusion that strength wins battles.
And God was dismantling something deeper than walls.
He was dismantling self-reliance.
Because if Israel fought and won, they would trust their swords.
But if they walked and won—
They would trust God.
And this is where it hits you.
Because your “Jericho” isn’t just your problem.
It’s your pride.

The need to fix yourself.
The urge to control outcomes.
The silent belief that if you try harder, you’ll finally break through.
But God interrupts that narrative and says:
“Put down your weapons.”
Not because the battle isn’t real.
But because you are not the savior in this story.
💔 SHAME → REDEMPTION
Let’s go deeper.
Some of you aren’t just tired.
You’re ashamed.

Ashamed that you’re still struggling.
Ashamed that you’re still circling the same issue.
Ashamed that after all your prayers… you’re still here.
Walking.

Same temptation.
Same weakness.
Same quiet battle no one sees.
And shame says:
“Real Christians don’t struggle like this.”
But Scripture says something different.
📖 “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
No condemnation.

Not less condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
No condemnation.
Which means your Jericho isn’t proof that God abandoned you.
It’s proof that God is working on you.
✝️ GOSPEL TURN — THIS IS WHERE EVERYTHING CHANGES
Because Jericho is not the main story.
Jesus is.
You see, Jericho had walls.
But your greatest wall is sin.

A barrier you cannot climb.
A separation you cannot fix.
📖 “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
And no amount of walking… striving… or self-improvement can tear it down.
So what did God do?
He didn’t ask you to circle your sin.
He sent His Son to crush it.

Jesus lived the life you couldn’t live.
Perfect. Sinless. Obedient.
Then He went to the cross—
Not as a victim.
But as a substitute.
📖 “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree…” — 1 Peter 2:24

Every failure.
Every secret.
Every shame you hide.
Placed on Him.
And when Jesus said:
“It is finished.” (John 19:30)
That wasn’t poetic.
That was a declaration.
The wall between you and God?
Destroyed.
Not by your effort.
But by His sacrifice.
And three days later—
He rose.
Because the victory wasn’t temporary.
It was eternal.
📖 “If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” — John 8:36
🔥 RESOLUTION — YOUR JERICHO MOMENT
So what do you do now?
You walk.
Not to earn victory.
But because victory has already been declared in Christ.
You obey.
Not because it makes sense.
But because God is trustworthy.
You keep showing up.
Even when nothing moves.
Because faith is not proven in outcomes.
It’s proven in obedience.
Hear this clearly:
You are not circling in vain.
Every step of obedience is stacking pressure in the unseen.
Every prayer is hitting heaven.
Every moment of surrender is weakening something you can’t yet see.
And one day—
Suddenly.
Unexpectedly.
Undeniably.
The wall will fall.
❤️ HEART INVITATION
But before your situation changes—
God wants your heart.

Not your performance.
Not your perfection.
Your surrender.
Maybe today is your Day 1.
Or your Day 6.
Or maybe you’re tired of walking altogether.
Then hear this:
Jesus is not waiting for you to get it right.
He’s inviting you to come home.
📖 “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28
Lay down your pride.
Bring your shame.
Confess your sin.
Trust in Jesus—not yourself.
Because the greatest miracle isn’t walls falling.
It’s a sinner being saved.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He sounded righteous.
paragraphs: He sounded righteous.
But heaven called it empty.

Two men walked into the same place…
but only one walked out right with God.

And here’s the part that should disturb you—
the “good man” was the one rejected.
Pause.
Because this story is not about them.
It’s about you.

It’s about the quiet thoughts you never confess.
The subtle comparisons you don’t notice anymore.
The silent belief that God must be pleased… because you’re not as bad as others.
That’s where it begins.

Slow.
Polished.
Religious.

The Pharisee didn’t curse.
He didn’t cheat.
He didn’t live a scandalous life.
He prayed.
He fasted.
He gave.
And yet… he was lost.
Why?
Because his righteousness had a mirror.
Not a cross.
“God, I thank You that I am not like other men…” (Luke 18:11)
Do you hear it?

Not desperation.
Not surrender.
Not worship.
Comparison.
Pride dressed in prayer language.
He wasn’t talking to God.
He was presenting himself.
And if we’re honest… this spirit slips into us easier than we admit.

It hides in church attendance.
It breathes in ministry service.
It whispers in our thoughts when we see someone fall:
“At least I’m not like that.”
That sentence feels small.
But it is spiritually lethal.

Because the moment you measure yourself against others,
you stop measuring yourself against God.
And God is not comparing you to them.
He is holy.
Perfect.
Untouched by sin.
Scripture says:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
Not some.
All.
That includes the Pharisee.
That includes you.
That includes me.

So while the Pharisee stood tall, listing his achievements like a résumé,
another man stood far off.
A tax collector.
A traitor in his culture.
A sinner with a reputation.
He didn’t look up.
He didn’t perform.
He didn’t pretend.
He broke.
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13)
No excuses.
No comparisons.
No self-defense.
Just truth.
Raw.
Unfiltered.
And Jesus said something that flips religion upside down:
“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other.” (Luke 18:14)
Justified.
Declared righteous before God.
Accepted.
Clean.
Not because he improved himself.
Not because he earned it.
But because he threw himself on mercy.
Let that sink in.

The worst man in the room…
was the only one who went home right with God.
Why?
Because pride locks the door to grace.
But humility opens it wide.

James 4:6 says,
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
Not ignores.
Opposes.
That means the Pharisee didn’t just miss God…
He stood against Him without realizing it.
And here is the tension we must face:
You can look holy… and still be far from God.
You can speak right… act right… serve right…
And still trust the wrong thing.
Yourself.
Your discipline.
Your consistency.
Your morality.
But none of those can save you.
Because the problem is deeper than behavior.
It’s sin.
And sin is not cleaned by effort.
It is forgiven by blood.
This is where everything turns.
This is where the Gospel steps in.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who think they are already righteous.
He came for sinners who know they are not.
“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick… I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” (Mark 2:17)
On the cross, Jesus took what the Pharisee refused to admit:
Sin.
Your sin.
My sin.

The hidden pride.
The silent arrogance.
The subtle self-trust.
He carried it.
And He paid for it.
Fully.
Completely.
And then He offers something no human effort can produce:
His righteousness.

2 Corinthians 5:21 says,
“For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.”
Did you catch that?
Not earn.
Become.
In Him.
Through Christ alone.
This is the difference between religion and the Gospel.

Religion says:
“Fix yourself, then come to God.”

The Gospel says:
“Come to God, because you cannot fix yourself.”
The Pharisee stayed standing.
The tax collector bowed low.
And heaven moved toward the one who humbled himself.
So let me ask you—honestly:

Are you praying to God…
or performing for Him?

Are you depending on Christ…
or subtly trusting yourself?
Do you secretly believe you are “doing better” than others…
And that somehow makes you safer?
That is a dangerous place to stand.
Because the ground of self-righteousness looks solid…
Until eternity exposes it.
But there is another way.
A better way.
A saving way.
Come low.
Not with your record.
Not with your excuses.
Not with your comparisons.
Come like the tax collector.
And say it from the core of your being:
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
And don’t stop there.
Look to Jesus.
Because mercy is not just a feeling.
It is a Person.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
He died.
He rose.
And He alone makes sinners right with God.
This is your moment.
Drop the mask.
Lay down the performance.
Abandon the quiet pride you’ve been protecting.
He is not asking for your résumé.
He is asking for your heart.
Broken.
Honest.
Open.
And here’s the promise:
“The one who humbles himself will be exalted.” (Luke 18:14)
God lifts the low.
He fills the empty.
He saves the honest.
So come.
Right now.
Right where you are.
No perfect words required.
Just a real surrender.
This is not coincidence.
This is invitation.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They didn’t die in rebellion.
paragraphs:
They didn’t die in rebellion.
They died in worship.
Let that sit.

Because that means it’s possible to be close to God…
and still be completely out of line with Him.

Two men.
Chosen.
Anointed.
Standing in the presence of glory.

And in one moment—
fire fell.

Not the kind that blesses.
The kind that consumes.
Why?
What did they do that was so serious… that God responded with fire?
Here’s the tension most people don’t want to face:

They weren’t atheists.
They weren’t idol worshipers.
They weren’t outside the system.

They were inside.
Serving.
Leading.
Wearing the garments.

And still—
they offered something God never asked for.

“Nadab and Abihu… offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which He had not commanded them. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them…”
— Leviticus 10:1–2
Catch that phrase.
“Which He had not commanded them.”
That’s the whole issue.

Not just what they did—
but that God never asked for it.
This is where it gets uncomfortably personal.

Because today, we don’t carry censers and incense—
but we still bring God things He never asked for.

Performance instead of purity.
Emotion instead of obedience.
Noise instead of surrender.

We raise hands… but resist His Word.
We sing loud… but live quiet rebellion.
We serve publicly… but hide privately.
And we call it worship.

But heaven is not moved by what feels spiritual.
Heaven responds to what is obedient.

Some scholars interpret that Nadab and Abihu may have used the wrong source of fire—
not the fire from the altar God had ignited (Leviticus 9:24),
but something man-made.
That detail matters.
Because it reveals something deeper:
They replaced God’s fire with their own.
And God would not accept it.
Pause.

How much of what we offer today…
is powered by our own fire?

Our ideas.
Our timing.
Our preferences.
Our platform.

Instead of:
“Lord, what have You commanded?”
This is the danger of familiarity.

They had seen glory before.
They had been in holy spaces.

And somewhere along the way—
holy became common.

And when holy becomes common…
obedience becomes optional.
But God responds:

“Among those who are near Me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.”
— Leviticus 10:3
God is not adjusting Himself to us.
We are called to align with Him.
This is not about fear-based religion.
This is about rightly seeing God.

Holy.
Pure.
Set apart.
Not to be approached casually.
And here’s the part that hits hardest:
You can be active in ministry… and still be offering strange fire.

You can preach—
and still not obey.

You can lead—
and still not surrender.

You can be seen as spiritual—
and still be out of alignment with God.
That realization brings shame.
The quiet kind.
The kind that whispers:

“Have I been doing this wrong?”
“Is my worship real?”
“Have I been offering God… something He never asked for?”
Stay with me.
Because this is where everything turns.
The story of Nadab and Abihu is not just a warning.
It’s a signpost pointing forward.

Because if approaching a holy God requires perfect obedience—
then who can stand?

Not Nadab.
Not Abihu.
Not you.
Not me.
That’s why we need Jesus.

“For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses… yet without sin.”
— Hebrews 4:15
Jesus never offered strange fire.
Not once.

Every step.
Every word.
Every act.
Perfect obedience.

“I always do the things that are pleasing to Him.”
— John 8:29

Where Nadab and Abihu failed—
Jesus fulfilled.
And then…
He did something scandalous.
He didn’t just live perfectly.
He died in our place.

“Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that He might bring us to God…”
— 1 Peter 3:18
Let that land.

The fire that should have consumed us—
fell on Him.

The judgment we deserved—
He absorbed.
So now…
We don’t come to God with our own fire.
We come through Christ.

“Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace…”
— Hebrews 4:16
Not confidence in ourselves.
Confidence in Jesus.
This is the shift:

From strange fire
to saving grace

From
“Look what I brought”
to
“Jesus, I need what You’ve done.”
So what do we do now?
We repent.

Not just of obvious sin—
but of self-made worship.

We lay down the need to control.
To impress.
To perform.
And we ask:
“Lord… what have You commanded?”
Because true worship is not built on creativity alone.
It is built on obedience to God’s Word.

“God is spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth.”
— John 4:24
Truth matters.
His way matters.
Right now—this is personal.
Not theoretical.
What are you offering God… that He never asked for?
What needs to be surrendered?
What needs to be realigned?
You are not too far gone.
You are not disqualified.
You are not beyond grace.
But you must come the right way.
Through Jesus.
If this is you—don’t ignore it.
This is not guilt.
This is God calling you back.
Say it.
Mean it.
Let it be real:
“Jesus, I surrender my way. Teach me Yours.”
If this woke you up…
From strange fire to saving grace — because Jesus rewrites everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He looked anointed.
paragraphs: He looked anointed.
But heaven had already turned away.
And nobody in the crowd could see it.
That’s the danger.

Because you can look right…
and be wrong where it matters most.

You can carry the crown…
and still lose the heart.
Saul was everything people wanted.

Tall. Strong. Commanding.
The kind of man who made a nation feel secure just by standing there.
Scripture says, “There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people” (1 Samuel 9:2).
He looked like a king.
And that was enough… for them.
But not for God.
Here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Because Saul’s story is not just ancient history.
It’s a mirror.
We know how to look right.
We know how to say the right words, post the right verses, raise the right hands in worship, smile at church, lead when people are watching.
But inside?
There are cracks.
Hidden compromises.
Silent negotiations with sin.
Private fears that control public decisions.
Saul didn’t lose the kingdom overnight.
He drifted.
Slowly.
Quietly.
Dangerously.
One compromise at a time.
One act of partial obedience dressed up as “good enough.”
One moment of choosing people’s approval over God’s command.
Until finally, the truth came out.
“I was afraid of the people and so I gave in to them.” (1 Samuel 15:24)
Read that again.
The king… ruled by fear.
The leader… led by the crowd.
The anointed… controlled by approval.
This is the real issue.
Not appearance.
Authority.
Heart.
Saul feared people more than he feared God.
And when fear of people sits on the throne of your heart… God does not.
Let that sink in.
Some of us are not walking in obedience because we’re still listening to the wrong voices.

“What will they think?”
“What will I lose?”
“What if I’m rejected?”
So we edit our obedience.
We delay repentance.
We manage sin instead of killing it.
We perform instead of surrendering.
And like Saul, we keep the image intact while the soul is collapsing.
But God sees it.
Every hidden motive.
Every quiet compromise.
Every moment we chose approval over obedience.
“Man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)
That verse should shake you.
Because you can fool people.
You can even fool yourself.
But you cannot fool God.
And here’s the hardest truth:
God rejected Saul as king (1 Samuel 15:26).
Not because he lacked talent.
Not because he lacked influence.
But because his heart refused full obedience.
Some scholars interpret Saul’s rejection as a gradual spiritual hardening—a pattern of disobedience that revealed where his allegiance truly was.
And that’s the warning.
Partial obedience is still disobedience.
Delayed obedience is still rebellion.
And outward success can hide inward decay… for a while.
But not forever.
Now stop.
Because this is where grace breaks in.
Because if Saul’s story ended with rejection, we would all be in trouble.
But the Bible doesn’t just give us Saul.
It gives us Jesus.
Saul was chosen because he looked like a king.
Jesus came looking like anything but.
“He had no beauty or majesty to attract us to him… nothing in his appearance that we should desire him.” (Isaiah 53:2)
Let that flip your expectations.
The true King didn’t arrive with height, armor, or outward impressiveness.
He came in humility.
In weakness.
In obedience.
Where Saul grasped for approval, Jesus surrendered to the Father.

Where Saul said, “I feared the people,”
Jesus said, “Not my will, but yours be done.” (Luke 22:42)

Where Saul preserved his image,
Jesus gave up His life.
And here is the Gospel:
Jesus took the place of people like Saul.
And people like us.
Every moment you chose image over integrity…
Every time you feared people more than God…
Every hidden sin you thought nobody saw…
Christ saw it.
And still went to the cross.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” (2 Corinthians 5:21)
That is not surface-level grace.
That is blood-bought redemption.
This is not behavior modification.
This is heart transformation.
But don’t miss this:
Grace is not permission to stay the same.
Grace is the power to finally change.
You cannot hold onto your image and receive His transformation at the same time.
Something has to die.
Your pride.
Your fear.
Your need for approval.
Your hidden sin.
It must come into the light.
Because healing does not happen in hiding.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)
Not manage.
Cleanse.
Not cover up.
Restore.
This is your moment.
Not to look right.
But to be made right.
So ask yourself:
Who are you really obeying?
What fear is controlling your decisions?
What sin are you protecting because it costs too much to surrender?
And hear this clearly—
God is not impressed by your image.
But He is ready to transform your heart.
Right now.
Not when you fix yourself.
Not when you feel worthy.
Now.
Come out of hiding.
Drop the performance.
Bring the real you before the real King.
Repent.
Not as shame.
But as return.
Because the same God who rejected Saul’s disobedience…
welcomes every broken sinner who comes through Jesus.
That includes you.
So here’s your step:
Stay close.
This is where transformation begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Israel did not wake up one morning and suddenly reject God.
paragraphs: Israel did not wake up one morning and suddenly reject God.
It happened quietly.
Slowly.
Almost reasonably.
They came to Samuel with what sounded like a practical request:
“Give us a king.”
At first glance, nothing about that sounds rebellious. It sounded organized. Strategic. Even responsible.

Every other nation had a king.
Kings led armies.
Kings built strong nations.
Kings made people feel secure.
Israel simply wanted to be like everyone else.
But God revealed something deeper behind their request.
“They have not rejected thee, but they have rejected Me.”
That sentence changes everything.
Because the problem was never really about leadership.
It was about trust.
Israel already had something that no other nation on earth had.
They had God Himself as their King.

He led them through the wilderness.
He defeated their enemies.
He delivered them from oppression.
He spoke to their prophets.
He guided their nation.
But the problem with God as King is this:
You cannot control Him.
You cannot predict Him.
You cannot manage Him.
And sometimes people prefer a visible authority over an invisible God who demands faith.
So Israel looked at the nations around them and said something dangerous:
“We want what they have.”
That sentence has ruined many destinies.
Because comparison is often the beginning of compromise.
Instead of appreciating the unique calling God gave them, they started measuring themselves against cultures that did not even know God.
They traded being set apart for fitting in.
And honestly… that temptation still exists today.
People want what looks impressive.
They trust charisma more than character.
They admire power more than obedience.
They follow influence more than truth.
And sometimes believers begin craving the very systems God never designed for them.
The most dangerous spiritual drift rarely starts with open rebellion.
It usually starts with quiet comparison.
“We want to be like them.”
Samuel warned them what their request would bring.
He told them what a human king would do.
He would take their sons.
He would take their daughters.
He would take their land.
He would take their crops.
He would take their freedom.
In other words:
The thing they wanted so badly would eventually cost them more than they expected.
That is another powerful lesson hidden inside this story.
Sometimes what we demand outside God’s will comes with a price we refused to count.
But the people refused to listen.
They insisted.
And God allowed it.
Not because it was the best plan.
But because sometimes God allows people to experience the consequences of what they stubbornly demand.
That reality should humble all of us.
Because not every answered prayer means God approved the desire.
Sometimes it simply means He allowed the request.
Israel wanted a crown they could see.
But they rejected the King who had always been protecting them.
And if we are honest, we can fall into the same pattern.
We may never say, “I reject God.”
But our choices can slowly drift in that direction.
Every time we trust culture more than Scripture.
Every time we prefer popularity over holiness.
Every time we admire the world’s systems more than God’s wisdom.
Every time we value fitting in more than standing apart.
That is how spiritual drift begins.
Not loudly.
Quietly.
Almost logically.
One of the most dangerous desires a believer can develop is the desire to be normal when God has called them to be different.
Israel was never meant to look like the surrounding nations.
They were meant to reflect the glory of God.
They were meant to live under a different authority.
A holy authority.
A divine authority.
A King no human crown could replace.
But they traded something eternal for something visible.
And history shows how heavy that decision became.
The truth is, many people still struggle with the same choice today.
Trust God.
Or trust what looks impressive.
Follow God's ways.
Or follow what everyone else is doing.
Depend on divine leadership.
Or choose what feels easier to control.
This story forces a question into every heart that reads it:
Do we truly want God to reign… or do we just want something that makes us feel secure?
Because those two desires are not always the same.
Israel wanted security.
But security without God always becomes bondage.
Power without God always becomes oppression.
And leadership without God eventually becomes corruption.
The lesson from this moment in Scripture is powerful and sobering:
Not every step forward is progress.
Sometimes it is departure.
And sometimes the most spiritual thing a person can do is refuse the pressure to become like everyone else.
Because God's people were never designed to blend in with the world.
They were designed to reveal a different Kingdom.
A better Kingdom.
An eternal Kingdom.
And unlike Israel's human kings…
The true King we serve does not take.
He gives.
He does not enslave.
He saves.
He does not exploit.
He redeems.
And His reign is not built on power.
It is built on love, truth, and righteousness.
So the next time the world’s systems start looking more attractive than God’s ways, remember this moment in Israel’s history.
Remember what they traded.
Remember what it cost.
And remember the warning hidden inside their request.
Sometimes the greatest spiritual danger is not rebellion.
It is the quiet desire to be like everyone else.
Engagement Question
Have you ever experienced a moment in your life where you realized you were slowly drifting toward what the world values instead of what God was calling you to?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Jonathan
paragraphs:
The Character I Almost Overlooked: Jonathan
Loyalty that surrendered a throne.
Most people remember David.

The giant killer.
The shepherd king.
The man after God’s own heart.
But hidden inside David’s story is one of the most remarkable men in Scripture.
Jonathan.
And the truth is… many of us almost overlook him.
Not because he lacked courage.
Not because he lacked influence.
But because his greatness was revealed in something our world rarely celebrates:
He willingly stepped aside.
Jonathan was not just any man in Israel.

He was the son of King Saul.
The natural heir to the throne.
The man who should have become the next king.

By tradition.
By bloodline.
By royal right.
The crown should have been his.
Yet Jonathan saw something most people would have resisted.
He saw God’s hand on David.
Scripture tells us in 1 Samuel 18:1 that the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and he loved him as his own soul.
But that love was tested in a way most friendships never are.

Because the man he loved…
was the man who would replace him.
Imagine the tension.

Every victory David won made Saul jealous.
Every song sung about David made the palace uneasy.
"Saul has slain his thousands, but David his tens of thousands." (1 Samuel 18:7)
Those words could have turned Jonathan into David’s enemy.
But they didn’t.
Instead of jealousy, Jonathan chose loyalty.
Instead of rivalry, Jonathan chose honor.
Instead of defending his future, he defended God’s will.
In 1 Samuel 18:4, Jonathan did something deeply symbolic.
He took off his robe, his armor, his sword, his bow, and his belt and gave them to David.
This was not just generosity.
This was prophetic humility.
Those items represented royal authority and warrior identity.
Jonathan was, in a sense, saying:
"I recognize what God is doing. And I will not stand in its way."
That moment alone reveals a powerful truth:
Some of the strongest faith is not seen in what we gain… but in what we willingly release.
Jonathan could have competed with David.
He could have manipulated the situation.
He could have protected his position.
Instead, he became David’s protector.
When Saul tried to kill David, Jonathan warned him.
When David was hiding in the wilderness, Jonathan went to strengthen his hand in God.
1 Samuel 23:16 says:
"Jonathan went to David at Horesh and helped him find strength in God."
Think about that.
The man who could have been king was helping the future king survive.
That level of loyalty is rare.

Because most people celebrate their friends…
until those friends begin stepping into the opportunities they wanted.
But Jonathan’s heart was different.
He understood something that many people struggle to accept:
God’s calling is not a competition.
Just because someone else is chosen does not mean you are forgotten.
Jonathan’s story teaches us a difficult but beautiful lesson.
You can be close to greatness without being consumed by comparison.
You can celebrate another person’s destiny without feeling threatened.
You can support someone else's calling even when it costs you recognition.
Jonathan shows us what humility actually looks like.
Not false humility.
Not polite words.
But real surrender.
Because sometimes the hardest test of character is not whether you can carry a crown.
It is whether you can lay one down.
And Jonathan did.
He stayed loyal to David even when his own father turned against him.
He defended David in dangerous moments.
He strengthened David in seasons of fear.
And he never tried to sabotage what God had chosen.
That is why Jonathan’s life quietly asks a powerful question:
Can you honor what God is doing in someone else’s life… even when it doesn’t center you?
That question exposes something deep in the human heart.
Because comparison is one of the oldest struggles in history.
It began with Cain and Abel.
It shows up in families, friendships, ministries, workplaces, and communities.
But Jonathan chose a different path.
He chose love over envy.
He chose loyalty over ambition.
He chose obedience over entitlement.
And that choice makes him one of the most honorable men in the Bible.
Here is something many people miss:
Jonathan never became king.
But his character still reigns through Scripture.
His story reminds us that faithfulness is not measured by titles.
It is measured by the condition of the heart.
Some people fight their entire lives trying to sit on a throne.
Jonathan teaches us that true greatness is revealed in those who trust God enough to step back when He says so.
And maybe that is the lesson many of us need today.
Not every door that closes is a loss.
Not every opportunity that passes us by was meant for us.
Sometimes God is writing a different story.
And sometimes the most beautiful role we can play is the one that says:
"I will honor what God is doing — even if I am not the center of it."
Jonathan may not have worn the crown.
But he wore something greater.
Integrity.
Loyalty.
Humility before the will of God.
And in a world obsessed with being first…
Jonathan reminds us that heaven also honors those who are willing to stand beside someone else’s calling.

Scripture:
1 Samuel 18:1–4
1 Samuel 19:1–7
1 Samuel 20:12–17
1 Samuel 23:16–18

Reflection Question:
Do you think it is harder to trust God while waiting for your own opportunity, or while watching someone else step into the opportunity you hoped for?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: God hates it.
paragraphs:
God hates it.
And you’re still entertaining it.
Sit with that.

Because this isn’t about them.
Not the corrupt.
Not the violent.
Not the obvious sinners.
This is closer.
Closer than you think.

You’ve heard “God is love.”
But you were never told…
what He hates.

And maybe that’s why some things in your life
still feel… untouched.
Unconfronted.
Unrepented.

Because if you really saw it the way God sees it—
you wouldn’t flirt with it anymore.
You’d run.
Let me open the tension wider.

What if the very thing you’ve been justifying…
is on God’s hate list?

What if the quiet attitudes, the hidden patterns,
the “it’s not that bad” moments—
are the very things heaven calls abomination?
Not to shame you.
But to wake you.

“There are six things that the Lord hates,
seven that are an abomination to Him…”
— Proverbs 6:16–19
This is not poetic exaggeration.
This is divine exposure.
Let’s walk through it.
Slow.
Honest.
Uncomfortable.
“Haughty eyes…”
Pride.
Not loud arrogance.
Subtle superiority.
The silent belief that you’re okay without surrender.

You still pray—
but you don’t bow.

You still sing—
but you don’t submit.

You still post—
but you don’t repent.
Pride doesn’t always look like rebellion.
Sometimes it looks like control.
“A lying tongue…”
Not just lies you tell others.
But lies you tell yourself.

“It’s just this once.”
“I can stop anytime.”
“God understands.”
Yes—He understands.
And He still calls it sin.
“Hands that shed innocent blood…”
You say, “That’s not me.”
But Jesus said:

“Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment…”
— Matthew 5:22

Hatred begins in the heart
long before it reaches the hands.

Character assassination.
Online tearing down.
Cancel culture disguised as righteousness.

You didn’t spill blood—
but you crushed a soul.
“A heart that devises wicked plans…”
Not accidental sin.
Intentional.
Planned.
Rehearsed.

You knew it was wrong—
but you still prepared for it.
You created opportunity for darkness.
And called it freedom.
“Feet that are swift to run to evil…”
This one cuts deep.
Because it’s not about falling.
It’s about running.

When temptation shows up—
you don’t resist.
You lean in.
You anticipate.
You even enjoy the chase.

Something inside you
is being trained…
to love what destroys you.
“A false witness who breathes out lies…”
Twisting truth.
Selective honesty.
Narratives shaped to protect your image.
You didn’t lie fully—
just enough.

And God says:
I see the whole thing.
“And one who sows discord among brothers.”
This one is quiet.
Deadly.
Church-breaking.
Friendship-ending.
Spirit-grieving.

Gossip.
Division.
Subtle seeds of offense.

You didn’t explode—
you whispered.

And suddenly…
unity died.
Let’s stop pretending.
This list?
It’s not out there.
It’s in here.
Pride.
Lies.
Hidden anger.
Secret sin.
Division.
This is where shame creeps in.
That heavy feeling.
That voice whispering:

“See? This is who you are.”
“You’re too far gone.”
“You can’t change.”
But that voice is lying too.
Because Scripture doesn’t stop at exposure.
It leads to redemption.
Listen carefully.
This is the turning point.
God doesn’t reveal sin to destroy you.
He reveals it to save you.

Because the same Bible that says God hates sin
also says this:

“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
— Romans 5:8
Not after you fixed yourself.
Not after you cleaned up.
While you were still in it.
Jesus didn’t come for perfect people.

He came for proud hearts.
For liars.
For the divided.
For the double-minded.
For you.
At the cross, something holy and terrifying happened.

The full weight of what God hates—
sin, rebellion, corruption—
was poured out.
Not on you.
On Christ.

“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree…”
— 1 Peter 2:24

Every lie.
Every proud thought.
Every hidden scheme.
Nailed.
Crushed.
Paid for.
This is the Gospel:

You are more sinful than you want to admit—
and more loved than you can imagine.
But grace is not permission.
It’s transformation.

“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us… and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— 1 John 1:9
Not manage.
Not excuse.
Cleanse.
That means the story doesn’t end with:
“God hates this.”
It continues with:
“God can change this.”
So here’s the real question:

What are you still holding
that God is calling you to release?
The pride?
Drop it.
The lie?
Confess it.
The secret sin?
Bring it into the light.
The division you started?
Go back. Make it right.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.

Because delayed obedience
is still disobedience.
This isn’t about behavior modification.
This is about surrender.

Jesus didn’t die
so you could manage sin.

He died
so you could be free from it.
And freedom doesn’t begin with effort.
It begins with repentance.
A turning.
A breaking.
A coming home.

Right now—yes, right now—
you can pray:

“Jesus, I see it.
I’ve justified what You hate.
Forgive me.
Change me.
I surrender.”
And heaven doesn’t hesitate.
Grace doesn’t delay.
Mercy doesn’t say, “Try harder first.”
It runs.

“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
— Romans 8:1
No condemnation.
But there is transformation.
This is not just content.
This is confrontation.
This is invitation.
This is God reaching for you.
Let Him.
If this pierced your heart, don’t ignore it.
Declare it.
who needs truth wrapped in grace.
when comfort returns.
If this stirred something in you…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: David’s story contains a truth many believers struggle to accept.
paragraphs: David’s story contains a truth many believers struggle to accept.
God sometimes prepares your greatest season in the darkest places.
Before David ever wore a crown, he lived in caves.

Not one cave.
Many caves.
After the prophet Samuel anointed him as the future king of Israel (1 Samuel 16:13), David’s life did not suddenly become easier. In fact, it became more dangerous.

The oil of anointing was still fresh…
Yet David was running for his life.
King Saul, consumed by jealousy, began hunting him. The man God had chosen to lead Israel was suddenly hiding in wilderness strongholds and caves (1 Samuel 22:1).
Imagine the confusion.

One day you are told that God has chosen you.
The next day you are sleeping on stone floors, hiding in darkness, unsure if you will survive the night.
But here is the powerful truth hidden in David’s story:
The cave was not a detour from David’s destiny.
The cave was part of it.
God often builds leaders in places where nobody is watching.
Inside those caves, David was not wasting time.
He was learning.
He was learning to trust God when circumstances made no sense.
He was learning to lead broken people. The Bible tells us that when David hid in the cave of Adullam, people who were distressed, in debt, and discontent gathered around him (1 Samuel 22:2).
These were not polished soldiers.
These were hurting men.
Yet in that cave, David began developing the leadership that would one day shape a kingdom.
The cave turned followers into warriors.
It also tested David’s heart.
One of the most powerful moments happened in another cave.
Saul entered the cave where David and his men were hiding (1 Samuel 24:3).
David had the perfect opportunity to end his suffering. His enemy was vulnerable. His men even encouraged him to take the throne by force.
But David refused.
Instead of killing Saul, David only cut off a corner of Saul’s robe. And even that troubled his conscience (1 Samuel 24:5).
Why?
Because David understood something many people miss.
Just because you can take something does not mean God wants you to.
David refused to grab the crown before God’s timing.
That moment in the cave revealed David’s true character.
Power did not begin on the throne.
It began in restraint.
The cave exposed the difference between Saul and David.
Saul tried to control everything.
David learned to trust God with everything.
That is why the cave matters so much.
Caves remove the distractions of public life. They strip away applause, reputation, and recognition.
In the cave, there is only you and God.
And that is often where the deepest transformation happens.
Many of the Psalms David wrote came from these hiding places.
Psalm 57 and Psalm 142 are prayers from the cave.
Listen to the honesty in David’s words:
“I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills his purpose for me.” (Psalm 57:2)
David did not pretend everything was fine.
He cried.
He prayed.
He wrestled with fear and pressure.
Yet he continued to trust God’s purpose.
That is faith.
Faith is not pretending life is easy.
Faith is believing God is still working when life is hard.
Some of the strongest believers in Scripture were shaped in hidden places.
Joseph had a prison.
Moses had a wilderness.
Elijah had a desert.
And David had caves.
God often does His deepest work where nobody sees it.
Because hidden seasons reveal the true condition of the heart.
Anyone can worship when life is successful.
But the cave asks a harder question:
Will you still trust God when the promise feels far away?
Will you still honor God when revenge is possible?
Will you still obey God when nobody would blame you for taking shortcuts?
David answered those questions in the cave.
And those answers shaped the king he would become.
Years later, when David finally took the throne, he carried lessons that could only be learned in darkness.
Humility.
Dependence.
Patience.
Reverence for God’s authority.
The crown did not make David great.
The cave prepared him for greatness.
And that truth still speaks to us today.
Many people today are in what feels like a “cave season.”
You may feel hidden.
You may feel delayed.
You may feel like your life does not match the promises you believe God has spoken.
But David’s story reminds us of something powerful:
Hidden does not mean forgotten.
God sees the cave.
He sees the prayers whispered in the dark.
He sees the tears nobody else notices.
He sees the quiet obedience when no one is applauding.
And often, those unseen moments are shaping the future more than public victories ever could.
The cave is where God teaches patience.
The cave is where He refines motives.
The cave is where He prepares hearts for responsibilities they are not yet ready to carry.
Because a throne without preparation can destroy a person.
But a throne after the cave produces wisdom.
David entered caves as a fugitive.
He left them as a man after God’s own heart (Acts 13:22).
So if you are in a cave season right now, do not assume God has abandoned your story.
He may be preparing it.
The place that feels like delay may actually be development.
The place that feels hidden may actually be sacred.
Because sometimes…
God builds kings in caves.
What is one lesson God has taught you during a hidden or difficult season of your life?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She was in the room… but never in his heart.
paragraphs: She was in the room… but never in his heart.

Chosen by circumstance.
Rejected by desire.
And some of you know exactly what that feels like.

You show up.
You give your best.
You love deeply.
But somehow… you’re still not the one.

Still not picked.
Still not preferred.
Still not pursued.
And here’s the question that haunts the quiet places:
“What’s wrong with me?”
Leah lived inside that question.

Every morning, she woke up beside a man who didn’t choose her.
Every glance reminded her—you were the substitute.
Every moment whispered—you are tolerated, not treasured.
And if we’re honest?

Some of us are not just wounded by people…
We are shaped by rejection.

We perform for love.
We compete for attention.
We exhaust ourselves trying to earn what should have been freely given.
Because deep down, there’s a hidden shame saying:
“If I were enough… they would have chosen me.”
But here’s where the story cuts deeper.
Genesis doesn’t soften it.
“When the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb…” — Genesis 29:31
Let that settle.
God saw.

Not ignored.
Not overlooked.
Not minimized.
Seen.

The pain you hide behind your smile?
Seen.

The silent comparisons?
Seen.

The nights you questioned your worth?
Seen.
God doesn’t need an announcement to notice your suffering.
But Leah’s response reveals something painfully human.
She names her sons like cries for validation.

Reuben — “Now my husband will love me.”
Simeon — “The Lord heard that I am unloved.”
Levi — “Now my husband will become attached to me.”
Do you hear the ache?

She kept receiving blessings…
But still begging for love.

She kept being used by God…
But still trying to be chosen by man.
And that’s where shame quietly takes root.

Because when blessings don’t fix your broken identity…
You start believing something deeper is wrong with you.
Let’s be real.
You can be:

Successful… but still feel unseen.
Faithful… but still feel unwanted.
Used by God… but still feel unloved.
Because external fruit does not automatically heal internal wounds.
Then comes the shift.
A holy interruption.
A moment where heaven breaks into heartbreak.
When Judah is born, Leah says:
“This time I will praise the Lord.” — Genesis 29:35
This time.
Not:
“Maybe now I’ll be enough.”
Not:
“Maybe now he’ll choose me.”
No.
“This time… I will praise the Lord.”
That is not resignation.
That is revelation.

Leah stopped chasing validation…
And started anchoring her identity in God.
She moved from:

“See me.”
to
“God already does.”
And here is where the Gospel explodes into the story.

Judah—Leah’s son—became the line of kings.
From that line came David.
And from that line came Jesus Christ.
Let that hit you.

The woman who felt unchosen…
Was chosen to carry the bloodline of the Savior.
This is not accidental.
This is redemption.
Because Jesus didn’t just come through Leah’s line…
He came for Leah’s pain.
Isaiah says:
“He was despised and rejected by men… a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief.” — Isaiah 53:3
Jesus knows rejection.
Not theoretically.
Personally.

He was not chosen by the crowd.
Not defended by His friends.
Not spared from the cross.
He was rejected… so your rejection wouldn’t define you.
Here is the Gospel—clear and unfiltered:
You and I have sinned.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
And part of that sin?
We build our worth on human approval.
We idolize being chosen.
We let people’s opinions shape our identity.
That’s not just pain.
That’s misplaced worship.
But Jesus stepped in.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not when you were chosen.
Not when you were enough.
While you were still broken.
And through Him:
“In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ…” — Ephesians 1:5
Do you see it?
You are not waiting to be chosen.
In Christ—you already are.
This is where shame loses its voice.
Because your identity is no longer:

Rejected.
Second choice.
Not enough.
Your identity becomes:

Forgiven.
Adopted.
Loved.
So what do you do with that ache?
That deep, lingering question:
“Why wasn’t I chosen?”
You bring it to Jesus.

Not polished.
Not filtered.
Not pretending you’re okay.
You bring the raw version.

The insecure version.
The tired version.
The version that still compares and still hurts.
And you let Him speak something stronger than rejection:
“You are mine.”
Repent—not just of sin…
But of believing that human love is your savior.
Surrender the need to be validated by people.
Receive the love that was nailed to a cross for you.
Because here’s the truth most people never hear:
Being unchosen by people may have been the very thing that positioned you to be claimed by God.
So stop begging for seats at tables God never assigned to you.
Stop shrinking to fit into someone else’s preference.
Stop rewriting your worth based on who walked away.
Look at the cross.
That is your proof.
You were worth dying for.
Prayer:

Lord Jesus,
Heal the places in me that still feel rejected.
Forgive me for building my identity on human approval.
Teach me to rest in the truth that I am chosen in You.
Break every lie that says I am not enough.
Anchor me in Your love that never shifts.
In Your name, amen.
If this hit your heart… don’t ignore it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She didn’t break the command.
paragraphs:
She didn’t break the command.
She added to it.
And that was enough to break everything.
Look again.

Not at the fruit.
Not at the serpent.
Look at the sentence.

Because buried in Eve’s words…
is the seed of every distortion you and I still believe today.

God said:
“You shall not eat of the tree…” (Genesis 2:17)

Eve said:
“You shall not eat… nor shall you touch it…” (Genesis 3:3)
God never said that.

One extra line.
One small exaggeration.
And suddenly…

God feels stricter than He is.
Closer to a tyrant than a Father.
More about restriction than relationship.
That’s the open door.

Because when God feels unreasonable…
sin starts to look reasonable.

When God feels harsh…
disobedience starts to feel justified.

And just like that—
truth doesn’t need to be denied…
just edited.
Let this hit you.

The first deception in human history
didn’t begin with rebellion.
It began with a misrepresentation of God’s Word.
And we’re still doing it.
You say:
“God knows my heart… He’ll understand.”
Or…
“I’ve messed up too much… God won’t take me back.”

Both feel real.
Both sound convincing.
Both are additions.
Here’s the tension.

Some of us make God softer than He is—
to excuse our sin.

Others make God harsher than He is—
to excuse our shame.
But both roads lead to the same place:
Distance from Him.
Listen carefully.
God doesn’t need your edits.

He is already perfectly holy.
Perfectly just.
Perfectly good.

When you add to His Word,
you don’t protect His holiness—
you distort His character.
And distortion is dangerous.

Because once you believe a false version of God,
you will respond to Him incorrectly.
You’ll either run into sin…
or run away from grace.
Scripture warns us clearly:
“Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and you be found a liar.” — Proverbs 30:6

That’s not just a command.
That’s protection.

Because adding to God’s Word
creates a god who doesn’t exist.
And a false god can’t save you.
Now here’s where it gets deeper.
The serpent didn’t start with a lie.
He started with a question.
“Did God really say…?” (Genesis 3:1)
And Eve responded…
with a distorted version.
That’s all the enemy needed.

Because once truth is slightly bent,
it becomes easier to fully break.
Be honest.
Where have you added to what God said?

Where have you made Him stricter…
or softer…
than He actually is?

Where have you rewritten His voice
to match your fear… or your desire?
This is where pride hides.
Not in loud rebellion.
But in subtle editing.
“I know what God said… but…”

That “but” has destroyed more lives
than open defiance ever did.
But here’s the turning point.
Because the story didn’t end in a garden.
It continued in a wilderness.

Where Eve distorted God’s Word…
Jesus defended it perfectly.

When Satan tempted Him, Jesus didn’t add.
He didn’t twist.
He didn’t soften.
He said:
“It is written…” (Matthew 4:4)

Exact.
Precise.
Unedited.

And where Adam and Eve fell through distortion—
Jesus stood in truth.
But He didn’t stop there.

Because perfect obedience alone
wasn’t enough to save you.
So Jesus went further.
To a cross.
And on that cross…

He carried every lie you believed.
Every distortion you accepted.
Every moment you edited God
to justify sin or magnify shame.
All of it.
Laid on Him.
“For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
That’s the Gospel.
Not behavior modification.
Not self-correction.

But full redemption
through Jesus Christ alone.
Hear this clearly.
Your problem is not just that you’ve sinned.
Your problem is that you’ve believed lies about God.
And your solution is not trying harder.

Your solution is seeing Him rightly—
through Jesus.
Because Jesus is not an edited version of God.
He is the exact image.
“The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His being…” — Hebrews 1:3

If you want to know what God is like—
look at Christ.

Not your fear.
Not your feelings.
Not your assumptions.
Christ.
So what now?
Stop editing.
Start surrendering.
Come back to what God actually said.

Not what culture says.
Not what trauma whispers.
Not what your guilt screams.
His Word.
His truth.
His Son.

And if you’ve been running—
because you thought God was too harsh…
Come home.

He is holy, yes.
But He is also merciful.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us…” — 1 John 1:9

And if you’ve been hiding—
because you made God too soft…
Wake up.

Grace is not permission to stay in sin.
It’s power to be free from it.
“Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” — Romans 6:1–2
This is your moment.
Not to tweak your theology.
But to realign your heart.
Repent.

Not just from sin—
but from believing a distorted God.
Return to truth.
Return to Christ.
Say it if you mean it:

“Jesus, I surrender what I thought You were.
Show me who You truly are.”
If this exposed something in you…

From distortion to truth.
From shame to redemption.
Because Jesus doesn’t just correct your words—
He redeems your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They didn’t just dislike Joseph.
paragraphs: They didn’t just dislike Joseph.
They hated him.

Not because he stole from them.
Not because he lied to them.
Not because he harmed them.
They hated him for something far more dangerous.
A dream.

A dream that did not come from ambition.
A dream that did not come from ego.
A dream that came from God.
Genesis 37 tells us something uncomfortable about the human heart: sometimes the moment God places favor on someone’s life, jealousy wakes up in the room.

Joseph was the young son of Jacob. Seventeen years old. Still growing. Still learning how to carry the weight of revelation. And his father gave him a robe that screamed what everyone already felt—Joseph was loved differently.
The robe was visible.
But the dream?
The dream was explosive.
Joseph dreamed of sheaves in the field bowing down to his sheaf. Later he dreamed of the sun, moon, and eleven stars bowing down before him.
It was not a random dream.
It was prophetic.
And when Joseph shared it… the room turned cold.
Scripture says plainly:

“And his brothers hated him even more for his dreams and his words.”
— Genesis 37:8

Jealousy does not need evidence.
It only needs comparison.
And comparison quickly becomes resentment.
The brothers began to look at Joseph and see something unbearable: God’s hand on his life.
They could not silence the dream.
So they decided to silence the dreamer.
Let that sink in.
Sometimes the people who know your name the longest struggle the most with your calling.
Joseph’s brothers did not see destiny.
They saw competition.
They did not see God’s plan.
They saw a threat.
So hatred started whispering inside their hearts. And hatred, if left alone, eventually becomes action.

First came the mockery.
Then the distance.
Then the conspiracy.
One day Joseph was simply obeying his father—walking across the fields to check on his brothers.
From a distance they saw him coming.
And instead of saying, “Here comes our brother,” they said something chilling:
“Here comes this dreamer.” (Genesis 37:19)
Not Joseph.
The dreamer.
His identity had already been reduced to the thing they despised.
Jealousy will always try to rewrite someone’s identity.
And in that moment they plotted something dark.
“Come now, let’s kill him and throw him into one of these cisterns…” (Genesis 37:20)
All because of a dream.
Think about that.
A teenager with a God-given vision nearly lost his life because envy had grown unchecked.
But here is where the story begins to whisper something deeper.
Joseph’s brothers thought they were ending the dream.
But God was only beginning the journey.
They stripped him of the robe.
They threw him into a pit.
Eventually they sold him into slavery.
If you stopped the story there, it would look like the dream failed.
It would look like jealousy won.
It would look like God’s promise collapsed under human cruelty.
But Scripture reveals something stronger than hatred.
Providence.
What the brothers meant as destruction, God was weaving into deliverance.
The pit was not the end.
It was the doorway.
Years later, Joseph would rise from slavery to become the governor of Egypt. The same brothers who betrayed him would one day stand before him in desperation during famine.
And the dream they hated?
It would come true.
But Joseph’s story does not end with revenge.
It ends with grace.
Joseph looked at the very men who sold him and spoke one of the most powerful lines in the entire Bible:

“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good…”
— Genesis 50:20
That is the miracle of God’s sovereignty.
People can hate the dream.
They cannot stop the Author of the dream.
But the story of Joseph is also pointing us to Someone greater.
Another beloved Son.
Another rejected one.
Another man betrayed by those close to Him.
Jesus Christ.

Like Joseph, Jesus was hated without cause.
Like Joseph, He was betrayed for silver.
Like Joseph, He was stripped and handed over to suffering.
But through the rejection of Christ, God accomplished the greatest rescue in human history.
The cross looked like defeat.
But it was redemption.
Joseph saved nations from famine.
Jesus saves souls from sin.
And here is the question this story quietly asks every one of us:
What do you do when someone else carries a dream from God?
Do you celebrate it?
Or do you resent it?
Jealousy is a dangerous fire. It burns relationships, distorts identity, and blinds hearts to the goodness of God.
But the Gospel offers a better way.
Instead of competing with others, Christ invites us to surrender to Him.
Because the greatest dream is not fame.
Not power.
Not recognition.
The greatest dream is redemption.
And that dream is available to every person through Jesus.
Maybe someone mocked what God placed in your heart.
Maybe people misunderstood your obedience.
Maybe the road you’re walking feels like a pit instead of a promise.
Listen carefully.
God is not finished writing your story.
The pit is not proof that the dream died.
Sometimes the pit is simply where God prepares the dreamer.

Stay humble.
Stay faithful.
Stay close to Christ.
Because what God begins, no hatred can cancel.
And what God promises, no pit can bury.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
🔥 ENGAGEMENT QUESTION
Have you ever experienced jealousy or rejection because of something God placed in your heart?

People may hate the dream.
But they cannot stop God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You thought the valley meant God left you.
paragraphs: You thought the valley meant God left you.
But what if it’s the only place He gets this close?
Because most of us don’t fear the dark…
We fear what it exposes.

The weakness.
The failure.
The secret you buried under “I’m okay.”
And suddenly, the valley feels louder than your faith.
You smile in public.
But inside?
You’re tired of pretending.

Tired of carrying guilt that doesn’t wash off.
Tired of replaying mistakes you can’t undo.
Tired of wondering if God is silently disappointed in you.
So you pray softer.
You hide deeper.
You scroll faster.
Anything to avoid that quiet moment where your soul whispers:
“Something is not right.”
And here’s the tension we don’t talk about—
The valley doesn’t create your shame.
It reveals it.

Everything you hid in the noise of comfort
becomes deafening in the silence of struggle.

That addiction you said you could control.
That compromise you justified.
That pride you disguised as strength.
Now it’s all there.
Unfiltered.
Uncovered.
And you hate it.
Because deep down, you know—
You can’t fix yourself.
“But here’s what we miss…”
The valley was never meant to destroy you.

It was meant to strip you of the illusion
that you could save yourself.
Psalm 23 says:
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me…” (Psalm 23:4)
Not around.
Through.
Some scholars interpret the “valley of the shadow of death” as a real, dangerous ravine shepherds had to guide sheep through—narrow, dark, filled with predators and uncertainty.
But the key is this—
The danger was real.
Yet the presence of the shepherd was more real.
David doesn’t deny fear.
He defies it.
Why?
“For You are with me.”
Not “I am strong.”
Not “I figured it out.”
Not “I overcame my past.”
No.
“You are with me.”
That’s the difference.
Because shame says:
“Hide.”
God says:
“Come closer.”
Shame says:
“You’ve gone too far.”
God says:
“I stepped into your darkness.”
And this is where the Gospel explodes into the valley—
You are not just walking through shadows.
You were once dead in sin.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
Not some.
All.
Your pride.
Your secret habits.
Your hidden thoughts.
Your quiet rebellion.
Sin isn’t just what you did.
It’s what separated you from God.
And the weight of that?
You feel it in the valley.
Because valleys don’t numb you.
They wake you up.
And here’s the hard truth—
No amount of self-improvement, discipline, or “trying harder” can erase sin.
You can adjust behavior.
But you can’t cleanse your heart.
You can hide from people.
But not from God.
And that’s where most people stop—
Convicted.
Exposed.
Ashamed.
But not yet free.
Because they never make the turn.
The Gospel turn.
Listen carefully—
God didn’t wait for you to climb out of the valley.
He came down into it.
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us…” (John 1:14)
Jesus Christ didn’t stand at a distance shouting instructions.
He stepped into our broken world.
He walked our dust.
Felt our pain.
Faced our temptation—yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
And then He did what no one else could do—
He took your sin.
Your shame.
Your guilt.
And carried it to the cross.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Not when you cleaned yourself up.
Not when you became worthy.
While you were still in the valley.
And on that cross—
Jesus didn’t just feel pain.
He absorbed judgment.
“The Lord has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.” (Isaiah 53:6)
Every hidden thing.
Every secret struggle.
Every failure you replay at night.
Placed on Him.
And when He said, “It is finished” (John 19:30),
He wasn’t speaking poetry.
He was declaring payment.
Complete.
Final.
Enough.
And then—
He walked through death itself.
And came out alive.
“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:36)
This is the truth most people miss:
The valley is not where God abandons you.
It’s where He confronts what’s killing you—
so He can free you from it.
But freedom requires something most avoid—
repentance.
Not just feeling bad.
Not just regret.
Repentance means turning.
Leaving sin.
Surrendering control.
Trusting Jesus not just as Savior—
but as Lord.
And that’s uncomfortable.
Because it means letting go of what you’ve been holding onto.
Even if it’s destroying you.
But here’s the invitation—
You don’t have to carry this anymore.
You don’t have to pretend.
You don’t have to stay stuck in cycles that keep breaking you.
Jesus is not waiting to shame you.
He’s calling you to Himself.
Right here.
Right now.
In the valley.
“Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28)
Not temporary relief.
Real rest.
For your soul.
So let me ask you—
What are you still hiding?
What are you still justifying?
What are you afraid to surrender?
Because the same Shepherd who walks with you…
is also the Savior who died for you.
And He’s not asking for perfection.
He’s asking for surrender.
Today.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you “feel ready.”
Now.
Whisper it if you have to:
“Jesus, I can’t carry this anymore.”
That’s where freedom begins.
And if this stirred something deep in your spirit…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From Jesus Saying “Follow Me”
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From Jesus Saying “Follow Me”
Two words.
That is all Jesus said.

No long explanation.
No roadmap.
No list of guarantees.
Just two words that changed the direction of ordinary lives forever:
“Follow Me.”

It sounds simple when we read it today.
But imagine hearing it in that moment.

Peter was standing near his fishing nets.
Matthew was sitting at a tax booth.
Others were busy with routines, responsibilities, and the ordinary rhythm of life.
