But others will quietly provide the donkey.
And heaven sees all of it.
Jesus once said something that reveals how God views these acts:

“Whoever gives even a cup of cold water… will by no means lose his reward.”
— Matthew 10:42
In God's Kingdom, faithfulness is never small.
The world celebrates fame.
But heaven celebrates obedience.
The unnamed man reminds us of something beautiful:
You do not have to be famous to be faithful.

You do not have to be seen to matter.
You do not have to lead the parade to be part of the purpose.
Sometimes your role is simply to release what God asks for.
And when you do, something incredible happens.
Your ordinary life becomes connected to God's extraordinary story.
So maybe the real question today is this:
What donkey in your life is still tied up?

Is it your time?
Your talent?
Your resources?
Your influence?
Your calling?
Your obedience?
What is God asking you to untie?
Because the truth is simple:
Anything surrendered to Jesus can carry glory.
And somewhere in heaven’s record…

There is still room for unnamed people
who simply loosen the rope when the Lord asks.
Reflection Question for Engagement
What is one “ordinary” thing in your life that you believe God might be asking you to surrender for His purpose?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They welcomed Jesus with praise…
paragraphs: They welcomed Jesus with praise…
…and then demanded His crucifixion.

That shift did not happen overnight.
It only looked sudden.

Because the truth is—
the seeds of rejection were already hidden inside their praise.
Jerusalem knew how to celebrate Him.

They laid down garments.
They waved palm branches.
They shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” (Matthew 21:9)

It was loud.
It was emotional.
It looked like revival.
But heaven sees deeper than volume.
Because a few days later, another sound rose from the same city:
“Crucify Him.” (Luke 23:21)
And that is one of the most uncomfortable warnings in all of Scripture:
You can praise Jesus… and still resist Him.
Pause there.

Because this is not just about them.
This is about us.
The crowd welcomed Jesus as long as He matched their expectations.

They thought He came to overthrow Rome.
They expected political power, immediate victory, visible dominance.
But Jesus came for something deeper.

He came to confront sin.
He came to call for repentance.
He came to establish a Kingdom not built on force—but surrender.
And when He didn’t become the King they imagined…
their praise collapsed.

“Their problem was not that they rejected Jesus later.
It was that they misunderstood Him from the beginning.”
That’s the warning.
Because many people still do this today.
We celebrate the parts of Jesus that feel good.

The Provider.
The Healer.
The Miracle Worker.
The One who opens doors.
But what happens when Jesus becomes the One who corrects you?

What happens when His Word confronts your lifestyle?
Your habits?
Your hidden compromises?
What happens when following Him costs you something?

Because the same crowd that shouted “Hosanna”
could not handle a Messiah who didn’t serve their agenda.
And here’s the uncomfortable truth:
A faith built on expectations will turn on God when He doesn’t follow your script.
Let that sink in.
Because many people don’t walk away from God due to lack of evidence…
They walk away because God didn’t meet their expectations.

He didn’t answer fast enough.
Didn’t move the way they wanted.
Didn’t protect their plans.
So slowly…

admiration turns into frustration.
And frustration—if left unchecked—turns into resistance.

“The same voice that praises God in comfort
can question Him in discomfort.”
The crowd didn’t suddenly become sinful on Friday.
Their hearts were already divided on Sunday.

They wanted a King without surrender.
A Savior without Lordship.
A crown without a cross.
And that is still one of the greatest dangers in modern faith.

Because it is possible to follow Jesus publicly…
but resist Him privately.

To sing about surrender…
but negotiate obedience.

To lift your hands in worship…
but hold back areas of your life He’s asking for.

“Not every ‘Hosanna’ comes from a surrendered heart.”
“Emotion can be real… and still be shallow.”
“Crowds can be loud… and still be lost.”
This is why Jesus never trusted crowds.

John 2:24 says He did not entrust Himself to them,
because He knew what was in man.
He could see the difference between excitement and commitment.
Between admiration and allegiance.

Between people who love what He does…
and people who submit to who He is.
So the real question is not:
“Do I praise Jesus?”
The real question is:
“Do I still follow Him when He doesn’t match my expectations?”
Because real discipleship is revealed under pressure.

When obedience becomes uncomfortable.
When answers are delayed.
When the path doesn’t make sense.
That’s where true loyalty is tested.

“The crowd was present for the entrance…
but absent at the cross.”
Don’t miss that.
Because it’s easy to follow Jesus when He’s being celebrated.
But will you stay when He’s being rejected?

Will you stay when obedience costs you reputation?
Comfort?
Control?
Will you stay when following Him feels lonely?
Because the cross reveals what the crowd could not sustain.
And here’s the deeper reality:

Jesus did not come to fit into your life.
He came to take over it.

He will bless you—but He will also break pride.
He will heal you—but He will also correct you.
He will lift you—but He will also lead you through surrender.

“Christ is not just someone to be admired.
He is Lord to be obeyed.”
And if we are not careful…

we can create a version of Jesus
who never confronts us,
never stretches us,
never calls us higher.
But that version of Jesus does not exist in Scripture.
The real Jesus will always lead you through transformation.
And transformation requires surrender.
So before you say “Hosanna” again…
ask yourself:

Is He only my Savior?
Or is He truly my Lord?

Because the most dangerous place to be
is not far from Jesus…

It is close to Him—
without ever surrendering to Him.

“The distance between praise and betrayal
is shorter than we think
when surrender is missing.”
May we not be people who celebrate Him in moments…
but resist Him in decisions.
May our worship go deeper than emotion.
May our faith survive discomfort.
May our loyalty remain—even when the crowd changes.
Because real love does not just wave palm branches.
It stays faithful… even at the cross.

Engagement Question:
Be honest—have you ever experienced a moment where following Jesus became uncomfortable, and you felt the tension between surrender and resistance?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She was called a dog…
paragraphs:
She was called a dog…
and still refused to leave.
Let that sit for a second.

Because most of us?
We would’ve walked away offended.
Closed the door.
Unfollowed Jesus.
But she stayed.
Why?

Because when your child is suffering…
pride dies fast.
She came desperate.

Not polished.
Not religious.
Not qualified.

A Syrophoenician woman.
An outsider.
A Gentile in a Jewish story.

And her daughter? Tormented. Broken.
Possessed by a demon she could not cast out, control, or explain.
This wasn’t theory.
This was war inside her house.
So she finds Jesus.
Falls at His feet.
Cries out:
“Lord, help me!”
(Matthew 15:25)
And then…
Silence.
At first, Jesus doesn’t answer.
Imagine that.

The Savior of the world…
not responding to your cry.

The disciples? Annoyed.
“Send her away.” (Matthew 15:23)

Translation:
“She’s loud. She’s desperate. She doesn’t belong.”
Have you ever felt that?

Like your pain is too much…
your story too messy…
your presence too inconvenient?
Then Jesus speaks.
And what He says shocks us.
“I was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel.” (Matthew 15:24)
And then:
“It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” (Matthew 15:26)
That word.
Dogs.
It hits.
Let’s not soften it.
This is tension.

Some scholars interpret this moment not as rejection, but as revelation—Jesus exposing the boundary that people believed existed between “insiders” and “outsiders”… before tearing it down through her faith.
But in real time?
It felt like rejection.
And here’s where most people leave.

Offended.
Hurt.
Triggered.

“God didn’t answer me.”
“So I’m done.”
But not her.
She doesn’t argue.
She doesn’t defend her dignity.
She leans in.
Lower.
Deeper.
Humbler.
“Yes, Lord…”
Let that sink in.
She AGREES.
“Yes, Lord—yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master’s table.” (Matthew 15:27)
That is not weakness.
That is faith stripped of pride.
That is a heart that says:

“I may not deserve it…
but I know You are merciful.”
This is where pride dies.

And many of us never get our miracle
because we refuse to come this low.

We want blessing…
without surrender.

We want breakthrough…
without humility.

We want Jesus…
without bowing.
But Scripture is clear:
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)
Not ignores.
Opposes.
Her posture unlocked something.
Jesus responds:
“O woman, great is your faith! Be it done for you as you desire.” (Matthew 15:28)

And instantly—
her daughter is healed.

No ritual.
No delay.
Just grace.
Here’s the deeper truth most people miss:
This story is not about a woman winning an argument.
It’s about a sinner finding mercy.
Because if we’re honest…
We are her.
Outsiders.
Unclean.
Not entitled to the table.
The Bible says:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
That includes you.
That includes me.
Sin isn’t just what we do.
It’s who we are apart from Christ.

Pride.
Rebellion.
Self-rule.
We don’t just need help.
We need rescue.
And this is where the Gospel explodes into the story.
Because Jesus didn’t just give crumbs.
He gave His life.
The same Jesus who spoke to that woman…
Would later go to the cross.

Rejected.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Crucified.
Not for His sin.
For ours.
“God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Do you see it?
She asked for crumbs.
Jesus offers a covenant.
She came as a stranger.
Through the cross, we are invited as sons and daughters.
Ephesians 2:13 says:
“But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.”
You don’t have to beg under the table anymore.
The table has been opened.
But only through Jesus.
Not through good works.
Not through religion.
Not through trying harder.
“Jesus said to him, ‘I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.’” (John 14:6)
Here’s the turning point:
The woman came with humility…
And left with power.
Because she recognized something many still miss today:

Grace is not earned.
It is received by faith.
But faith requires surrender.
And surrender kills pride.
So let me ask you:

Are you still standing…
or are you ready to kneel?
Because some of you are still negotiating with God.
Still holding onto control.
Still saying:
“I’ll come… but on my terms.”
That door doesn’t open.
The Kingdom opens to those who say:
“Yes, Lord.”

Even when it hurts.
Even when it humbles.
Even when it costs everything.
Maybe your life feels like her house right now.

Chaos.
Darkness.
Something you cannot fix.
Hear this:

One word from Jesus
can break what has been tormenting you for years.
But will you come?
Not with pride.
Not with entitlement.
But with desperate, surrendered faith?
Say it:
“Lord… even a crumb from You is enough.”

And then trust Him
for more than crumbs.
Because at the cross…
He didn’t hold back.
Heart Check:
Where is pride still blocking your breakthrough?

What have you refused to surrender
because it would cost your image, your control, your comfort?
Come lower.
Not to be rejected.
But to be received.
grace is still available.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t just find treasure.
paragraphs: He didn’t just find treasure.
He exposed what he was willing to lose.

What if the reason you feel empty…
is not because God is absent—
…but because you’re still holding on to what He’s asking you to release?
There’s a man in the dust.

Sweat on his brow.
Dirt under his nails.
A life that looked… ordinary.
Until one moment broke everything open.
A glint.
A spark.
Something buried beneath what everyone else walked past.
And suddenly—
His entire life became a decision.
This is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because the story of Matthew 13:44 is not soft.
It’s confrontational.
It cuts.
“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.” — Matthew 13:44 (ESV)
Did you catch that?
In his joy… he sold everything.

Not regret.
Not pressure.
Not obligation.
Joy.
But let’s be honest.
Most of us don’t feel joy when God starts touching our attachments.
We feel exposed.
Because deep down—
we know what we’re clinging to.
That hidden relationship.
That secret sin.
That pride you disguise as “strength.”
That image you protect so no one sees the real you.
You say, “It’s not that serious.”
But your soul knows.
It’s costing you more than you admit.
Here’s the tension:
The man didn’t accidentally own the treasure.
He had to choose it over everything else.
And this is where shame creeps in.
Because if we’re real—
we’ve chosen lesser things.
Again.
And again.
And again.
You knew it wasn’t right… but you stayed.
You felt the conviction… but you silenced it.
You heard God whisper… but you delayed obedience.
And now there’s this quiet weight inside you.
Not loud.
But heavy.
Shame.
The kind that says:
“You had your chance.”
“You’re too far gone.”
“You’ve already chosen wrong too many times.”
But listen carefully.
That voice?
That is not the voice of Jesus.
Because the Gospel does not say:
“Sell everything perfectly, then come to Me.”
No.
The Gospel says:
“You couldn’t afford the treasure… so I paid for you.”
Let me take you deeper.
Some scholars interpret this parable as the believer recognizing the infinite value of God’s Kingdom and surrendering everything in response.
Others see something even more staggering:
Jesus is the man in the story.
He saw the field.
Broken.
Sin-filled.
Dust-covered humanity.
And He saw something hidden in it.
You.
And what did He do?
He didn’t negotiate.
He didn’t hesitate.
He didn’t hold back.
He gave everything.
“Though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you by His poverty might become rich.” — 2 Corinthians 8:9
The cross was not partial payment.
It was total surrender.
Your sin?
Paid.
Your shame?
Carried.
Your past?
Nailed.
“God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Do you see it now?
You are not the only one being asked to give everything.
Jesus already did.
And now—
the invitation is not condemnation.
It’s response.
Not “earn it.”
But “receive it.”
But here’s the truth most people avoid:

You cannot hold on to your sin
and fully embrace the Kingdom.
Not because God is cruel.
But because sin will keep suffocating what He’s trying to revive.
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.” — Luke 9:23
This is where redemption begins.
Not in perfection.
But in surrender.
Right now—
there’s something in your life you keep burying.
Hoping no one sees.
Hoping God will just… overlook it.
But He doesn’t expose to shame you.
He reveals to heal you.
The same God who sees your hidden sin…
also offers hidden grace.
And grace is not weak.
Grace is not passive.
Grace is powerful enough to break chains you thought were permanent.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us… and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
Not manage.
Not ignore.
Cleanse.
This is your moment.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you “feel ready.”
Now.
What are you still holding onto?
That you already know is not worth the cost?
Let it go.
Not because you’re strong—
but because Jesus is worth more.
And here’s the beautiful reversal:
When you surrender everything…
you don’t end up empty.
You end up free.
Free from pretending.
Free from hiding.
Free from the exhausting weight of trying to control everything.
Because the treasure was never the field.
It was Him.
Jesus is the Kingdom.
Jesus is the reward.
Jesus is the treasure your soul has been searching for in everything else.
So come.
Not polished.
Not perfect.
But honest.
Repent.
Turn.
Lay it down.
And receive what you could never earn.
If this is you—
Make it real.
you remember what’s truly worth everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The plague was killing thousands…
paragraphs: The plague was killing thousands…
And the camp of Israel was silent.

No sermons.
No repentance.
No urgency.
Just compromise spreading like wildfire through a nation that once trembled at the voice of God.
Then one man stood up.
And everything changed.
In Book of Numbers chapter 25, Israel had arrived at one of its darkest moments in the wilderness journey.

The people who had seen the Red Sea split…
The people who had eaten manna from heaven…
The people who had heard the thunder of God at Sinai…
Now bowed their heads before idols.
It began with seduction.

The Moabite women invited Israelite men into their feasts.
What looked like romance quickly became spiritual betrayal.

Meals turned into pagan rituals.
Desire turned into idolatry.
And before long, the people of Israel were bowing to Baal of Peor.
Scripture says it plainly:
“Israel yoked themselves to Baal of Peor. And the anger of the LORD burned against them.” — Numbers 25:3
Sin always promises pleasure.
But it always delivers death.
And judgment came swiftly.
A plague broke out in the camp.

People began collapsing.
Families watched loved ones die.
Fear spread through the tents of Israel.
By the time it ended, 24,000 people were dead.
Let that sink in.
Twenty-four thousand.

Not because God is cruel…
But because sin is deadly.
And yet the tragedy deepened.
Right in the middle of the crisis — while leaders were weeping at the entrance of the Tabernacle — an Israelite man brazenly walked into camp with a Midianite woman.

Open rebellion.
Public defiance.
In front of everyone.

No shame.
No fear of God.
And that is when one man refused to stay silent.
His name was Phinehas.
Phinehas was the grandson of Aaron, the high priest.
He saw what was happening.

The idolatry.
The arrogance.
The destruction spreading through the nation.
And the Bible says something remarkable:
“Phinehas son of Eleazar… saw this, he left the assembly, took a spear in his hand, and followed the Israelite into the tent…” — Numbers 25:7–8
With decisive zeal for the holiness of God, Phinehas executed judgment on the man and the woman engaged in rebellion.
And immediately…
The plague stopped.
Scripture records it with chilling clarity:
“Then the plague against the Israelites was stopped.” — Numbers 25:8
God Himself affirmed the act.
He declared that Phinehas had shown zeal for His honor, and because of that zeal, the destruction was halted.
But here is the deeper truth many miss.
Phinehas was not just ending a scandal.
He was standing in the gap.
One act of righteous zeal stopped a national catastrophe.
Yet this story points to something even greater.
Because Phinehas held a spear…
But centuries later, another man would face a spear too.
His name is Jesus Christ.
Where Phinehas stopped a plague temporarily, Jesus came to stop the ultimate plague — sin and death.
Humanity had joined itself to idols far worse than Baal.

Pride.
Lust.
Greed.
Self-worship.
The infection had spread through every heart.
Scripture declares:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
The plague of sin is universal.
But instead of destroying us…
Jesus stepped into the gap.
He did not pick up a spear.
He received one.

At the cross, Roman soldiers drove nails through His hands and feet.
And after He died, a soldier pierced His side with a spear.
The judgment we deserved fell on Him.
The wrath we earned was poured out on Him.
And through His sacrifice, the plague of sin can finally be stopped.
Not by human zeal.
But by divine mercy.
So what does Numbers 25 say to us today?
It reminds us of three sobering truths.
1. Sin is never harmless.
What begins as temptation can become national destruction.
Private compromise eventually becomes public consequences.
Sin always spreads.
2. God is holy.
The same God who parted the sea still hates sin.
His love is real — but His holiness is not negotiable.
Grace does not redefine sin.
Grace rescues us from it.
3. True salvation comes through Jesus alone.
Phinehas stopped one plague.
But Jesus defeated the plague that enslaves every human soul.
Through His blood, forgiveness is offered.
Through His resurrection, new life begins.
Through repentance and faith, we are made clean.
So the question is not just about ancient Israel.
The question is about us.
What idols have we tolerated?
What compromises have we excused?
What sins have we allowed to remain hidden?
The good news of the Gospel is this:
No matter how deep the plague has spread…
Jesus still saves.
Turn to Him.

Confess your sin.
Lay down your idols.
Receive the grace purchased at the cross.
Because the same God who judged sin in Numbers also offers mercy through His Son.
And His mercy is greater than our rebellion.
Someone you know may be fighting a hidden plague of sin tonight.
And they need to hear that freedom is possible through Christ.
Because the story of Scripture is always the same:

From rebellion…
To redemption.

From judgment…
To grace.

From death…
To life.

Numbers 25: The zeal that stopped the plague.
The cross: The love that saves the world.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You saw it coming… and you said nothing.
paragraphs: You saw it coming… and you said nothing.
Read that again.
Because this is where it starts to hurt.
You knew something was off.
You felt it in your spirit.

The quiet drift.
The hidden compromise.
The “it’s not that serious” lie slowly eating someone alive.
And God nudged you.
“Say something.”
But you didn’t.
Not because you didn’t care.
But because you were afraid.

Afraid of losing the friendship.
Afraid of sounding judgmental.
Afraid of being rejected.
So you chose silence.
And silence felt safer…
Until it didn’t.
Here’s the open loop most people never close:
What if your silence didn’t protect them…
What if it actually cost them?
What if the very thing you avoided saying…
was the very thing God wanted to use to save them?
This is where the weight of being a watchman hits.
Not ancient history.
Not just some Old Testament role.
This is now.
This is you.
God said through the prophet:
“Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me.” — Ezekiel 3:17
And then He says something that should shake us:
“If I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and you give him no warning… his blood I will require at your hand.” — Ezekiel 3:18
Let that sit heavy.
This isn’t about being dramatic.
This is about divine responsibility.
We live in a generation that celebrates silence.

“Stay in your lane.”
“Mind your own business.”
“Don’t judge.”
But the Bible doesn’t call that love.
It calls that negligence.
Because real love doesn’t watch someone walk toward destruction and stay quiet.
Real love speaks.
Even when it shakes.
Even when it costs.
Even when it’s uncomfortable.
But here’s the tension…
Because if we’re honest?
We’ve all failed here.
You.
Me.
All of us.
We saw the warning signs in someone else…
But ignored the warning signs in ourselves.
Secret sin.
Hidden pride.
Compromise we renamed as “struggle.”
We needed a watchman too.
And sometimes…
we silenced the voice God sent.
This is where shame creeps in.

“You should have said something.”
“You knew better.”
“You failed.”
And it’s true.
We did.
But this is not where the story ends.
Because God, in His mercy, didn’t leave us with failing watchmen.
He sent the Perfect One.
Jesus Christ
Jesus didn’t stand at a distance and shout warnings.
He stepped into our danger.
He didn’t just see sin coming…
He carried it.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not when we got it right.
Not when we finally spoke up.
Not when we fixed ourselves.
While we were still sinners.
At the cross, something divine happened.
The responsibility we failed to carry…
the warnings we didn’t speak…
the lives we couldn’t save…
Jesus took it all.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.” — 1 Peter 2:24
The blood that should have been on our hands…
was placed on His.
This is grace.
Not earned.
Not deserved.
Given.
But grace doesn’t make us passive.
It transforms us.
Now, we don’t speak as guilty watchmen trying to avoid punishment.
We speak as redeemed sons and daughters who have seen what silence can cost…
and what love can save.
“Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others.” — 2 Corinthians 5:11
Not condemn.
Not control.
But persuade.
With truth.
With tears.
With love.

Some scholars interpret the role of the watchman as specifically prophetic for Israel, but the principle echoes through the New Testament: believers are called to speak truth, restore gently, and warn faithfully (Galatians 6:1, James 5:20).
This isn’t about shouting louder.
It’s about loving deeper.
So let’s make it personal.
Who has God been putting on your heart?
The friend drifting.
The sibling compromising.
The person smiling on the outside but drowning in secret.
And deeper than that…
Where have you been ignoring God’s voice?
What sin have you been excusing?
What warning have you been resisting?
This is your moment.
Not to feel condemned.
But to be awakened.
Because the same Jesus who forgave you…
is now calling you.
To speak.
To love.
To warn.
To restore.
Not perfectly.
But faithfully.
You don’t need the perfect words.
You just need a surrendered heart.
So today…
Break the silence.
Send the message.
Start the conversation.
Say the thing God has been pressing on your spirit.
And if you’re the one who’s been running…
the one hiding…
the one drifting…
hear this:
You are not too far gone.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
Come back.
Not to religion.
Not to performance.
But to Jesus.
He is still saving.
Still restoring.
Still calling.
Don’t wait until it’s too late.
If this hit your heart…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They were chosen by God…
paragraphs:
They were chosen by God…
—but still losing battles in secret.
Read that again.

Chosen.
Anointed.
Used.
And yet… breaking inside.
That’s the detail most people miss.

We celebrate the victories.
The miracles.
The moments God moved through them.
But we ignore the fractures beneath the surface.

The fear in Gideon’s chest.
The pride creeping into Samson’s strength.
The silent compromises of David’s heart.
The hesitation in Moses’ voice when God called him.
And if we’re honest…
That story sounds a little too familiar.

Because you can be showing up in public—
serving, leading, posting, smiling—
while privately battling things no one else sees.

Secret sin.
Quiet shame.
Hidden cycles you swore you’d already broken.
You love God.
But there are rooms in your heart you still won’t let Him enter.
And here’s the tension:
God can use you… even while something in you is still undone.
But that is not the goal.
That is mercy.
Not maturity.
Not freedom.
Not transformation.
Look at what Scripture reveals:
“Now the Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon…” — Judges 6:34
Yet just chapters later, Gideon builds an ephod that leads Israel into idolatry (Judges 8:27).
“Then the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson…” — Judges 14:6
Yet Samson’s life was marked by impulsive desire and moral compromise (Judges 16).
“The Lord is my shepherd…” — Psalm 23:1

David could write worship that still shakes the earth—
yet he also fell into adultery and orchestrated death (2 Samuel 11).
Feel the weight of that.

God’s power can rest on a person…
while their private life is still at war.
Some scholars interpret these moments as evidence of God’s covenant faithfulness despite human failure. Others emphasize them as warnings—showing that gifting is never a substitute for godliness.
Either way, the message is clear:
Anointing is not the same as surrender.
And that should shake you—in the best way.
Because maybe you’ve been measuring your spiritual health by what God does through you…
instead of what God is doing in you.

Miracles don’t always mean maturity.
Platform doesn’t always mean purity.
Impact doesn’t always mean intimacy with God.
Let that sink in.

You can cast out demons…
and still be bound in secret.

You can lead others…
and still be lost in certain areas.
That’s why Jesus said:
“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven…” — Matthew 7:21–23
That verse is not meant to scare you away.
It’s meant to wake you up.
Because God never intended to just use you.
He wants to transform you.

Deeply.
Fully.
Honestly.
And this is where everything shifts.
Because the story of imperfect deliverers is not pointing to them.
It’s pointing to the One they could never be.
Jesus Christ.
The only Deliverer with no cracks.

No compromise.
No hidden sin.
No divided heart.

Where others were empowered temporarily,
Jesus is righteous eternally.

Where others saved for a moment,
Jesus saves forever.
“For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.” — Hebrews 4:15
Let that hit your heart.

He understands your struggle—
but He is not trapped by it.
And because of that…
He can actually set you free.

Not manage your sin.
Not hide your shame.
Destroy it.
This is the Gospel:
You are not just flawed.
You are a sinner in need of rescue.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
But God did not leave you there.

Jesus stepped into your mess—
lived the life you couldn’t live—
died the death you deserved—
and rose again so you could be made new.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
This is not behavior modification.
This is resurrection.
You don’t need better discipline first.
You need surrender.
Real surrender.

Not partial obedience.
Not selective repentance.
Everything.
Because here’s the truth most people avoid:

God is not impressed with your performance
if your heart is still divided.
He doesn’t just want your gift.
He wants you.
All of you.

The parts you show…
and the parts you hide.
So let me ask you—
What are you still keeping from Him?

That habit?
That mindset?
That relationship?
That secret no one knows?
Bring it into the light.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
Cleanse.
Not cover.
Not ignore.
Cleanse.
You don’t have to live split anymore.

Public strength.
Private struggle.
That’s not freedom.
Jesus didn’t die so you could manage sin.
He died so you could be free from it.
Completely.
This is your moment.
Not to feel condemned.
But to come home.

Drop the mask.
Lay down the weight.
Stop performing.
Start surrendering.
Say it plainly:
“Jesus, I give You everything.”
Not just your strengths.
Your secrets too.
And watch what happens when grace meets honesty.
Freedom.
Real freedom.
If this hit you where it hurts… where it’s real…
And if this stirred something deep in you…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t steal the money.
paragraphs: He didn’t steal the money.
He just kept a part of it… and pretended it was everything.

And somehow—
that was enough to shake heaven.

Because the most dangerous sin isn’t always loud rebellion.
Sometimes it’s quiet deception wrapped in spiritual language.

Ananias didn’t walk into the room looking like a liar.
He walked in looking like a disciple.
That’s what makes this terrifying.

He brought an offering.
He laid it down publicly.
He positioned himself where faithful people stood.
But something was off.
Not in his hands.
In his heart.

Acts 5 tells us that while others were selling everything in genuine surrender, Ananias “kept back part of the proceeds”—and then presented it as if it was the full sacrifice (Acts 5:1–2). Peter confronts him and says something chilling: “Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 5:3).
Pause.
He didn’t lie to impress people.
He lied in the presence of God.
And that’s where this cuts deep.

Because we think the issue is the amount.
God says the issue is the motive.

We think it’s about generosity.
God says it’s about integrity.
Here’s the tension:

Ananias wanted the recognition of surrender
without the reality of surrender.

And if we’re honest…
that spirit didn’t die in Acts 5.
It just learned how to hide better.

We post the Scripture.
We say the right things.
We show up where spiritual people gather.
But deep inside?

There are compartments we haven’t surrendered.
Hidden negotiations we haven’t confessed.
Delayed obedience we keep excusing.
Let me ask you something—

What part of your life looks surrendered…
but isn’t?

What are you presenting to God
that is only partial truth dressed as full devotion?
Some don’t even realize it.

They’ve convinced themselves:
“At least I gave something.”
But God never asked for something.
He asked for everything.

Jesus said it plainly in Luke 9:23:
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.”

Not selectively.
Not partially.
Daily.
Here’s the hidden struggle nobody talks about:

You can serve in ministry
and still protect your pride.

You can give financially
and still withhold your heart.

You can look surrendered
and still be strategically disobedient.
And the scariest part?
People might applaud it.
But heaven won’t.
Read that again.
Because Acts 5 doesn’t just reveal judgment.
It reveals how seriously God takes authenticity.

Peter says, “You have not lied just to human beings but to God” (Acts 5:4).
And in that moment, Ananias falls.
Not because God hates him.
But because God was protecting the purity of a newborn Church.
Some scholars interpret this moment as a unique act of divine judgment in a critical time of the early Church’s formation—yet the warning still stands for us today:
God sees what we fake.
And He loves us too much to let us build a life on deception.
Here’s the AHA moment:
God is not after your performance—He’s after your honesty.
Let that sink in.
Because everything changes when you realize this:

You don’t need to impress God.
You need to be real with Him.
SPIRITUAL MIRROR:

If your private life doesn’t match your public worship,
you’re not walking in surrender—you’re managing an image.
And that image will eventually collapse.
But here’s where grace walks in.
Because the story of Ananias is not just a warning.
It’s an invitation.

An invitation to stop pretending.
To stop curating a version of yourself that looks holy but avoids the cross.
Jesus didn’t die for your image.
He died for you.
The real you.

The struggling you.
The divided you.
The one who’s tired of hiding.
Romans 5:8 says, “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

Not when you got it right.
Not when you became consistent.
Not when you finally gave everything.
While you were still holding back.
That’s grace.
But grace is not permission to pretend.
It’s power to repent.
And repentance is not just saying sorry.
It’s surrendering fully.

No filters.
No edits.
No hidden portions.
Just you and Jesus.
Here’s the conviction:
Partial surrender is still resistance.

You can’t follow a crucified Savior
while protecting a comfortable secret.
But here’s the hope:

The same Jesus who sees your hidden places
is the same Jesus who offers you a clean heart.
1 John 1:9 promises, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not shame you.
Cleanse you.
Restore you.
Rebuild you.
So come out of hiding.
Come out of performance.
Come out of partial obedience.
You were not created to manage an image.
You were called to live in truth.
And truth is where freedom begins.

If you feel this in your chest right now…
that’s not condemnation.
That’s conviction.
And conviction is God calling you back.
Right now.
Not later.
Not when it’s convenient.
Now.
Lay it down.
All of it.

The part you show.
The part you hide.
The part you’re afraid to lose.

Because what you surrender to Jesus
He doesn’t destroy—
He redeems.

Take it slow.
Let God work.

You don’t have to rush—
but you do have to respond.
And the next message might uncover what you’ve been avoiding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You thought God ignored you.
paragraphs: You thought God ignored you.
But what if He was listening… to the prayers you never even said out loud?

Because Hannah didn’t scream.
She didn’t perform.
She didn’t impress anyone in the room.
She broke.
And somehow… that was enough to move heaven.
Here’s the part we don’t talk about.
Some of your deepest prayers never make it past your lips.

They sit in your chest.
Heavy.
Unspoken.
Untranslated.
You come to church smiling… but inside, you’re negotiating with disappointment.

You say, “I’m okay.”
But your soul whispers, “I’m tired.”

Tired of waiting.
Tired of hoping.
Tired of pretending your faith isn’t quietly bleeding.
Hannah knew that place.
Scripture says she was “deeply distressed and prayed to the Lord and wept bitterly” (1 Samuel 1:10). Not polished. Not pretty. Just raw.
And when she prayed, her lips were moving… but her voice was gone.
Silent.
And the priest thought she was drunk.
Misjudged.
Misread.
Misunderstood.
Let that sink in.
The moment she was closest to God… she looked the most broken to people.

AHA REVELATION LINE:
Sometimes your deepest spiritual breakthrough looks like emotional collapse to those who don’t understand your battle.
Read that again.
We’ve been trained to believe that strong faith looks composed.
But Hannah shows us something dangerous and freeing:

Faith doesn’t always look strong.
Sometimes it looks shattered… but surrendered.
Now let me ask you something.
When was the last time you were honest with God without editing yourself?

Not the “blessed and highly favored” version.
Not the “I’m good, Lord” version.
The real one.

The one that trembles.
The one that questions.
The one that feels like it might fall apart mid-prayer.
Or have you been offering God filtered faith… while hiding your real pain?
Here’s the quiet struggle nobody admits:
Delayed obedience.
You’re waiting for God to fix something before you fully surrender something.

“I’ll trust You… when You answer.”
“I’ll obey… when it makes sense.”
But partial surrender is still resistance.

And God is not moved by performance.
He is moved by truth.
Psalm 34:18 says the Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit.

Not the polished.
Not the impressive.
The crushed.

SPIRITUAL MIRROR STATEMENT:
You don’t need a louder voice—you need a more surrendered heart.
Because here’s where it gets uncomfortable.

Some people don’t have unanswered prayers…
They have unoffered ones.
You stopped asking.
You stopped believing.
You buried your desire because disappointment felt safer than hope.

And now your silence isn’t surrender…
it’s self-protection.
But Hannah’s silence was different.
It was surrendered.
She poured out her soul before the Lord (1 Samuel 1:15), not to manipulate God… but to meet Him.
And that’s the shift.

She didn’t just want a child.
She wanted God.
And when God gave her Samuel, she gave him back.
That’s dangerous faith.

Faith that says:
“Even if You bless me, I won’t idolize the blessing.”

Conviction line:
Some of us don’t want God—we want what God can give.
Let that confront you.

Because the Gospel is not about God improving your life.
It’s about God reclaiming your heart.
And this is where everything turns.
Because Hannah’s story whispers something deeper than answered prayer.
It points to Jesus.
You see, centuries later, another cry would rise…
Not silent—but forsaken.
On the cross, Jesus cried, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Matthew 27:46)

The silence Hannah felt…
Jesus absorbed fully.
Why?
So that your silence would never mean God’s absence again.
This is the Gospel:

Your sin separated you.
Your striving cannot fix you.
Your silence cannot hide you.
But Jesus stepped in.

He lived the life you couldn’t live.
Died the death you deserved.
And rose again so you could be restored.
Not improved.
Redeemed.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

Not when you figured it out.
Not when you cleaned yourself up.
While you were still broken.
That means your silent prayers don’t disqualify you.
They reveal you.
And grace meets you there.
Identity shift:

You are not the one God forgot.
You are the one God is forming.

You are not unheard.
You are being drawn deeper.
Another AHA moment:
God is not just answering your prayer—He is transforming your posture.
Hannah walked in empty.
She walked out seen.
And before the answer even came… her countenance changed (1 Samuel 1:18).
Why?
Because peace came before provision.
That’s the miracle we skip.
So what about you?

Are you waiting for God to change your situation…
or are you allowing Him to change you?

Right now.
In the silence.
In the waiting.
In the tension.
This is your moment.
Not to perform.
But to pour out.

Talk to Him.
Honestly.
Messy if needed.

Repent where you’ve hardened your heart.
Return where you’ve drifted.
Receive what Jesus already paid for.
If you don’t know Him yet—this is your invitation.
Not to religion.
To relationship.

Jesus is not waiting for your perfection.
He’s calling for your surrender.
And if you’ve been walking with Him but quietly drifting…
Come back.
He hasn’t moved.
If this pierced you, don’t ignore it.
Stay close.
There’s more He wants to reveal in the silence.
No pressure. Just nourishment for your soul.)
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Because Exodus 31 hides a shock most believers miss.
paragraphs: Because Exodus 31 hides a shock most believers miss.
When God announced the building of the Tabernacle—the most sacred structure Israel would ever see—you might expect Him to choose a prophet, a priest, or a famous spiritual leader.
But He didn’t.
God chose a craftsman.

A man with tools in his hands.
Dust on his skin.
Calluses on his fingers.
His name was Bezalel.
And the Lord said something that should shake every believer awake:
“See, I have called by name Bezalel… and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship.” — Exodus 31:2–3
Pause there.
The first person in the Bible explicitly described as being filled with the Spirit of God was not introduced as a preacher, king, or miracle worker.

He was an artist.
A builder.
A craftsman.
Let that sink in.
Because many people believe a dangerous lie:
That God only values what happens on a stage.
But Exodus 31 destroys that idea.
God anoints hands.
Hands that design.
Hands that sew.
Hands that carve wood.
Hands that melt gold.
Hands that work quietly while others stand in the spotlight.
Bezalel was chosen to help build the Tabernacle, the sacred tent where God's presence would dwell among Israel. Every measurement, every woven thread, every hammered piece of gold mattered.
Why?
Because the Tabernacle wasn’t just architecture.
It was theology in wood, gold, and fabric.

The Ark.
The lampstand.
The altar.
The veil.
Every detail preached a message:

God is holy.
Sin is serious.
And sinners cannot approach Him casually.
Yet God made a way.
But here’s the deeper layer most people miss.
The Tabernacle was never meant to be the final answer.
It was a shadow.
A prophetic picture pointing forward to someone greater.
Jesus Christ.
The Gospel of John reveals the connection when it says:
“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” — John 1:14
That word dwelt literally means “tabernacled.”
Jesus became the true meeting place between God and humanity.
Where the Tabernacle had curtains, Christ tore the veil.
Where priests offered sacrifices daily, Jesus offered Himself once for all (Hebrews 10:10–12).
Where the Ark symbolized God's throne, Christ now sits at the right hand of the Father as our living High Priest.
The Tabernacle was the shadow.
Jesus is the reality.
But there’s something else in this story that cuts straight into the heart.
Many people want the platform.
But God often calls people to the workbench.
We crave recognition.
God often assigns faithfulness.
We want applause.
God looks for obedience.
Bezalel was not building his own brand.
He was building something for God’s glory.
And here’s the astonishing truth:
The Spirit of God empowered him not just for worship—but for craftsmanship.
Meaning this:
Your skill can be sacred.
Your work can be worship.
Your profession can become a platform for God's glory.
The Spirit who filled Bezalel is the same Spirit who empowers believers today.

Whether you design…
Build…
Write…
Code…
Teach…
Repair…
Lead…
Create…
When your life belongs to Christ, everything becomes holy ground.
But let’s be honest.
Many of us have used our talents for the wrong things.
Hands meant for worship have been used for sin.
Minds designed for creativity have been consumed by pride.
Skills given by God have been twisted for self-glory.
That’s the scandal of the human heart.
But here’s the miracle of the Gospel:
Jesus doesn’t just forgive sinners.
He redeems them.
He restores what sin tried to destroy.
He takes broken lives and rebuilds them into something beautiful.
Just like Bezalel shaped gold for the Tabernacle, Christ shapes redeemed sinners into living stones for His kingdom.
The apostle Peter writes:
God is still building.
But now the structure is not made of curtains and wood.
It’s made of redeemed people.
Men and women saved by grace.
Former rebels turned into worshipers.
Former sinners turned into testimonies.
And here’s the invitation.
Stop chasing recognition.
Start pursuing obedience.
Stop measuring your life by visibility.
Start measuring it by faithfulness.
Because the same God who called Bezalel by name still calls people today.
He calls the unseen.
The overlooked.
The ordinary.
And He fills them with His Spirit to build something that lasts beyond this life.
So here’s the question:
Are you using what God gave you for His glory?
Or are you still building your own kingdom?
Because one day, every work will be tested by fire (1 Corinthians 3:13).
Only what was built for Christ will remain.
But here is the hope that changes everything.
Even if your past is filled with failure…
Even if your hands have built the wrong things…
Jesus can still redeem your story.
Repent.
Turn to Christ.
Trust the One who died for sinners and rose again.
And let Him take your life—your gifts, your skills, your story—and use them for His glory.
Because the greatest Builder in the universe is still at work.
And He is not just building a tabernacle.
He is building His Kingdom.
And the invitation is open.
Follow Jesus.
Surrender your life.
And become part of the masterpiece God is crafting through grace.
Because the world celebrates fame…
But heaven celebrates faithfulness.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They tried to make him famous…
paragraphs:
They tried to make him famous…
but he refused to take the credit.
And that’s what makes this story dangerous.

Because most of us don’t fall when we’re weak.
We fall when we’re seen.

A man who couldn’t walk for years suddenly stands.
Bones strengthen. Ankles lock. Muscles respond.

And in seconds—
the invisible becomes undeniable.

The crowd gasps.
Eyes widen.
Attention shifts.
Not to God.
To Peter.
And here’s the tension—don’t miss this.

This was the perfect moment to build a name.
A following.
A reputation.
One miracle… and you can become someone.
But Peter does something that will confront your soul.
He rejects the spotlight.
Let’s be honest.

We don’t always sin in rebellion.
Sometimes we sin in applause.

You prayed—and it worked.
You spoke—and people listened.
You led—and it succeeded.
And slowly… subtly… silently…
You start believing the power is yours.

Not fully.
Not consciously.
But enough.

Enough to enjoy the credit.
Enough to crave the recognition.
Enough to forget where it came from.
That’s the quiet danger.

Pride doesn’t always roar.
Sometimes it whispers, “You did good.”
But Peter interrupts the illusion.
“Why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk?” (Acts 3:12)
Feel the weight of that.
He refuses to let admiration turn into idolatry.
He refuses to let a miracle become a mirror.
He refuses to let people confuse the vessel with the Source.
And then he redirects everything.
“By faith in the name of Jesus, this man… has been made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through Him that has completely healed him.” (Acts 3:16)

Not my power.
Not my holiness.
Not my reputation.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Here’s the deeper truth.
Peter wasn’t always like this.

This is the same man who once said,
“Even if all fall away… I never will.”
Confidence.
Boldness.
Self-assurance.
And then?

He denied Jesus.
Three times.
In one night.
That failure broke something in him.
Or rather—
It broke him open.

Because when you’ve seen your own weakness up close…
you stop pretending you’re strong.

When you’ve failed publicly…
you stop craving public praise.

When grace rescues you from your worst moment…
you stop acting like you deserve your best ones.
Some scholars interpret Peter’s bold humility here as the fruit of deep repentance after his denial. Not perfection—but transformation.
And that’s where many miss it.

Humility is not thinking less of yourself.
It’s seeing yourself accurately before a holy God.

Broken.
Dependent.
Carried by grace.
Let me say something that might sting a little:
If God answered your prayers the way you secretly want credit… would you still point people to Jesus?
Or would you start collecting what belongs to Him?
Because Scripture is clear:
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)
Not ignores.
Opposes.

That means pride doesn’t just slow your walk with God.
It puts you in resistance against Him.
But here’s the beauty of the Gospel.

God doesn’t just expose pride.
He redeems people trapped in it.
Peter is proof.

A man who once boasted in his loyalty
becomes a man who boasts only in Christ.

A man who once failed under pressure
becomes a man who stands under power.
Not because he improved himself.
But because Jesus restored him.
After the resurrection, Jesus didn’t discard Peter.
He pursued him.
“Do you love Me?” (John 21:15–17)
Not: “Why did you fail Me?”
But: “Will you return to Me?”
That’s grace.

Not earned.
Not deserved.
But freely given.
And that’s the invitation for you.
Because maybe your struggle isn’t loud sin.
Maybe it’s quiet pride.

The need to be seen.
The hunger to be affirmed.
The subtle shift from “God did it” to “I did well.”
And you feel it.
That tension.
That internal applause you don’t want to admit.
Listen carefully.

The power flowing through your life is real.
But it was never yours.
“For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)
Everything you carry is borrowed glory.

Every gift is grace.
Every open door is mercy.
Every impact is Jesus moving through you.
So what do we do?
We return it.
We give the glory back.
Not as a performance.
But as surrender.
Right now—pause.
Check your heart.
Where have you been taking credit?
Where have you been enjoying attention more than honoring Christ?
Where have you subtly stepped onto a throne that was never yours?
This is not condemnation.
This is invitation.
Repent.
Not with shame.
But with clarity.
Turn back.
Step down.
Lift Him up.
Because the goal was never for people to see you.
It was always for people to see Jesus.

Crucified for your sin.
Risen for your salvation.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.” (Romans 3:23–24)
That includes pride.
That includes you.
So come back.

Not polished.
Not pretending.
But honest.
And let your life say:

“The power is real…
but the glory belongs to Jesus.”
Let it be your declaration.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He thought he was ready.
paragraphs: He thought he was ready.
But heaven was silent.
And Moses moved anyway.
That’s the part we don’t like to admit.
Because it feels… familiar.

You saw something wrong.
You felt something burning.
You knew—“This has to change.”
But no one talks about what happens when passion outruns obedience.

Moses looked both ways before he struck (Exodus 2:12).
Not for God.
For witnesses.
Let that sink in.

He checked if people were watching…
but didn’t check if God had spoken.
And in one moment, zeal became sin.
Read that again.

This wasn’t random anger.
This was misdirected calling.
Acts 7:25 says Moses supposed his people would understand that God would deliver them through him…
…but they didn’t.
Because God never told Moses to act that way.
And here’s the uncomfortable truth:

You can be called by God…
and still move in a way that God never commanded.
That’s where many fall.
Not in ignorance.
But in assumption.

We feel the burden…
and crown ourselves the solution.

We sense purpose…
and skip surrender.

We carry conviction…
but refuse correction.
And somewhere deep inside, there’s a voice whispering:
“You don’t need to wait. Just act.”
But that voice isn’t always God.
Sometimes it’s pride dressed like urgency.
Sometimes it’s insecurity trying to prove something.
Sometimes it’s hidden frustration that hasn’t learned how to kneel yet.
Let me ask you something:
What are you forcing right now that God never told you to carry?
What are you trying to fix with your hands that only God can redeem with His power?
Because here’s the AHA moment:
The same passion that reveals your calling can also expose your immaturity.
Moses wasn’t wrong to care.
He was wrong to control.
And that difference cost him 40 years.
Forty.
Years.
Not because God rejected him.
But because God refused to use an unbroken vessel for a holy assignment.
Hebrews 11:24–25 shows Moses would later choose suffering with God’s people over the pleasures of Egypt.

But before that faith…
there was failure.

Before the staff…
there was a sword.

Before deliverance…
there was a dead body in the sand.
And maybe that’s your story too.
Not publicly.
But privately.

Hidden compromises.
Delayed obedience.
Silent pride.

You still pray.
You still show up.
But there are areas where you’ve already decided:
“I’ll handle this myself.”
This is where it gets real.
Because self-reliance doesn’t just slow your calling.
It can distort it.
Moses tried to save one man by killing another.
Jesus came to save all men by giving Himself.
That’s the difference.

One acted in human strength.
The other moved in divine surrender.
And here’s the Gospel:
You and I—we’ve all done this.
We’ve all tried to fix what only Christ can redeem.
We’ve all buried things we hoped no one would find.
Sin.
Shame.
Control.
But Numbers 32:23 says, “Be sure your sin will find you out.”
And it did for Moses.
The next day, when he tried to play peacemaker, the Hebrew men said:
“Who made you ruler and judge over us?” (Exodus 2:14)
Translation?
“You’re not sent. You just stepped in.”
That hit deeper than the crime.
Because it exposed the truth:
Calling without confirmation leads to confusion.
And maybe someone needs to hear this:

Just because you feel ready…
doesn’t mean God has released you.

Just because it burns…
doesn’t mean it’s time.

Just because you can…
doesn’t mean you should.
That’s not limitation.
That’s protection.
Here’s the spiritual mirror:
Are you submitted… or just passionate?
Because passion can make you loud.
But only surrender makes you usable.
And this is where grace breaks in.
God didn’t cancel Moses.
He sent him to the wilderness.
Not to destroy him.
To reshape him.
Acts 7:30 says after forty years, God appeared to Moses in a burning bush.
Forty years later.
Same calling.
Different man.
Because God is not just concerned with what you do.
He’s concerned with who you become.
And hear this clearly:
God would rather delay your assignment than allow your pride to destroy it.
That’s mercy.
That’s love.
That’s grace.
And ultimately, that’s the Gospel.
Because where Moses failed…
Jesus fulfilled.
Where Moses struck in anger…
Jesus stretched out His hands in mercy.
Where Moses took a life…
Jesus gave His life.
Romans 5:8 declares that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not when we got it right.
Not when we waited perfectly.
But in our failure.
In our rushing.
In our pride.
Jesus stepped in and said:
“I’ll carry what you tried to control.”
That’s redemption.
That’s grace.
That’s why your story isn’t over.
You may have acted too soon.
Spoken too fast.
Moved without permission.
But if you turn back…
If you surrender…
If you lay down the need to control…
God can still use you.
Not as you were.
But as you are becoming.
You are not the savior.
Jesus is.
And that’s good news.

Because it means the pressure is off…
and the invitation is open.
Come back to Him.
Let Him lead.
Let Him shape.
Let Him decide the timing.
If this hit something deep in you…
This isn’t about content. It’s about consecration.
And next time…
we’ll talk about what Moses learned in the wilderness that changed everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jonah’s story begins with a sentence that should shake every believer.
paragraphs: Jonah’s story begins with a sentence that should shake every believer.
“Now the word of the Lord came to Jonah…” (Jonah 1:1)

That alone is a privilege many people pray for.
To hear God clearly.
To receive direction.
To be trusted with an assignment.
But Jonah’s story also reveals something uncomfortable.
Hearing God is not the same as obeying God.
God told Jonah exactly what to do:
“Arise, go to Nineveh…”
But the next line is one of the most sobering verses in Scripture.
“But Jonah rose up to flee…”

Not toward Nineveh.
Toward Tarshish.
The opposite direction.
And that is the warning I see in Jonah’s story.

Because Jonah did not run from confusion.
He ran from clarity.

He knew the assignment.
He just didn’t want it.
And if we’re honest, this is where Jonah’s story begins to feel very close to home.
Many people say they are waiting for God to speak.
But sometimes the real struggle isn’t that God is silent.
Sometimes the real struggle is that God already spoke, and obedience would cost more than we want to give.
Jonah did not misunderstand God.
He resisted God.
And resistance often looks quieter than rebellion.

It doesn’t always look like open sin.
It often looks like delay.

“I’ll do it later.”
“Maybe next season.”
“I’m not ready yet.”
“Someone else will do it.”
But delayed obedience slowly becomes directional disobedience.
Jonah didn’t stay still.
He moved.

He bought a ticket.
He boarded a ship.
He started traveling.
But movement does not always mean you are in God’s will.
You can move fast in the wrong direction.
And here is one of the most dangerous parts of the story.
Tarshish had a boat ready.
That means the escape route was available.
And that reveals something many people overlook:
Not every open door is from God.
Some doors are simply opportunities to disobey more comfortably.
Jonah found a ship.
He found sailors.
He found transportation.
Everything looked possible.
But possibility is not the same as permission.
And then the storm came.
The Bible says:
“The Lord sent a great wind upon the sea.” (Jonah 1:4)
Notice something important.
The storm wasn’t random.
God sent it.
Not because God hated Jonah.
But because God loved him too much to let him run unchecked.
Sometimes the storm in your life is not punishment.
Sometimes it is interruption.
A divine disruption designed to stop a direction that would destroy your purpose.
And here is the part of the story that chills me the most.
While the sailors were panicking…
Jonah was asleep.
Think about that.
The storm was violent.
The ship was breaking apart.
The sailors were praying.
Cargo was being thrown overboard.
But Jonah was downstairs… sleeping.
That is what happens when a heart becomes comfortable avoiding obedience.
You can learn how to sleep in a storm instead of surrendering in it.
You can grow so used to running from God that the urgency fades.
And when that happens, the danger is not the storm.
The danger is spiritual numbness.
A numb conscience is more dangerous than loud chaos.
But there is another warning hidden in this story.
Jonah’s decision didn’t only affect Jonah.
The sailors were caught in a storm connected to someone else’s disobedience.
That’s the thing about calling.
When God assigns something to your life, it is rarely only about you.
Your obedience protects people.
Your obedience influences people.
Your obedience opens doors for people.
And sometimes your resistance creates storms that spill into spaces you never intended to affect.
But here is the mercy in the story.
God didn’t abandon Jonah.
God pursued him.

Through wind.
Through waves.
Through a storm.
Because God refuses to easily release the people He has called.
The storm was not only correction.
It was grace refusing to let Jonah disappear from his purpose.
And maybe that’s the message someone needs to hear today.
If you feel like your life is being shaken…
If you feel like the waters are rough…
If you feel like God keeps confronting the same issue in your heart…
It might not be rejection.
It might be mercy.
God loves you too much to let you outrun your assignment.
Jonah teaches us something powerful.
You can run from the place God called you to…
But you cannot outrun the God who called you.
And sometimes the greatest turning point in a life is the moment someone finally admits:
“I have been running.”
Because the moment you stop running…
The moment you surrender…
The moment you turn back toward the direction God originally spoke…
That is when storms begin to lose their authority.
That is when peace begins to return.
And that is when purpose begins to breathe again.
So the question Jonah’s story leaves us with is not simply:
“Has God spoken?”
The deeper question is:
“Are we running from what He already said?”
📖 “But Jonah rose up to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.” — Jonah 1:3
Let me ask you something honestly:
Have you ever felt like Jonah — knowing what God wants, but struggling to surrender to it?
Share your thoughts below. Your story might encourage someone else who is wrestling with obedience right now.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He was ready to start a war… and God said, “Stop.”
paragraphs: He was ready to start a war… and God said, “Stop.”
Pause.
Because this is where most of us fail.
You think the real danger is losing.
No.
The real danger is winning a fight God never told you to fight.

Rehoboam had the numbers.
180,000 warriors.
Steel sharpened.
Blood pressure rising.

This wasn’t just strategy.
This was pride… dressed as justice.
And maybe that’s where this hits you.
Because not all your battles are holy.
Some of them are just your ego… screaming.
Here’s the tension:

You feel justified.
You feel wronged.
You feel like silence means weakness.

So you prepare your words.
Sharpen your response.
Load your emotions like weapons.
You’re ready.
Ready to “set things right.”
But what if heaven is not backing your fight?
What if God is not in your anger?
What if you’re about to destroy something God actually allowed?
Enter a man most people skip.
Shemaiah.

No army.
No rank.
No applause.
Just a message.

“You shall not go up or fight against your relatives… for this thing is from Me.”
— 1 Kings 12:24
Let that sink in.
“This thing… is from Me.”
God was saying:
“This conflict you hate… I allowed it.”
And that changes everything.
Some scholars interpret this as God’s judgment unfolding through the division of the kingdom.
Others see it as a moment where God restrains greater destruction.
But both agree on this:
God was in control—even in the chaos.
And He was not giving permission to fight.
This is where pride gets exposed.

Because pride doesn’t ask,
“Is God in this?”

Pride asks,
“How do I win this?”

Pride wants control.
Vindication.
The last word.
But God wanted obedience.
And here’s the miracle:
Rehoboam listened.

He had the power to crush.
But he chose to surrender.
He put the weapon down.
And a civil war… never happened.
Now lean in.
Because this is not just ancient history.
This is your life.

Your family.
Your relationships.
Your hidden arguments.

The messages you almost sent.
The words you almost said.
The bridges you almost burned.
Let me ask you something raw:

How many battles have you fought…
that God never authorized?

How many relationships died…
not because of truth…
but because of pride?

How many times did you say,
“I’m just being real,”

when really…
you were just being ruled by your flesh?
Scripture doesn’t stay silent here.

“What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?”
— James 4:1

The war outside you…
is revealing the war inside you.
And that’s the deeper problem.
Because the greatest civil war is not between people.
It’s between you and God.
You want control.
God calls for surrender.
You want justice on your terms.
God offers mercy through His Son.
Here is the truth we cannot soften:
You and I were not neutral.

“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
— Romans 5:8

We were sinners.
Rebels.
Enemies.

Not misunderstood.
Not slightly off.
Lost.
And yet…
Jesus didn’t come with an army to destroy us.
He came with a cross to save us.

While we were raising weapons of pride,
He stretched out His hands in surrender.

While we demanded our way,
He said,

“Not My will, but Yours be done.”
— Luke 22:42

While we deserved judgment,
He took it.

“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree…”
— 1 Peter 2:24
This is the Gospel:

Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
But grace is greater.

Jesus absorbed the wrath.
Paid the debt.
Opened the way.
Shemaiah stopped a physical war.
Jesus stops the eternal one.

So now the question is not:
“Are you right?”
The question is:
Are you surrendered?

Because you can win arguments…
and lose your soul.

You can be justified in your logic…
and still be far from God.

You can speak truth…
with a heart that is not submitted to Truth Himself.
Maybe today…
God is sending you your own Shemaiah moment.
Not through a prophet standing in front of you…
But through this message.
Put the weapon down.

The bitterness.
The pride.
The need to prove yourself.
Lay it down.
Repent.

Not just of what you did…
but of what is ruling your heart.
Turn to Jesus.

Not as a concept.
Not as a backup plan.
As Lord.
As Savior.
As the only One who can make peace where you’ve been making war.

“He Himself is our peace…”
— Ephesians 2:14

Not your effort.
Not your control.
Him.
And here’s the beauty:
You don’t have to clean yourself up first.
You don’t have to win first.
You don’t have to fix everything.
You just have to come.
Come with your pride.
Come with your anger.
Come with your mess.
And watch what grace does with surrendered hearts.
Some of you are one decision away…
From saving something you were about to destroy.
Don’t miss this moment.
Let it confront you.
Let it change you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t want the cup.
paragraphs: He didn’t want the cup.
Let that sink in.
The Savior you worship… asked if there was another way.
And still—He drank it.
Why?

Because surrender is not about what you feel.
It’s about who you trust.
And that is where most of us break.

Because we say “God, Your will be done”—
but inside, we’re negotiating.

We want obedience… with conditions.
Surrender… with escape routes.
Faith… but only if it feels safe.
And here’s the tension:
What do you do when God’s will contradicts your desire?

What do you do when obedience costs you something real—
your pride,
your relationship,
your plan,
your timeline,
your secret sin?
That’s where Gethsemane stops being a story…
…and starts becoming a mirror.
Because if we’re honest—
Some of us are not struggling with God’s silence.
We’re struggling with His answer.
“No.”
“Wait.”
“Let it go.”
“Die to that.”
And it exposes something uncomfortable:
We don’t just want God’s will.
We want control.
We want to be saved—
but not surrendered.
We want the crown—
but not the cross.
We want resurrection—
but not death.
And Jesus steps into that exact tension.

Luke 22:42 says:
“Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
Don’t rush past that.
Feel it.

This is not a calm prayer.
This is not soft spirituality.
This is agony.
The Gospel of Luke even records that His sweat became like drops of blood (Luke 22:44).
This is a man under crushing weight.
And yet—
He doesn’t rebel.
He doesn’t run.
He doesn’t rewrite the Father’s will to fit His comfort.
He surrenders.
Fully.
Completely.
Holy.
Some scholars interpret this moment as the full weight of humanity’s sin beginning to press upon Christ—even before the cross—revealing both His true humanity and His perfect obedience.
And here’s the part that should shake you:
Jesus was sinless.
You are not.
He had every right to resist.
You and I—
we are the ones who created the cup.

Our sin.
Our pride.
Our hidden rebellion.
Our secret compromises.
That cup?
It had your name on it.

Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities…”
He didn’t just drink suffering.
He drank your judgment.
My sin deserved that cup.
Your shame deserved that cup.
Every hidden thing you thought nobody saw—
God saw it.
And still…
Jesus said yes.
This is where the Gospel explodes into clarity.
Because Christianity is not about you trying harder to surrender.
It’s about Jesus surrendering perfectly in your place.

Romans 5:8 says:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when you got your life together.
Not when you cleaned up your act.

While you were still running,
still hiding,
still pretending—
He chose the cross.
That’s grace.
Not earned.
Not negotiated.
Given.
But here’s the turning point you cannot ignore:
Grace is free.
But it is not cheap.

Because the same Jesus who said,
“Not my will, but Yours”—
now calls you to follow Him.

Luke 9:23:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”
That’s where pride dies.
That’s where control breaks.
That’s where secret sin gets dragged into the light.
And I know—
that’s uncomfortable.
Because surrender feels like loss.
It feels like you’re giving up the only thing holding your life together.
That relationship you know God is convicting you about.
That habit you keep justifying.
That version of your future you refuse to release.
But listen carefully:
What you’re holding onto…
might be the very thing keeping you from freedom.
Jesus didn’t surrender to destroy you.
He surrendered to save you.
And when He calls you to surrender—
it’s not to take life from you.
It’s to give you real life.

John 10:10:
“I came that they may have life and have it abundantly.”
But abundant life does not grow in control.
It grows in surrender.
So here’s the question:
What is your “cup”?
What is the thing you’re asking God to remove—
but deep down, you know He’s asking you to trust Him through it?
This is your Gethsemane moment.
Not on a hill in Jerusalem—
but right where you are.
In your room.
In your silence.
In that tension you’ve been avoiding.
And the invitation is not condemnation.
It’s grace.
You don’t have to clean yourself up first.
You don’t have to pretend you’re strong.
Come honest.
Come broken.
Come real.
And say what Jesus said—
even if your voice shakes:
“Not my will…
but Yours.”
That prayer may feel like death.
But in Christ—
it leads to life.
Because the same Jesus who knelt in the garden…
walked out of the grave.
And if you belong to Him—
your surrender is never the end of your story.
It’s the beginning of redemption.
Right now—
pause.
Search your heart.
What are you still controlling?
What are you refusing to release?
Lay it down.
Not halfway.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Repent.
Turn from the sin you’ve been hiding.
Turn from the pride you’ve been protecting.
Turn toward Jesus—
the One who already carried your cup.
And trust Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He walked into the battlefield… and nobody even flinched.
paragraphs: He walked into the battlefield… and nobody even flinched.
Not even his own brothers believed he belonged there.
And that’s where the story turns.

Because the most dangerous thing about being overlooked…
is not what people think about you—
it’s what you start believing about yourself.
David wasn’t just facing Goliath.

He was facing every silent lie that whispers:
“You’re not enough.”
“You don’t belong here.”
“Go back to where you came from.”
And if you’re honest…
You’ve heard those voices too.
Not out loud.
But in the quiet.

In the delay.
In the unanswered prayers.
In the seasons where everyone else seems to be “chosen”… and you’re still in the field.
Let me ask you something.
How many times have you obeyed God halfway… because you felt unqualified the whole way?
How many callings have you delayed because you’re waiting to “feel ready”?
There’s a kind of struggle we don’t talk about.
Not rebellion.
But hesitation.
Not open sin.
But quiet disobedience dressed as “humility.”
Read that again.
David could’ve stayed with the sheep.
He could’ve said, “I’m not trained. I’m not strong. I’m not like them.”
But he didn’t.

Because while others saw a boy,
God had already seen a king.
Scripture says in 1 Samuel 16:7 that “the Lord looks on the heart.”

Not your resume.
Not your following.
Not your perfection.
Your heart.
And here’s the tension—
You can have the right heart… and still feel completely overlooked.
That’s the battlefield nobody prepares you for.
Because being unseen doesn’t feel spiritual.
It feels painful.
It feels like rejection.
It feels like God forgot to call your name.
But here’s the revelation—
God often hides what He intends to reveal with power.
David’s victory didn’t start in the valley.
It started in obscurity.

In the fields.
In the silence.
In the unseen battles with lions and bears (1 Samuel 17:34–37).
That’s where faith was forged.
Not in front of applause.
But in front of God.
And here’s the AHA moment:

The place you feel most overlooked…
may be the place God is training you most intensely.
Because when David finally stood before Goliath, he didn’t borrow Saul’s armor.
He brought his history with God.

He said in 1 Samuel 17:45,
“I come against you in the name of the Lord of hosts…”
Not confidence in self.
Confidence in God.
And that changes everything.
But let’s go deeper.
Because this isn’t just David’s story.
It’s yours.
And it’s ultimately about Jesus.
Because there was another One who was overlooked.
Isaiah 53:2 says He had “no form or majesty that we should look at Him… no beauty that we should desire Him.”
Jesus didn’t look like a king.
He didn’t fit expectations.

He was rejected.
Mocked.
Crucified.
And here’s the spiritual mirror—
The same heart that overlooks God’s chosen… is the same heart that resists surrender.
That’s us.
We don’t just feel overlooked.
Sometimes, we overlook God.
We delay obedience.
We hide compromise.
We justify sin because “no one sees it.”
But Scripture is clear: “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
That’s the real giant.
Not Goliath.
Sin.

Pride.
Self-reliance.
Hidden rebellion.
And no stone can defeat that.
No discipline.
No self-improvement.
Only Jesus.
Because on the cross, Christ didn’t just fight for you—
He stood in your place.

2 Corinthians 5:21 says,
“He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.”
That’s the Gospel.
Not “try harder.”
But “surrender deeper.”
Not “prove yourself.”
But “receive what Christ has already done.”
And here’s the conviction—
You don’t need a bigger platform.
You need deeper repentance.
You don’t need more validation.
You need real surrender.
Because God is not looking for impressive people.
He is looking for surrendered hearts.
Identity shift:
You are not the forgotten one.
You are the chosen one in preparation.
You are not disqualified by your weakness.
You are positioned for God’s power.
“But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise… what is weak to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).
This is where it gets personal.

What if the reason you feel overlooked…
is because God is protecting you from being platformed before you’re formed?
What if the delay is mercy?
What if the hidden season is grace?
Because a premature spotlight can destroy what private obedience is trying to build.
David wasn’t late.
He was ready.
And when the moment came—
One stone.
One surrender.
One God.
And the giant fell.
So what about you?
What giant are you facing right now?

Fear?
Comparison?
Secret sin?
Spiritual numbness?
Bring it to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Repent where you’ve delayed.
Surrender where you’ve resisted.
Trust where you’ve doubted.
He sees you.
Hebrews 4:13 says nothing in all creation is hidden from God’s sight.
That should convict you.
And comfort you.
Because the same God who sees your sin…
is the same God who offers you grace.
Right now.
Not when you’re better.
Now.
If this stirred something in you… don’t ignore it.
Stay rooted. Stay grounded.
And next time… we’re going deeper into what happens after the giant falls—because victory has its own battles.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She was the last woman anyone expected God to use.
paragraphs: She was the last woman anyone expected God to use.

Her city was wicked.
Her reputation was worse.
And yet… when heaven looked at Jericho, one house was marked for mercy.
Her name was Rahab.
And her story begins on a night filled with fear, whispers, and a knock at the door.
Two Israelite spies had slipped quietly into Jericho.

They were not tourists.
They were not merchants.
They were scouts from the people of God.
Jericho was already trembling with rumors. Stories had spread across the land like wildfire: the God of Israel had split the Red Sea… crushed kings… and was now marching toward Canaan.
The walls of Jericho were strong.
But the hearts inside those walls were melting.
And somehow, of all the places the spies could go… they entered Rahab’s house.
A prostitute.
A woman the “respectable” people avoided.
A woman whose life was defined by survival, compromise, and whispered shame.
But here is where the story flips.
Because God often walks straight into the houses religion refuses to enter.
That night, soldiers from the king came knocking.
“Bring out the men who came to you.”
The spies had been discovered.
Death was seconds away.
Rahab had a choice.
Protect the spies… and risk execution.
Or betray them… and save her life.
She made her decision.
Rahab rushed the men up to her roof and hid them under stalks of flax.
Then she faced the soldiers.

“They already left,” she said.
