There is peace waiting.
There is clarity waiting.
And yes—there is restoration.
Not partial.
Whole.
Not surface-level. Real transformation.
But right now—
This is your moment.
Don’t wait for fire to fall.
Walk out while grace is calling.
If this hit you…
For your soul.
Next post?
We’re going deeper into the moment Lot hesitated… and what almost cost him everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They came back from the same land.
paragraphs: They came back from the same land.

Same hills.
Same giants.
Same cities with walls that touched the sky.

But ten men saw terror…
…and two men saw God.
That’s the thunderclap inside Numbers 14.

Twelve spies walked into the Promised Land.
They tasted the grapes.
They saw the abundance.
They carried proof of blessing back to Israel.
But something happened on the journey home.
Fear started whispering.
And by the time they reached the camp, ten of them were preaching panic.

“We can’t attack those people.”
“They’re stronger than we are.”
“We looked like grasshoppers to them.”
Grasshoppers.
Think about that.

God had just split the Red Sea.
God had crushed Pharaoh’s army.
God fed them manna from heaven.
God led them by fire and cloud.

Yet one look at giants…
and suddenly the people forgot the God who moved oceans.
Fear has a way of shrinking memory.

It erases miracles.
It rewrites history.
It edits God out of the story.
And that’s exactly what happened in the camp of Israel.
Panic spread like wildfire.

People cried all night.
Families wailed in their tents.
The crowd started talking about something shocking.
They wanted to go back to Egypt.

Back to chains.
Back to whips.
Back to slavery.
Why?
Because fear makes bondage feel safer than faith.
But then two men stood up.
Joshua.
Caleb.
While the crowd shouted and fear roared, these two tore their clothes and lifted their voices with a different report.
Listen to their words:

“The land we passed through is exceedingly good.
If the Lord delights in us, He will bring us into this land and give it to us…
Only do not rebel against the Lord.
And do not fear the people of the land…
The Lord is with us. Do not fear them.”
— Numbers 14:7–9
Notice something powerful.
Joshua and Caleb did not deny the giants.

They didn’t say the land was empty.
They didn’t pretend the enemy was weak.
They simply refused to magnify the giants more than God.
And that’s the battle many of us are fighting today.
Your giants might not be warriors with spears.
Your giants might be:

Debt.
Addiction.
A broken marriage.
A secret sin you keep hiding.
A diagnosis that scares you.
A past that keeps whispering shame.
The giants are real.
But here’s the truth Joshua and Caleb understood:
Giants are loud… but they are not Lord.
God is.
And when you compare the size of your problem to the greatness of God, everything changes.
But here’s where the story cuts deeper.
The people didn’t celebrate Joshua and Caleb.
They tried to stone them.
Why?
Because truth often offends people who have already decided to believe fear.
Unbelief hates courageous faith.
And the consequence was devastating.
God declared that the generation who refused to trust Him would wander in the wilderness for forty years.
An entire generation missed the promise because they believed the wrong report.
Let that sink in.

Ten voices of fear
overpowered
two voices of faith.
But here’s the Gospel thread woven through this story.
Joshua’s name in Hebrew is Yehoshua.
It means:
“The Lord saves.”
The Greek version of that name is Jesus.
Joshua pointed forward to someone greater.
Because humanity has always struggled with unbelief.

Like Israel, we grumble.
We doubt.
We rebel.
We retreat.
But Jesus came as the greater Joshua.
Where Israel failed, He obeyed perfectly.
Where we doubted, He trusted the Father.
And when the ultimate giant—sin and death—stood before us, Jesus didn’t retreat.
He went straight to the cross.
The cross looked like defeat.
But three days later…
The stone rolled away.
The grave lost its grip.
And the greatest giant humanity ever faced was crushed under the victory of Christ.
That means something powerful for you today.
Your fear doesn’t get the final word.
Your past doesn’t get the final word.
Your shame doesn’t get the final word.
Jesus does.
So today, you have a choice.

You can listen to the ten spies—
the voices of doubt, fear, anxiety, and despair.
Or you can listen to the voice of faith that says:
“The Lord is with us. Do not fear.”
Maybe your giant still stands tall.
Maybe the battle still looks intimidating.
But remember this:

The God who split seas
is still the God who moves mountains.

The God who carried Israel
is still the God who carries you.

And the Savior who walked out of the grave
is still rewriting broken stories today.
So stand up.
Lift your eyes.
Stop calling yourself a grasshopper when you belong to the King.
Because faith doesn’t say the giants are small.
Faith says God is greater.
And when you trust Him…
Even giants become bread.
Someone out there is staring at a giant and forgetting the size of their God.
Remind them.
Because the Lord is with us.
Do not fear them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Some stories in the Bible feel small at first glance.
paragraphs: Some stories in the Bible feel small at first glance.

A few verses.
One man.
One moment.
But hidden inside them are truths that can reshape how you see yourself… and how you see God.
Ehud is one of those stories.
Israel had drifted again.
They did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and as a result, they fell under the oppression of Moab (Judges 3:12). This wasn’t a quick setback. It lasted eighteen years.

Eighteen years of pressure.
Eighteen years of limitation.
Eighteen years of wondering if things would ever change.
And then something shifted.
“They cried unto the Lord…”
That’s where deliverance always begins.

Not with strength.
Not with strategy.
But with surrender.
And the Bible says, “The Lord raised them up a deliverer, Ehud…” (Judges 3:15).
Pause there.

God didn’t just send help.
He raised a person.
And that person didn’t look like the obvious choice.
Ehud was left-handed.

In that time, that wasn’t just a random detail. It made him different in a world built around right-handed strength. Most warriors trained, fought, and carried weapons in a way that assumed right-hand dominance.
Ehud didn’t fit that mold.
But what made him different… made him effective.
Let that settle.
Because some of you have spent years trying to fix what God may have designed.

You’ve tried to blend in.
Tried to adjust.
Tried to become more “normal.”

But God is not looking for copies.
He works through design.
Ehud’s left hand wasn’t a weakness in God’s eyes.
It was part of the plan.
The Bible says Ehud made a double-edged dagger and strapped it to his right thigh (Judges 3:16). That detail matters.
Why?
Because guards expected weapons on the left side, drawn by the right hand.
Ehud didn’t fit the expectation.
And because of that, he passed through unnoticed.
What people didn’t expect… God had already prepared.
This is where the lesson gets deeper.

Your difference is not just identity.
It may be strategy.

The way you think.
The way you process.
The way you’ve lived.
Even the things that made you feel out of place…
God can position all of it for purpose.

Ehud gained access to King Eglon.
He stood in a private moment that no one else had.
And in that moment, he acted.

Now, let’s be clear—this is a historical account of deliverance during a specific time in Israel’s history. It is not a command for us to imitate his actions. But it does reveal how God can use a person, in their context, to bring about freedom.
Ehud moved with courage.

He didn’t freeze in fear.
He didn’t shrink in doubt.
He stepped into the assignment placed in front of him.
And everything changed.
After that moment, Ehud escaped, rallied Israel, and led them into victory over Moab (Judges 3:27–29).
And then comes a line that should stop you:
“So Moab was subdued that day… And the land had rest for eighty years.” (Judges 3:30)
Eighty years of peace.
Let that sink in.

One life.
Raised by God.
Willing to act.
Changed the trajectory of a nation for generations.
That is the weight of obedience.

We often think our lives are small.
Our actions are insignificant.
Our obedience doesn’t matter that much.
But Scripture shows us something different.

God can take one surrendered person…
and use them to bring freedom far beyond what they can see.
So the question is not:
“Am I the most qualified?”
Ehud wasn’t.
The question is:
“Am I willing to be used?”
Because God is not limited by what people expect.

He is not restricted by your background.
He is not intimidated by your differences.
He is not searching for perfection.
He is looking for availability.
And sometimes…

The thing you thought disqualified you
is the very thing He designed to position you.

Ehud didn’t become someone else.
He didn’t try to match the system around him.
He allowed God to use who he was.
And through that, deliverance came.

So before you dismiss your story…
before you hide what makes you different…
before you assume God can’t use you…
Remember this:
God often hides His strategy inside what the world overlooks.

You are not disqualified because you are different.
You are not forgotten because you are unseen.
You are not useless because you don’t fit expectations.
You may be positioned.
And when your moment comes…
Will you step forward?
Because your obedience might not just change your life.
It might bring freedom to others too.
Memorable lines to carry with you:

What people overlook, God often prepares.
Your difference may be part of your assignment.
God doesn’t need the obvious—He uses the available.
Hidden does not mean useless.
One act of obedience can echo for generations.

Engagement Question:
What is something in your life you once saw as a weakness… that God might actually want to use?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He led millions…
paragraphs:
He led millions…
but secretly wished he could disappear.

Not from enemies.
From the people he was called to serve.
You won’t hear this in most sermons.

Not the breaking voice.
Not the quiet collapse behind obedience.
Because leaders are supposed to be strong.
Right?
But Moses…
was unraveling.

And if you’ve ever smiled in public
while breaking in private—
this is for you.

They complained.
Constantly.

Not once.
Not twice.
Relentless.

“No water.”
“No meat.”
“We miss Egypt.”
Imagine that.

They were rescued from slavery—
and still romanticized bondage.
And Moses had to absorb it all.

Every complaint.
Every accusation.
Every unmet expectation.
Day after day.
Soul pressure.
Until something inside him cracked.
Listen carefully.
This is not rebellion.
This is emotional fatigue.

“I cannot carry all these people by myself; the burden is too heavy for me.”
— Numbers 11:14
That’s not a weak man speaking.

That’s a faithful man
who has reached his limit.
Let’s get honest.
Some of you are there right now.

Still showing up.
Still serving.
Still saying “I’m okay.”
But inside?
You’re tired.
Not just physically.
Spirit-level tired.
The kind of tired sleep can’t fix.
And here’s the hidden struggle:
You feel guilty for being tired.
Because God called you.
Because people depend on you.
Because quitting feels like failure.
So you carry it.
Silently.
Until the weight starts whispering lies:

“You’re not enough.”
“You’re failing them.”
“You should be stronger.”
But look at Moses again.
He didn’t pretend.
He brought his breaking point to God.

Raw.
Unfiltered.

“If this is how you are going to treat me, please go ahead and kill me…”
— Numbers 11:15
That’s heavy.
Some scholars interpret this as Moses expressing deep despair, not rebellion—but an overwhelmed heart crying out under unbearable leadership pressure.
God didn’t cancel him.
God didn’t shame him.
God responded.
Watch this.
Grace doesn’t always remove the assignment.
Sometimes it redistributes the weight.

“Gather for me seventy men… and I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them. They will help you carry the burden…”
— Numbers 11:16–17
God didn’t say, “Try harder.”
He said, “You were never meant to carry this alone.”
Let that hit.

Some of you are drowning…
not because you’re weak—
but because you’re carrying what God never asked you to carry alone.
But don’t miss the deeper layer.
Moses is not the end of the story.
He’s a shadow.
A signpost.
Pointing forward.
Because where Moses said:
“I can’t carry them…”
Jesus said:
“I will.”
This is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement.
Not emotional management.
Substitution.

“Surely He took up our pain and bore our suffering…”
— Isaiah 53:4

“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree…”
— 1 Peter 2:24
Jesus didn’t just feel your burden.
He carried it.
To the cross.
Fully.
Willingly.
Completely.

Your burnout.
Your resentment.
Your silent frustration.
Even the thoughts you’re ashamed to admit:
“I don’t want to do this anymore.”
He carried that too.
But here’s the turning point.
You don’t just admire Jesus.
You come to Him.

“Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.”
— Matthew 11:28
Not a temporary break.
Not distraction.
Rest for your soul.
And here’s the truth we often avoid:

You cannot receive that rest
while pretending you’re fine.

You cannot experience His strength
while clinging to self-reliance.

You cannot be filled
while refusing to empty yourself.
This is where repentance comes in.
Not just turning from sin—
but turning from self-sufficiency.
From pride that says:
“I can handle this.”
From fear that says:
“If I let go, everything will fall apart.”
Listen.
God is not asking you to collapse.
He’s asking you to surrender.
There’s a difference.
Collapse is giving up.
Surrender is handing over.
Moses reached the edge—
and met provision.
You can too.

But only if you stop hiding your fatigue
and start bringing it to Jesus.
So let me ask you—

What are you carrying
that Jesus already died to carry for you?
The expectations?
The pressure?
The emotional weight of everyone around you?
Lay it down.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Whisper it if you have to:
“Jesus… I’m tired.”
“I can’t carry this.”
“I give this to You.”
That’s not weakness.
That’s worship.
And watch what happens.
He won’t crush you.
He will meet you.
He will hold you.
He will restore you.

Because the same God
who strengthened Moses—

now lives in you
through Christ.
You are not alone in this.
You never were.
If this hit your heart…
for the days the weight comes back.
From burden to breakthrough.
From exhaustion to encounter.

From silent breaking…
to sacred surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 969 YEARS… AND HE STILL COULDN’T ESCAPE IT.
paragraphs: 969 YEARS… AND HE STILL COULDN’T ESCAPE IT.
Let that hit you.

Almost a thousand years to live…
and still—
death won.
But there’s something deeper here you’re not seeing yet.
Something unsettling.
Something personal.
Because Methuselah’s story isn’t just about him…
It’s about you.

You wake up.
You scroll.
You laugh.
You work.
You hide.
And somewhere in the quiet corners of your soul—
You know something isn’t right.

That habit you keep excusing.
That pride you keep feeding.
That secret you hope nobody ever finds out.
You tell yourself:
“Later.”
“I’ll fix it someday.”
“I still have time.”
That’s the lie.
Because if a man had 969 years…
and still ended in a grave—
What makes you think time is your savior?
The Bible doesn’t dramatize it.

No poetry.
No explanation.
Just a line that echoes like a hammer:
“All the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died.” — Genesis 5:27
That’s it.
No matter how long he lived—
He still faced the same end as everyone else.
Because the problem was never the length of life.
It was the condition of the heart.
And here’s where it gets heavier.
Some scholars interpret Methuselah’s name to mean:
“When he dies, it shall be sent.”
And right after his death—
The flood came.
Judgment didn’t come early.
God waited.

Year after year.
Decade after decade.
Century after century.
Why?
Because God is not eager to destroy—
He is patient to save.
“The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise… but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance.” — 2 Peter 3:9
Do you see it?
Methuselah’s long life wasn’t just about longevity.
It was mercy on a timer.
Every extra year was another chance for humanity to turn back.
But they didn’t.
They kept living like judgment would never come.
Like sin had no consequence.
Like God would just overlook everything.
Sound familiar?
We do the same thing.

We normalize what God calls sin.
We celebrate what God calls broken.
We delay what God calls urgent.
And we assume—
We have time.
But time has never saved anyone.
Here’s the truth we don’t like to face:
Sin is not just a mistake.
It’s rebellion.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
Not some.
Not the worst.
All.

That includes the quiet sinner.
The secret struggler.
The “good” person with hidden compromise.
Sin separates.
“For the wages of sin is death…” — Romans 6:23
Not just physical death—
Spiritual separation from God.
Forever.
That’s the flood we don’t talk about anymore.
Because right here—
Right at the weight of that truth—
Everything changes.
Methuselah lived 969 years…
But Jesus Christ lived about 33.
And yet—
Those 33 years did what 969 never could.
Jesus didn’t just live long.
He lived perfect.

No sin.
No compromise.
No hidden darkness.
“He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.” — 1 Peter 2:22
And then—
He did something no one expected.
He took your place.
On the cross, Jesus absorbed the full weight of sin.
Not just the visible ones—
The secret ones.
The ones you think you’ve hidden well.
The ones that still whisper to you at night.
“God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
That’s the exchange.
Your sin.
For His righteousness.
Your guilt.
For His grace.
Your death sentence—
For His eternal life.
And then—
Three days later—
The grave broke.
“He is not here; He has risen, just as He said.” — Matthew 28:6
Death didn’t win.
Time didn’t win.
Sin didn’t win.
Jesus did.
So now the question shifts.
It’s no longer:
“How long will I live?”
It becomes:
“What am I doing with the life I’ve been given?”
Because you don’t need 969 years to get right with God.
You need one surrendered moment.
Right now.
Not later.
Not someday.
Now.
Maybe this is your Methuselah moment.
The space where God is still giving you time.
Not to drift—
But to return.
Repent.
That means turn.
Not just feel bad—
Change direction.

Lay down the pride.
Confess the sin.
Stop hiding.
And come to Jesus.
Because grace is not earned over time.
It is received in surrender.
“Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” — Romans 10:13
Not might.
Not maybe.
Will.
So let me ask you—
What are you still holding on to?
That sin?
That bitterness?
That double life?
Is it worth your soul?
This is your moment.
Don’t waste it.
If you’re ready—
Pray this in your heart:

“Jesus, I surrender.
I confess my sin.
I need Your mercy.
Save me. Change me. Make me new.”
Now don’t keep this quiet.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Some people think the servant in Matthew 25 was punished because he lost the talent.
paragraphs: Some people think the servant in Matthew 25 was punished because he lost the talent.
But that is not what happened.
He didn't lose it.
He buried it.
And that is what makes this story so unsettling.

The servant did not steal the money.
He did not waste it on reckless living.
He did not gamble it away.
When the master returned, he was even able to say something that sounded responsible:
"Look. Here is what you gave me."
He still had it.

Still intact.
Still safe.
Still untouched.
And yet the master called him wicked and lazy.
Why?
Because in the Kingdom of God, faithfulness is not measured by what you protect from risk…
It is measured by what you are willing to steward for growth.
The servant thought safety was wisdom.
But Heaven saw something different.
Heaven saw fear disguised as responsibility.
And that is the warning hidden inside this parable.
The servant himself revealed the real issue when he spoke to the master.

"I was afraid."
(Matthew 25:25)
That one sentence explains everything.
Fear made him bury what he was meant to multiply.
Fear convinced him that doing nothing was better than risking failure.
Fear made him believe that preserving the gift was enough.
But buried things do not grow.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal for many of us.
Because not everyone destroys their calling through rebellion.
Some people lose their calling through hesitation.
Not through sin.
Through delay.
Through hiding.
Through waiting for the perfect moment that never comes.

They bury their voice.
They bury their gift.
They bury their opportunity.
They bury the assignment God placed in their hands.
Not because they hate God.
But because they are afraid.

Afraid of failing.
Afraid of criticism.
Afraid of being seen.
Afraid of stepping into responsibility.
So they convince themselves that doing nothing is safer.
But the parable exposes a powerful truth:
Unused potential is not neutral in the Kingdom of God.
When God entrusts something to a life, He expects it to move.
He expects it to grow.
He expects it to serve others.
And sometimes the greatest tragedy is not when someone ruins their gift…
It is when they hide it so deeply that it never touches the world.
Think about how many talents are buried today.
Ideas that were never started.
Ministries that were never launched.
Words that were never spoken.
Callings that were never pursued.
Acts of obedience that were delayed so long they eventually disappeared.
Not because God didn't give the talent.
But because fear convinced someone to dig a hole instead of planting a seed.
One of the most sobering parts of the story is that the servant also misunderstood his master.
He described the master as harsh.
Demanding.
Difficult.
And when your view of God becomes distorted, your stewardship becomes distorted too.
If you believe God is only waiting to punish you, you will hide.
If you believe God is impossible to please, you will hesitate.
If you believe God only wants perfection, you will never risk obedience.
But the two faithful servants understood something different.
They trusted the character of their master.
So they worked.
They invested.
They took responsibility.
They multiplied what was placed in their hands.
And when the master returned, he said something every believer longs to hear:
"Well done, good and faithful servant."
Not perfect servant.
Faithful servant.
That is the difference.
Faithfulness is not about having the biggest gift.
It is about refusing to bury what God entrusted to you.
You do not need five talents to please God.
You just need the courage to use the one you were given.
Because the real danger is not always rebellion.
Sometimes the real danger is hesitation that lasts too long.
The servant buried one talent.
But in doing so, he buried something even more tragic.
He buried his opportunity to be faithful.
And that warning still echoes today.
Some people are not running from their calling.
They are quietly hiding it in the ground.
Waiting.
Hesitating.
Delaying.
Protecting it from risk.
But buried things never multiply.
And one day, every steward will face the same question the master asked in the parable:
"What did you do with what I gave you?"
That question searches every heart.
Your gift matters.
Your calling matters.
Your obedience matters.
What God places in your hands was never meant to stay buried.
It was meant to grow.
It was meant to serve.
It was meant to multiply.
And sometimes the most dangerous prayer we can pray is not "Lord, give me more."
It is the quiet question:
"Lord… have I buried what You already gave me?"

📖 Matthew 25:25
"I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth."

Discussion Question:
What is one gift, calling, or opportunity people often bury out of fear without even realizing it?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Three days. Three temptations. Three denials.
paragraphs: Three days. Three temptations. Three denials.
Throughout the Bible, the number three appears at some of the most decisive moments in the story of God’s people.

Not as superstition.
Not as numerology.
But as a pattern of confirmation, testing, and transformation.
Again and again, Scripture shows us that the third moment often reveals the turning point.

Sometimes it reveals weakness.
Sometimes it reveals faith.
Sometimes it reveals the beginning of redemption.
And once you start noticing it, you see it everywhere in the biblical story.
Before Jesus began His public ministry, He was led into the wilderness.
For forty days He fasted.
At His weakest physical moment, Satan came with three temptations (Matthew 4:1–11).

First, he challenged Jesus to turn stones into bread.
Then he tempted Him to throw Himself from the temple.
Finally, he offered the kingdoms of the world.
Three temptations.
Each one attacking something deeper than hunger.

Identity.
Trust.
Authority.
And three times Jesus answered with the same weapon:
“It is written.”
The third temptation did not break Him.
It revealed Him.
Later, on the darkest night of the Gospel story, another set of three moments unfolds.

Peter, the disciple who boldly promised,
“Even if all fall away, I will not” (Mark 14:29).
But in the courtyard of the high priest, fear replaced courage.
A servant girl recognized him.
“You also were with Jesus.”
Peter denied it.
Then someone else asked.
He denied it again.
Then a third voice insisted.
And Peter denied Jesus for the third time.
Immediately the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us something heartbreaking happened next.
“The Lord turned and looked at Peter.” (Luke 22:61)
Three denials.
Three failures.
Three moments Peter wished he could erase.
But God was not finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met His disciples by the Sea of Galilee.
Peter had gone back to fishing.
Maybe he believed his failure had disqualified him.
Maybe he thought the story was over.
But Jesus did something remarkable.
Three times He asked Peter a question.
“Simon, son of John, do you love Me?” (John 21:15–17)
Three times.
The same number as the denials.
Not to shame him.
But to restore him.
For every denial, Jesus gave Peter a chance to declare love again.
And after each answer, Jesus gave a command:
“Feed my lambs.”
“Take care of my sheep.”
“Feed my sheep.”
Peter’s worst failure became the doorway to his calling.
Then there are the three days that changed history.
After the crucifixion, Jesus was placed in a tomb.
The stone was sealed.
Roman guards stood watch.
Hope seemed buried.
But Jesus had already told His disciples what would happen.
“The Son of Man must be killed and after three days rise again.” (Mark 8:31)
Three days of silence.
Three days of grief.
Three days when it looked like darkness had won.
But the third day was never meant to be the end.
It was the moment God would rewrite the story.
The stone rolled away.
The tomb was empty.
Death was defeated.
And the world would never be the same.
Even earlier in Scripture, the pattern appears.
Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of a great fish before being delivered (Jonah 1:17).
Later, Jesus would say that Jonah’s experience was a sign pointing to His own resurrection (Matthew 12:40).
Paul spent three days blind after encountering Christ on the road to Damascus before receiving sight and stepping into his mission (Acts 9:9–18).
Three days.
Three moments.
Three turning points.
The Bible also establishes an important principle in Deuteronomy 19:15:
“A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.”
In other words, truth is confirmed through repetition.
And throughout Scripture, the number three often marks divine confirmation.
A moment God wants people to recognize.
A moment where the heart is revealed.
A moment where a decision becomes unavoidable.
But maybe the most powerful lesson is this:
God often meets us in the third moment.

The third temptation.
The third failure.
The third day.
The moment when we think everything is over.
Peter thought his third denial defined him.
The disciples thought the third day meant defeat.
But God was writing a different ending.
Because in the hands of God, the third moment is often where redemption begins.
Maybe you are in a “second moment” right now.

Still in the struggle.
Still in the silence.
Still in the uncertainty.
But the biblical pattern reminds us of something powerful.
The story is not finished yet.
Because sometimes…
the third moment is where everything changes.

The third prayer.
The third attempt.
The third day.
And suddenly what looked like the end becomes the beginning of something God had planned all along.
Which “three moment” in the Bible has impacted you the most?

Peter’s restoration?
Jesus’ resurrection after three days?
Jonah’s three days in the fish?
Let’s learn from Scripture together.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 3 Truths About Your Identity in Christ
paragraphs: 3 Truths About Your Identity in Christ
Most people live their entire lives believing the wrong story about themselves.
The enemy loves that.
Because if he can control what you believe about who you are, he can influence how you live, how you pray, how you fight temptation, and how you walk with God.
Many believers still carry labels that Jesus already removed.

• Failure
• Shame
• Not good enough
• Too broken
• Too sinful
• Too far gone
But the Gospel tells a completely different story.
The cross did not just forgive your sins.
The cross gave you a new identity.
And when you understand who you are in Christ, everything changes.
Here are 3 powerful truths about your identity in Christ.
1. You Are Forgiven
This is where the Gospel begins.
Jesus did not die to make bad people slightly better.
He died to forgive sinners completely.
The blood of Christ was not partial payment.
It was full payment.
That means if you have repented and trusted in Jesus, your sins are not hanging over your head waiting to be exposed.
They have been paid for.
Scripture says:

"If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
— 1 John 1:9
Forgiveness is not based on how well you perform.
It is based on what Jesus finished on the cross.
The enemy will try to remind you of your past.
But God reminds you of the cross.
Your past may explain your story.
But it does not define your identity.
If God has forgiven you, stop agreeing with the voice that says you are still condemned.
2. You Are Adopted
Salvation is not just forgiveness.
It is family.
When God saves you, He does not treat you like a tolerated outsider.
He brings you into His household.
Scripture says:

"But to all who did receive Him, who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God."
— John 1:12
Think about that.
The Creator of the universe did not just rescue you.
He adopted you.
That means:
You are not spiritually homeless.
You are not unwanted.
You are not alone.
You are a son or daughter of the King.
Adoption means God does not relate to you merely as a judge.
He relates to you as a Father.
And good fathers do not abandon their children.
They discipline them.
They guide them.
They restore them.
They love them.
You belong to Him.
3. You Are Redeemed
Redemption is a powerful biblical word.
It means to buy back something that was lost.
Humanity was enslaved to sin.
But Jesus paid the ransom to set us free.
Scripture says:

"In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses."
— Ephesians 1:7
Redemption means your life is not useless.
Your past is not wasted.
God can take broken stories and turn them into testimonies of grace.
Many of the strongest believers once had the darkest pasts.
Because redemption does not erase your story.
It transforms it.
Your pain can become purpose.
Your scars can become ministry.
Your testimony can become someone else's hope.
You Are a New Creation
All of this leads to the powerful truth found in today's verse:

"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come."
— 2 Corinthians 5:17
Notice what the verse says.
It does not say you are a slightly improved version of your old self.
It says you are new.
The old identity ruled by sin is no longer your master.
Yes, believers still battle temptation.
Yes, we still grow in sanctification.
But our identity has changed.
You are no longer defined by:

• your worst sin
• your darkest season
• your past mistakes
• your failures
You are defined by Christ.

Forgiven.
Adopted.
Redeemed.
This is who you are.
Not because you earned it.
But because Jesus secured it.
Why This Matters
Identity shapes behavior.
If you believe you are still the old person, you will keep living like the old person.
But when you understand who you are in Christ, you start living differently.
You resist sin differently.
You pray differently.
You walk with confidence before God.
Not arrogance.
But confidence rooted in grace.
A Challenge For You Today
Stop rehearsing the lies of your past.
Start declaring the truth of God's Word.
Remind your soul:

I am forgiven.
I am adopted.
I am redeemed.
I am a new creation in Christ.
And if you needed to hear this today, you are not here by accident.
God is reminding you of who you really are.
If you believe this truth, declare it.
And if someone you love needs this reminder,
Someone scrolling today needs to remember their identity in Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jerusalem had walls.
paragraphs: Jerusalem had walls.
Massive stone walls.
Inside those walls were the temple, the priests, the sacrifices, the crowds, and the religious center of the nation. Inside the city was where people believed holiness lived.
But when Jesus was crucified…
He was not killed inside the city.
He was taken outside the gate.
That detail is not random.
It is deeply theological.
And once you see it, the cross becomes even more powerful.
In the Old Testament system, certain things were taken outside the camp or outside the city.
The bodies of sacrificial animals whose blood was brought into the sanctuary were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27).
People with severe impurity were sent outside.
Criminal executions were carried out outside.
Outside was the place of rejection.
Outside was where shame was displayed.
Outside was where the unclean things were taken.
So when Jesus was led through the gates of Jerusalem carrying His cross, something profound was happening.
The Son of God was being treated like the rejected.
Hebrews 13:11–12 explains it clearly:

“For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp.
So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through His own blood.”
Jesus did not just die for sin.
He became the rejected sacrifice.
He stepped into the place where the condemned were sent.
He allowed Himself to be counted among the cursed.
Galatians 3:13 says:
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.”
Think about that for a moment.
The Holy One of God…
treated like an outcast.
The King of Heaven…
led outside the city like a criminal.
The Creator of the world…
rejected by His own creation.
But here is the beautiful reversal of the Gospel.
The place of rejection became the doorway to redemption.
Jesus went outside the gate so that sinners could be brought inside the family of God.
He stepped into shame so we could step into grace.
He stepped into exile so we could come home.

“The place where humanity rejected Him
became the place where God accepted us.”
And maybe that is why this detail resonates so deeply with us.
Because many people today feel like they are outside.
Outside the circle.
Outside God’s mercy.
Outside forgiveness.
Outside hope.
Some people feel outside because of their past.
Others feel outside because of their failures.
Some feel outside because they think they’ve gone too far.
But the cross tells a different story.
Jesus willingly walked outside the gate to reach the people who thought they were beyond the gate.
He did not stay in the center of religious comfort.
He stepped into the place of disgrace.
“Grace walked into rejection so the rejected could be redeemed.”
The cross was not placed in the center of the city.
It was placed where the broken were.
Where the criminals were.
Where the condemned were.
And that is exactly where Jesus chose to stand.
Right in the middle of humanity’s guilt.
Right in the middle of our shame.
Right in the middle of our brokenness.
Imagine the moment.
The city gates behind Him.
Roman soldiers pushing Him forward.
A heavy wooden cross cutting into His shoulders.
Blood running down His face from the crown of thorns.
The crowd watching.
Some mocking.
Some crying.
And Jesus walks forward.
Not resisting.
Not escaping.
Not calling angels.
Because He knows what is happening.
He knows the sacrifice must be made.
The Lamb of God must be offered.
And that Lamb must be taken outside the gate.
The writer of Hebrews then gives believers a powerful challenge.
Hebrews 13:13 says:
“So let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the reproach He endured.”
In other words:
If Jesus was willing to be rejected for us…
We should never be ashamed of Him.
Following Christ may not always place us in the center of cultural acceptance.
Sometimes it means standing outside the gate too.
But the place of rejection with Christ is better than the place of comfort without Him.
Because outside the gate…
Is where redemption happened.
Outside the gate…
Is where mercy was purchased.
Outside the gate…
Is where the greatest act of love in history took place.
And the gate that closed behind Jesus…
Opened forever for us.
“The place of rejection became the doorway to redemption.”
“Grace walked into exile so we could come home.”
“Jesus was taken outside the gate so sinners could be brought inside the family.”
If this message speaks to you, take a moment to reflect:
Have you ever felt like you were outside — distant from God, unworthy, or beyond forgiveness?
And how does it change your perspective knowing that Jesus walked outside the gate specifically to bring people like us back inside?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She didn’t lose her son.
paragraphs:
She didn’t lose her son.
She surrendered him.
And that’s where most of us stop reading.

Because surrender sounds holy…
until it costs you something you love.

She prayed for him with tears no one heard.
She carried him in a womb that once felt like a grave.
She held him, fed him, named him.
Samuel.
Her miracle.
Her proof that God still listens.
But here’s the tension we don’t like:

God answered her prayer…
then asked for the answer back.
And this is where shame whispers…
“What kind of mother gives her child away?”
“What if you misheard God?”
“What if surrender is just loss dressed up in faith?”
Let’s be honest.
Some of us don’t struggle with unanswered prayers.
We struggle with answered prayers that require surrender.
You prayed for the job—now it’s pulling you away from God.
You prayed for the relationship—now it’s testing your obedience.
You prayed for the blessing—now it’s becoming your idol.
And deep down…
You feel it.
That quiet conviction.
That holy discomfort.
That whisper:
“Will you give it back to Me?”
Hannah stood at that exact crossroad
No applause.
No validation.
Just a choice.

Cling…
or consecrate.
And she chose what most of us avoid:
She let go.
“For this child I prayed, and the Lord has granted me my petition that I made to Him. Therefore I have lent him to the Lord. As long as he lives, he is lent to the Lord.” — 1 Samuel 1:27–28
Let that sink in.
She didn’t just receive a blessing.
She returned it.
Here’s the deeper truth most people miss
Hannah’s story is not just about motherhood.
It’s about ownership.
We say, “God blessed me with this.”
But we live like, “This belongs to me.”
And that’s where the fracture begins.
Because blessings can quietly become idols.
Not evil.
Just… elevated.
Above obedience.
Above surrender.
Above God Himself.
And this is where shame tightens its grip
Not loud.
Subtle.
“You can follow God… just not that far.”
“You can obey… just not with this.”
“You can surrender… but keep something for yourself.”
So we negotiate.
Half-surrender.
Partial obedience.
Delayed yes.
And we call it wisdom.
But Scripture calls it something else.
The Scripture cuts deeper than we expect
“Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.” — Proverbs 3:5
All.
Not most.
Not comfortable parts.
Not what costs little.
All.
Now here’s the turning point
Because this is not just Hannah’s story.
It’s pointing to Someone greater.
Another Son.
Given.
Not borrowed.
Not returned.
Given.
“For God so loved the world, that He gave His only Son…” — John 3:16
Feel the contrast.
Hannah gave Samuel to serve in a temple.
God gave Jesus to die on a cross.
Hannah released in faith.
God released in sacrifice.
And here’s where redemption breaks through
Because you and I?
We haven’t surrendered perfectly.
We’ve held on.
Clung tightly.
Chosen comfort over obedience.
Delayed God.
Ignored conviction.
Turned blessings into idols.
That’s called sin.
Not just wrongdoing—
misplaced worship.
But Jesus didn’t come to shame you for that.
He came to save you from it.
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Before you fixed it.
Before you surrendered.
Before you got it right.
He gave Himself.
Fully.
Completely.
No negotiation.
This is the Gospel
You don’t earn God’s love by surrendering perfectly.
You receive God’s grace because Jesus surrendered perfectly.
On the cross, He didn’t hold back.
Not His body.
Not His blood.
Not His will.
“Not My will, but Yours be done.” — Luke 22:42
That’s the surrender we couldn’t live.
So He lived it for us.
And died in our place.
And rose again—
So that we wouldn’t just admire surrender…
We could be transformed by it.
Now the question turns back to you

What are you holding…
that God is asking you to release?
Not because He wants to take from you—
But because He wants to free you.
From fear.
From control.
From silent idols.
From the exhausting pressure of holding everything together.
Listen carefully
Hannah didn’t lose her son.
She placed him in God’s hands.
And what God holds—
He doesn’t waste.
Samuel didn’t disappear.
He stepped into purpose.
And maybe that’s your breakthrough

What feels like loss…
might actually be alignment.

What feels like surrender…
might actually be release into calling.
So here’s your invitation
Stop negotiating with God.
Stop delaying obedience.
Stop holding what was never yours to keep.
Come to Jesus.
Not with polished faith—
But with honest surrender.
Repent.
Turn from control.
Trust Him again.
Lay it down.
And watch what He does with what you release
Because the cross already proved this:
God is not trying to take from you.
He’s trying to save you.
🔥 Engagement
🙏 Follow CTA
If this stirred something in you…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He cried over the son who betrayed him.
paragraphs: He cried over the son who betrayed him.
Not in anger.
In agony.
He won the battle…
…but lost his boy.
And that changes everything.
Because this is not just a story about a fallen prince.
This is a mirror.
And if you look closely enough—
you might see yourself in Absalom.
Or worse…
you might hear your Father’s voice in David’s cry.
Absalom was not an outsider.
He was royalty.

Chosen bloodline.
Position. Privilege. Identity.
And still—
he chose rebellion.
He stole hearts behind closed gates (2 Samuel 15:6).
Spoke smooth words.
Built influence quietly.
Plotted loudly in secret.
And here’s the dangerous part:
He didn’t look like a villain.
He looked like success.
Handsome. Charismatic. Admired.
The Bible even says:
“In all Israel there was no one so much to be praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom…” (2 Samuel 14:25)
Let that sink in.
You can look perfect—
and be completely lost.
This is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because some of us know how to perform righteousness…
while entertaining rebellion.
We lift hands in worship—
but keep certain doors locked.
We speak “God bless you”—
while quietly resisting His authority.
We wear the image of a son—
but live like we have no Father.
That’s Absalom.
And if we’re honest—
that’s us.
Rebellion doesn’t always shout.
Sometimes it whispers.
“I know better.”
“I’ll do it my way.”
“I don’t need to submit.”
And it feels powerful—
until it isn’t.
Because sin has a direction.
And it never leads home.
Absalom rode into battle full of confidence.
But he left hanging—
caught in a tree.
Helpless.
Exposed.
Suspended between heaven and earth.
(2 Samuel 18:9)
That image is haunting.
Because that’s what sin does.
It lifts you—
then traps you.
Promises freedom—
then paralyzes you.
Makes you feel above everything—
until you’re stuck between everything.
And then comes the moment no one prepares for.
The end.
The consequence.
The silence after rebellion.
Absalom dies.
Not reconciled.
Not restored.
Still running.
And then—
the cry.

“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you…”
(2 Samuel 18:33)
Don’t rush past that.
Feel it.
That is not political grief.
That is not royal disappointment.
That is a father’s heart breaking open.
Here’s the tension:
David loved a son who rejected him.
And that’s where this story shifts from history…
to revelation.
Because David’s words carry a longing he could not fulfill:
“Would I had died instead of you.”
He wanted to take his son’s place.
But he couldn’t.
That’s the limit of even the greatest human love.
And this is where the Gospel explodes into the story.
What David wished to do—
Jesus actually did.
You are not just reading about Absalom.
You are reading about yourself.
Because the Bible says:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way…” (Isaiah 53:6)
That’s rebellion.
Not just behavior—
direction.
A heart turned away from God.
But the verse doesn’t end there.
“…and the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.”
That’s Jesus.
Where Absalom hung helpless in a tree—
Jesus hung willingly on a cross.
Not trapped—
but surrendered.
Not for His rebellion—
but for ours.
This is not poetic symmetry.
This is divine substitution.
“Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures.” (1 Corinthians 15:3)
Let’s make it plain:
You deserve the consequence.
He took it.
You ran.
He pursued.
You rebelled.
He redeemed.
That is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement.
Not religious performance.
Not behavior management.
Rescue.
Through Jesus Christ alone.
But here’s the question that won’t leave you:
Are you still running?
Still building your own kingdom?
Still negotiating with sin?
Still calling rebellion “freedom”?
Because here’s the truth most people don’t want to hear:
Delayed judgment is not canceled judgment.
And grace is not permission to stay lost.
“Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness… not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4)
That word—repentance.
It means turn.
Not feel bad.
Turn.
Come home.
Because unlike Absalom—
your story is not over yet.
You are still breathing.
Which means grace is still reaching.
The Father is not standing with a sword.
He’s calling with a heart.
But the way back is not pride.
It’s surrender.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)
That’s the promise.
Not partial forgiveness.
Full cleansing.
Not shame preserved.
Shame erased.
So what are you holding onto that is not worth your soul?
What are you defending that Christ already died to free you from?
This is your moment.
Not tomorrow.
Not someday.
Now.
Lay it down.
Say it:
“Jesus, I’ve been running. I surrender.”
And watch what grace does.
If this hit you—
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He had everything.
paragraphs: He had everything.
Power. Position. Provision.
But one vineyard—just one—became the fire that exposed the famine in his soul.
Pause there.

Because this is not just Ahab’s story.
This is ours.

In 1 Kings 21:1–16, a king looks out from his palace and sees something that does not belong to him. Naboth’s vineyard. Close enough to admire. Close enough to crave. Close enough to forget every blessing already sitting in his hands.
And in a moment, desire mutates.
Into jealousy.
Into entitlement.
Into quiet rage.

Ahab was not denied by God.
He was denied by a boundary.
And instead of honoring it, he resented it.
That is where jealousy begins—not in lack, but in comparison.
Read the text carefully.

Ahab goes home “sullen and vexed.”
He lies on his bed.
Turns his face away.
Refuses to eat.
A king… reduced to a sulking child.
Why?
Because someone else obeyed God.
Naboth refused to sell the vineyard because it was his inheritance—given by the Lord, protected by covenant (Leviticus 25:23–28). This was not stubbornness. This was obedience.
But jealousy does not respect obedience.
It resents it.
And here is the dangerous turn:
When jealousy is not confronted, it recruits others.
Enter Jezebel.

Cold.
Strategic.
Unbothered by righteousness.
She does what jealousy always dreams of doing—she just does it louder.

False witnesses are raised.
A righteous man is accused.
An innocent man is executed.
Naboth dies.
And Ahab… takes the vineyard.
Listen carefully:
Jealousy will make you comfortable benefiting from sins you didn’t physically commit.
That is how deep the corruption goes.

You may not throw the stone…
but you will enjoy the silence after.
This is not just ancient history.
This is modern reality.
Jealousy whispers:

“Why them and not you?”
“You deserve that life.”
“God is holding out on you.”
And if you believe that lie long enough, you will start calling sin “strategy.”

You will justify shortcuts.
You will excuse compromise.
You will celebrate outcomes without questioning the cost.
And slowly, quietly, your heart will harden.
But God sees.
He always sees.
In the very next verses (1 Kings 21:17–29), God sends the prophet Elijah with a message that cuts through the illusion:
“Have you killed and also taken possession?”
That question still echoes today.

Have you compromised and called it favor?
Have you envied and called it motivation?
Have you resented and called it ambition?

God is not fooled by polished outcomes.
He examines the heart.
And here is the weight of truth:
Jealousy is not a small sin.
It is a direct challenge to the wisdom of God.

It says,
“Lord, You made a mistake with my life.”
That is dangerous ground.
But here is where grace breaks in.
Because the story of Ahab exposes the disease…
But the Gospel reveals the cure.
Where Ahab took innocent blood to gain what he wanted…
Jesus gave His innocent blood to redeem those who wanted what was never theirs.
Let that settle.
On the cross, Christ bore not just our obvious sins—but the hidden ones.

The quiet comparisons.
The silent resentments.
The moments we smiled at others while grieving their blessing in secret.
Jesus carried that.

He was stripped so you could be clothed.
He was rejected so you could be accepted.
He was crushed so your corrupted desires could be made clean.
This is not behavior modification.
This is heart transformation.
Because the answer to jealousy is not trying harder to be content.
It is seeing Christ clearly enough that everything else loses its grip.

When you realize what you already have in Jesus—
forgiveness, sonship, purpose, eternity—
comparison starts to look small.
Not because your desires disappear…
…but because your soul is finally satisfied.
So here is the invitation:
Bring your jealousy into the light.
Name it.

Don’t rename it.
Don’t excuse it.
Don’t spiritualize it.
Confess it.
“Lord, I have been angry at Your goodness to others.”
And watch what He does.
He does not crush the repentant.
He restores them.
Even Ahab, in a rare moment of humility later in the chapter, humbled himself—and God responded with mercy (1 Kings 21:27–29). Not because Ahab deserved it… but because God is that gracious.
How much more for those who come through Christ?
So today—

Release the comparison.
Release the bitterness.
Release the quiet competition in your heart.
What God has for you is not delayed by someone else’s blessing.
And what He withholds is never cruelty—it is wisdom.
You don’t need their vineyard.
You need your Savior.
And in Him… you already have enough.

Key Scripture: 1 Kings 21:1–16
Truth to carry: Jealousy consumes what gratitude could have protected—but Christ restores what sin has corrupted.
“What have I been secretly resenting that God never assigned to me?”
Then surrender it.
Right now.
Because from scandal to grace—Jesus still rewrites everything.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He had everything.
paragraphs:
He had everything.
And still ended up begging… for a drop.
Pause.
Let that disturb you.
Because Gospel of Luke 16 is not fiction to entertain—it is truth to awaken. Jesus pulls back the curtain of eternity and shows us something we would rather not see:
A man can live admired… and die unprepared.

The rich man wore purple—status, influence, visible success.
Every day felt like a celebration.
Every meal, a feast.
Every moment, comfort.
At his gate?
Lazarus.

Broken skin.
Open sores.
Empty stomach.
Dogs showing more compassion than people.
And here is the silence that screams:

The rich man never touched him.
Never fed him.
Never saw him.

Not because he couldn’t…
—but because he wouldn’t.
That is the danger.

Not loud rebellion.
Not dramatic evil.
Just a slow, quiet indifference that hardens the soul until mercy feels optional.

Then suddenly—
death interrupts the story.

No warning.
No extension.
No negotiation.

Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham’s side.
The rich man is buried—and wakes up in torment.
And just like that…
Everything flips.

The one ignored on earth is comforted in eternity.
The one celebrated on earth is now crying out in agony.
Listen closely.

The rich man doesn’t ask for escape.
He asks for relief.
“Send Lazarus… just a drop of water.”
Even in hell, he still sees Lazarus as someone beneath him.

That’s how deep sin can go.
It doesn’t just blind you—it reshapes how you see people, even in judgment.
And Abraham answers with a reality that should shake every comfortable heart:
“Between us and you, a great chasm has been fixed.”
Fixed.

No crossing.
No second chance.
No “I’ll get serious later.”
Eternity is not adjustable.
Now feel the tension rise—

The rich man suddenly becomes an evangelist.
“Send someone to warn my family!”
He believes a miracle will wake them up.
But heaven responds with something sharper than fire:
“They have Moses and the Prophets… let them hear them.”
In other words:
God has already spoken.
And then comes the line that echoes through history:
“If they do not listen… neither will they be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.”
There it is.
The shadow of the Gospel breaking through the warning.
Because Someone did rise.
Jesus Christ.

Still—many delay.
Still—many assume there is time.
Listen to me carefully.

The rich man was not condemned for having wealth.
Scripture never teaches that wealth itself is sin.
He was condemned because his heart was untouched by God.

No repentance.
No compassion.
No evidence that he knew the Lord he claimed to honor.
Faith that never moves toward mercy is not saving faith.

Because when grace enters a heart—
it changes how you see people at your gate.

You begin to notice.
You begin to care.
You begin to act.

Not to earn salvation—
but because salvation has already begun to transform you.
And here is the Gospel turn—
We are not just observers in this story.
We are the rich man.

Blessed with time.
Access to truth.
Moments of conviction.
And yet, how often do we step over what God is pointing at?
But Jesus…
He is not like the rich man.

He didn’t step over us.
He stepped toward us.
We were Lazarus—spiritually bankrupt, wounded by sin, unable to save ourselves.
And Christ came close.

He touched the unclean.
He carried our shame.
He took the fire we deserved.
On the cross, He cried out—not for a drop of water—but under the full weight of judgment.
Why?
So that sinners like us could cross from death to life.
So that the “great chasm” would not trap us—but be bridged by His blood.
This is not just a warning.
This is mercy screaming through a story.
So here’s the question that refuses to leave:
Are you living comfortably… but spiritually asleep?
Are you hearing God’s Word… but delaying obedience?
Are you surrounded by truth… but untouched by grace?
Because one day—

The gate will close.
The roles will be revealed.
And eternity will speak without interruption.
But not today.
Today, grace is still calling.
Turn.

Not tomorrow.
Not when it’s convenient.
Now.

Turn from the illusion that success equals security.
Turn from the coldness that ignores people God places in your path.
Turn from a faith that is only words.
Turn to Jesus Christ.

The risen Savior.
The only bridge across the chasm.
The only One who can take a dead heart and make it alive again.
And when He saves you—
You won’t just look up to heaven.
You will start looking differently at the people right in front of you.
The gate will no longer be a boundary.
It will become a mission.

Because eternity is real.
Souls are real.
And the Gospel is still powerful enough to rewrite any ending.
This is your moment.
Choose Christ.
Before the story becomes yours.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He stood in front of fire…
paragraphs:
He stood in front of fire…
and felt colder than ever.

Because when God calls you—
it doesn’t always feel like power.
Sometimes… it feels like exposure.

Moses saw the burning bush.
Flames dancing.
Branches alive but not consumed.
Holy.
Unexplainable.
Undeniable.
You would think that moment would ignite courage.
But it didn’t.
It exposed fear.
In Exodus 3–4, God speaks clearly:

“I have seen the suffering of My people…
I am sending you.”

Not a suggestion.
A commission.
And Moses?
He starts pulling back layer after layer of resistance.
“Who am I?”

That’s not humility.
That’s insecurity talking loud.

“I’m not enough.”
“I don’t belong in that room.”
“I can’t carry that weight.”
Sound familiar?
Then he says:
“What if they don’t believe me?”
Now it’s rejection.

Because it’s one thing to hear God—
it’s another to face people.
The fear of being dismissed, laughed at, questioned.
So Moses stalls.
Then he goes deeper:
“I’m not eloquent.”
Now it’s inadequacy.

He’s not just afraid of the mission—
he’s afraid of how he’ll look doing it.
Because calling often puts you where your weakness is most visible.
And finally… the raw truth breaks out:
“Please, Lord… send someone else.”
There it is.
Not confusion.
Not lack of evidence.
Just fear… dressed as an excuse.
Let’s not pretend we’re different.

We don’t stand in deserts with burning bushes—
but we’ve all had moments where God nudged us.

Speak.
Forgive.
Lead.
Repent.
Step out.
And instead of moving… we calculate.
Delay.
Deflect.
Why?
Because calling is costly.

It pulls you out of hiding.
It confronts your past.
It demands surrender.
And Moses had a past.

A man he killed.
A life he ran from.
An identity he buried in the wilderness.

So when God said, “Go back to Egypt,”
He wasn’t just sending Moses to Pharaoh.
He was sending him back to the place of his failure.

Some scholars interpret Moses’ hesitation as trauma resurfacing—an exile forced to face the land he escaped. Others see it as humility that slipped into fear. But Scripture makes one thing unmistakable:
God never withdraws the call.
And here’s the turning point that changes everything:
God doesn’t argue with Moses’ weakness.
He answers it with His presence.
“I will be with you.” (Exodus 3:12)
Read that again.

God didn’t say, “You’re strong enough.”
He didn’t say, “You’ll figure it out.”
He said, “I’m going with you.”
That’s the difference.

Calling is not about your capability.
It’s about God’s presence.
But don’t miss this—

God does get angry in Exodus 4:14.
Not because Moses is weak…
But because Moses keeps resisting after God has already promised Himself.
There’s a line between honest fear and hardened refusal.
And Moses was getting close.
Yet even there—grace shows up.

God sends Aaron.
God provides signs.
God stays faithful.
Because when God calls, He also carries.
Now here’s where the story crashes into us.
Because Moses isn’t the only one who struggled to say yes.
We all have our burning bush moments.
Moments where God interrupts our normal and says:

“Come closer.”
“Take off your sandals.”
“This is holy ground.”
And we feel it—

That tension between what is safe…
and what is sacred.
But the greater story doesn’t end with Moses.
It points forward.
To a better obedience.
A perfect surrender.
Jesus Christ faced His own moment in a garden.
Not a burning bush—
But crushing weight.
Not a command to go to Pharaoh—
But a cross.
And where Moses said, “Send someone else…”
Jesus said:
“Not My will, but Yours be done.” (Luke 22:42)
That’s the Gospel.

Where we hesitate—He obeyed.
Where we shrink back—He stepped forward.
Where we run—He stayed.
All the way to the cross.

For your fear.
For your excuses.
For your sin.
So now when God calls you—
It’s not a threat.
It’s not pressure.
It’s an invitation grounded in grace.

Because the One who calls you…
already died for you…
already rose for you…
already walks with you.
You don’t have to be fearless.
You just have to be willing.
Maybe your “Egypt” is a conversation you’ve been avoiding.
Maybe your “Pharaoh” is a habit you refuse to confront.
Maybe your calling feels too big, too heavy, too exposing.
And deep down, you’ve been whispering:
“Lord… send someone else.”
But what if He’s still saying:
“I will be with you.”

Not when you’re perfect.
Not when you’re ready.
Not when you feel strong.
Now.
This is your moment.

Not dramatic.
Not loud.
But real.
Will you keep running?

Or will you finally turn…
step closer to the fire…
and say yes?
Pause.
Pray.
Respond.
Because delayed obedience is still resistance.
And God’s call doesn’t disappear—it waits.
Step into it.
Even trembling.
Especially trembling.

Because the same God who met Moses in the wilderness
is meeting you right here.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: God was never mentioned… but your sin still is.
paragraphs: God was never mentioned… but your sin still is.
Read that again.

Because silence doesn’t mean innocence.
And hidden doesn’t mean unseen.
You’ve mastered it, haven’t you?
The art of looking okay.

Smiling in public.
Serving in church.
Posting Bible verses.
While hiding battles no one hears.

The addiction you renamed “stress.”
The pride you call “confidence.”
The compromise you buried under “I’m still learning.”
And here’s the tension:

If no one sees it…
does it still matter?

If God feels silent…
does He still care?
If there’s no lightning, no judgment, no exposure…
Are you really in danger?
This is where Esther confronts you.
Because the Book of Esther never mentions God…
…but it exposes something terrifying:
God can be silent… and still be sovereign.
A whole empire moved.

A queen positioned.
A king disturbed in his sleep.
A decree reversed.
No “God said.”
No prophet speaking.
No miracle breaking the sky.
And yet—
Everything was orchestrated.
Now lean in.
Because this is where it gets uncomfortable.
You think silence means permission.

You think because judgment hasn’t come…
you’re safe.
But Scripture says otherwise.
📖 Ecclesiastes 8:11
“Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, the heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil.”
Let that sink in.
Delay is not approval.
Silence is not agreement.
God’s patience is not your permission.
You kept going…
because nothing happened.
You crossed the line…
and the ground didn’t open.
You entertained the thought…
and no voice stopped you.
So you assumed—
“I’m fine.”
But Esther whispers:
God doesn’t need to announce Himself to be in control.
And that should shake you.
Because while you were hiding…
God was still writing.
While you were justifying…
God was still watching.
While you were delaying repentance…
God was still giving you time.
Time.
Not to continue.
But to turn.
Here’s the deeper wound:
Sin doesn’t just live in what you do.
It lives in what you hide.

The secret thoughts.
The quiet compromises.
The things you hope never come to light.
📖 Luke 8:17
“For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.”
Everything hidden…
will be revealed.
Not maybe.
Not if.
Will.
And suddenly Esther feels closer to home.
Because just like God was unseen in Persia…
He is unseen in your secret places.
But not absent.
Never absent.

Some scholars interpret the silence in Esther as intentional—
a divine design to teach us to recognize God even when He seems hidden.
And maybe that’s the point.
Because your life right now?
It might feel like Esther.

No voice.
No signs.
No interruption.
But don’t confuse silence with safety.
Let’s go deeper.
Because this is where grace breaks in.
Esther didn’t stay passive.
She stepped forward.
Risked everything.
Faced the king.
“For such a time as this.” (Esther 4:14)
And here’s where the Gospel explodes into the story:

Esther risked her life to stand before a king…
hoping for mercy.

Jesus gave His life to stand in your place…
offering you mercy.
You don’t have to guess if God sees you.
The cross answers that.
📖 Romans 5:8
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when you cleaned up.
Not when you confessed everything.
Not when you fixed your life.
While you were still hiding.
That secret sin?
Jesus saw it.
That shame you buried?
Jesus carried it.
That guilt you can’t shake?
Jesus paid for it.
This is the Gospel:

You are more sinful than you admit…
but more loved than you ever imagined.
Sin demands exposure.
But grace offers redemption.
And here’s the turning point:
You can keep hiding…
or you can come into the light.
📖 1 John 1:9
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not shame you.
Not reject you.
Cleanse you.
But it requires something:
Confession.
Honesty.
Surrender.
No more pretending.
No more hiding behind silence.
No more mistaking delay for approval.
Because the same God who was silent in Esther…
spoke loudly through Jesus.
The cross is not subtle.
It is not quiet.
It is God declaring:
“I see you… and I came for you.”
So here’s the question you can’t avoid:
What are you still hiding?
Not from people.
From God.
And are you ready to bring it into the light?
This is your moment.
Not tomorrow.
Not when it gets worse.
Now.
Whisper it if you have to.
Pray it through tears.
But don’t leave this moment unchanged.
Jesus is not waiting to expose you.
He’s waiting to restore you.
Step out of the shadows.
Come into grace.
If you’re ready…
And let this be the day silence ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He looked like he was losing.
paragraphs: He looked like he was losing.

Not winning.
Not strong.
Not ready.
Losing.

Because sometimes the most dangerous moment in your life…
is not when the enemy surrounds you—
…it’s when fear exposes what’s inside you.
And Jehoshaphat was exposed.

A king.
A leader.
A man of God.
And yet the Scripture says it plainly:
“Jehoshaphat was afraid…” (2 Chronicles 20:3)
Let that sit.
Afraid.

Not composed.
Not confident.
Not in control.
Afraid.
And here’s the tension we don’t like to admit:

You can be chosen by God…
and still shaken by life.

You can pray…
and still panic.

You can lead others…
and still feel like you’re about to collapse inside.
But here is where everything shifts.
Not when the enemy retreats.
Not when the situation improves.
But when a man finally stops pretending he’s enough.
Because Jehoshaphat didn’t hide his fear.
He redirected it.
“He set himself to seek the Lord…” (2 Chronicles 20:3)
That line is everything.

He didn’t run to strategy first.
He didn’t gather weapons first.
He didn’t protect his image.
He sought God.
Let me speak straight to your soul:
Some of you are not losing because the battle is too big.
You are losing because you keep fighting it without surrender.
You keep carrying what was never yours.
You keep trying to be your own savior.
And deep down…
you know it.
Jehoshaphat stands before God and prays something raw:
“We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on You.” (2 Chronicles 20:12)
No filters.
No fake strength.
No spiritual performance.
Just truth.
We don’t know.
But we’re looking at You.
This is where pride begins to die.

Because pride says:
“I’ve got this.”

Faith says:
“I don’t… but God does.”
And then comes the Word of the Lord:
“Do not be afraid or discouraged… For the battle is not yours, but God’s.” (2 Chronicles 20:15)
Read that again.
Not yours.
God’s.
Some of you are exhausted because you’re trying to win battles God never assigned you to carry.
You’re trying to control outcomes that belong to Him.
You’re trying to fix what only grace can redeem.
And then…
Jehoshaphat does something that makes no human sense.
He sends singers.
Not soldiers.
Worshipers… to the frontlines.
While the threat is still real.
While the fear is still present.
While the outcome is still unseen.
They begin to sing:
“Give thanks to the Lord, for His steadfast love endures forever.” (2 Chronicles 20:21)
This is not denial.
This is not delusion.
This is war.
Spiritual war.
Because worship declares:
“God, You are still God—even when I feel like I’m losing.”
And as they worship…
God moves.

The enemy collapses.
Confusion breaks out.
Victory comes—not by human strength—
…but by divine intervention.
But don’t miss this.
This story is not ultimately about Jehoshaphat.
It’s about you.
And it’s about a deeper war.
Because the greatest battle you face…
is not outside of you.
It’s inside you.
Sin.
Pride.
Rebellion.
The quiet resistance to surrender.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
That’s the real battlefield.
And here’s the truth we avoid:
You cannot win this war on your own.

No discipline.
No self-improvement.
No effort.
Can save you.
And this is where Jesus steps in.
Not as a helper.
As a Savior.
Where you were surrounded by sin…
He stepped into the battlefield.
Where you were condemned…
He took the sentence.
“God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Jesus didn’t just fight your battle.
He finished it.
At the cross, He absorbed the wrath we deserved.
Through His resurrection, He crushed death itself.
“It is finished.” (John 19:30)
Not partial victory.
Not temporary relief.
Finished.
So now the call is not:
“Try harder.”
It’s:
Repent.
Surrender.
Believe.
Because the same pride that says “I’ve got this” in life…
is the same pride that keeps people from Christ.
Some of you are still trying to fix yourself before coming to Jesus.
You’re still trying to clean up your life before surrendering.
You’re still fighting a war He already paid for.
Stop.
Bring your fear.
Bring your failure.
Bring your shame.
And say what Jehoshaphat said:
“Lord… I don’t know what to do.
But my eyes are on You.”
Because grace meets you there.
Not when you’re strong.
But when you finally surrender.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us… and to cleanse us.” (1 John 1:9)
This is your moment.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.
Lay the battle down.
Let Jesus be your victory.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: God never gets tired.
paragraphs: God never gets tired.

He never runs out of strength.
He never reaches a limit.
The Bible is clear about this.

Isaiah 40:28 says:
"The Lord is the everlasting God… He will not grow tired or weary."
So when we read Genesis 2:2–3, something surprising happens.
It says:
“By the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing; so on the seventh day He rested from all His work. Then God blessed the seventh day and made it holy.”
But this raises an honest question.
If God never gets tired…
Why did He rest?
The answer is deeper than most people realize.
God was not resting because He was exhausted.
He was establishing a rhythm for humanity.
The Hebrew word used for “rested” in Genesis is “shavat.”
It does not mean collapsing from fatigue.
It means to cease, to stop, to pause.
God finished His creative work and then intentionally stopped.
And when He stopped, He did something profound.

He blessed the day.
He made it holy.
This was the first time in the Bible that time itself was declared sacred.
Not a mountain.
Not a temple.
Not an altar.
A day.
Think about that.

Before sin entered the world…
Before humanity experienced exhaustion…
Before the chaos of life began…
God already built rest into the structure of creation.
That means rest was never meant to be a luxury.
It was meant to be a rhythm of life.
Yet today, most people live the opposite way.
We live in a world that glorifies constant movement.

Busy schedules.
Endless productivity.
Nonstop work.
Many people measure their worth by how much they produce.
But the rhythm of creation tells a completely different story.
Your value does not come from how much you do.
Your value comes from who created you.
God rested to show humanity something we easily forget:
Life is not only about building.
It is about belonging.
When God stopped on the seventh day, creation was complete.
Nothing was missing.
Nothing needed improvement.
And God looked at what He had made and called it very good.
That moment teaches us something powerful.
Rest is not laziness.
Rest is trust.
When you rest, you are declaring something with your life:
“I trust God enough to stop working.”
That is why the Sabbath later became one of the most important commands given to Israel.
In Exodus 20:8–11, God told His people:
"Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy… For in six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth… but He rested on the seventh day."
God was inviting His people to live in the same rhythm He demonstrated at creation.
Work faithfully.
But do not forget to stop.
Because constant striving slowly convinces us that everything depends on us.
And that is a dangerous illusion.
Rest reminds us of a truth we desperately need:
God is the Provider.

Not our hustle.
Not our strength.
Not our constant activity.
Even Jesus later reinforced this principle when He said:

"The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath."
— Mark 2:27
In other words, God did not design rest as a burden.
He designed it as a gift.
A pause.
A reset.
A sacred moment where we step away from the noise of life and remember who we belong to.
Because when life becomes nothing but work, achievement, and pressure…
We slowly lose sight of the One who gave us life in the first place.
The seventh day is a reminder that our identity is not found in endless productivity.
You are not a machine.
You are a soul created by God.
And sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is not do more.
It is to stop long enough to remember Him.
The rhythm of creation is still speaking today.
Work faithfully.
Build what God has called you to build.
Be diligent.
Be responsible.
But never forget the lesson written into the very fabric of creation:
Even God paused.
Not because He needed rest.
But because we would.
And the God who created the universe knew something about humanity that we often forget:
A life without sacred pauses eventually becomes a life without peace.
So the next time you feel guilty for slowing down…
Remember the seventh day.
God built rest into creation before He built anything else into human life.
And maybe that is because the Creator knew something we are still learning today:
The soul needs stillness to remember God.
And sometimes the holiest thing you can do…
Is simply stop.

Genesis 2:2–3
"By the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing; so on the seventh day He rested from all His work."

Reflection Question:
Do you think modern life has made it harder for people to practice the kind of rest God designed? Why or why not?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He walked down the mountain carrying stone.
paragraphs:
He walked down the mountain carrying stone.
But what he was really carrying… was the mirror of the human heart.

Thunder cracked across Sinai.
Lightning split the sky.
A mountain burned like a furnace.
And a nation trembled.

Not because of war.
Not because of enemies.
But because God was speaking.
In Exodus 20, the Lord Himself declared ten words that would shake history. These were not philosophical ideas. Not suggestions for self-improvement.
They were commands from the Creator of the universe.

Commands written not on parchment.
But on stone.
Because God’s holiness does not bend.
The Ten Commandments begin with a declaration that changes everything:
“I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” — Exodus 20:2
Before the law… there was deliverance.

God rescued Israel first.
Then He showed them how to live.
Grace came before the command.
And then the thunder of heaven spoke:
You shall have no other gods before Me.

Not wealth.
Not power.
Not pleasure.
Not self.
God alone belongs on the throne.
You shall not make idols.
Because the infinite God cannot be reduced to something we can control.
Yet humanity keeps trying.

We carve idols from wood.
We craft them from ambition.
We polish them with success.
And then we bow.
You shall not take the name of the Lord in vain.
God’s name is not decoration for our lips while our hearts wander.
His name is holy.
Remember the Sabbath day.

One day to stop striving.
One day to remember the Provider.
Rest is an act of faith.
Honor your father and mother.
Because God builds societies on the foundation of family.
You shall not murder.
Every human life carries the fingerprint of God.
You shall not commit adultery.
Marriage is covenant, not convenience.
You shall not steal.
God calls us to trust His provision.
You shall not bear false witness.
Truth protects justice.
Lies destroy it.
And then the final commandment pierces deeper than behavior:
You shall not covet.

Not your neighbor’s house.
Not their spouse.
Not their life.

God moves past actions…
and reaches straight into the human heart.
And here is the uncomfortable truth.
If we are honest, the Ten Commandments do not simply expose ancient Israel.
They expose us.
Who among us has never placed something before God?
Who has never desired what belongs to someone else?
Who has never spoken words that wounded truth?
Jesus made the law even sharper.

He said anger can carry the seed of murder.
Lust can carry the seed of adultery.
Suddenly the commandments are not ten distant rules.
They become a mirror.
And in that mirror we see something unsettling.
We see that the problem of humanity is not merely broken systems.
It is the human heart.
The law reveals it.
The law exposes it.
But the law cannot heal it.

The commandments are perfect…
but we are not.
And that is why Sinai was never meant to be the final mountain.
Another hill would rise in history.
Not with thunder.
But with nails.
Outside Jerusalem stood three crosses.
On the center cross hung Jesus Christ.
