The royal magicians—the ones who had once tried to imitate the miracles—attempted to appear before Moses.
But Scripture records a humiliating detail:
“The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils.” — Exodus 9:11
The men who once pretended power were now covered in proof that they had none.
Their rituals failed.
Their spells collapsed.
Their bodies betrayed them.
False power always collapses when it collides with the authority of the living God.
Egypt had many gods of healing.
Priests prayed to them.
People trusted them.
But when disease spread across the nation…
Not one of those gods answered.
The plague exposed a terrifying truth:

False gods can promise protection,
but they cannot stop judgment.
Yet the most tragic part of the story is not the boils.
It is Pharaoh’s heart.
Scripture tells us something sobering:
“But the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not listen to them.” — Exodus 9:12
Before this moment, Pharaoh had already hardened his own heart multiple times.
He ignored warnings.
He resisted truth.
He watched miracle after miracle and still chose pride.
Eventually something frightening happened.
His heart became fixed in rebellion.
This is one of the most serious warnings in Scripture.
Sin does not just damage behavior.
Sin hardens the heart.
Ignore God long enough, and eventually the voice of conviction grows quiet.
The danger of sin is not just what it does to your life.
The danger of sin is what it does to your ability to repent.
But hidden inside this terrifying plague is a deeper message.
The boils were more than a physical disease.
They were a picture of the human condition.
Because sin behaves the same way.
At first it hides beneath the surface.

Invisible.
Secret.
Contained.
But eventually…
It breaks through.

Sin surfaces in anger.
In pride.
In addiction.
In shame.
What began as something hidden becomes something painfully visible.
The sixth plague reminds us of something uncomfortable:
Humanity’s greatest disease is not on the skin.
It is in the heart.
And no human power can cure it.

Not religion.
Not rituals.
Not wealth.
Not influence.
Only one person can heal what sin has infected.
His name is Jesus Christ.
When Jesus walked the earth, He did something revolutionary.
He touched the sick.
He healed lepers.
He restored bodies others refused to come near.
But the greatest miracle was not physical healing.
The greatest miracle was forgiveness.
On the cross, Jesus carried the deeper plague of humanity—our sin.
The prophet Isaiah wrote:
“By His wounds we are healed.” — Isaiah 53:5
Think about that.
Egypt suffered wounds of judgment.
But Christ carried wounds of redemption.
The boils of Exodus revealed the sickness of rebellion.
The wounds of Christ reveal the cure of grace.
Here is the question that still echoes today.
Will we respond like Pharaoh?
Or will we respond with repentance?
Because God’s warnings are not acts of cruelty.
They are acts of mercy.
Every warning is an invitation to turn.
Every conviction is a doorway to grace.
And today that invitation is still open.
No matter how deep the wound of sin may be.
No matter how long the rebellion has lasted.
No matter how visible the damage has become.
Jesus still heals hearts.
Not just skin.
He restores souls.
If this message stirred something in you, pause for a moment.
Reflect.
Repent.
Return to Christ.
Because the greatest miracle in Scripture is not a plague.
It is redemption.
And that redemption is still available today.
Someone scrolling tonight may need to remember that no wound is too deep for the grace of Christ.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The sky didn’t just darken.
paragraphs:
The sky didn’t just darken.
It exploded.

Ice the size of stones.
Fire flashing through the storm.
Thunder tearing the heavens open like a warning from eternity.
Egypt had never seen anything like it.
And neither had the world.
This was the 7th plague.

Not random weather.
Not natural disaster.
Not coincidence.
Judgment.
But hidden inside the thunder was a whisper of mercy.
Let me show you.
Pharaoh had heard the warning again and again.
“Let My people go.” — Exodus 9:13

But pride is stubborn.
Power is intoxicating.
And a hardened heart does not listen easily.

Egypt had already seen the Nile turn to blood.
They had endured frogs, gnats, flies, livestock death, and painful boils.
Yet Pharaoh refused to bow.
So God escalated the warning.
Through Moses, the Lord spoke:

“Send therefore now, and gather thy cattle, and all that thou hast in the field… for upon every man and beast which shall be found in the field… the hail shall come down upon them, and they shall die.” — Exodus 9:19
Did you catch that?
Before the storm came…
God warned them.
Judgment was coming — but mercy opened the door first.
And then the sky broke.
“And the LORD sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground… so there was hail, and fire mingled with the hail, very grievous.” — Exodus 9:23–24
Imagine it.
Hailstones crashing like falling boulders.
Lightning ripping across the sky like burning spears.
Fire dancing through the storm.

Fields shattered.
Trees ripped apart.
Livestock collapsing in the open fields.
Egypt’s gods of sky and weather were silent.
Powerless.
Because this storm was not about climate.
It was about authority.
God was revealing a truth Pharaoh refused to accept:
The Lord alone rules heaven and earth.
But here is the part that should stop us cold.
Some Egyptians listened.
Scripture says:
“He that feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh made his servants and his cattle flee into the houses.” — Exodus 9:20

Those who believed the warning…
were spared.

Those who ignored it…
suffered loss.

Same storm.
Different outcomes.
The difference?
Whether they feared the Word of the Lord.
The hail devastated Egypt.
But in the land of Goshen—where the Israelites lived—
there was no hail.
Not one stone.
Not one flame.
God was drawing a line in the storm.

Protection for His people.
Judgment for rebellion.
Finally Pharaoh cracked.
He called for Moses and Aaron and said:
“I have sinned this time: the LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.” — Exodus 9:27
For a moment, it sounded like repentance.
But it wasn’t.
Because when the storm stopped…
Pharaoh’s heart hardened again.
He wanted relief.
Not transformation.
He wanted the pain gone.
But not God as Lord.
And that’s the uncomfortable mirror.
How many people cry out to God only during the storm?
“Lord help me!”
“Lord save me!”
“Lord I’ll change!”
But when the thunder fades…
So does the promise.
Pharaoh’s story is not just ancient history.
It is a warning.
Because the Bible teaches something even more sobering.
The plagues of Egypt were shadows.
Foreshadows of a greater judgment coming upon the world.
The book of Revelation describes hail, fire, and divine wrath again falling upon the earth (Revelation 16).
History is moving toward a final moment when God will confront evil fully.
But just like in Egypt—
Mercy comes first.
And that mercy has a name.
Jesus Christ.
At the cross, the storm of judgment fell.
But it did not fall on us.
It fell on Him.
Jesus bore the wrath our sins deserved so that anyone who repents and trusts in Him can receive forgiveness, restoration, and eternal life.
Not because we earned it.
But because grace stepped into the storm.
The 7th plague teaches something unforgettable:
God warns before He judges.
God calls before He condemns.
God opens a door before the storm arrives.
The question is not whether the warning exists.
The question is whether we will listen.
Because just like the Egyptians who ran their animals inside—
those who take God at His Word find refuge.
So if this message found you today…
Don’t harden your heart like Pharaoh.
Don’t wait for the next storm to take God seriously.
Turn to Christ.
Run to the refuge while mercy still calls.
Because the same God who sent the hail…
also sent a Savior.
And His grace is stronger than any storm.
If this message moved you, share it so someone else can hear the warning and the hope.
Someone out there is standing in the field while the clouds are gathering.
And they need to know there is still time to run inside.
“He who feared the word of the LORD… fled into the houses.” — Exodus 9:20
Choose wisely.
Choose Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t wait for sunrise.
paragraphs: He didn’t wait for sunrise.
He didn’t wait for clarity.
He didn’t wait for confirmation from people who would never understand.
He moved… while it was still dark.
That’s how Matthew 2 unfolds—not like a calm devotional scene, but like a midnight evacuation under divine command.

“Get up,” the angel said.
“Take the child and His mother. Escape… because death is coming.”
(See Matthew 2:13)

No applause.
No backup plan.
No map.
Just a word from God… and a decision.
Joseph chose obedience.
Feel the weight of that moment.

A young father.
A fragile mother.
A sleeping child who carried the weight of eternity.
And outside?

A king with power.
A city unaware.
A massacre already forming in the shadows.

This is not a gentle nativity anymore.
This is war.
And Joseph becomes a shield.

Not because he is perfect.
Not because he is fearless.
But because he trusts the voice of God more than the comfort of staying.
Let that confront you.

Because many of us want clarity before obedience.
We want safety before surrender.
We want guarantees before movement.
But heaven often speaks like this:
“Move now… understand later.”
Joseph didn’t argue.

He didn’t negotiate timelines.
He didn’t say, “Lord, let me pray about it for three more days.”
The Bible says, he got up… and left that very night.
Immediate obedience is not emotional—it is spiritual alignment.
And sometimes, delay is dangerous.
Because what God is trying to protect in your life… the enemy is already targeting.
Read that again.
There are things growing in you right now—callings, convictions, purity, purpose—and hell is not passive about it.
Herod wasn’t.

Herod didn’t send a warning email.
He sent soldiers.
Matthew 2:16 tells us he ordered the killing of children in Bethlehem.

Evil was real.
Violence was imminent.
And the only thing standing between life and death… was obedience to God’s voice.
Joseph obeyed—and Jesus lived.
But don’t miss the deeper truth.

Joseph protected Jesus physically…
But Jesus would later save Joseph eternally.
That flips everything.
Because sometimes we think our obedience makes us the hero.
It doesn’t.
It simply places us under the covering of the true Hero.
The child in Joseph’s arms was not just a child.
He was the Lamb of God.
The same Jesus who escaped Herod… would one day walk straight into crucifixion.
No escape.
No detour.
No angel saying, “Run.”
Why?
Because the mission was no longer preservation—it was sacrifice.
He would carry the cross Joseph could never carry.
He would take the punishment Joseph deserved.
He would die… for the very sins of the man who once carried Him to safety.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we saved Jesus.
But that Jesus came to save us.
So when God says “Get up,” it is not to burden you.
It is to align you with His protection, His purpose, His plan of redemption.
Some of you are being warned right now.
Not by fear—but by conviction.
There’s a relationship that feels normal… but it’s quietly killing your spiritual life.
There’s a habit you keep excusing… but it’s eroding your sensitivity to God.
There’s a place, a compromise, a secret… and the Spirit keeps whispering:
“Leave.”
“Move.”
“Get up.”
And you keep waiting.

Waiting for it to be easier.
Waiting for it to be less costly.
Waiting for it to make sense.
But Joseph shows us—obedience is often urgent.
Because delay can expose what God is trying to protect.
Listen carefully:
You don’t need full understanding… to take the next right step.
You just need trust.
Trust the God who sees what you cannot.
Trust the God who warns before destruction.
Trust the God who protects not just your body—but your soul.
And here’s the beauty:

Even when your obedience feels small…
God is weaving it into a story that is eternal.
Joseph probably didn’t fully grasp it that night.
He just walked.

Step by step.
Through darkness.
Toward a foreign land.
Holding a promise he didn’t fully understand.
But heaven saw everything.
And history would never be the same.
So today—this is your moment.

What is God asking you to leave?
What is He asking you to protect?
What is He asking you to trust Him with?
Don’t overthink what God already made clear.
Get up.
Move.
Obey.
Because the same Jesus Joseph carried… is now calling you.

Not just to protect what is holy—
but to receive the salvation only He can give.
If you’ve been running, hiding, delaying—this is your invitation.
Turn back.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
He is not just the child who was saved.
He is the Savior who saves.
Right now.
Right where you are.
And His grace is still reaching… even into your hesitation.
Someone is one decision away from obedience that could change everything.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They didn’t warn you about this kind of sin.
paragraphs:
They didn’t warn you about this kind of sin.
Because it doesn’t look like rebellion… it looks like normal.
You’re not running from God.
You’re just… blending in.

Scrolling what they scroll.
Laughing at what they laugh at.
Desiring what they desire.

Still praying.
Still believing.
Still calling yourself “Christian.”
But something feels off.
Quiet.
Heavy.
Convicting.
Because deep down, you feel it.

That subtle tension in your chest.
That whisper you keep ignoring.
“This isn’t who you are anymore.”
But you don’t want to lose it.

The attention.
The pleasure.
The approval.
The feeling of being accepted.
So you stay.

Half in.
Half surrendered.
Half alive.
Let me say what most won’t:
Half-hearted Christianity is not harmless.
It’s war.

And you’re standing in the middle…
trying to hold hands with both sides.
📖 “You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.” — James 4:4
That word “adulterous” isn’t random.
It’s relational.

God is not just your Creator.
He calls Himself your Husband (Isaiah 54:5).

So when your heart clings to the world…
it’s not just distraction.
It’s spiritual betrayal.
Let that land.
This isn’t about rules.
This is about love.

Who has your affection?
Who shapes your desires?
Who defines your worth?

Because whatever you love most…
you will obey without question.
Some scholars interpret “the world” here not as people, but as a system opposed to God—values, desires, and patterns driven by pride, self-glory, and rebellion (see 1 John 2:15–16).
And that system is subtle.
It doesn’t scream, “Reject God.”
It whispers:

“Just this once.”
“You deserve it.”
“No one will know.”
And slowly…

Your convictions fade.
Your hunger for God dulls.
Your sensitivity to sin weakens.
Not overnight.
But drip… by drip… by drip.
Here’s the part that hits hardest:

You can sing worship songs…
and still be in love with the world.

You can post Bible verses…
and still crave validation more than holiness.

You can look on fire publicly…
while quietly entertaining what nailed Jesus to the cross.
This is the tension:
Secret sin always feels safe—until it costs you intimacy with God.
But don’t miss this.
Don’t stop at verse 4.
Because right after confrontation…
comes grace.
📖 “But He gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.’” — James 4:6
More grace.

Not less when you fail.
Not less when you drift.
More.
Here’s the Gospel.
You and I chose the world.

We chased it.
Loved it.
Justified it.
And that choice made us enemies of God (Romans 5:10).
But instead of leaving us there…
Jesus stepped in.
He lived the life we refused to live—fully surrendered, fully obedient.
He died the death we deserved—bearing the weight of our sin, our compromise, our divided hearts.
📖 “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not when you cleaned up.
Not when you fixed your habits.
While you were still choosing the world.
And on that cross…
Jesus didn’t just forgive your sin.
He broke its power.
📖 “Our old self was crucified with Him… so that we would no longer be slaves to sin.” — Romans 6:6
So now…
You’re not stuck.
You’re not trapped.
You’re not too far gone.
But you are being called.
📖 “Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.” — James 4:7–8
This is your moment.

Not tomorrow.
Not when it’s convenient.
Now.
What are you still holding onto?
What part of “the world” still has your heart?
What secret compromise are you protecting?
Be honest.
God already sees it.
And He’s not waiting to condemn you.
He’s waiting to restore you.
Drop it.
All of it.

The sin you’ve normalized.
The habit you’ve hidden.
The identity you’ve built outside of Him.
Come back.
Not halfway.
Not casually.
Fully.
Because Jesus didn’t die for a portion of your heart.
He died for all of you.
And here’s the beauty:
When you let go of the world…
You don’t lose life.
You finally find it.
📖 “Whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.” — Matthew 16:25
This isn’t restriction.
This is rescue.
So right now—wherever you are—
Pray this:

“Lord, I’ve been holding onto things that pull me away from You.
I repent.
I turn from the world.
I choose You.
Cleanse my heart.
Make me whole again.
Teach me to love what You love.
In Jesus’ name. Amen.”
If this hit you deep…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They weren’t blind… and that was the problem.
paragraphs: They weren’t blind… and that was the problem.

They could read.
Teach.
Lead.
But they could not see.
And here’s the tension you can’t ignore:

What if the reason you haven’t changed…
is because you’re convinced you don’t need to?

What if your greatest weakness
is the belief that you’re already strong?
Let’s go deeper.
Because this is not about ancient Pharisees.
This is about us.

You can sit in church every Sunday…
and still resist the voice of God.

You can know the lyrics…
but never surrender your life.

You can quote Scripture…
and still protect your pride.
That’s the danger of spiritual blindness.
It doesn’t feel like darkness.
It feels like control.
Like confidence.
Like “I’m okay.”
But beneath that calm surface…
There’s a quiet resistance.
A subtle refusal.
A hidden voice that whispers:
“I don’t need to change.”
This is the emotional trigger—pride → humility.
Because pride doesn’t always shout.
Sometimes it sits quietly in your chest…

nodding along with truth
while refusing to bow to it.
Jesus confronted this directly.
Not the broken.
Not the sinners who knew they were lost.
But the ones who thought they were already found.

“For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind will see and those who see will become blind.”
Some Pharisees who were with him heard him say this and asked, “What? Are we blind too?”
Jesus said, “If you were blind, you would not be guilty of sin; but now that you claim you can see, your guilt remains.”
Let that settle.
Jesus is not condemning ignorance.
He’s confronting false sight.
Because the most dangerous place to be…

is thinking you see clearly
when you are actually missing God.
Some scholars interpret this passage as a reversal:

The physically blind receive both physical and spiritual sight,
while the spiritually proud—those confident in their own righteousness—
are exposed as truly blind.
And if we’re honest…
That’s uncomfortable.
Because pride is subtle.
It dresses up like maturity.
It sounds like wisdom.
It even uses Bible language.
But pride resists surrender.
Pride edits conviction.
Pride negotiates with sin.
You feel it when God nudges you…
“Let go of that relationship.”
“Forgive that person.”
“Confess that hidden sin.”
“Stop pretending.”
And instead of obeying…
you explain.
You delay.
You justify.
That’s not confusion.
That’s blindness.
And here’s the hard truth:
You cannot heal what you refuse to admit.
But don’t miss this—
The story doesn’t end in exposure.
It turns to grace.
Because in the same chapter…
there’s a man who was truly blind.
No status.
No reputation.
No image to protect.
And when Jesus touched him—
everything changed.
Not because he earned it.
Not because he understood everything.
But because he was willing to receive.
That’s the Gospel turn.
Don’t miss it.
You are not saved by being right.
You are saved by surrendering to Jesus.
📖 Ephesians 2:8–9
“For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God—not by works, so that no one can boast.”
Grace destroys pride.
Because you can’t earn what Jesus already paid for.
At the cross—
your pride is exposed.
Your sin is revealed.
Your illusion of control is shattered.
But also—
your debt is paid.
Your shame is covered.
Your eyes can finally open.
📖 2 Corinthians 4:4–6

“The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers… For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ made his light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of God’s glory displayed in the face of Christ.”
Read that again.
Blindness is real.
But so is light.
And that light has a name:
Jesus Christ.
He doesn’t just inform you.
He transforms you.
He doesn’t just point to truth.
He is the Truth.
And here’s the invitation—
not to the perfect…
but to the honest.
If there’s even a flicker inside you saying,
“Lord… maybe I’ve been seeing wrong…”
Don’t silence it.
That’s not weakness.
That’s grace breaking through.
So right now—
drop the image.
Release the pride.
Stop defending what God is trying to heal.
Pray this, not polished… but real:

“Jesus, I don’t want to just think I see.
I want to truly see You.
Break my pride.
Open my eyes.
I surrender.”
Because the miracle isn’t just sight.
It’s new life.
📖 2 Corinthians 5:17
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here!”
You don’t have to stay blind.
You don’t have to fake clarity.
You don’t have to carry the weight of pretending.
Jesus is still opening eyes.
Today.
Right now.
Even yours.
And if this stirred something deep in your spirit…
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He was never supposed to win.
paragraphs: He was never supposed to win.

A boy with a sling…
standing in a valley where trained warriors refused to stand.
Across the battlefield towered a giant whose armor alone weighed more than the courage of Israel’s army that day.
For forty days, morning and evening, the giant stepped forward.

Mocking.
Roaring.
Defying the people of God.
His name was Goliath of Gath (1 Samuel 17).
And every time he shouted his challenge, the same thing happened.
Silence.

Helmets lowered.
Spears stayed still.
Even King Saul — the tallest man in Israel — did nothing.
Because fear can paralyze even the strongest-looking people.
But then a shepherd arrived.
Not a soldier.
Not a warrior.
A delivery boy carrying bread and cheese for his brothers.
His name was David.
And the moment David heard Goliath’s voice echo across the valley, something inside him ignited.
Not pride.
Not anger.
Holy conviction.
David asked a question nobody else dared to ask:

“Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?”
— 1 Samuel 17:26
Notice something powerful here.
Everyone else saw how big Goliath was.
David saw how big God is.
That changed everything.
When Saul heard that this young shepherd was willing to fight, he tried to clothe David with royal armor.

Helmet.
Breastplate.
Sword.
But David could barely move.
So he took it off.
Because borrowed armor cannot replace personal faith.
David walked toward the battlefield with what God had already trained him with:

A shepherd’s staff.
A sling.
And five smooth stones from the brook (1 Samuel 17:40).
But the real weapon wasn’t the sling.
It was trust in the Lord.
When Goliath saw David approaching, the giant laughed.
A boy?
With a stick?
This insulted him.
But David answered with one of the most powerful declarations in the Bible:

“You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts.”
— 1 Samuel 17:45
Then David said something even deeper:

“The battle is the LORD’s.”
— 1 Samuel 17:47
And in one lightning moment that history would never forget—
The shepherd ran forward.
The sling spun.
The stone flew.
And the giant fell.
One stone.
One strike.
The enemy who terrified an entire nation collapsed into the dust.
But the real story of David and Goliath is not simply about courage.
It is about God’s glory.
The Lord was showing Israel that victory does not come from weapons, size, or human strength.
It comes from trusting Him.
That is why Scripture says:

“So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone.”
— 1 Samuel 17:50
But the story points even deeper than that.
David in this moment becomes a shadow of a greater Champion.
Israel stood helpless before an enemy they could not defeat themselves.
David stepped forward as their representative.
He fought the battle for them.
And when he won, the victory became their victory.
This is exactly what Jesus Christ has done for us.
Humanity stood in a deeper valley.
The enemy was not a giant from Gath.
The enemy was sin, death, and Satan.
No human strength could defeat it.
No religion could defeat it.
No good works could defeat it.
So God sent a Champion.
Jesus Christ stepped into the battlefield of the cross.
Where the world expected defeat, God delivered victory.
What looked like weakness became the crushing blow against the enemy.
Through His death and resurrection, Jesus defeated the powers that enslaved us.
That is why the Gospel is not advice.
It is victory news.

“But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
— 1 Corinthians 15:57
So when you look at this story again, ask yourself something honestly:
What is your Goliath?
Fear?
Shame?
Addiction?
Hidden sin?
The lie that you are too small, too broken, or too late for God to use?
Listen carefully.
The same God who brought down Goliath is still at work today.
And the same Savior who conquered sin still calls sinners to Himself.
You do not defeat your giants by trusting in yourself.
You defeat them by running toward God in faith.
That is the message of this valley.
And it is the message of the cross.
The battle belongs to the Lord.
And through Jesus Christ, the victory is already written.
If this story stirred something in your heart, share it so someone else can hear the truth today.
Because the world is full of people standing in valleys…
Waiting for someone to remind them that God still brings giants down.
📖 Scripture: 1 Samuel 17
🔥 Key Truth: “The battle is the LORD’s.” — 1 Samuel 17:47
Because here we tell the stories shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most people barely notice Andrew when they read the Gospels.
paragraphs: Most people barely notice Andrew when they read the Gospels.

His name appears quietly in the list of disciples.
He rarely speaks long sentences.
He never preaches a famous sermon.
He is not standing in the spotlight like Peter.
And yet, if you follow the small moments where Andrew appears, a powerful pattern emerges.
Andrew kept bringing people to Jesus.
Not preaching.
Not leading crowds.
Simply bringing people.
The first time we meet Andrew, he had just encountered Jesus. Something about that moment changed him immediately. And what was the very first thing he did?
He went looking for someone.
John 1:41 tells us:
“He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, ‘We have found the Messiah.’ And he brought him to Jesus.”
He brought his brother.
That brother was Simon Peter.

The same Peter who would later preach at Pentecost.
The same Peter who would lead thousands to Christ.
The same Peter whose name echoes throughout church history.
But before Peter stood before thousands, he was simply a man being led to Jesus by his brother.
Andrew.
Think about that for a moment.
The man who preached to thousands was first brought by someone who never sought the spotlight.
Andrew reminds us of something modern culture often forgets:
Not every kingdom builder stands on a stage.
Some simply open the door.
And Andrew kept doing this again and again.
In John 6, a massive crowd had gathered around Jesus. Thousands were hungry. The disciples were trying to figure out how to feed them.
That is when Andrew noticed something small.
A boy.
With five barley loaves and two fish.
It did not look like enough.
It probably seemed insignificant compared to the size of the crowd.
But Andrew still brought the boy to Jesus.
John 6:9 records Andrew saying:
“Here is a boy with five small barley loaves and two small fish, but how far will they go among so many?”
Andrew didn’t know what Jesus would do.
But he brought what he found.
And Jesus multiplied it.
Five loaves and two fish fed more than five thousand people.
Imagine if Andrew had ignored the boy because the offering looked too small.
But Andrew had the heart of someone who believed that anything placed in the hands of Jesus could become more than enough.
Then later in John 12, some Greeks came to Jerusalem during the festival. They wanted to see Jesus.
They approached Philip first.
Philip then went to Andrew.
And together they brought the request to Jesus.
Once again, Andrew was part of connecting people who were seeking the Savior.
He kept doing the same simple thing.
Bring people to Jesus.
It may sound small.
But heaven never calls it small.
Andrew teaches a lesson many believers overlook today.
We often measure spiritual impact by visibility.
We celebrate the preacher with the microphone.
We admire the leader with the platform.
But the Kingdom of God has always grown through quiet faithfulness.
Through invitations.
Through introductions.
Through conversations.
Through one person pointing another person to Christ.
Andrew never wrote a Gospel.
Andrew never stood on the Mount of Transfiguration giving a speech.
Andrew never became the most famous apostle.
But Andrew brought Peter.
Andrew brought the boy with the loaves.
Andrew helped bring seekers to Jesus.
And those moments became part of miracles.
The truth is, many of the greatest things God does begin with someone doing something that seems very ordinary.
A conversation.
An invitation.
A message.
A prayer.
A simple “Come and see.”
Andrew’s life whispers a powerful truth to every believer who feels unseen.
You do not have to be the loudest voice to have eternal impact.
You do not have to lead the crowd to change someone’s destiny.
Sometimes the greatest spiritual influence is simply guiding one person toward Christ.
And you may never fully see what happens next.
Andrew probably never imagined how far Peter’s influence would reach.
But heaven remembers.
God sees the quiet obedience that history sometimes overlooks.
In a world that constantly pushes people to be seen, Andrew shows us a different kind of faithfulness.
Faithfulness that does not need recognition.
Faithfulness that simply keeps pointing people to Jesus.
Quiet faithfulness.
Consistent obedience.
Small acts placed in God’s hands.
Those are the things God multiplies.
So if you have ever felt overlooked…
If your faith feels quiet…
If your role feels small compared to others…
Remember Andrew.
Because sometimes the person who simply brings someone to Jesus becomes part of a story far bigger than they ever imagined.
And eternity will reveal just how powerful one introduction can be.
So here is the real question for us today:
Who in your life might be one invitation away from meeting Jesus?
And what could happen if you simply did what Andrew did…
and brought them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Thirty-two thousand soldiers stood ready for war.
paragraphs: Thirty-two thousand soldiers stood ready for war.
Then God said something that shattered Gideon’s confidence:
“You have too many men.” (Judges 7:2)
Too many?
Israel was facing the vast Midianite army — a force so large the Bible describes them as “like locusts in number” (Judges 7:12). Their camels were countless. Their camp filled the valley.

And God looked at Gideon’s army…
and said it was too big.
Let that sink in.
Most of us pray for more before we move.

More resources.
More support.
More certainty.
More numbers.
But in Judges 7, God does the opposite.
He starts subtracting.

First, Gideon announces:
“If anyone is afraid, you may go home.”
22,000 men leave.
Just like that.
Imagine watching two-thirds of your army walk away before the battle even starts.
But God wasn’t finished.

The Lord then tested the remaining men at the water. Some scholars interpret this moment as a test of alertness or readiness, but the text itself simply records that God used it as the means to reduce the army again (Judges 7:5–7).
After the test?
Only 300 men remained.
Three hundred.
Against an army that filled an entire valley.
And then God declared the reason behind it all:
“Lest Israel boast against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’” (Judges 7:2)
Do you see it?
God reduced the army on purpose.
Because the human heart loves to steal God’s glory.
If Israel had won with 32,000 men, they might have said:

“We were stronger.”
“We had better strategy.”
“We deserved the victory.”
So God stripped away their confidence in themselves.
Until the only explanation left was Him.
This is one of the most uncomfortable patterns in Scripture:

God often removes what we think we need…
before He reveals what He has already provided.
Think about Gideon that night.
No massive weapons.
No giant army.
Just 300 men, each holding a trumpet, a jar, and a torch.
That was the battle plan.
Not swords.
Not shields.
Trumpets.
Clay jars.
Torches hidden inside.
From a military perspective, it sounded ridiculous.
But God was writing a story that would echo through history.
When the moment came, the 300 surrounded the Midianite camp at night.
Then suddenly—

Trumpets blasted.
Jars shattered.
Torches burst into the darkness.
And the men shouted:
“A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” (Judges 7:20)
Panic exploded through the Midianite camp.
Confusion spread.
The enemy turned their swords on each other and fled into the night.
And Israel won.
Not because they were strong.
But because God was.
The victory of Gideon’s 300 men reveals a powerful truth that still confronts us today:
God’s power shines brightest when human strength runs out.
We live in a world obsessed with numbers.

Followers.
Likes.
Money.
Influence.
Platforms.
But heaven measures victory differently.
God does not need massive numbers to accomplish His will.
He can change history with one shepherd boy and a sling.
He can launch the church through twelve ordinary disciples.
He can defeat sin and death through one crucified Savior.
The pattern of Gideon ultimately points us forward to Jesus Christ.
At the cross, the world thought it was witnessing weakness.
A beaten man.
A crown of thorns.
A criminal’s execution.
But what looked like defeat was actually the greatest victory in human history.
Through the cross, Jesus defeated sin.
Through the resurrection, He crushed death.
Through grace, He saves sinners like us.
Just like Gideon’s army, salvation does not come through human strength.
It comes through God’s power alone.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.”
No boasting.
No self-glory.
Only grace.
Maybe you’re in a season where your “army” feels small.
Maybe resources are shrinking.
Maybe support has disappeared.
Maybe the odds feel impossible.
Do not assume God has abandoned you.
He may be doing exactly what He did with Gideon.
Reducing what you trust in…
So you will learn to trust Him alone.
Because when God wins the battle, no one can confuse who deserves the glory.
And that is the kind of victory that changes lives.
So here’s the question that Judges 7 leaves hanging in the air:
What if your “300 season” is not your weakness…
but the stage where God plans to reveal His power?
Trust Him.
Obey Him.
Walk forward even when the numbers look small.
Because the God who delivered Gideon with 300 men is the same God who still works miracles today.
And the greatest miracle of all?
A sinner redeemed through Jesus Christ.
📖 Scripture: Judges 7:2–7, Judges 7:19–22
🔥 If this message strengthened your faith, share it so someone else can remember:
God doesn’t need big numbers to do big miracles.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He asked for more…
paragraphs:
He asked for more…
but what he really needed was less of himself.
Pause.
Because that’s where most people get it wrong.

You think you need more strength.
More influence.
More open doors.
But what if the real problem… is what you’re still holding on to?
Elisha stood at the edge of something terrifying.
His mentor—his covering, his voice, his safety—was about to be taken.

The chariots of fire were coming.
The mantle was about to fall.
And suddenly… the shadow he lived under would disappear.

No more hiding behind Elijah.
No more borrowed authority.
No more second place.
Just him.
And the weight of calling.
That’s where the tension lives.

Because deep down, we all want what Elisha asked for—
a double portion.

Double favor.
Double anointing.
Double impact.
But we skip the part nobody posts about:

The loneliness.
The fear.
The crushing realization that if God doesn’t come through… you’re not enough.
And that’s the truth we avoid.
You’re not enough.

Not holy enough.
Not strong enough.
Not pure enough.
And that hidden gap?
That’s where shame starts whispering.

“You’re a fraud.”
“You can’t carry this.”
“You’ve failed too many times.”
So instead of surrendering, we compensate.

We perform.
We pretend.
We build a version of ourselves that looks spiritual… but is starving inside.
Listen carefully.
Elisha did not pretend.
He didn’t mask insecurity with confidence.
He faced it.
And then he said something dangerous:

“Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me.”
— 2 Kings 2:9
That was not ambition.
That was desperation.
In Hebrew context, the “double portion” was the inheritance of a firstborn son (Deuteronomy 21:17). Elisha wasn’t asking to be greater than Elijah.
He was saying:
“I am stepping into sonship. I accept the responsibility. But I cannot do this without God.”
Some scholars interpret this as a request not for power, but for capacity—the spiritual weight required to carry what was coming.
And that hits differently.
Because you don’t need hype.
You need capacity.
You don’t need applause.
You need transformation.
And here’s where it cuts deep—
God will not pour a double portion into a divided heart.
Let that sit.

If you’re still feeding secret sin…
If pride is still sitting on the throne…
If repentance is optional in your life…
Then what you’re asking for would actually destroy you.
Because power without purity is poison.
And influence without intimacy is empty.
That’s why the story doesn’t end with the request.
Elijah responds:

“You have asked a hard thing…”
— 2 Kings 2:10
Hard.
Not impossible.
But costly.

Because what Elisha was really asking for…
was a life fully surrendered to God.
And here’s the Gospel turn—don’t miss this.
Elisha needed the Spirit to continue Elijah’s work.
But we need something deeper.
We need salvation.
Because the greatest barrier isn’t lack of power—
It’s sin.

Your sin.
My sin.
The hidden, quiet, respectable, destructive sin.

“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
— Romans 3:23
And no amount of effort, discipline, or spiritual activity can fix that.
You don’t need a better strategy.
You need a Savior.
That’s why Jesus came.
Not to upgrade your life—but to resurrect your dead heart.

“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
— Romans 5:8
At the cross, Jesus took your shame.

Not minimized it.
Not ignored it.
He absorbed it.

Every hidden compromise.
Every moment of pride.
Every failure you keep replaying at night.
Paid for.
Completely.
And then He rose again—
Not just to prove power…
But to offer new life.

“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.”
— 2 Corinthians 5:17
That’s your double portion.
Not status.
Not spotlight.

But a new heart.
A new Spirit.
A new identity as a son or daughter of God.
And from that place—
God entrusts more.
Not to impress people…
But to reflect Him.
So here’s the question:

Are you asking for more…
while resisting surrender?

Are you chasing impact…
while avoiding repentance?

Are you praying for a double portion…
but refusing to die to yourself?
Because the real miracle is not what God does through you.
It’s what He transforms in you.
Today, the invitation is not hype.
It’s holiness.
Not performance.
But repentance.
Come honest.
Come broken.
Come without the mask.
Jesus is not intimidated by your weakness.
He is ready to redeem it.
But you must turn.
You must surrender.
You must say—

“Lord, I don’t just want what You can give…
I want You.”
And when that becomes your prayer—
He doesn’t just fill you.
He changes you.
Completely.
This is your moment.
Come back to it. Pray through it.
And if this stirred something in you—
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She wasn’t supposed to be there.
paragraphs: She wasn’t supposed to be there.
Unclean. Untouchable. Unwanted.
But somehow… she still reached.

And that reach?
It broke every rule society placed on her.
Because shame will always try to silence you before grace can reach you.
Twelve years.

Twelve years of bleeding.
Twelve years of hiding.
Twelve years of hearing whispers when she walked by… or worse—seeing people step away.
Can you feel that?

That quiet humiliation.
That invisible label stamped on your life: “Stay back.”
Maybe yours isn’t physical.

Maybe it’s the sin nobody knows about.
The addiction you keep promising God you’ll quit… but don’t.
The thoughts you’d be ashamed to say out loud.
The version of you that smiles in public but crumbles in private.
And here’s the lie shame keeps repeating:

“You’ve gone too far.”
“You’re too dirty.”
“God helps people better than you.”
So you stay in the crowd.

Close enough to see Jesus…
But never close enough to touch Him.
But this woman?
She was done listening to shame.

She didn’t wait to be invited.
She didn’t clean herself up first.
She didn’t fix her condition before coming.
She came bleeding.
She came broken.
She came anyway.
Scripture says:

“And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind Him and touched the fringe of His garment, for she said to herself, ‘If I only touch His garment, I will be made well.’ Jesus turned, and seeing her He said, ‘Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well.’ And instantly the woman was made well.” — Matthew 9:20–22
Don’t miss this.
She didn’t touch His hand.
She didn’t earn His attention.
She touched the edge.
And that was enough.
Because it was never about how strong her grip was.
It was about who she was reaching for.
But here’s what should shake you…

According to the law (Leviticus 15), her condition made her ceremonially unclean.
Anything—or anyone—she touched would also be considered unclean.
Which means by human standards…
She should have made Jesus unclean.
But instead…
Jesus made her clean.
That’s the Gospel hiding in plain sight.
Your sin doesn’t contaminate Christ.
His holiness consumes your sin.
Let that sink in.

You’ve been afraid to come close because of what you’ve done.
But the very thing you think disqualifies you… is the reason He came.
“For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
Jesus didn’t avoid the unclean.
He absorbed the cost.
At the cross, He took your shame, your hidden sin, your private battles—every stain—and bore it fully.
Not halfway.
Fully.
Some scholars interpret this moment with the woman as more than just physical healing—it’s a preview of the cross itself. A Savior who does not withdraw from impurity, but steps into it to redeem.
And when He turned and called her “daughter”…
That wasn’t just healing.
That was restoration of identity.
She went from outcast… to family.
From shame… to belonging.
From hiding… to being seen.
And here’s the part we miss.
Jesus stopped for her.
In a crowd full of noise, pressure, urgency—He stopped.
For one trembling touch.

That means your quiet prayer?
He hears it.

That hidden struggle?
He sees it.
That moment where you almost gave up?
He’s closer than you think.
But here’s the turning point…
She had to reach.
Faith is not passive agreement.
Faith moves.
Faith presses.
Faith risks being seen in the middle of shame.
And maybe that’s where you are right now.
Stuck between fear and faith.
Between hiding and reaching.
Between “What if God rejects me?” and “What if He doesn’t?”
Let me tell you the truth your shame doesn’t want you to hear:
Jesus is not repelled by your brokenness.
He responds to your reaching.
But the Gospel goes deeper than healing your situation.
It transforms your standing.
You are not just someone God tolerates.
Through Christ, you become someone God adopts.
“But to all who did receive Him, who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God.” — John 1:12
This is not behavior modification.
This is resurrection.
This is not “try harder.”
This is “come closer.”
So what are you waiting for?

More guilt?
More hiding?
Another year of pretending you’re fine?
Or…
Will you reach?
Right now.

Not when you’re better.
Not when you’ve fixed yourself.
Not when your life looks more “Christian.”
Now.

Bring the addiction.
Bring the secret.
Bring the shame you’ve buried so deep you don’t even name it anymore.
Bring it to Jesus.

Because the same Savior who stopped for her…
Is still stopping for people like you.
And when you reach Him, you won’t just find healing.
You’ll find a Savior who calls you family.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The moment that divided Israel did not begin with rebellion.
paragraphs: The moment that divided Israel did not begin with rebellion.
It began with a conversation.
When Rehoboam became king, the people of Israel came to him with a request that sounded reasonable.
“Lighten the heavy burden your father placed on us, and we will serve you.”

They were not threatening revolt.
They were offering loyalty.
All they asked for was mercy.
So Rehoboam did something wise at first.
He asked for advice.
And this is where the story becomes painfully revealing.
The older counselors—men who had served under Solomon—gave him counsel that was both simple and powerful.
They told him:
“If you will serve the people today, speak kindly to them, and answer them gently… they will be your servants forever.”
In other words:

Leadership is not secured through intimidation.
It is secured through humility.
But Rehoboam didn't like that answer.
Because humility often feels weak to people who are trying to prove themselves.
So he asked another group for advice.
The young men he grew up with.
The ones who understood his pride better than they understood wisdom.
Their counsel sounded stronger.
More aggressive.
More impressive.
They told him:
“Tell the people this — my little finger is thicker than my father’s waist.”
“My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.”

It was bold.
It was intimidating.
It was powerful.
And it was incredibly foolish.
Rehoboam chose the advice that made him sound strong instead of the advice that would have made him wise.
And in a single arrogant response…
A kingdom shattered.
Ten tribes walked away.
Israel divided.
And a decision made in pride created consequences that would echo for generations.
This is why the story of Rehoboam is so relevant today.
Because most people don't lose things suddenly.
They lose them through small moments where pride wins over wisdom.
Rehoboam did not lack counsel.
He lacked the humility to accept the right counsel.
And that is a dangerous place for any person to be.
Because pride has a strange way of disguising itself.
Sometimes pride looks like confidence.
Sometimes pride sounds like strength.
Sometimes pride feels like standing your ground.
But pride often rejects the very voices God places in our lives to protect us.
Think about it.
How many relationships have been damaged because someone refused wise advice?
How many leaders have collapsed because they surrounded themselves with people who only told them what they wanted to hear?
How many families, ministries, businesses, and friendships have been fractured because correction was rejected?
Rehoboam teaches us something uncomfortable.
The loudest voices around you are not always the wisest ones.
And the voices that challenge you the most may be the ones trying to save you.
The older counselors understood something Rehoboam didn't.
Authority is strongest when it is tempered with humility.
Power that refuses wisdom eventually destroys itself.
Rehoboam inherited one of the greatest kingdoms in the ancient world.
But inheritance cannot replace character.
Position cannot replace maturity.
And a crown cannot protect someone from the consequences of pride.
That is the tragedy of this story.
The kingdom did not have to split.
It wasn't inevitable.
It wasn't unavoidable.
It happened because a young king chose ego over wisdom.
And that decision reshaped history.
Which leads to a question every one of us should ask ourselves.
Who do we listen to when our pride is on the line?
Do we surround ourselves with voices that affirm our ego?
Or do we allow wise voices to challenge us—even when it stings?
Because wisdom often arrives wrapped in discomfort.
Correction rarely feels flattering.
But those moments of humility can save us from years of regret.
One of the most dangerous things a person can become is unteachable.
When someone stops listening…
When they refuse correction…
When they only accept voices that reinforce their desires…
They begin walking down the same road Rehoboam did.
And that road leads to division.
Division in families.
Division in leadership.
Division in communities.
Division in hearts.
Rehoboam thought harshness would make him look powerful.
Instead, it revealed his insecurity.
True strength is not proven through intimidation.
True strength is proven through wisdom.
The strongest leaders are not the ones who speak the loudest.
They are the ones humble enough to listen before they speak.
Because sometimes the difference between preservation and destruction is a single decision.
A single response.
A single moment of humility.
Rehoboam reminds us that pride can divide what wisdom could have preserved.
And sometimes the most important question we can ask ourselves is this:
Am I listening to wisdom…
Or am I just listening to the voices that agree with me?

Scripture
1 Kings 12:1–19
2 Chronicles 10:1–19
Discussion Question
Have you ever realized later that someone tried to warn you… but pride made it hard to hear at the time?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most people don’t realize this about the parable of the wise and foolish builders.
paragraphs: Most people don’t realize this about the parable of the wise and foolish builders.

The difference between them was not intelligence.
It was not opportunity.
It was not even what they heard.
They both heard the same words.
The difference was what they did with those words.

Jesus said the wise man built his house on rock.
The foolish man built his house on sand.
At first glance, the two houses probably looked the same.

Both had walls.
Both had roofs.
Both looked like shelter.
From a distance, you might not even notice the difference.
But the real difference was hidden underground.
And that is how life often works.
Many people build impressive houses.

Successful careers.
Public influence.
Beautiful images of strength and stability.
But heaven does not measure your life by what stands on the surface.
Heaven measures your life by what holds it up underneath.
Because foundations are built where nobody is watching.

The digging is hidden.
The work is slow.
The process is costly.
But that unseen work determines everything.
And then Jesus said something that should stop all of us for a moment.

The rain descended.
The floods came.
The winds blew.
In other words, storms are not unusual in life.
They are inevitable.
Everyone will face storms.

Storms of pressure.
Storms of disappointment.
Storms of loss.
Storms of temptation.
Storms that shake everything you thought was secure.
And when those storms arrive, something powerful happens.
Storms reveal foundations.

A storm does not create weakness.
It exposes it.

Some lives collapse not because the storm was too strong…
but because the foundation was never strong enough.
And that is the warning hidden inside this parable.
The foolish builder was not someone who rejected Jesus.
He heard Jesus.
He listened to the teaching.
He was close to the truth.
But he did not build his life on it.
That may be one of the most sobering realities in Scripture.
You can be near the truth and still build on sand.
You can admire wisdom and still ignore it.
You can hear sermons, read Scripture, attend church, and still construct your life on things that cannot survive pressure.
Sand foundations today might look like this:
Building your identity on success.
Building your worth on approval.
Building your security on money.
Building your peace on circumstances.
Building your direction on feelings.
All of those things can feel stable… until the storm arrives.
But sand always shifts under pressure.
The wise builder understood something deeper.
He understood that truth is not meant to be heard only.
It is meant to be obeyed.
Jesus said the wise man is the one who hears His words and does them.
Not just inspired by them.
Not just impressed by them.
But shaped by them.
This means the foundation of a strong life is not emotion.
It is obedience.
It is the quiet daily decision to align your life with the words of Christ.
Obedience when it is easy.
Obedience when it is difficult.
Obedience when no one else sees.
Those decisions are like stones placed under your house.
And one day, those stones will hold you up.
Notice something else about the story.
The wise builder still faced the storm.
Following God does not remove every storm from your life.
Faith does not guarantee calm weather.
But it gives you something stronger than the storm.
It gives you a foundation the storm cannot destroy.
That is the promise hidden inside this parable.

A life built on Christ may be shaken…
but it will not collapse.
And maybe the most important question this story asks us is not about the storm.
It is about the foundation.
Because every person reading this is building something.
You are building a life.
You are building habits.
You are building decisions.
You are building a future.
And the truth is this:
One day the rain will fall.
One day the winds will rise.
One day the flood will push against everything you have built.
And when that moment comes, appearance will not matter.
Image will not matter.
Reputation will not matter.
Only the foundation will matter.
Three truths from this story that are worth remembering:
A beautiful house on a weak foundation is just a future ruin.
Storms don’t destroy everyone equally, because not everyone built the same way.
And the life that stands the longest is the life built on obedience to Christ.
So today the real question is not:
“How strong does my life look?”
The real question is:
What is my life built on?
Because storms reveal what sunshine hides.
And foundations decide what remains standing.
📖 Matthew 7:24–27
ENGAGEMENT QUESTION

Be honest:
What do you think people today most often build their lives on instead of the rock of Christ?
Approval? Money? Success? Feelings?
I’d love to hear your thoughts.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Some people think rejecting God’s Word protects them from it.
paragraphs: Some people think rejecting God’s Word protects them from it.
King Jehoiakim believed that.
And his story in Jeremiah 36 is one of the most chilling scenes in the Bible.
Because this king did something few people in Scripture ever dared to do.
He burned the Word of God.
But what happened next reveals a lesson every generation needs to hear.
The prophet Jeremiah had been warning Judah for years.
God told him to write down every prophecy He had spoken—every warning about the coming judgment of Babylon if the nation refused to repent.

Jeremiah dictated the message to his scribe, Baruch.
The scroll was read publicly in the temple.
The message spread quickly through Jerusalem.
Officials were shaken.
So they brought the scroll to the king.
This moment could have changed everything.

The nation was already on the edge of disaster.
If the king humbled himself, repentance could have spread through the land.
But Jehoiakim’s reaction revealed the true condition of his heart.
It was winter.
The king sat in his palace with a fire burning in a brazier beside him.
As the scroll was read aloud, something shocking happened.
After only a few columns were read…
Jehoiakim cut the scroll with a knife.
Then he threw the piece into the fire.
More of the scroll was read.
Again he cut it.
Again he burned it.
Piece by piece.
Line by line.
God’s message was thrown into the flames.
The Bible records something terrifying about this moment:

“Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments.”
— Jeremiah 36:24
In the ancient world, tearing your garments was a sign of repentance and fear before God.
But the king and his servants sat there calmly while God’s Word burned.
No trembling.
No humility.
No repentance.
Just defiance.
But here is the truth Jehoiakim did not understand.
Burning the scroll did not erase the message.
God spoke again.
Jeremiah was instructed to write another scroll.
And the Bible says something remarkable:

“And there were added besides unto them many like words.”
— Jeremiah 36:32
In other words…
The message didn’t disappear.
It became even stronger.
The king tried to silence God’s Word.
But heaven simply wrote it again.
This story is not just about an ancient king.
It is about the human heart.
Because many people today do something very similar.
They do not literally burn Scripture.
But they remove the parts they don’t want to hear.
They ignore the warnings.
They avoid conviction.
They reshape God’s message until it feels comfortable.
But truth does not change because we dislike it.
God’s Word is not fragile.
It does not depend on human approval.
Kings may reject it.
Cultures may mock it.
Generations may ignore it.
But what God speaks remains true.
Jehoiakim thought destroying the scroll gave him control.
But history shows the opposite.
Judah fell.
Babylon came.
Jerusalem was devastated.
And the king who burned God’s warning could not escape the consequences of ignoring it.
The fire in the brazier did not stop the fire of judgment.
There is a powerful lesson here.
Sometimes the most dangerous moment in a person’s life is when they hear God’s Word clearly—and still refuse to respond.
Not ignorance.
Not confusion.
But conscious rejection.
Jehoiakim heard the message.
He understood the warning.
And he chose contempt.
Yet even in this story, we see something incredible about God.
God did not owe Judah another warning.
But He sent one.
The scroll was written again.
The message returned.
That reveals something about the heart of God.
He continues to speak—even after people resist Him.
Warnings are not cruelty.
They are mercy.
Conviction is not condemnation.
It is an invitation to turn before it is too late.
So the question this story leaves us with is simple but serious.
What do we do when God’s Word confronts us?
Do we humble ourselves?
Or do we quietly cut away the parts we do not want to obey?
Because rejecting truth does not remove accountability.
Ignoring God does not silence Him.
And burning the scroll does not stop the message.
Three lines from this story should stay with us:

You can burn the scroll.
But you cannot burn the truth.

You can silence the messenger.
But you cannot silence God.

You can reject the warning.
But you cannot escape the consequences.
Jehoiakim tried to destroy the message.
But thousands of years later…
We are still reading it.
The scroll survived.
The Word remained.
And the lesson still speaks.

📖 Jeremiah 36:23–24
"And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire… yet they were not afraid."

Reflection Question:
If God confronted your life with a truth today, would you receive it… or would you try to burn the scroll?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 450 prophets screaming.
paragraphs: 450 prophets screaming.
One prophet praying.
And an altar drowning in water.
That’s where the fire of God fell.

Mount Carmel was not just a mountain that day.
It was a courtroom.
Israel had been limping between two opinions for years.

They claimed to know the God of Abraham…
but their hearts bowed to Baal, the so-called storm god worshiped by the surrounding nations.

King Ahab allowed it.
Queen Jezebel promoted it.
The nation followed it.
And heaven went silent.

For three years and six months there was no rain on the land (1 Kings 17:1; James 5:17).
The drought was not random.
It was a direct confrontation.
Because Baal was supposed to control rain.
Yet the skies stayed shut.
Why?
Because the Lord was exposing a lie.
So God sent His prophet.
Elijah walked onto Mount Carmel and spoke words that still echo through history:

“How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.”
— 1 Kings 18:21
The people said nothing.
Silence is often the language of a divided heart.
Then Elijah proposed the challenge.

Two altars.
Two sacrifices.
No fire.
“The god who answers by fire — He is God.” (1 Kings 18:24)
The crowd agreed.
The prophets of Baal went first.
From morning until noon they cried out.
“Baal, answer us!”
Nothing.

They danced around the altar.
Nothing.
Elijah even mocked them:
“Maybe your god is deep in thought… or traveling… or sleeping!” (1 Kings 18:27)
Still nothing.
So the prophets escalated.
They cut themselves with swords and spears — a common pagan ritual meant to attract divine attention.
Blood ran down their arms.
They screamed.
They begged.
They performed.
The Bible says they raved until evening.
But the verdict was clear:

“There was no voice. No one answered. No one paid attention.”
— 1 Kings 18:29
That line alone exposes every false god humanity has ever trusted.
Money cannot answer.
Fame cannot answer.
Pleasure cannot answer.
Power cannot answer.
Idols always demand everything…
and return silence.
Then Elijah stepped forward.
No theatrics.
No self-harm.
Just faith.
First, he rebuilt the altar of the Lord, which had been torn down (1 Kings 18:30).
Twelve stones.
One for each tribe of Israel.
A reminder that this was not just Elijah’s God.
This was the covenant God of the nation.
Then Elijah made the miracle even harder.
He poured water on the sacrifice.
Once.
Twice.
Three times.

The altar was soaked.
The trench around it filled with water.
In human terms, it was impossible for fire to start.
But Elijah wanted everyone to know something:
When God moves, no one can mistake it.
Then the prophet prayed.
Not a long prayer.
Not dramatic.
Just simple faith.

“Answer me, O Lord, answer me, that this people may know that you, O Lord, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back.”
— 1 Kings 18:37
And immediately…
fire fell.
Not a spark.
Not a small flame.
The Bible says the fire of the Lord consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the dust, and even the water in the trench (1 Kings 18:38).
Heaven answered.
The crowd fell face down.
And they cried out:
“The Lord, He is God! The Lord, He is God!” (1 Kings 18:39)
That was the real victory of Mount Carmel.
Not just fire.
But hearts turning back.
And that’s where this story collides with us today.
Because Baal didn’t disappear.
He just changed names.
Today Baal looks like success.
Baal looks like lust.
Baal looks like approval.
Baal looks like money.
Baal looks like anything we trust more than God.
Modern idols don’t stand in temples.
They sit in our pockets.
They live in our ambitions.
They whisper lies that sound like freedom.
But they never answer.
Never save.
Never satisfy.
Only God answers by fire.
And the greatest fire God ever sent wasn’t on Mount Carmel.
It was at the cross.
Because our hearts were the broken altars.
Our sins were the sacrifice.
And Jesus stepped into the place we deserved.
On the cross, Christ took the judgment for every idol we have ever loved more than God.
Then three days later…
God answered again.
Not with fire.
But with an empty tomb.
The resurrection declared to the world:
Jesus Christ alone is Lord.
So the question of Elijah still stands.
Not on Mount Carmel.
But in your heart.
How long will you limp between two opinions?
If the Lord is God…
follow Him.
No divided heart.
No half devotion.
No secret idols.
Just surrender.
Because when the true God shows up, fake gods fall.
Always.
And grace still calls wandering hearts home.
Someone you know might be standing on their own Mount Carmel today.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He was eighty-five years old… and he asked for the mountain.
paragraphs: He was eighty-five years old… and he asked for the mountain.
Read that again.

Not a chair.
Not a quiet corner.
Not a peaceful retirement.
A mountain.
And not just any mountain.
The one filled with giants.
That moment is recorded in Book of Joshua 14:12, when Caleb stood before Joshua and made one of the boldest declarations in Scripture:

“Now therefore give me this mountain, of which the LORD spoke in that day; for you heard in that day how the Anakim were there, and that the cities were great and fortified. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall be able to drive them out as the LORD said.”
But to feel the weight of those words… you have to rewind the story.
Forty-Five Years of Waiting
Forty-five years earlier, Caleb was not eighty-five.
He was forty.
In Book of Numbers 13, Moses sent twelve spies into the Promised Land.
They saw abundance.
They saw fortified cities.
They saw giants.
Ten spies came back shaking.
They said, “We cannot attack these people; they are stronger than we are.”
Fear spread through the camp like wildfire.
But two men stood against the tide.

Caleb…
and Joshua.
Caleb silenced the crowd and declared:
“We should go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly do it.” (Numbers 13:30)
Not because Israel was powerful.
But because God had spoken.
The Price of Faith
Faith has a cost.
Israel refused to trust God.
They chose fear instead.
Because of that rebellion, the entire generation wandered in the wilderness for forty years.
Everyone who doubted God’s promise died in the desert.
Everyone…
except two men.
Joshua.
And Caleb.
God said Caleb had “a different spirit” and followed Him fully (Numbers 14:24).
But here is what many people forget:
Caleb still had to wait.
Forty years wandering.
Five more years fighting when Israel finally entered the land.
Forty-five years… holding onto a promise.
Most People Lose the Fire
Think about it.
Forty-five years.
Dreams fade that long.
Vision fades.
Strength fades.
But Caleb’s faith did not fade.
When the land was finally being divided, Caleb stepped forward.
Wrinkles on his face.
Gray in his beard.
Scars from battles.
But the fire inside him was still alive.
He told Joshua:

“I am this day eighty-five years old.
Yet I am as strong this day as on the day that Moses sent me.” (Joshua 14:10–11)
Then came the line that echoes through history.
“Now therefore give me this mountain.”
The Mountain of Giants
The mountain Caleb requested was Hebron.
The territory of the Anakim — the giant warriors that once terrified Israel.
Most people would avoid that place.
Caleb asked for it.
He didn’t want the easiest land.
He wanted the place where God’s promise would be proven.
Because faith does not run from giants.
Faith walks straight toward them with God.
The Secret of Caleb’s Strength
Notice something powerful in his words.
Caleb did not brag about his strength.
He didn’t say, “I can defeat them.”
He said:
“If the LORD will be with me… I shall drive them out.” (Joshua 14:12)
That is the heart of biblical courage.
Not confidence in self.
Confidence in God’s presence.
The Gospel Behind the Mountain
Caleb’s story is not just about bravery.
It points us to something deeper.
The greatest giants are not the Anakim.
They are sin, death, and judgment.
No human strength can defeat them.
But Jesus Christ did.
At the cross, Jesus faced the greatest mountain humanity could never climb.
Sin.
Shame.
The wrath of God against evil.
And He conquered it.
Three days later, the empty tomb proved that the greatest giant had fallen.
Because of Jesus:

• Sin can be forgiven
• Shame can be erased
• Broken lives can be restored
• Eternal life is offered freely to those who repent and believe
The victory Caleb experienced in the land points forward to the greater victory of Christ.
A Question for You
What mountain has God placed before you?
Is it obedience you keep delaying?
A sin you keep hiding?
A calling you keep ignoring?
Many people spend their lives waiting for a valley.
But God sometimes calls His people to mountains.
Difficult places.
Impossible places.
Places where His power will be seen.
Faith Doesn’t Retire
Our culture worships comfort.
God calls for courage.
Caleb reminds us that faith does not expire with age.
You are never too old to trust God.
Never too broken to start again.
Never too late to step into what God promised.
Because when the Lord is with you…
giants fall.
Remind them of Caleb.
Remind them of the God who keeps His promises.
And remember:
Don’t retire your faith.
Ask God for the mountain.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They almost killed Him… in church.
paragraphs: They almost killed Him… in church.

Not in the streets.
Not in a battlefield.
In a place where Scripture was read.
And that should disturb you.
Because the same spirit still lives today.

You can sit in the presence of truth…
and still resist it.

You can hear Jesus…
and still want Him gone.

Not out loud.
But in your heart.
Look again at that moment.
“All those in the synagogue, when they heard these things, were filled with wrath… and led Him to the brow of the hill… that they might throw Him down over the cliff.”
Pause.
These weren’t outsiders.

These were listeners.
Regulars.
People who knew the sound of Scripture.

They didn’t explode when Jesus healed.
They didn’t react when He spoke kindly.
They snapped when He exposed them.
That’s the tension.
We love a Jesus who comforts.
We struggle with a Jesus who confronts.

We celebrate grace…
until grace demands repentance.

We post verses…
until those verses point at us.
And suddenly…

The same lips that say “Amen”
start whispering, “Too much.”
Let me ask you something that might shake you:
What part of Jesus are you secretly resisting?
Is it His call to forgive someone who hurt you?
“For if you forgive others… your heavenly Father will also forgive you.”
Is it His command to walk away from a hidden sin?
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification…”
Is it His authority over your plans, your desires, your control?
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily…”
Because here’s the truth we don’t like to say out loud:
Sometimes we don’t reject Jesus completely.
We just try to push Him to the edge.
That’s what Nazareth did.

They didn’t deny He spoke well.
They didn’t deny His power.
They just refused His authority.

They wanted inspiration…
not surrender.

They wanted miracles…
not transformation.

They wanted a Savior…
but not a Lord.
And before you point at them—
Look inward.
Because pride doesn’t always shout.

Sometimes it sits quietly in church…
arms crossed…
heart closed.

Sometimes it sings worship songs
while resisting conviction.

Sometimes it looks holy on the outside
but is negotiating obedience on the inside.
That is the most dangerous place to be.
Close to Jesus.
But unmoved by Him.
Here’s the weight of it:
Their anger wasn’t random.
Jesus confronted their assumption that they deserved special favor.
He reminded them that God’s grace reached outsiders.
That stung their pride.
Some scholars interpret this moment as a direct challenge to religious entitlement—Jesus exposing the human tendency to think we are “worthy” while others are not.
And that exposure triggered rage.
Because pride doesn’t like being dethroned.
But don’t miss this.
Don’t miss this.
Jesus walked away from that cliff.
“But passing through the midst of them, He went away.”
Why?
Because it wasn’t time.
The cross was still ahead.
And when that time came…
He didn’t walk away.
He walked toward it.
That’s the Gospel.

The same Jesus they tried to throw away
chose to be lifted up on a cross.
Not forced.
Willing.
“No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord.”
He took the rejection.
He absorbed the wrath.
He carried the sin—not just of violent crowds—
But of quiet resistance.
Of hidden pride.
Of selective obedience.
Of hearts that say, “I’ll follow You… but only this far.”
And this is where everything turns.
Because the story doesn’t end at the cliff.
It ends at an empty tomb.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when we were fully surrendered.
Not when we had it all together.
While we were still resisting Him.
That means this:
Even if you’ve been pushing Jesus to the edges of your life…
He is still reaching for you.
Even if you’ve been avoiding the parts of truth that confront you…
Grace is still calling your name.
Even if pride has been sitting on the throne of your heart…
There is still a King who invites you to step down—and be free.
This is your moment.
Not to admire Jesus.
Not to analyze Him.
But to surrender.
Fully.
No conditions.
No hidden corners.
No “except this part.”
Because partial surrender is still resistance.
Let Him be Lord.
Not just Savior.
Let Him confront you.
Not to shame you—
But to free you.
Because every command of Christ is not a cage.
It’s a key.
So here’s the question that won’t leave you:
Are you drawing closer to Jesus…
Or quietly pushing Him away?
Stop.
Pray.
Be honest.
“Jesus, I surrender the part of me that resists You.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t reject Jesus.
paragraphs:
He didn’t reject Jesus.
He just said… “later.”
And that was enough to lose everything.

You think delay is harmless.
You think you still have time.
But what if “later” is the most dangerous word your soul has ever whispered?

What if the greatest threat to your calling is not rebellion—
but hesitation dressed as wisdom?
Stay with me.
Because this is where many fall… quietly.
There’s a man in Scripture who almost followed Jesus.
Almost.

Not a criminal.
Not a blasphemer.
Not a mocker.
Just… not ready yet.
“Lord, I will follow thee; but let me first go bid them farewell…” — Luke 9:61
Sounds reasonable, right?

Family matters.
Closure.
Timing.
But heaven saw something deeper.
A divided heart.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable.

Because that man…
might be you.
You say:

“I’ll fully surrender after I fix my life.”
“I’ll let go of that sin when I’m stronger.”
“I’ll commit to God when things calm down.”
But things never calm down.

Sin never politely waits its turn.
And your heart?
It doesn’t stay neutral.
It hardens.

Slowly.
Silently.
Dangerously.
Let me say it plainly:
Delayed obedience is disobedience in disguise.
And it feels spiritual.
It sounds wise.
But it’s deadly.
Jesus didn’t comfort the man’s delay.
He confronted it.
“No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.” — Luke 9:62
Sharp.
Unfiltered.
Full of mercy.
Because Jesus sees what we refuse to admit:
You cannot follow Him while negotiating your surrender.

Some scholars interpret this passage as a warning against divided loyalty—
that looking back represents a heart still tied to the old life.
And if that’s true…
Then “later” is not about time.
It’s about attachment.
Let’s get honest.
What are you still holding on to?

A relationship God already told you to release?
A secret sin you’ve learned to hide well?
A version of your life where you stay in control?
You want Jesus…
But not at the cost of everything.
That tension?
That’s the battlefield of your soul.
Because Jesus is not asking to be part of your life.
He is calling you to surrender it.
Completely.
And here’s the truth most people avoid:
Every “later” makes your heart less responsive to God.

Conviction fades.
Sensitivity dulls.
Compromise normalizes.
Until one day…
You don’t feel anything anymore.
That’s how people drift.
Not with a loud “no.”
But with a quiet, repeated… “not yet.”
But listen carefully.
This is not where the story ends.
Because Jesus doesn’t just warn.
He rescues.
The same Christ who spoke those hard words…
Walked toward a cross for people like us.

For the hesitant.
For the double-minded.
For those who delayed, denied, and ran.
Scripture says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not when you were ready.
Not when you were consistent.
Not when you stopped saying “later.”
While you were still in it.
That’s grace.

Unearned.
Undeserved.
Unstoppable.
And through His death and resurrection, Jesus made a way.
A real way.

Not self-improvement.
Not behavior management.
But transformation.
Sin is real.
It separates us from God.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
And the cost is serious.
“For the wages of sin is death…” — Romans 6:23
But the verse doesn’t end there.
“…but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” — Romans 6:23
That’s the Gospel.
Not “try harder.”
Not “come back later.”
But:

Repent.
Return.
Receive.
Now.
You don’t clean yourself up first.
You come as you are.

Broken.
Conflicted.
Honest.
And you surrender.
Because Jesus didn’t say, “Follow me when you’re ready.”
He said:
“Follow me.” — Matthew 9:9
Immediate.
Personal.
Non-negotiable.
So let me ask you something—no filters, no excuses:
How many times have you said “later” to God?
And what has it cost you?

Peace?
Clarity?
Intimacy with Him?
You feel it, don’t you?
That quiet nudge.
That tension in your chest.
That whisper saying:
“Come back.”
That’s not guilt trying to crush you.
That’s grace trying to wake you.
Today is not random.
This moment is not accidental.
You are being invited.
Again.
Not to religion.
Not to performance.
But to a Person.
Jesus Christ.
And He is not asking for perfection.
He is asking for surrender.
So stop looking back.
Stop negotiating.
Stop delaying what your soul already knows.
Come now.
Not tomorrow.
Not when it’s convenient.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.
Pray this in your heart if you mean it:

“Lord Jesus, I’ve been saying ‘later.’
But today, I surrender.
Forgive my sin.
Change my heart.
Teach me to follow You fully.
Right now.”
If this hit you—
Sit in it.
Respond to it.
Move.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)
