title: You can look strong…
paragraphs:
You can look strong…
and still be silently breaking inside.

Because sometimes the loudest pain…
is the one nobody hears.
You’ve mastered the smile.

You say “I’m okay.”
You say “God is good.”
You say “I’m blessed.”
But deep down?
You’re tired of pretending.

Tired of editing your prayers so they sound acceptable.
Tired of filtering your emotions so you don’t look weak.
Tired of carrying questions you’re scared to say out loud.
And here’s the tension—

What if the version of you that people admire…
is the version of you that God never asked for?

What if your polished faith
is actually hiding your honest heart?
Job didn’t play that game.
He lost everything.

Children.
Health.
Security.
Peace.
And when the weight of it crushed him…
He didn’t perform.
He didn’t sanitize his words.
He didn’t pretend everything made sense.
He cried.

Loud.
Unfiltered.
Uncomfortable.
“Why did I not perish at birth?” (Job 3:11)
That’s not a Sunday-school prayer.
That’s a shattered man speaking truth in the presence of God.
And here’s what should shake you—
God did not silence him.
God did not reject him.
God listened.
Let that confront you.
Because some of us have been taught that real faith sounds clean.
But Scripture shows us that real faith sounds honest.
“The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.” (Psalm 34:18)
Not the polished.
Not the perfect.
The broken.
The crushed.
The ones who don’t have the strength to fake it anymore.
Some scholars interpret Job’s cries as bordering on complaint, even wrestling dangerously close to accusation.
But here’s the weight of it—
God still called Job “blameless and upright” (Job 1:8).
Meaning this:
Your honesty does not disqualify you.
It might actually be the evidence that your relationship with God is real.
But let’s go deeper.
Because Job’s story exposes something in us.

We are more comfortable performing before people
than being real before God.

We fear looking weak in front of others
more than we fear living fake before the Lord.
That’s pride.
And pride will suffocate your soul slowly, quietly, convincingly.
It tells you:

“Keep it together.”
“Don’t let them see.”
“Don’t say that to God.”
But pride cannot heal you.
It can only hide you.
And what is hidden cannot be transformed.
Here’s the turning point—
Job’s story doesn’t end in despair.
But it also doesn’t resolve because Job figured everything out.
It resolves because God revealed Himself.
And this is where the Gospel explodes into the story.
Because Job points forward to Someone greater.
Jesus Christ.
Unlike Job, Jesus was truly innocent.
Yet He suffered more deeply than any human ever could.
Not just physically.
But spiritually.
On the cross, Jesus cried out:
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46)
Do you see it?

The Son of God Himself
entered the place of honest anguish.
Not as rebellion—
But as redemption.
He took on our sin.

Our hidden shame.
Our silent struggles.
Our unspoken questions.
“God made Him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” (2 Corinthians 5:21)
This is the Gospel:
You don’t need to perform your way to God.
Jesus already paid your way to Him.

Your sin—paid.
Your shame—covered.
Your brokenness—not rejected, but pursued.
But here’s the part you cannot skip—

Grace is free.
But it is not cheap.
It calls you to come as you are…
and to leave transformed.
Repentance is not pretending you’re okay.
It’s admitting you’re not—
and turning fully to Christ.

Not halfway.
Not filtered.
Fully.
Because partial surrender is still hidden pride.
And God is not after your performance.
He is after your heart.
The real one.
The messy one.
The one you’ve been trying to clean up before showing Him.
Listen carefully—
God already sees it.
And still invites you closer.
So stop editing your prayers.
Stop pretending in His presence.
Stop hiding behind spiritual language while your soul is bleeding.
Bring Him your real heart.
Say it.

“Lord, I’m tired.”
“Lord, I’m confused.”
“Lord, I’m struggling.”
“Lord, I need You.”
That is not weakness.
That is worship.
Because worship is not perfection.
It is surrender.
Right here.
Right now.
You don’t need another motivational quote.
You need an encounter with Jesus.
So let me ask you—
What are you still hiding from God?
What prayer have you been too afraid to say?
What pain have you been disguising as strength?
Bring it into the light.
Today.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.
Because healing begins where honesty lives.
And grace flows where pride dies.
Sit with it.
Respond to it.
Let God meet you in it.
Type “OPEN MY HEART” if you’re done pretending.
And if this stirred something deep in your spirit…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He was on his knees…
paragraphs:
He was on his knees…
and heaven was already standing.
Because this is where most people get it wrong.
They think Paul lost.
They think the sword won.
They think suffering means defeat.

But what if the moment that looked like failure…
was actually the loudest victory heaven ever heard?
Let’s get honest.
Some of you are living in quiet shame right now.
Not public.
Not obvious.
But deep.
Hidden.

You smile in church…
but inside, you replay your past like a courtroom that never adjourns.

The words.
The choices.
The compromise.
The secret sin no one else knows.
And it whispers:

“You’ve gone too far.”
“You had your chance.”
“God may forgive others… but not you.”
Paul would understand that voice.
Because before he was a preacher…
He was a persecutor.
Not just a sinner.
A violent enemy of the Church.
“Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.” — Acts 8:3
That’s not a mistake.
That’s a pattern.
That’s not weakness.
That’s destruction.
He didn’t accidentally oppose Jesus…
He hunted His people.
Imagine the weight of that.

The faces he saw dragged away.
The cries he ignored.
The blood he approved.
If anyone had a reason to live in permanent shame…
It was Paul.
But then—
Everything shattered.
On a road to Damascus, breathing threats and violence…
Jesus showed up.
Not with applause.
Not with approval.
But with truth.
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?” — Acts 9:4
And in that moment…
Paul realized something terrifying—and beautiful:
His sin wasn’t just against people.
It was against Christ.
Here’s where most people expect the story to end.

Judgment.
Condemnation.
Final rejection.
But Jesus does something scandalous.
He doesn’t destroy Paul.
He calls him.
This is the part religion struggles to explain.
Because religion says:
“Fix yourself, then come.”
But Jesus says:
“Come… and I will fix what you cannot.”
Paul later writes this, and you can feel the weight behind every word:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners—of whom I am the foremost.” — 1 Timothy 1:15
Did you catch that?
Not “I was.”
“I am.”

Even as an apostle…
he never forgot who he had been.
Not to stay in shame—
But to magnify grace.

Some scholars interpret Paul’s words here as a posture of ongoing humility, not self-condemnation—he wasn’t denying transformation, but declaring that apart from Christ, he still recognized his deep need for grace.
Now look back at the execution ground.

Chains on his wrists.
Sword in the air.
Dust rising.
Soldiers watching.
This is the end… right?
No.
This is the evidence.
Because a man like Paul does not face death like that unless something—no, Someone—has completely rewritten him.
Listen to his final declaration:
“I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” — 2 Timothy 4:7
That’s not denial.
That’s not delusion.
That’s certainty.
Here’s the truth that will break chains if you let it:
Paul was not confident in himself.
He was confident in Christ.
Because the Gospel is not:
“Try harder.”
“Do better.”
“Be worthy.”
The Gospel is this:

You are a sinner.
You cannot save yourself.
Your past is real.
Your guilt is justified.
But—
Jesus Christ stepped into your place.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not when you improved.
Not when you cleaned up.
While you were still in it.
On the cross, Jesus absorbed the full weight of sin—
Not partially.
Not temporarily.
Completely.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
Read that again.
No condemnation.
Not less condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
None.
So when Paul knelt before that sword…
He wasn’t thinking:
“I hope I did enough.”
He knew:
“Jesus already did.”
And that changes everything.
Because your story is not defined by your worst moment.
It is defined by what you do with Jesus.
So let me ask you—honestly:

What are you still carrying…
that Jesus already paid for?

The addiction?
The hidden habit?
The regret?
The identity built on failure?
Why are you holding onto chains…
that have already been broken?
This is your moment.
Not to perform.
Not to pretend.
But to surrender.
Repent.
That doesn’t mean just feeling bad.
It means turning.
Agreeing with God about your sin—and choosing His way over yours.
Come to Jesus.
Not later.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.
Because the same grace that stopped Paul on the road…
Is reaching for you in this very moment.
You are not too far gone.
You are not too broken.
You are not the exception to grace.
You are the reason grace exists.
If this hit your heart—
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re not unqualified.
paragraphs: You’re not unqualified.
You’re exposed.
And that terrifies you.
Because deep down… you know the truth.

If people really saw your thoughts, your habits, your hidden cycles—
they wouldn’t call you “chosen.”
They would walk away.

So you try harder.
Act cleaner.
Speak nicer.
Serve louder.
But inside?
You feel like a fraud.
And here’s the tension you don’t want to admit:

What if the reason you feel unworthy…
is because you actually are?

What if your weakness isn’t just insecurity—
but evidence of something broken?

Not just mistakes.
Sin.

Not just failure.
Rebellion.
And no amount of self-improvement can fix that.

This is where most people stop reading.
Because this is where it gets uncomfortable.
But stay.
Because this is where grace begins to breathe.
We live in a world obsessed with qualification.

Degrees.
Status.
Platforms.
Perfection.
Even in church, we quietly believe:

“God uses the strong.”
“God uses the clean.”
“God uses the consistent.”
But Scripture interrupts that illusion.
Hard.
“But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong.” — 1 Corinthians 1:27
Read that again.
God didn’t accidentally use the weak.
He chose them.
Intentionally.
On purpose.
Why?

So no one can stand before Him and say,
“I did this.”
So no one can take His glory and wear it like a crown.
Your weakness is not a disqualification.
It is the stage where God makes His power undeniable.
Look at the pattern.

Moses—afraid, insecure, slow of speech (Exodus 4:10).
David—forgotten in the field, then later broken by sin (2 Samuel 11).
Rahab—a woman marked by a past she couldn’t erase (Joshua 2).
Peter—bold with his mouth, weak in his loyalty (Luke 22:61–62).
Paul—a man who hunted Christians before becoming one (1 Timothy 1:13).
These are not side characters.
These are central figures in God’s story.

And every one of them had a reason to say,
“God, I’m not the one.”
But God doesn’t build His kingdom with flawless people.
He builds it with surrendered ones.
Here’s the part we must not skip.
Their weakness wasn’t the point.
Their repentance was.
Because God does not excuse sin.
He redeems sinners who turn back to Him.
“Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.” — Proverbs 28:13
Did you catch that?

Confess.
Forsake.

Not hide.
Not justify.
Not rename.
This is where many want grace… without surrender.
Forgiveness… without repentance.

But the Gospel is not God saying,
“You’re fine as you are.”

It’s God saying,
“You’re not okay—but I love you too much to leave you there.”
And this is where Jesus steps in.

Not as a motivational speaker.
Not as a life coach.
But as Savior.
Because your biggest problem is not your insecurity.
It’s your sin.
And sin separates you from God.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
That includes you.
That includes me.
No exceptions.
But God didn’t leave us in that condition.
He entered it.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not after you fixed yourself.
Not after you became consistent.
While you were still broken.
Still failing.
Still hiding.
Jesus stepped onto the cross and took your place.

Your shame.
Your guilt.
Your punishment.
All of it.
“So that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
That is not behavior modification.
That is transformation.

From guilty… to forgiven.
From lost… to found.
From dead… to alive.
Not because you qualified yourself.
But because Christ qualified you through His sacrifice.
So what do you do now?
You stop performing.
And you start surrendering.
You stop hiding.
And you start confessing.
You stop trying to earn what can only be received.
“Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out.” — Acts 3:19
Repentance is not shame.
It is the doorway to freedom.
It’s not God pushing you away.
It’s God calling you home.
Listen carefully.
Your past is real.
Your sin is serious.
But it is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
Not even close.
Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20).
That doesn’t mean you take sin lightly.
It means you take Jesus seriously.
So if you feel unqualified…
Good.
That means you’re finally seeing clearly.
Now bring that honesty to Christ.
Not later.
Not when you feel better.
Now.
Tell Him the truth.
All of it.
And watch what He does with surrendered weakness.
Respond.
Type “OPEN MY HEART” if you’re ready to stop hiding and start surrendering.
Come back to it when the lies return.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She was already dead.
paragraphs: She was already dead.
And everyone in the room knew it.

No pulse.
No breath.
No hope.
But Peter didn’t panic.
That’s the part we skip too fast.
Because when you stand in a room filled with loss—real loss, not theory—you either perform… or you fall to your knees.
Peter chose the floor.
Why?
Because he knew something we forget when shame is loud and failure feels final.

There are moments where talking won’t fix it.
Explaining won’t fix it.
Trying harder won’t fix it.
Some things only move… when God moves.
Acts 9 doesn’t give us a polished miracle story. It gives us tension.

Widows crying.
Clothes in their hands—evidence of Tabitha’s kindness.
A body laid still in an upper room.
And then Peter walks in—not as a hero—but as a desperate man who knows his limits.
He sends them all out.
Silence fills the room.
And then—
He kneels.
Let that sink in.
Before resurrection came… surrender came first.
Before power was displayed… dependence was chosen.
Before the miracle… there was a man admitting, “God, if You don’t move, nothing will.”
That’s where many of us break.
Because we don’t like that place.
We like control.
We like looking strong.
We like hiding the fact that inside, something in us has already died.

Dead passion.
Dead purity.
Dead prayer life.
Dead hunger for God.
And we cover it up with activity, with church language, with filtered faith.
But God is not moved by performance.
He is drawn to surrender.
“But Peter put them all outside, knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, ‘Tabitha, arise.’ And she opened her eyes…” — Acts 9:40
Don’t miss it.
He didn’t start with the miracle.
He started with God.
Some scholars interpret this moment as Peter intentionally following the pattern of Jesus in Mark 5:40–41—removing the noise, creating space, depending fully on the Father.
Because real power is not imitation.
It’s connection.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Tabitha wasn’t raised because she was famous.
She was known for good works. Quiet service. Hidden love.
And yet—even she died.
Let that confront us.
Faithfulness does not exempt you from broken moments.
You can serve, love, give… and still face loss.
So what do you do when your life doesn’t match your obedience?
When you did right… but it still fell apart?
When you prayed… but it still died?
This is where shame creeps in.

“Maybe I failed God.”
“Maybe I’m not enough.”
“Maybe this is the end.”
But hear this clearly:
Death is not always the end of the story.
Not when Jesus is involved.
Because the same Jesus who empowered Peter in that room is the One who walked into our greatest problem—sin—and didn’t just visit it…
He carried it.
We weren’t just struggling.
We were spiritually dead.
“...you were dead in your trespasses and sins…” — Ephesians 2:1
Not weak.
Dead.
No ability to fix ourselves. No power to resurrect our own hearts.
But Jesus didn’t stand at a distance.
He stepped in.

He lived the life we couldn’t live.
Died the death we deserved.
Took the weight of sin, shame, and judgment on the cross.
And then—
He rose.
Not metaphorically.
Literally.
“Christ died for our sins… He was buried… He was raised on the third day…” — 1 Corinthians 15:3–4
That changes everything.
Because now, resurrection is not just something God does.
It’s who He is.
So when Peter said, “Tabitha, arise,” it wasn’t Peter’s power.
It was borrowed authority from a risen Savior.
And that same Jesus is still speaking today.
Not just to dead bodies.
But to dead hearts.
To hidden shame.
To secret sin you thought no one knew.
To that quiet failure you buried under “I’m fine.”
And He’s not shouting condemnation.
He’s calling you.
To rise.
But notice—Tabitha didn’t raise herself.
She responded.
That’s where repentance comes in.
Not behavior management.
Not trying harder.
Turning.
From sin. From self. From control.
And trusting fully in Jesus.
That’s where grace meets you.
Not when you clean yourself up.
But when you finally admit you can’t.
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” — James 4:6
Pride says, “I got this.”
Humility says, “Lord, I need You.”
And that’s the turning point.
That’s where life begins again.
So let me ask you—honestly:
What in your life feels dead right now?

Your prayer life?
Your purity?
Your calling?
Your closeness with God?
Don’t dress it up.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because the same Christ who raised from the grave is not intimidated by your condition.
He’s inviting you out of it.
Today.
Right now.
Not after you fix yourself.
Now.
Kneel before you speak.
Surrender before you strive.
Call on Him before you quit.
And watch what God does with what you thought was over.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most people think the Pharisees were condemned because they were openly sinful.
paragraphs: Most people think the Pharisees were condemned because they were openly sinful.
But that is not the truth.
The Pharisees were condemned because they looked holy while loving applause more than God.

They prayed.
They taught Scripture.
They fasted.
They followed religious rules with extreme discipline.
From the outside, they looked like the most devoted people in society.
But Jesus saw something deeper.
He saw the hidden hunger inside their hearts.
They didn’t just want to serve God.
They wanted people to notice them serving God.

They loved the important seats in public gatherings.
They loved the respectful greetings in marketplaces.
They loved the titles that made people admire them.
And slowly, without realizing it, their desire for recognition replaced their desire for righteousness.
That is the lesson the Pharisees teach us.
And it is far more relevant today than most people realize.
Because human nature has not changed.
Even in spiritual spaces, the heart can begin craving something dangerous:
Recognition.

We want to be seen as wise.
We want to be seen as faithful.
We want to be seen as spiritual.
But when the desire to appear righteous becomes stronger than the desire to be righteous, the soul begins to drift.
This is why Jesus spoke some of His strongest warnings to the Pharisees.
Not because they rejected religion.
But because they turned religion into a performance.
They polished the outside of the cup.
But inside, pride was growing quietly.
And that warning still echoes today.
Because a person can know Scripture and still crave admiration.
A person can serve in ministry and still secretly hope people notice them.
A person can speak about humility while silently enjoying the praise that follows.
And here is the uncomfortable truth:
Public praise can slowly replace private purity.
At first it feels harmless.
Someone compliments your faith.
Someone applauds your leadership.
Someone admires your wisdom.
But if the heart is not guarded, something subtle happens.
You begin feeding on that applause.
And when that happens, the motivation slowly shifts.
You are no longer serving God alone.
You are serving the image of being admired.
The Pharisees remind us that spiritual pride often wears religious clothing.
It speaks the right language.
It stands in the right places.
It performs the right actions.
But beneath the surface, the heart is craving something other than God.
And Jesus exposed that reality.
He said they loved human praise more than the praise that comes from God.
Think about that for a moment.
They preferred the approval of people over the approval of heaven.
And that is a terrifying exchange.
Because human applause is loud, but it fades quickly.
God’s approval is quiet, but it lasts forever.
The Pharisees built reputations that impressed crowds.
But Jesus looked straight through the reputation and saw the heart.
And that is the part of this story that should humble all of us.
Because the temptation to perform spiritually still exists.
Especially in a world where everything can be seen.
Where platforms are public.
Where faith can be displayed.
Where recognition can come instantly.
It is possible to build a public image of devotion while neglecting the private place where God actually shapes a person.
But God is not looking for impressive appearances.
He is looking for surrendered hearts.
He is not impressed by titles.
He is not moved by public recognition.
He looks at what happens when no one is watching.
When the crowd is gone.
When the spotlight disappears.
When the only audience left is heaven.
That is where real faith lives.
The Pharisees teach us a lesson that every believer must wrestle with:
It is possible to look close to God while being far from Him.
That is why humility matters.
That is why secret prayer matters.
That is why obedience in hidden places matters.
Because the truest faith is not the one that attracts applause.
The truest faith is the one that would still obey God even if nobody noticed.
Even if nobody praised it.
Even if nobody celebrated it.
Because at the end of the day, one question matters more than every title, compliment, or reputation.
Not:
“Did people admire me?”
But:
“Was God pleased with my heart?”
The Pharisees chased admiration.
But Jesus calls us to something deeper.
Not performance.
Not reputation.
Not applause.
But quiet, genuine surrender.
And the people God trusts the most are often not the ones standing in the brightest spotlight.
They are the ones faithfully walking with Him in the shadows where only God can see.
Because the greatest reward is not public praise.
The greatest reward is hearing God say:
“Well done.”
Scripture

Matthew 23:5–7
“Everything they do is done for people to see…”
Engagement Question
Be honest:
Have you ever caught yourself wanting recognition for doing something spiritual?
Let's talk about it below.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most people believe great victories require great numbers.
paragraphs: Most people believe great victories require great numbers.

A large army.
A powerful leader.
Overwhelming strength.
But one of the most powerful moments in Scripture began with something very different.
Just two men.

In 1 Samuel 14, Israel was paralyzed with fear. The Philistines had superior weapons, superior numbers, and superior military power. Israel’s army was hiding in caves, trembling, discouraged, and unsure of what to do.
Even King Saul, the leader of the nation, was sitting under a tree with his soldiers, waiting.

Waiting for a plan.
Waiting for courage.
Waiting for something to change.
But Jonathan, Saul’s son, saw the moment differently.
Instead of staring at the problem, he looked at the power of God.
And without announcing it to the entire army, Jonathan turned to his armor bearer and said something that reveals the heart of true faith:

“Come, let’s go over to the outpost of those uncircumcised men. Perhaps the Lord will act in our behalf. Nothing can hinder the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few.”
— 1 Samuel 14:6
Think about that.

Jonathan did not say, “We have the numbers.”
He did not say, “We are stronger.”
He said something far deeper.
God is not limited by numbers.
This is the lesson.
So many people delay obedience because they believe they need more support before they can move.

More people.
More approval.
More resources.
More certainty.
But Jonathan teaches us that faith does not wait for the crowd.
Faith moves when it knows God is able.
Notice something powerful about Jonathan’s words.
He says, “Perhaps the Lord will act.”
That statement is not doubt.
It is humility.
Jonathan was not arrogantly assuming victory. He was acknowledging that the outcome belonged to God. But he also understood something important:
God often moves when someone has the courage to step forward.
Jonathan and his armor bearer began climbing the rocky pass toward the Philistine outpost. It was dangerous. They were exposed. The enemy had the higher ground.
From a military perspective, it made no sense.
But from a faith perspective, it made perfect sense.
Because Jonathan knew that God can turn impossible situations into turning points.
And that is exactly what happened.
As Jonathan and his armor bearer attacked, the Lord sent panic into the Philistine camp. Confusion spread through their army. The ground trembled. Chaos erupted among the enemy forces.
What started with two men suddenly became a national victory.
The entire battle shifted.
But notice something important.
The breakthrough did not begin with the whole army.
It began with one man willing to trust God and one man willing to stand beside him.
Sometimes we underestimate the power of one obedient step.

One prayer.
One decision.
One act of courage.
One moment where someone says, “God is able, even if the odds say otherwise.”
The truth is, many people are stuck in life because they keep measuring their possibilities by what they see around them.
Jonathan measured the moment differently.
He didn’t ask, “How many are with us?”
He asked, “Can God do this with few?”
And the answer was yes.
It has always been yes.
Throughout Scripture, God repeatedly works through what seems small:

David with a sling against a giant.
Gideon with only three hundred men.
A young boy’s lunch feeding thousands.
Twelve disciples turning the world upside down.
Again and again, the Bible reminds us that God’s power is not dependent on human abundance.
In fact, sometimes God chooses the small beginning so that His power is unmistakable.
That means your situation may not be as hopeless as it feels.
You may feel outnumbered.
You may feel unsupported.
You may feel like the resources around you are too small to make a difference.
But Jonathan’s story reminds us of something powerful:
God is not weakened by your small beginning.
He is not intimidated by the odds.
He does not need a crowd to begin a breakthrough.
Sometimes the only thing standing between fear and victory is one person who is willing to believe that God can move.
Jonathan stepped forward.
And history changed.
So here is the question this story leaves us with:
What if the breakthrough you are waiting for is on the other side of a step you have been afraid to take?
What if the courage you feel stirring inside you is not reckless—but faith?
What if God is simply waiting for someone to climb?
Jonathan’s story is not just about a battle long ago.
It is a reminder that heaven still honors courageous faith.
Because even today, nothing can hinder the Lord from saving—whether by many or by few.
What do you think is the hardest part about stepping out in faith when you feel like you are standing alone?
Your answer might encourage someone who needs courage today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Imagine being the one sheep.
paragraphs: Imagine being the one sheep.

Not the ninety-nine safely gathered in the field.
Not the ones that stayed close to the shepherd.
Not the ones who never wandered too far.
But the one that drifted.
The one that slowly moved away from the safety of the flock, step by step, until the familiar voices faded and the landscape turned unfamiliar and dangerous.
That is the story Jesus tells in Luke 15:4–7.
But if we read it carefully, we discover something deeper than a simple story about sheep.
It is a revelation of the heart of God.
Jesus asked a powerful question:
“Suppose one of you has a hundred sheep and loses one of them. Doesn't he leave the ninety-nine in the open country and go after the lost sheep until he finds it?” (Luke 15:4)
Notice something important.

The shepherd does not say,
“Well, ninety-nine is still a good number.”
He does not calculate the loss as acceptable.
He does not shrug and move on.
He searches.
The story is not about the intelligence of the sheep.
Sheep are known for wandering. They are not strong navigators. When they get lost, they often become trapped, frightened, and unable to find their way back.
The power of the story is not the sheep’s ability.
It is the shepherd’s determination.
Jesus reveals that God does not ignore the one who is lost.
He pursues.
And He keeps searching “until he finds it.”
Those four words carry incredible hope.
Until he finds it.

Not for a few minutes.
Not only while it is convenient.
Not only while the sheep deserves it.
The shepherd searches until the rescue happens.
Many people believe the lie that once they wander too far, they have crossed a line that cannot be undone.
They believe their failures have placed them beyond God's attention.
But Jesus tells this story to destroy that lie.
The lost sheep represents the wandering soul.

The person who drifted from faith.
The one who got distracted.
The one who followed the wrong voice.
The one who feels surrounded by the thorns of regret, confusion, and distance.
And instead of condemnation, Jesus describes a shepherd who moves toward the lost.
Even more powerful is what happens when the sheep is found.
Jesus says the shepherd joyfully puts it on his shoulders and carries it home.
Notice what the shepherd does not do.

He does not scold the sheep.
He does not lecture it about its mistakes.
He does not leave it to walk back alone.
He lifts it.
He carries it.
This moment reveals something profound about grace.
Sometimes restoration is not about our strength to return.
Sometimes it is about the Shepherd carrying us when we cannot walk anymore.
Jesus then makes the meaning unmistakable.
“I tell you that in the same way there will be more rejoicing in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need to repent.” (Luke 15:7)
Heaven celebrates rescues.
Not perfection.
Not performance.
Rescue.
Think about that.
All of heaven erupts in joy when one lost person turns back to God.

One life.
One story.
One soul.
This tells us something about the value God places on people.
You are not just a number in a crowd.
You are not invisible to heaven.
You are not too far gone.
You are the sheep worth searching for.
But there is another lesson hidden inside this parable.
The heart of the Shepherd should become the heart of His followers.
If Jesus moves toward the lost, His people cannot become comfortable ignoring them.
We cannot build communities that celebrate the ninety-nine while forgetting the one who quietly disappeared.
The mission of the church has always been the same mission of the Shepherd:
Seek the lost.
Love the wandering.
Restore the broken.
Carry the weak.
This parable reminds us that God’s love is not passive.
It moves.
It searches.
It rescues.
And if you have ever had a season where you felt lost — spiritually distant, confused, or overwhelmed — this story was told for you.
Because the Shepherd in Jesus’ story is not fictional.
It is a picture of Christ Himself.
The Son of Man said it clearly in Luke 19:10:
“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
That is the mission of Jesus.
He searches.
He finds.
He carries.
And heaven rejoices.
So the next time you read the story of the lost sheep, remember this:
You may feel lost.
But you are never beyond the reach of the Shepherd.
And sometimes the greatest miracle is not that we found our way back.
It is that He came looking for us.

What part of this story speaks to you the most:
The wandering sheep… or the Shepherd who refused to stop searching?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The voice in your head is not always your friend.
paragraphs: The voice in your head is not always your friend.
Sometimes… it’s the very thing pulling you away from God.

You hear it when you’re alone.
When the noise dies down.
When no one is watching.
And it sounds like you.
But it’s not.
Because that voice keeps whispering things that God never said.
And deep down… you know something is off.

It tells you to stay silent about your sin.
It tells you to delay repentance.
It tells you that “it’s not that serious.”
But the longer you listen… the heavier your soul feels.
The quieter God becomes.
And the louder that other voice gets.
Let’s expose it.
Because some of you are being discipled… not by the Holy Spirit—
…but by the wrong voice.

That voice says:
“Just this once won’t hurt.”

So you click.
You hide.
You justify.
And then comes the shame.

But instead of running to God…
you run further away.
That’s not conviction.
That’s deception.

That voice says:
“You’re already too far gone.”

So you stop praying.
You stop showing up.
You slowly disappear from the presence of God.
Not because God left—
…but because you believed a lie.

That voice says:
“You deserve this.”

So pride rises.
Submission fades.
And suddenly, your feelings outrank Scripture.
You start editing God’s Word to fit your lifestyle.
And you don’t even realize—
you’ve made yourself your own god.
Listen.
This is not new.
This is ancient.
“Did God really say…?” — Genesis 3:1
That was the serpent’s first strategy.
Not to destroy Eve immediately—
but to distort the voice she trusted.
Because if he can corrupt the voice you follow…
he can control the life you live.
But here’s where it gets dangerous.
Some of you think the voice is yours.
You’ve lived with it so long…
you’ve mistaken bondage for personality.
Shame for identity.
Noise for truth.
Let Scripture cut through the confusion:
“My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me.” — John 10:27
Jesus didn’t say His sheep hear many voices.
He said they know His.
Clear.
Personal.
Alive.
So if the voice you’re listening to is pulling you away from Him…
it’s not Him.
If it feeds fear more than faith…
it’s not Him.
If it condemns you without pointing you back to grace…
it’s not Him.
Because the voice of Jesus does something different.
It doesn’t ignore your sin—
but it doesn’t trap you in it either.

It exposes…
then invites.

Convicts…
then restores.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
Notice that.
No condemnation.
Not “less condemnation.”
None.
But here’s the truth we don’t like:

You cannot experience that freedom…
while clinging to the wrong voice.
This is where the Gospel steps in.
Not as a concept.
Not as motivation.
But as rescue.
You and I—we’ve all listened to the wrong voice.

We chose sin.
We justified it.
We hid in it.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
That’s the diagnosis.
No one escapes it.
But God didn’t leave us there.
He didn’t just shout correction from heaven.
He came down.
In flesh.
In Jesus Christ.
And on the cross—

every lie you believed…
every sin you hid…
every voice that chained you—
was nailed there with Him.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not when you cleaned yourself up.
Not when you figured it out.
While you were still lost.
Still listening to the wrong voice.
Jesus didn’t die just to forgive you.
He died to free you.
To break the authority of every voice that isn’t His.
And then He rose.
Because the wrong voice always ends in death—
but the voice of Christ leads to life.
So now the question is not:
“Do you hear voices?”
You do.
We all do.
The real question is:
Which one are you following?
Because one voice will lead you deeper into hiding.
And one voice is calling you out of the grave.
Right now… you can feel it.
That tension.
That pull.
That quiet conviction rising in your chest.
That’s not shame.
That’s God calling you home.
Don’t numb it.
Don’t delay it.
Come back.
Repent.
Turn from the voices that have been shaping your life.
And surrender again to Jesus.
You don’t need to fix everything first.
You just need to respond.
“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.” — Hebrews 3:15
Today.
Not tomorrow.
Not when it’s convenient.
Now.
Let Him retrain your ears.
Let Him renew your mind.
Let Him restore your soul.
Because the voice you follow…
will determine the life you live.
If this hit your heart, don’t ignore it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He built bigger barns…
paragraphs: He built bigger barns…
…but forgot he was dying.
You can feel it, can’t you?
That quiet lie we whisper to ourselves:
“Just a little more… then I’ll be secure.”

More money.
More savings.
More control.
Then I’ll rest.
But what if your “later”… never comes?
Jesus told a story that cuts deeper than comfort.
A man wasn’t wicked in the way we usually define it.

He didn’t steal.
He didn’t kill.
He didn’t oppress.
He just… succeeded.
His land produced abundantly. Overflowing. Beyond expectation.
And suddenly, he had a problem most people pray for.
“What shall I do? I have no place to store my crops.” — Luke 12:17
Sounds familiar?

Blessing became his burden.
Provision became his obsession.
Increase became his identity.
So he made a plan.
“I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones…” — Luke 12:18
Pause.
Listen carefully.

“I will…”
“My barns…”
“My grain…”
“My goods…”
That’s not planning.
That’s ownership without surrender.
That’s provision without God.
That’s pride dressed like wisdom.
And then comes the moment no one expects.

No warning.
No countdown.
No second chance.
“But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you…’” — Luke 12:20
Fool.
Not because he was rich.
But because he thought he was in control.
Here’s the uncomfortable truth:
You can be financially prepared… and spiritually bankrupt.
You can be building a future… that you will never live to see.
You can be admired by men… and empty before God.
This is not about money.
This is about the heart.
Because money just reveals what you trust.
And this man trusted his barns more than his Creator.
Let’s go deeper.
This isn’t just ancient history.
This is you.
This is me.
We build modern barns:

Bank accounts.
Career titles.
Business plans.
Insurance policies.
Backup strategies.
None of these are wrong.
But when they become your peace…
They become your god.
Scripture exposes it clearly:
“So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” — Luke 12:21
Not rich toward God.
That’s the real poverty.
You can have everything the world applauds…
…and still be empty where it matters most.
Now here’s where everything turns.
Because this story doesn’t end in condemnation.
It points to a Savior.
Jesus didn’t just tell this parable to warn you.
He told it to rescue you.
Because every one of us has lived like this rich fool.

We trusted ourselves.
We clung to control.
We built our lives without fully surrendering to God.
That’s sin.
Not just what we do.
But who we trust.
And sin always leads to death.
“For the wages of sin is death…” — Romans 6:23
Not just physical death.
Spiritual separation from God.
Eternal loss.
The kind no barn can protect you from.
But here is the Gospel.
The interruption of grace.
“…but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” — Romans 6:23
Jesus stepped into our illusion of control.
Lived the life we couldn’t live.
Died the death we deserved.
And rose again to offer what wealth never could:

Forgiveness.
Peace.
Eternal life.
The rich fool said:
“I will secure my future.”
Jesus said:
“Your soul is required.”
But on the cross…
Jesus said:
“It is finished.” — John 19:30
Meaning your future—if you trust Him—is no longer fragile.
It is secured in Him.
This is the turning point.
You don’t need bigger barns.
You need a surrendered heart.
You don’t need more control.
You need Christ.
So let me ask you, honestly:
What are you trusting right now?
What are you building your peace on?
What are you afraid to lose?
Because whatever you can’t surrender…
has already taken God’s place.
Jesus invites you today:
“Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth… but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven…” — Matthew 6:19–20
That’s not loss.
That’s wisdom.
That’s freedom.
Repent.
Not just of obvious sins…
But of self-reliance.
Of quiet pride.
Of thinking you can secure your life without God.
Turn to Jesus.
Not later.
Now.
Because the most dangerous lie is this:
“I still have time.”
You don’t need to fear that truth.
Because grace is still available.
Right now.
If your heart is beating…
God is calling.
Prayer:

Lord Jesus, I confess that I have trusted in what I can build more than in You. Forgive me for my pride, my fear, and my need to control. I surrender my life, my future, and everything I have into Your hands. Teach me to be rich toward God. Be my treasure, my peace, and my salvation. Amen.
If this hit your heart…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He rode a donkey… once.
paragraphs: He rode a donkey… once.
Now He rides into war.
And that should shake you.

Because the same Jesus people ignore today…
is the King they won’t escape tomorrow.
You’ve heard of Him as Savior.
Gentle. Patient. Forgiving.

The One who eats with sinners.
The One who touches the unclean.
The One who says, “Come to Me.” (Matthew 11:28)
But Revelation 19 doesn’t show Him reaching out…
It shows Him riding in.
And most people aren’t ready for that version of Jesus.
Let’s be honest.

We love a Jesus who forgives…
but we resist a Jesus who rules.

We want grace without surrender.
Mercy without repentance.
Salvation without transformation.

We say we follow Him—
but our pride still sits on the throne.

We sing worship songs—
but our secret sin still has a private room.

We post verses—
but our hearts haven’t bowed.
And deep down…
We think we still have time.
But here’s the tension you can’t ignore:

What if the Jesus you keep delaying…
is already standing at the edge of eternity?
What if mercy has an expiration date?

What if the next time heaven opens…
it’s not for salvation—but for judgment?
Revelation pulls the curtain back.
“And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse! The one sitting on it is called Faithful and True, and in righteousness He judges and makes war.” (Revelation 19:11)
Faithful.
True.
Not soft.
Not negotiable.
He doesn’t come asking.
He comes ruling.
“His eyes are like a flame of fire… and on His head are many diadems.” (Revelation 19:12)
Nothing hidden anymore.

Every secret thought.
Every private compromise.
Every moment you said, “It’s not that serious.”
Seen.
Fully.
By Him.
“From His mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations…” (Revelation 19:15)
He doesn’t need weapons.
His Word is enough.

The same Word you ignored.
The same truth you scrolled past.
The same conviction you silenced.
Now becomes the standard that judges.
And here’s where it hits.
Hard.
“He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.” (Revelation 19:15)
This is not symbolic anger.
This is holy justice.
Sin is not cute to God.

It’s not “just a phase.”
It’s not “who I am.”
It’s rebellion.
And rebellion meets judgment.
But wait.
Don’t miss this.
The One bringing judgment…
Is the same One who took it.

Before Revelation 19…
there was a cross.

Before the white horse…
there was a wooden beam.

Before the crown of many diadems…
there was a crown of thorns.
Isaiah saw it first:
“But He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities…” (Isaiah 53:5)
Jesus didn’t just come to warn you about judgment.
He stepped into it.
For you.
This is the Gospel.
Clear.
Unavoidable.
You are not judged because God hates you.
You are judged because sin is real.
And justice is holy.
But God made a way.
“God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Not when you fixed yourself.
Not when you got better.
While you were still in it.

Still hiding.
Still pretending.
Still delaying.
He died.
And now the question isn’t:
“Is Jesus coming back?”
He is.
The question is:
How will you meet Him?
As Savior?

Covered by His blood.
Forgiven. Restored. Free.
Or as Judge?
Exposed. Accountable. Without excuse.
Because you don’t get both versions at the same time.
Grace is offered now.
Judgment comes later.
But the window…
Is closing.

Some scholars interpret Revelation 19 as both a literal future event and a symbolic unveiling of Christ’s ultimate authority over all evil. But whether you read it symbolically or literally, the truth remains unshaken:
Jesus wins.
Sin loses.
And every heart will answer.
So let me ask you—no filters, no pretending:
What are you still holding onto?

That secret habit?
That pride you won’t release?
That delayed obedience?
You call it small.
He calls it sin.
But listen…
This is not a message to crush you.
This is a call to wake you.
Because the same King who rides in judgment…
Still offers mercy today.
“Seek the Lord while He may be found; call upon Him while He is near.” (Isaiah 55:6)
While He may be found.
Not forever.
Now.
You don’t clean yourself first.
You come as you are.
Broken. Guilty. Tired.
And you repent.
Turn.
Surrender.
Trust in Jesus—not your effort, not your morality, not your image.
Him alone.
Because only His blood saves.
Only His grace restores.
Only His name redeems.
And when you do…
Revelation 19 is no longer your fear.
It becomes your victory.
Because the King you see riding…
Is your King.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR GUILT IS TAKEN AWAY.
paragraphs: YOUR GUILT IS TAKEN AWAY.
Let that line slow you down for a second.

Not minimized.
Not explained away.
Not buried under religious performance.
Taken. Away.
That’s the scandal Isaiah experienced the moment heaven touched his life.
And it started with terror.
Isaiah did not walk into a cozy worship service.
He stepped into a collision with holiness.
“The Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple.” (Isaiah 6:1)
Seraphim hovered above Him like living flames.

Six wings.
Faces covered.
Feet covered.
Even sinless beings shielded themselves from the blazing purity of God.
And they cried out with thunder in their voices:
“Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts.”
Not loving, loving, loving.
Not merciful, merciful, merciful.
Holy.
The foundations of the temple shook.
Smoke flooded the room.
And in that moment, Isaiah stopped comparing himself to other people.
Because when you see God clearly…
You finally see yourself honestly.
Isaiah didn’t say:
“I’m doing my best.”
“I’m not that bad.”
“I’m better than most.”
No.
The prophet collapsed under the weight of truth.

“Woe is me! For I am undone.”
(Isaiah 6:5)
The Hebrew word means destroyed… unraveled… ruined.
Isaiah realized something devastating:
You can be religious and still be unclean.
He confessed:
“I am a man of unclean lips.”
Why lips?
Because lips reveal the heart.

The lies.
The gossip.
The pride.
The anger.
The hidden poison in words we thought nobody noticed.
And suddenly Isaiah realized:

The mouth meant to speak for God
…had been stained by sin.
Sound familiar?
Some of us know that feeling.
The moment when the Holy Spirit pulls back the curtain.

And the secret you hid.
The words you spoke.
The compromise you justified.
All of it suddenly stands under the light of God.
That moment feels terrifying.
But watch what happens next.
Because God did not destroy Isaiah.
He cleansed him.
One of the seraphim flew to the altar.
In his hand was a burning coal.
Fire from the place of sacrifice.
The angel touched Isaiah’s lips.
Imagine that moment.

Heat.
Shock.
Pain.
Not to punish him.
But to purify him.
And heaven declared something Isaiah could never declare over himself:

“Your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for.”
(Isaiah 6:7)
Did you see it?
Isaiah confessed his sin.
But God removed it.
Isaiah acknowledged the stain.
But God performed the cleansing.
Religion tells you:
“Fix yourself first.”
The Gospel says:
“Come broken. Jesus will cleanse you.”
That coal from the altar was not random.
It pointed forward.
Forward to a hill outside Jerusalem.
Forward to wood, nails, and blood.
Forward to Jesus Christ.
Because one day, the true altar would be the cross.
And the fire of God’s justice would not fall on us.
It would fall on Him.

Jesus carried our guilt.
Jesus bore our shame.
Jesus paid our debt.
So that heaven could say over sinners like you and me:
“Your guilt is taken away.”
Not because we improved ourselves.
But because Christ gave Himself.
And here’s the part many people miss.
The cleansing came before the calling.
Right after Isaiah was purified, he heard the voice of the Lord:
“Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?” (Isaiah 6:8)
Isaiah didn’t hesitate.
Not because he was perfect.
But because he had been forgiven.
He said:
“Here am I. Send me.”
God does not send flawless people.
He sends forgiven people.
People who remember what it felt like when grace touched their life.
People who know what it means to have guilt lifted off their chest.

People who once said, “Woe is me,”
but now say, “Use me.”
So let me ask you something honest.
What guilt are you carrying right now?

The secret sin?
The words you wish you could take back?
The failure nobody knows about?
You might feel like Isaiah:

Undone.
Exposed.
Unworthy.
But the message of the Gospel is this:
Grace still touches lips.
Not with a burning coal now…
But with the cleansing power of the cross.
Jesus did not come to shame sinners.
He came to save them.
And when His grace touches your life, heaven declares something the enemy hates hearing:
“Your guilt is taken away.”
Not postponed.
Not probation.
Gone.
Pause.
Pray.
Tell Jesus the truth about your life.
Because the same God who cleansed Isaiah is still cleansing sinners today.
And the moment grace touches your life…
Everything changes.

Your past loses its chains.
Your shame loses its voice.
Your future gets rewritten.
Because that’s what Jesus does.
He turns burning conviction into blazing redemption.
And suddenly the words that once condemned you become the testimony that frees others.
🔥 “Grace touched my life.”
Because someone you know needs to hear this today:
Your guilt is taken away.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Pride rarely announces itself loudly.
paragraphs: Pride rarely announces itself loudly.
It begins quietly.

Not with rebellion…
but with admiration of yourself.
And few stories in Scripture reveal the danger of pride more clearly than the fall of Lucifer.
Before Lucifer became the enemy of God, he was one of the most magnificent beings God ever created.
The Bible describes him as full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.

In Ezekiel 28:12–15, he is portrayed as a being of extraordinary splendor, adorned with precious stones and placed in the very presence of God. Some scholars understand this passage as describing the spiritual reality behind the king of Tyre — pointing to the fall of the one we know as Satan.
He was not created evil.
He was created glorious.
He stood close to the throne of God.
Imagine the privilege.
Imagine the beauty.
Imagine the authority.
But something dangerous began to grow inside his heart.
Not weakness.
Not ignorance.
Pride.
The tragedy of Lucifer is not that he lacked greatness.
The tragedy is that he mistook his greatness as something that belonged to him instead of something given by God.
Scripture reveals the moment the shift happened.
In Isaiah 14:13–14, we read the thoughts that formed in his heart:

“I will ascend into heaven.
I will exalt my throne above the stars of God.
I will sit on the mount of the congregation.
I will ascend above the heights of the clouds.
I will make myself like the Most High.”
Five times he said “I will.”
Pride always speaks that language.
“I will rise.”
“I will take.”
“I will become.”
“I will be greater.”
Lucifer was no longer satisfied reflecting God’s glory.
He wanted God’s position.
And that is the core danger of pride.
Pride is not simply thinking highly of yourself.
Pride is forgetting where your blessings came from.
The same beauty that once reflected God's glory became the mirror of his own admiration.
The same wisdom that once served God became corrupted by ambition.
And the same position that placed him near God became the stage for rebellion.
One of the most sobering realities in the Bible is this:
The first rebellion in the universe did not begin on earth.
It began in heaven.
Not in darkness.
But in glory.
Lucifer stood in the presence of God and still chose to exalt himself.
That is how deceptive pride can be.
Pride does not need poverty to grow.
It can grow in blessing.
It can grow in success.
It can grow in talent.
It can grow in influence.
And if it is not guarded against, it can grow even in spiritual leaders.
This is why Scripture repeatedly warns about the danger of pride.
In Proverbs 16:18, we read:
“Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.”
Lucifer’s fall became the ultimate example of that truth.
The one who tried to rise above all creation became the one cast down the farthest.
Jesus Himself referenced this moment when He said in Luke 10:18:
“I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.”
In a moment, the one who tried to ascend above the clouds was brought down.
The throne he tried to take became the judgment that expelled him.
And the glory he once carried was replaced with rebellion and ruin.
Lucifer’s story is not just ancient history.
It is a warning for every generation.
Because pride still whispers the same lies today.
“You deserve more.”
“You should be recognized.”
“You should be above others.”
“You should be the center.”
But the kingdom of God works in the opposite direction.
In God’s kingdom, humility rises while pride collapses.
Jesus taught in Matthew 23:12:
“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”
Lucifer tried to raise himself.
Jesus humbled Himself.
One tried to take the throne.
The other chose the cross.
And that contrast reveals one of the deepest lessons in Scripture:
Pride tries to climb.
Humility learns to bow.
Lucifer’s fall reminds us of something important.
Every gift we have — our abilities, opportunities, influence, and success — are not evidence of our superiority.
They are evidence of God’s grace.
The moment we begin to believe the glory belongs to us, we step onto the same dangerous path that Lucifer walked.
But the moment we remember where our blessings came from, pride loses its power.
Lucifer’s story is a warning.
But it is also a mirror.
Because every human heart faces the same decision:
Will we exalt ourselves…
or will we honor the One who gave us everything?
One path leads upward for a moment and downward forever.
The other bows today — and is lifted by God tomorrow.
So here is the question worth asking ourselves:
Have you ever caught pride quietly growing in your heart — especially after success or recognition?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The sacrifice wasn’t accepted… until the fire touched it.
paragraphs: The sacrifice wasn’t accepted… until the fire touched it.
That’s the part we don’t talk about enough.
In the Old Testament, God didn’t just ask for offerings—He commanded that they be burned on the altar (Leviticus 1). Not partially. Not symbolically. Completely.
Because fire reveals what words can hide.
It exposes whether something is truly surrendered… or just temporarily released.

You can place something on the altar and still be emotionally attached to it.
You can say “God, it’s Yours” while secretly hoping to reclaim it later.
You can give… and still not surrender.
But when the fire comes—everything changes.

Fire doesn’t negotiate.
Fire doesn’t leave portions untouched.
Fire finishes what surrender starts.
And that’s exactly why God required it.
“It is a burnt offering… an aroma pleasing to the Lord.” (Leviticus 1:9)

Not because God delights in smoke…
But because He honors hearts that hold nothing back.

The fire was never about destruction.
It was about transformation.

What goes into the fire is not wasted—
it is transferred.

From human hands…
to divine acceptance.
And here’s where it gets personal.

Because the system of burnt offerings didn’t end—
it evolved.
Romans 12:1 says:
“Offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God—this is your true and proper worship.”
Now the altar is no longer made of stone.
It’s your life.
And the fire?
It’s the daily cost of obedience.

It’s forgiving when you’re wounded.
It’s letting go when you want control.
It’s staying faithful when no one sees.
It’s saying yes to God… when it would be easier to walk away.
A living sacrifice is more difficult than a dead one.
Because it keeps choosing surrender.

Again.
And again.
And again.
And here’s the tension most people feel but rarely admit:

We don’t mind putting things on the altar…
We just don’t like when God sends the fire.
Because fire makes it real.

Fire means it’s no longer yours.
Fire means there’s no going back.
Fire means surrender has become irreversible.
And that’s where true worship begins.

Not in songs.
Not in words.
But in what you refuse to take back.
Some of the greatest delays in our spiritual lives aren’t because God said “no”…

But because we said “yes”…
without surrendering fully.

We placed it on the altar—
but resisted the fire.
And partial surrender will always produce partial transformation.

You can’t experience full obedience
while protecting a hidden exception.
That’s why Scripture consistently ties fire to God’s presence.

When Elijah rebuilt the altar, the fire fell (1 Kings 18).
When Solomon dedicated the temple, fire came down (2 Chronicles 7:1).
Fire is where heaven responds to surrender.
And maybe that’s the real question:

Do you want God’s presence…
or just His promises?
Because His presence often comes through fire.

Not to destroy you—
but to refine you.

Not to take from you—
but to reveal what truly owns your heart.
“Fire makes surrender final.”

And some things in your life will never change
until they are fully surrendered.

Some prayers won’t be answered
until something is fully released.

Some breakthroughs are waiting
on the other side of obedience that costs you something.
Because God doesn’t bless what you almost surrender.
He responds to what you fully give.
So take a moment and ask yourself honestly:

What is still in your hands…
that should already be in the fire?

Is it control?
A relationship?
A habit?
A fear?
A version of your life you don’t want to let go of?
Because the altar is still calling.
And the fire is not your enemy.

It is the evidence
that something has truly been given to God.

“God is not after your offering—He’s after your surrender.”
“You don’t partially burn what you fully give.”
“The altar is where control goes to die.”
“A living sacrifice is one that doesn’t climb back down.”
“What you keep back will always compete with what you say you surrendered.”
And here’s the hope in all of this:

Every sacrifice in the Old Testament pointed forward
to one final, perfect offering—
Jesus Christ.

He didn’t just go to the altar…
He became the sacrifice.

And unlike every other offering—
He gave everything.

Completely.
Willingly.
Without holding back.
So now, surrender is no longer about earning God’s favor.
It’s a response to the One who already gave everything for you.
Which means this:
You’re not losing anything in the fire.
You’re releasing it into the hands of a faithful God.
And whatever you fully surrender to Him…
He knows how to redeem, restore, or replace.
But it starts the same way it always has:

With an altar.
With a decision.
With a fire.
And nothing held back.

Engagement Question:
What is one thing God has been asking you to fully surrender—but you’ve been hesitant to let burn?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You pointed at them.
paragraphs:
You pointed at them.
But heaven was pointing at you.
Pause.
Because this is where it gets uncomfortable.
You saw their sin.

You felt it—
that quiet satisfaction…
that subtle “I’m better than this.”
But something inside you shifted.
Not conviction.
Comparison.
And now there’s a question hanging in the air:

What if the thing you hate in them…
is the thing you refuse to face in yourself?
Stay with me.
Because Jesus didn’t say this to the worst sinners.
He said it to the religious ones.

The careful ones.
The disciplined ones.
The “I would never do that” crowd.
And then He dropped a blade:
“Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the plank that is in your own eye?” — Matthew 7:3
A speck.
Tiny. Annoying. Visible.
A plank?
Massive. Obvious. Blinding.
And yet—ignored.
Here’s the truth we don’t like to admit:
Pride is the most invisible sin to the one who carries it.

You can spot lust in others.
You can call out compromise.
You can analyze behavior like a judge in a courtroom.
But pride?

It hides behind “discernment.”
It disguises itself as “righteous anger.”
It whispers, “You’re just being honest.”
Let’s get real.
You don’t just see their sin.
You study it.
Replay it.
Talk about it.
Build quiet cases in your mind.
And all the while…
Your own heart is drifting.
Jesus didn’t say ignore sin.
He said deal with yours first.
“First take the plank out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.” — Matthew 7:5
First.
That word confronts everything.

Because we want to fix others
before we surrender ourselves.
We want correction without confession.
We want clarity without cleansing.
But God doesn’t work that way.
Let me say something that might shake you:

You can be right about their sin…
and still be wrong before God.
Because God is not just looking at what you see.
He’s looking at how you see.
The Pharisees were experts in pointing out sin.
And yet Jesus said:
“This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” — Matthew 15:8
They were accurate.
But they were empty.
Correct.
But disconnected.
And maybe…
just maybe…
that’s where you are right now.
You’ve mastered spiritual language.
You know the Scriptures.
You can quote verses.

But when was the last time
you let those same Scriptures break you?
Here’s where everything shifts.
Because this isn’t just about behavior.
This is about the heart.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?” — Jeremiah 17:9
Your heart can justify anything.
Even your judgment.
Even your pride.
Even your silence.
So what’s the answer?
Not self-improvement.
Not trying harder.
Not pretending to be humble.
You need a Savior.
Because the same Jesus who exposed the plank…
…is the same Jesus who carried your cross.
Let this sink in:
While you were busy analyzing others—
He was fully aware of everything in you.

Every hidden motive.
Every quiet arrogance.
Every secret thought.
And still—
He chose the cross.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not after you fixed yourself.
Not after you became humble.
Not after you removed the plank.
While.
You.
Were.
Still.
A.
Sinner.
That’s grace.
Undeserved.
Unfiltered.
Unstoppable.
But grace doesn’t excuse pride.
It crushes it.
Because when you truly see the cross—
You lose the right to look down on anyone.
At the foot of the cross:

The liar and the leader stand equal.
The addict and the achiever kneel the same.
The broken and the “put together” are both desperate for mercy.
There is no “better.”
Only forgiven.
And that changes everything.
Now, instead of pointing fingers—
You extend hands.
Instead of exposing others—
You carry their burdens.
Instead of standing above—
You kneel beside.
That’s what real transformation looks like.
Not louder correction.
Deeper compassion.
So here’s the question you can’t avoid anymore:
What plank have you been protecting?
That attitude?
That pride?
That hidden sin you’ve renamed as “personality”?
Bring it to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not when it’s convenient.
Now.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
Faithful.
Just.
Willing.
You don’t have to hide.
You don’t have to pretend.
You don’t have to keep carrying what Jesus already died to remove.
This is your moment.
Not to scroll.
Not to agree.
To surrender.
Say it.
Mean it.
Let it break you.
Then let Him rebuild you.
And if this pierced something deep—
Come back to it.
Let it work on you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She refused to leave.
paragraphs: She refused to leave.

Not when the sun burned her skin by day.
Not when the cold crept into her bones by night.
Not when the vultures circled.
Not when the wolves drew near.
She stayed.

Rizpah.
A name almost lost in the margins of Scripture—until grief made her unforgettable.

In 2 Samuel 21:10, the Bible says she took sackcloth and spread it on a rock. From the beginning of harvest until the rains poured down, she kept watch over the bodies of her sons. She drove away birds by day. She fought off beasts by night.

No stage.
No spotlight.
No applause.

Just a mother.
And a love that refused to let dishonor win.
Sit with that for a moment.
Because this is not the kind of story we like to share. There is no instant miracle here. No sudden reversal. No angel breaking through the sky to fix everything in one moment.
Just a woman sitting in the tension between loss and loyalty.
And that tension exposes something in us.

We love stories where God moves quickly.
We celebrate breakthroughs that come overnight.
We repost testimonies that wrap up clean.
But what about the ones who wait?

What about the ones who sit on the rock…
guarding what’s broken…
holding onto what’s already gone?

Rizpah didn’t walk away from pain.
She planted herself in it.
Why?
Because love honors—even when the world has already moved on.
Her sons were publicly shamed. Their bodies left exposed as a sign of judgment. In that culture, that meant disgrace. Final. Visible. Uncovered.
But Rizpah said, “Not on my watch.”

She could not change what happened.
She could not reverse the judgment.
She could not bring them back.
But she could stand in the gap between shame and honor.
And she did.

Day after day.
Night after night.
Until something shifted.

Scripture tells us that when King David heard what Rizpah had done, he was moved. He gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan, along with the remains of those who had been left exposed, and gave them a proper burial.
And then this line drops like thunder:
“After that, God responded to the plea for the land.” (2 Samuel 21:14)
Did you catch it?

Heaven moved…
after a mother stayed.

No sermon.
No strategy.
No platform.
Just relentless, faithful presence in the place of pain.

Some scholars interpret this moment as a turning point—where Rizpah’s public act of honor awakened the conscience of the king, leading to restored dignity and, ultimately, divine response over the land.
In other words…

What looked like silent suffering
became catalytic obedience.
And suddenly, Rizpah is no longer just a grieving mother.
She is a mirror.
Because if we’re honest, we all have something we’ve been tempted to abandon.

A relationship that feels too far gone.
A calling that feels buried.
A part of our life marked by failure, regret, or shame.
And the world whispers, “Leave it. It’s over.”
But Rizpah whispers back, “Stay.”

Stay in prayer.
Stay in faith.
Stay in honor.
Stay when it hurts.
Stay when no one sees.
Because heaven does not overlook what the world ignores.
And this is where the Gospel explodes into the story.

Rizpah guarded the dead.
Jesus conquered death.

She sat on a rock of grief.
Christ rolled away the stone of the grave.

She fought off birds and beasts to preserve dignity.
Jesus disarmed sin and shame at the cross.

Where Rizpah could only delay decay,
Jesus defeated it completely.
Listen carefully—

The same God who saw Rizpah on that rock
sees you right now.

In your quiet fight.
In your hidden grief.
In your unseen obedience.
And He is not indifferent.
At the cross, Jesus took on the ultimate exposure. Public shame. Naked rejection. The full weight of sin laid bare before heaven and earth.
Why?
So that your story would not end in disgrace.

So that what was left exposed in your life
could be covered by grace.

So that what felt final
could be redeemed.
This is not just Rizpah’s story.
This is your invitation.

If you’ve been standing over something broken—
don’t walk away yet.

If you’ve been guarding something painful—
don’t lose heart.

If you’ve been sitting in a season that feels silent—
heaven is not ignoring you.

God sees.
God moves.
God redeems.

And through Jesus Christ, He does more than restore honor—
He gives new life.
So come to Him.

Bring the grief.
Bring the questions.
Bring the part of your life you thought was too far gone.

Lay it at the feet of the One who stepped into death
and walked out alive.
Because in Christ, the story never ends in shame.
It ends in resurrection.
Let Rizpah’s story speak again.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She thought the silence meant God had left.
paragraphs: She thought the silence meant God had left.
But the wilderness was never empty.
It just felt that way.
Hagar is crying.

Not soft tears.
Not poetic pain.
This is the kind of crying that comes when hope is already buried.

She’s out of water.
Out of options.
Out of strength.
And she walks away from her son because watching him die would break her faster than death itself.

That’s not just a moment.
That’s a collapse.
And if we’re honest… some of us know that place.

The place where you don’t post anymore.
Where you stop praying like before.
Where you still believe in God—but quietly wonder if He still sees you.
Here’s the tension.
Genesis 21 says Hagar lifted her voice and wept… but it also says God heard the voice of the boy (Genesis 21:17).
Wait.

She’s the one crying.
But God responds to the child?
Why?
Some scholars interpret this as God responding not just to loud pain—but to covenant purpose. Ishmael was not forgotten because God had already spoken over his life.
And that changes everything.

Because sometimes you feel ignored…
not because God is absent—
but because He’s working deeper than your understanding.
Read that again.

You’ve been crying about what’s dying…
while God is protecting what He promised.
Let me ask you something.

What have you silently concluded about God in your lowest moment?
And what if that conclusion is wrong?
Because here’s the truth we don’t say out loud:
Sometimes we obey halfway… then blame God fully.

Hagar was sent away, yes.
But her story started in compromise (Genesis 16).
A decision made in human effort… not divine trust.
And now she’s in a wilderness created by choices she didn’t fully control—but still had to endure.
Sound familiar?
This is where shame creeps in.

“This is my fault.”
“I deserve this.”
“God probably moved on from me.”
But the wilderness exposes something deeper than your failure.
It reveals what you believe about God when everything is stripped away.
Here’s the AHA moment:

The wilderness doesn’t prove God left you.
It reveals whether you trust Him when you can’t see Him.
And here’s the mirror:
You don’t just doubt God in pain… you redefine Him.

You start seeing Him as distant.
Selective.
Silent.
But Scripture cuts through that lie.
Genesis says, “God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water” (Genesis 21:19).
The well didn’t appear.
It was already there.
She just couldn’t see it.
Let that hit you.

Provision was present…
but perception was broken.
And that’s where many are stuck right now.

Not without help.
Not without grace.
Just without sight.
But here’s where it gets even deeper.
Hagar names God earlier in Genesis 16:13 as “El Roi”—the God who sees me.

Not saw.
Not will see.
Sees.
Present tense.

Even in compromise.
Even in consequence.
Even in collapse.
But don’t miss this—
Being seen by God doesn’t automatically mean being saved by Him.
That’s where Jesus enters the story.

Because Hagar was rescued from physical death…
but humanity still faced spiritual death.

And Scripture says, “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Not just Hagar.
All of us.
We didn’t just wander into a wilderness.
We chose it.

Sin separated us from God.
Not distance.
Not silence.
Sin.
But God didn’t just hear us crying from heaven.
He came down.
Jesus stepped into our wilderness.
He didn’t just watch suffering—He absorbed it.
On the cross, He cried out, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that you would never have to be truly forsaken.
That’s the Gospel.

Not self-repair.
Not religious effort.
Rescue.
Through Jesus alone.
Because “the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23).
Here’s the conviction you might not want—but need:
You can know Bible stories… and still be spiritually blind to the well right in front of you.
Church attendance doesn’t equal surrender.
Emotion doesn’t equal repentance.
And tears don’t equal transformation.
But grace?
Grace changes everything.
Because when God opens your eyes through Christ… you don’t just survive the wilderness.
You’re transformed in it.
You’re not just someone trying to make it anymore.

You are seen.
You are pursued.
You are redeemed.
Not because you earned it.
But because Jesus paid for it.
So here’s the invitation.
Stop running from the place where God is trying to meet you.
Stop interpreting silence as abandonment.
And stop believing that your story ends in the desert.
Lift your eyes.
The well is closer than you think.
Someone you love is silently breaking right now.
Stay close.
And the next message?
It’s for the ones who feel like they’ve gone too far to come back.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She didn’t whisper that prayer.
paragraphs:
She didn’t whisper that prayer.
She shouted it from a breaking soul.
“Give me children… or I die.”

That’s not poetry.
That’s pressure.
That’s pain turning into demand.
And if you’re honest…
You’ve prayed like that too.

Not out loud.
But deep inside—where nobody hears the desperation you try to hide.

“Lord, fix this now.”
“Lord, I can’t take this anymore.”
“Lord… why not me?”
And here’s the tension you don’t say:

You love God…
but you’re starting to resent what He hasn’t given.
Read that again.

Because Rachel wasn’t faithless.
She was just empty.

Loved by Jacob.
Chosen. Desired. Seen.
But still barren.
And that’s the contradiction that messes with your theology.

How can you be loved…
and still lacking?

How can you be chosen…
and still waiting?

How can God bless others in front of you…
while your prayer feels ignored?

Rachel saw Leah’s children.
And suddenly, her desire became comparison.
Her comparison became envy.
Her envy became desperation.
And desperation… started speaking louder than faith.
Let me ask you something:
What are you quietly angry at God about?
What blessing are you struggling to celebrate in others… because you’re still waiting for yours?

There’s a version of you that worships God publicly…
but questions Him privately.

No one sees it.
But God does.
And still—He doesn’t walk away.
Genesis 30:22 says, “Then God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb.”
Don’t rush that verse.

God remembered.
God listened.
God acted.

Not because Rachel prayed perfectly…
but because God is merciful.
Here’s the AHA moment:
God didn’t wait for Rachel to fix her heart before He responded—He responded to begin fixing her heart.
Let that sink in.
We think breakthrough comes after we become pure enough, patient enough, spiritual enough.
But sometimes…
Grace shows up while you’re still messy.

Still jealous.
Still struggling.
Still half-faith, half-frustration.

That’s not permission to stay there.
That’s proof God meets you there.
But here’s the warning:
When desire becomes demand, you stop trusting God—you start trying to control Him.
And God will never bow to your desperation.

He will answer…
but He will also transform.
Because the real issue was never just Rachel’s womb.
It was her heart.
And maybe…
that’s your story too.
SPIRITUAL MIRROR:
You don’t just want God to move—you want Him to move on your timeline.
And when He doesn’t…
You start rewriting who He is.

“Maybe He forgot me.”
“Maybe I’m not chosen.”
“Maybe I’m not enough.”
But Scripture never said God forgets His people.
Isaiah 49:15 whispers, “Can a mother forget her nursing child?… Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.”
So if God hasn’t moved yet…
It’s not neglect.
It’s purpose.
Because here’s where everything turns.
Rachel’s story doesn’t end with desperation.
It points to something deeper.
It points to Jesus.
Because every one of us knows what it means to feel barren.

Not physically—
but spiritually.
Empty.
Dry.
Trying… but still stuck.
Romans 3:23 says, “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
That’s the real barrenness.
A heart that cannot produce righteousness on its own.
And no amount of striving, comparing, or demanding can fix that.
But then—
Jesus steps in.

Not when we were ready.
Not when we were worthy.
But while we were still broken.
Romans 5:8 declares, “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
That’s the Gospel.

Not “clean yourself up first.”
Not “earn your miracle.”
But:
Come empty—and let Him fill you.

At the cross, Jesus carried your envy.
Your silent anger.
Your hidden disappointment with God.
He didn’t shame it.
He paid for it.
And through His resurrection, He offers something Rachel’s story was pointing toward all along:
Not just answered prayers…
But a transformed heart.
Identity shift:

You are not the one God forgot.
You are the one God is forming.

You are not delayed.
You are being prepared.
Conviction line:
Some of you don’t need a breakthrough—you need surrender.
Because the blessing you’re chasing might actually be revealing the idol you’re protecting.
And Jesus is not just here to give you what you want.
He’s here to become what you need.
So what now?
Bring it all.

The ugly prayer.
The impatient heart.
The quiet jealousy.
Lay it down.
Repent—not just of sin, but of trying to control God.
