That same choice still stands today.
Because the cross of Jesus is the ultimate Passover doorpost.
And the promise still echoes across history:

“When I see the blood, I will pass over you.”
— Exodus 12:13
If this message moved you, pause for a moment.
Reflect.
Because the story of the tenth plague is not just about judgment.
It’s about salvation.
It’s about the Lamb.
And it’s about the God who still rescues people from slavery to sin.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Some people in the Bible preached.
paragraphs:
Some people in the Bible preached.
Some performed miracles.
Some wrote the Scriptures we still read today.
But one man carried the message.
His name was Tychicus.
And if you blink while reading the New Testament, you might miss him completely.
His name appears only a few times. No dramatic speeches. No famous miracles. No chapters named after him.
Yet the apostle Paul trusted him with something incredibly important.
He trusted him with the message.
That alone should make us stop and think.
Because the letters Tychicus carried were not ordinary letters.
They were the letters to the churches.
Letters that would strengthen believers, correct false teaching, encourage the discouraged, and shape Christian theology for generations.
Some of the very Scriptures we read today were delivered by the hands of this quiet, faithful servant.
Think about that.

Before the church in Ephesus read Paul's words…
Before the believers in Colossae received instruction…
Before the encouragement reached struggling Christians…
Someone had to carry the message across long roads, uncertain terrain, and dangerous travel routes.
That someone was Tychicus.
Paul describes him this way:

“A beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord.”
— Ephesians 6:21
Those are not casual words.
Paul chose his words carefully.
He did not simply call him a messenger.
He called him beloved.
He called him faithful.
And he trusted him to represent him to entire churches.
In Colossians 4:7–8, Paul writes:
Did you notice something powerful there?
Tychicus was not just delivering a scroll.
He was delivering encouragement.
He carried the heart of the apostles with him.
He strengthened believers.
He represented the ministry.
He stood as a bridge between leaders and churches.
That kind of responsibility requires trust.
And trust is one of the highest currencies in the Kingdom of God.
Today we often measure significance by visibility.
We celebrate the ones on the platform.
The ones with the microphone.
The ones whose names everyone recognizes.
But the early church was built not only by famous leaders.
It was also built by faithful people like Tychicus.
People who could be trusted.
People who would not alter the message.
People who would deliver truth exactly as it was given.
People whose character spoke louder than their reputation.
The gospel moved forward because of men and women like him.
Reliable.
Steady.
Dependable.
And maybe that is why his story matters so much today.
Because many people feel invisible in their calling.
Maybe you are not the preacher.
Maybe you are not the leader everyone sees.
Maybe your role feels small.
Maybe you serve quietly.
Maybe you support others.
Maybe you carry responsibilities behind the scenes that few people ever notice.
But heaven notices.
The Kingdom of God has always been advanced by people who are faithful when nobody is watching.
People who will carry truth with integrity.
People who will serve without applause.
People who understand that obedience matters more than recognition.
Tychicus reminds us of a powerful truth:
You do not have to be the voice of the message to be essential to the mission.
Sometimes your role is to carry what God has entrusted to you.
Carry the encouragement.
Carry the responsibility.
Carry the calling.
Carry the truth.
And when you do that faithfully, you are participating in something far bigger than public recognition.
Because God does not measure greatness the way the world does.
He measures faithfulness.
Jesus once said:
“Well done, good and faithful servant.”
Not famous servant.
Not popular servant.
Faithful servant.
And that is exactly what Tychicus was.
Faithful enough for Paul to send him to multiple churches.
Faithful enough to represent apostolic leadership.
Faithful enough to strengthen believers across regions.
Faithful enough to carry words that would become part of the eternal Word of God.
That is not a small assignment.
That is sacred trust.
So if you ever feel like your role in the Kingdom is unnoticed…
Remember Tychicus.
He may not have written the letters.
But he carried them.
He may not have stood in every pulpit.
But he strengthened the churches.
He may not have been the headline.
But he helped deliver the message that would change the world.
And sometimes…
The most powerful ministries are the ones that history almost overlooks.
Because God is not only building His Kingdom through the famous.
He is building it through the faithful.
And heaven never overlooks those who can be trusted.
Scripture References

Ephesians 6:21–22
Colossians 4:7–8
2 Timothy 4:12
Titus 3:12
Reflection Question
Have you ever felt like your role in God's Kingdom was small or unnoticed? How does the story of Tychicus change the way you see faithfulness?
If this message encouraged you, share it so more people can remember the power of quiet faithfulness.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: FIVE.
paragraphs: FIVE.

You thought it was just a number.
But it keeps showing up… right when you’re at your worst.
You missed it.
Most people do.

Because we read the Bible for stories—
but God writes in patterns.

And five keeps appearing…
right where failure should have ended everything.
Right where shame should have had the final word.
But it didn’t.
Let me take you there.

Not to a perfect version of you—
but to the real one.
The one who knows what it’s like to fall… again.

The one who smiles in public but replays guilt in private.
The one who promised, “This is the last time…”
…but it wasn’t.
You ever feel that?
Like you’ve exhausted God’s patience?

Like heaven is keeping count—
and you’ve already gone too far?
Here’s where the tension breaks.
Because Scripture doesn’t hide broken people.
It exposes them.
Then it floods them with something they didn’t earn.
Five.
David picked up five smooth stones.

“Then he took his staff in his hand, chose for himself five smooth stones from the brook… and he drew near to the Philistine.”
— 1 Samuel 17:40
Five.
Standing before a giant that mocked him, defied God, and should have crushed him.
And yet—only one stone was used.
Why five?

Because even before the victory—
God was already declaring something deeper:
“This will not be about your strength.”
Now don’t miss this.

The law of God—His holy standard—
is written in the first five books of the Bible.
Genesis. Exodus. Leviticus. Numbers. Deuteronomy.
That law reveals something uncomfortable:
You don’t measure up.
I don’t either.

“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
— Romans 3:23
Not some.
All.
So here’s the tension:

God is holy.
You are not.

The law exposes it.
Your conscience confirms it.
And your past?
It reminds you.
So where does five—grace—fit into this?
Right here.
Right where you think it’s over.

Because the same Bible that gives the law…
introduces Jesus.

“For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”
— John 1:17
Do you see it?

Law reveals the problem.
Grace reveals the Savior.
And then this detonates everything you thought you knew about God:

“But where sin increased, grace increased all the more.”
— Romans 5:20
Read that again.
Not equal.
Not barely enough.
More.
You thought your sin disqualified you.
God says it became the stage where His grace would be displayed.
Let’s get real.

Your secret sin?
He saw it.

Your hidden addiction?
He knows it.
That thing you’re ashamed to even name?
He already carried it.
This is where most people run.
But this is exactly where God steps in.
Because grace is not God ignoring your sin.
Grace is God dealing with it fully—through Jesus Christ.
Here’s the Gospel—clear, unfiltered, undeniable:
You are a sinner.
Not just by mistake… but by nature.
And sin separates you from God.

“For the wages of sin is death…”
— Romans 6:23
That’s the cost.
Death. Separation. Judgment.
But don’t stop there.
Because the verse doesn’t end there.

“…but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
— Romans 6:23
Gift.
Not earned.
Not deserved.
Given.

Jesus lived the life you couldn’t live.
Perfect. Sinless. Obedient.
Then He died the death you should have died.
On the cross, your sin was not ignored—it was punished.
On Him.

“God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.”
— 2 Corinthians 5:21
That’s the exchange.
Your guilt… for His righteousness.
Your shame… for His acceptance.
Your death… for His life.
And three days later—
He rose.
Because grace doesn’t just forgive.
It restores.
It resurrects.
So what do you do with this?
You don’t clean yourself up first.
You don’t try harder.
You don’t wait until you feel worthy.
You repent.
You turn.
Not halfway.
All the way.

“Repent, then, and turn to God, so that your sins may be wiped out…”
— Acts 3:19
And you believe.
Not in yourself.
Not in religion.
In Jesus Christ alone.
This is your moment.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.

Because the same God who placed five stones in David’s hand…
is placing grace in front of you.
And this time—
It’s not about defeating a giant.
It’s about surrendering your heart.
Listen.
You are not beyond grace.
You are not too far gone.
You are not the exception.
Grace is still reaching.
Even now.
Even here.
Even for you.
So come home.
Drop the weight.
Confess the sin.
Receive the Savior.
And if something inside you is stirring—
That’s not emotion.
That’s invitation.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You can fool people…
paragraphs:
You can fool people…
…but you cannot fool God.

You can lift your hands in worship—
and still be hiding something you refuse to surrender.

And that tension right there?
That quiet, uncomfortable weight in your chest?
That’s not random.
That’s God knocking on the door you’ve been pretending doesn’t exist.
Because here’s the truth most people won’t say out loud:

You can build a whole “Christian life”
around avoiding one honest moment with God.

You can serve.
Lead.
Post Bible verses.
Say “God is good” with a steady voice—
while secretly negotiating with sin in the dark.
And the more you perform…
…the more you protect the mask.
You start editing your prayers.
Filtering your confessions.
Softening your convictions.
Because deep down, you’re afraid—
“If God really sees this… will He still want me?”
So you smile.
You show up.
You say the right things.
But inside?
There’s a war.
A quiet guilt that doesn’t leave.
A shame that keeps whispering,
“Don’t let them see the real you.”
Here’s where it gets dangerous.
Because performance doesn’t kill sin.
It hides it.
And what you hide… grows.
Jesus didn’t ignore this.
He exposed it.
📖 “Woe to you… you clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence.” (Matthew 23:25)
He wasn’t attacking broken people.
He was confronting hidden ones.
People who looked righteous—
but refused to be honest.
Let that sink in.
God is not impressed by your outside.
He sees the inside you’re trying to manage.
The thoughts you excuse.
The habits you justify.
The compromise you renamed “struggle.”
And some scholars interpret this passage as Jesus rebuking religious leaders specifically—
but the principle reaches all of us:
God is after the heart.
Not the performance.
Now here’s the turning point.
Don’t miss this.
Because if all you hear is exposure… you’ll run.
But if you hear the Gospel… you’ll come home.
You don’t have a sin problem that better behavior can fix.
You have a heart problem that only Jesus can redeem.
📖 “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
That includes the person preaching.
The one singing.
The one posting.
The one reading this right now.
Sin isn’t just what you do.
It’s who you are without Christ.
And no amount of performance can erase it.
But this is where grace explodes into the story.
📖 “But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Not when you cleaned yourself up.
Not when you fixed your image.
Not when you got consistent.
While you were still hiding.
Still struggling.
Still failing.
Jesus didn’t die for your mask.
He died for your real, unfiltered, exposed self.
And on that cross—
He took your sin.
Your shame.
Your secret.
Your double life.
He absorbed the judgment you were trying to avoid.
📖 “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree…” (1 Peter 2:24)
So you don’t have to carry them anymore.
But here’s the part many skip.
Grace is free—
but it’s not casual.
It calls for repentance.
Not pretending.
Not managing.
Not delaying.
Repentance means you stop hiding—
and start agreeing with God.
📖 “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just and will forgive us… and purify us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)
Confess.
Not perform.
Confess.
Not impress.
Confess.
And be cleansed.
This is your moment.
Not to try harder.
Not to fix your image.
But to come clean before a holy God who already sees everything—
and still chose the cross for you.
Imagine that.
The God who knows your worst—
offering you His best.
You don’t have to keep carrying this.
You don’t have to keep splitting your life into “public faith” and “private compromise.”
You don’t have to live exhausted from maintaining an illusion.
You can take off the mask.
Right now.
Say it honestly:
“Lord, this is who I really am.”
No filters.
No edits.
No performance.
And watch what happens.
Not rejection.
Not condemnation.
But mercy.
📖 “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” (Romans 8:1)
That’s not permission to keep hiding.
That’s freedom to finally be honest.
So here’s the invitation.
Drop the act.
Bring the secret into the light.
Stop negotiating with the sin that Jesus already died to break.
Run to Christ.
Not when you’re better.
Now.
And let Him do what performance never could—
make you new.
If this hit something deep in you…
That tug you feel?
That’s not emotion.
That’s conviction.
Type “OPEN MY HEART” if you’re ready to stop performing and start surrendering.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He was seconds away from becoming the villain in his own story.
paragraphs: He was seconds away from becoming the villain in his own story.

Sword drawn.
Jaw tight.
Breathing fire.
David—the anointed, the chosen, the future king—was marching toward bloodshed not because of war… but because of insult.

A man named Nabal had mocked him.
Dishonored him.
Returned evil for good.
And David snapped.
Four hundred men followed him into the heat of revenge. Not justice. Not righteousness. Revenge.
Pause.
Let that sink in.

A man after God’s own heart…
Almost became a man led by his own rage.
And here’s the truth we don’t like to admit:
You can be called by God… and still be one bad moment away from doing something you’ll regret forever.
Enter Abigail.

Not loud.
Not violent.
Not reactive.
But urgent.
Intentional.
Brave.
She runs toward the storm everyone else is avoiding. While David is charging forward with a sword, Abigail is running forward with wisdom.

Bread in her hands.
Wine prepared.
Heart surrendered.
And then—she does something powerful.
She falls before David.

Not because she is weak.
But because she understands something David almost forgot:
Humility can stop what anger accelerates.
She speaks.
And her words don’t just calm David… they confront him.

She reminds him who he is.
She reminds him who God is.
She reminds him what is at stake.
In 1 Samuel 25:31, she warns him that if he takes revenge, it will become “a burden” on his conscience—needless bloodshed that will haunt him when he becomes king.
That line cuts deep.
Because in that moment, Abigail isn’t just saving Nabal’s household…
She’s saving David’s future.
Let that hit you.
Sometimes God will send someone into your life—not to agree with your anger—but to interrupt it.
Not to validate your feelings—but to protect your calling.

And if you’re not careful…
you will silence the very voice God sent to save you.
David could have ignored her.

He had the power.
He had the army.
He had the justification—at least in his mind.
But instead…
He listens.
And everything changes.
David says in 1 Samuel 25:32–33:
“Praise be to the Lord… who has sent you today to meet me. May you be blessed for your good judgment and for keeping me from bloodshed this day…”
Don’t miss that.
David recognized that Abigail was God’s intervention.

Not coincidence.
Not inconvenience.
Divine interruption.
And here’s where it gets even deeper.
David was ready to take justice into his own hands.
But after he stops…
God Himself deals with Nabal.

No sword needed.
No revenge executed.
Just divine justice, in divine timing.
This is the part we struggle with.

Because we want closure now.
We want justice fast.
We want payback personal.
But Scripture shows us something better:
God does not need your anger to accomplish His justice.
Let that free you.
Because some of you are carrying the weight of something someone did to you.

The disrespect.
The betrayal.
The dishonor.

And you’re standing where David stood—
one decision away from reacting in a way that will cost you more than it’s worth.
Hear this clearly:

Not every offense deserves your reaction.
Not every insult requires your response.
Not every wrong is yours to repay.

And if you let your emotions lead…
you might win the moment but lose your peace, your witness, your future.
But there’s more.
This story doesn’t just point to wisdom.
It points to Jesus.
Because Abigail stood between a man of wrath and the people who would suffer for it.
She became a mediator.
A peacemaker.
A bridge between destruction and mercy.
And that is a shadow of Christ.
Because where David was about to shed blood in anger…
Jesus shed His blood in love.
Where David needed to be stopped from destroying others…
Jesus willingly allowed Himself to be destroyed to save us.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Do not take revenge… but leave room for God’s wrath.”
Why?
Because vengeance belongs to the Lord.
And grace… grace belongs to Jesus.
Who is your “Nabal” right now?
And more importantly…
Will you become David in his anger… or David after Abigail spoke?
Will you react?
Or will you surrender?
Will you take matters into your own hands?
Or will you trust God enough to let Him handle it?
Because one moment of restraint…
One act of obedience…
One decision to listen instead of lash out…
Could save you from becoming something you were never called to be.
Take a breath.
Lower the sword.
Let God be God.
And let grace rewrite what anger was about to destroy.
And if you’re the one struggling—
Not weakness.
Not defeat.
Surrender to God.
Because some battles are not won by fighting…
But by trusting the One who fights for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Moses did not lose his destiny in Egypt.
paragraphs: Moses did not lose his destiny in Egypt.
He just met the version of himself that could not carry it.
That is where most people misunderstand his story.

We often think Moses became a leader at the burning bush.
But the truth is… leadership did not begin with fire.
It began with failure.
In Exodus 2, Moses sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. Something inside him rises—anger, justice, urgency. He steps in, kills the Egyptian, and hides the body in the sand.
At first glance, it looks like courage.
But Scripture reveals something deeper.
Moses tried to deliver people before he was ready to depend on God.
And that is a dangerous place to be.
Because calling without surrender can lead to destruction.
The next day, when Moses tries to intervene again, he hears the words that expose everything:
“Who made you ruler and judge over us?”
In one moment, his identity collapses.

His position disappears.
His confidence shatters.
His future—at least in his mind—is over.
So he runs.

Not strategically.
Not spiritually.
Just… runs.

From Egypt.
From responsibility.
From the weight of what he did.
And maybe that is where this becomes personal.

Because some of us are not running from people…
We are running from moments.

Moments we wish we handled differently.
Decisions we regret.
Versions of ourselves we don’t want to face.
Moses carried that.
And for 40 years, he lived in Midian—not as a prince, not as a deliverer—but as a shepherd.

Quiet.
Hidden.
Forgotten.
Or at least… it felt that way.
But here is the part many people miss:
God never called Moses in Egypt.
He called him in the wilderness.
Let that sink in.

The place Moses thought was his ending…
was actually where God chose to speak.

In Exodus 3, there is no crowd.
No applause.
No platform.
Just a man, a desert, and a bush that burns without being consumed.
And from that fire, God calls his name.
“Moses… Moses.”

Not “deliverer.”
Not “leader.”
Not “chosen one.”
Just… Moses.
Because before God assigns purpose, He restores identity.
And this is where everything shifts.
Moses, the man who once acted boldly, now hesitates.
“Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?”

The same man who moved without thinking…
now feels completely unqualified.
Why?
Because the wilderness did something Egypt never could.
It stripped him of self-reliance.

It taught him silence.
It taught him patience.
It taught him dependence.
And here is the lesson most people overlook:

God did not use Moses in spite of the wilderness.
He used Moses because of it.
Those 40 years were not wasted.
They were preparation.

The desert trained his endurance.
The sheep trained his leadership.
The silence trained his listening.
So when God finally called him, Moses no longer trusted himself.
And that was exactly the point.
Because God was not looking for a man who believed in his own strength.
He was looking for a man who would rely on His.
That is why God responds to Moses’ insecurity with something powerful:
“I will be with you.”

Not “You are enough.”
Not “You’ve grown.”
Not “You’re ready.”
Just—“I am with you.”
Because the assignment was never about Moses being capable.
It was about God being present.
And that changes everything.
Some of you are frustrated because your life does not look like what you expected.

You thought you would be further by now.
You thought things would have happened already.
You thought that mistake disqualified you.
But Moses would tell you this:

Delay is not always denial.
Sometimes it is development.
You are not always buried when things go quiet.
Sometimes… you are being built.
Moses left Egypt as a fugitive.
He returned as a leader.

Not because his past disappeared—
but because God transformed his dependence.
And here is the truth that will challenge you:

You can be called and still be unprepared.
You can be gifted and still be unbroken.
You can have purpose and still need process.
Moses had all three.
And God took him through all of it.
So if you are in a wilderness season right now…

Do not rush it.
Do not resent it.
Do not mislabel it.

Because the very place you are tempted to call a setback
might be the place God is shaping the strength you will need later.
The wilderness is not where your story ends.
It is where your self-reliance does.
And when that finally breaks…
Purpose becomes clear.
So here is the question:

Are you running from your wilderness…
or allowing God to use it?

Because the difference between a fugitive and a leader
is not the absence of failure—
It is what God is allowed to do with it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Peter did not become bold in a moment.
paragraphs: Peter did not become bold in a moment.
He became bold through a process.
And if you miss that, you will misunderstand Pentecost.

Because Acts 2 is not just a story about power falling from heaven…
It is a story about a man who had already fallen—and been lifted back up.

This is the same Peter who once stood in the shadows of a courtyard fire…
And denied Jesus three times.

No crowd.
No threats of execution.
Just pressure.
Just fear.
Just the instinct to protect himself.
And he broke.
That is important.
Because sometimes we imagine that the people God uses most are the ones who never collapsed.
But Peter is proof that God often builds His strongest witnesses out of people who know exactly what it feels like to fail Him.
And not quietly.
Publicly.
Painfully.
Personally.
Peter didn’t just make a mistake—he denied the One he loved.
And when the rooster crowed, Scripture says he went out and wept bitterly.
That sound… that breaking… that moment…
That is part of his sermon too.
Because you cannot understand his boldness in Acts 2 unless you first understand his brokenness in Luke 22.
But here is where the story shifts.
Jesus didn’t discard Peter.
He restored him.
In John 21, Jesus didn’t shame him—He reinstated him.

Three times denied.
Three times restored.
“Do you love Me?”
That matters more than most people realize.

Because Peter’s authority did not come from perfection.
It came from restoration.
And then Pentecost came.
The Holy Spirit filled the room.
But more importantly—He filled the man.

And suddenly, the one who once said, “I do not know Him,”
stood up and said, “Let me tell you exactly who He is.”
That is the transformation.

Peter didn’t become someone else.
He became who he was always meant to be—after being healed.
And when he stood up to preach, he didn’t perform.
He proclaimed.

He didn’t soften the truth.
He didn’t adjust the message to please the crowd.
He said:

Jesus was crucified.
Jesus was raised.
Jesus is Lord and Messiah.
No hesitation.
No apology.
No fear.
And something powerful happened.
The Bible says they were “cut to the heart.”
That is what Spirit-filled truth does.

It doesn’t entertain.
It pierces.
It reaches places in people that clever words never can.

And when they asked, “What shall we do?”
Peter didn’t give them something comfortable.
He gave them something real.

Repent.
Turn.
Be baptized.
This is where the lesson gets personal.
Because many people today are waiting to feel “ready” before they speak, serve, or step into what God is calling them to do.
But Peter wasn’t ready because he was perfect.
He was ready because he was surrendered.
There is a difference.
Some of you are still silenced by your past.

Still replaying the moment you failed.
Still defined by the version of you that broke under pressure.
But Peter’s life is a loud contradiction to that mindset.

Because the same man who failed publicly…
was later used publicly.

The same voice that denied Jesus…
was later used to declare Him to thousands.
That means your worst moment does not have to be your final identity.
Let this settle deeply:
God does not waste repentance.
He doesn’t restore you just so you can sit quietly in shame.
He restores you so you can stand boldly in truth.
And maybe that’s what someone reading this needs to hear today.
You remember the night you failed.
But God remembers the morning He called you back.
You remember your weakness.
But God sees your surrender.
You remember the moment you broke.
But God sees the moment you said, “Lord, I still love You.”
And that is where everything begins again.
Peter’s story teaches us this:

Broken people can become bold people.
Restored people can become powerful witnesses.
Forgiven people can speak with a different kind of authority.
Not arrogance.
Not pride.
But conviction.
Because they know what grace feels like.

So if you’ve been hiding…
If you’ve been silent…
If you’ve been disqualifying yourself because of something in your past…
This is your reminder:
Peter hid once too.
But he didn’t hide forever.
And neither should you.

If Jesus has restored you, stand up.
If the Spirit has filled you, speak up.
If grace has reached you, don’t go back to silence.
Because your story is not over.
And sometimes…

The loudest testimony comes from the one who once said,
“I don’t know Him,”
but now lives to make Him known.
“Then Peter stood up… and addressed the crowd.” — Acts 2:14
So the question is:

What is God asking you to stand up and speak about…
that fear has been keeping you silent about?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Church is not called a building.
paragraphs: The Church is not called a building.

It is not called an institution.
It is not even primarily called an organization.

Scripture gives it a name that is far more intimate…
far more costly…
and far more revealing.
The Bride.
Let that sink in.

Because a bride is not something you use.
A bride is someone you love.
From the beginning, God has always spoken in the language of relationship.

In Genesis, a bride is formed.
In the Gospels, a Bridegroom arrives.
And in Revelation, a wedding is prepared.

This is not coincidence.
This is the storyline of redemption.
When Paul writes in Ephesians 5, he does not say Christ merely saved the Church.
He says:

Christ loved the Church
and gave Himself for her.
That means the cross was not just an act of rescue.
It was an act of devotion.

“The nails were not just driven by sin…
they were held by love.”
We often reduce salvation to forgiveness.
But Scripture expands it into something deeper.

You were not just forgiven.
You were chosen.

You were not just rescued.
You were pursued.

You were not just cleansed.
You were prepared.
Because a bride is not randomly selected.
She is intentionally chosen.
But here is where the message becomes uncomfortable…

Because if the Church is the Bride,
then our lives are not casual.
They are covenant.
Paul says in 2 Corinthians 11:2:
“I promised you to one husband, to Christ…”
That means our faith is not meant to be divided.

Not half-devoted.
Not distracted.
Not emotionally distant.
Because no bride stands at the altar with a divided heart.
And yet, this is where many believers quietly struggle.

We love God…
but we also love comfort.

We follow God…
but we still flirt with compromise.

We sing devotion…
but live distracted.

“The greatest threat to the Bride is not persecution…
it is distraction.”
Because distraction slowly erodes devotion.
And devotion is what defines a bride.
In Revelation 19, there is a powerful moment:

“The wedding of the Lamb has come,
and His bride has made herself ready.”
Notice that phrase.
Made herself ready.

Not earned salvation.
Not achieved perfection.
But prepared her heart.
Because holiness is not about pressure.
It is about preparation.

“God is not looking for a perfect Bride…
He is preparing a devoted one.”
This changes how we see obedience.
Obedience is no longer just duty.
It becomes desire.

Because when you love someone,
you don’t obey out of fear…
You respond out of affection.
Think about it.
A bride does not prepare for her wedding reluctantly.
She prepares with anticipation.

With focus.
With expectation.
With joy.
So why does God use this imagery?
Because He wants us to understand something many miss:

Christianity is not just about believing in Christ.
It is about belonging to Him.
And belonging changes everything.

It changes how you think.
How you live.
What you tolerate.
What you walk away from.
Because you are not just representing yourself anymore.
You are reflecting your Bridegroom.

“You don’t just carry His name…
you carry His heart.”
This is why compromise matters.
This is why purity matters.
This is why intimacy with God matters.
Not because God is trying to control you…
But because He is committed to you.
And here is the part that should humble all of us:
Christ did not choose a perfect Bride.
He chose a broken one.

A distracted one.
A wandering one.
And then He loved her anyway.

“Grace is not God lowering the standard…
it is God lifting the Bride.”

He washes.
He restores.
He refines.

Not to reject…
but to redeem.
This means your current struggle does not disqualify you.
Your weakness does not cancel your calling.
Your imperfections do not remove your identity.
Because the Bride is not defined by where she started…
But by who she belongs to.
And one day…
This will not be metaphor anymore.
It will be reality.
Revelation describes a moment where heaven opens…
And the Bride is ready.

Clothed in righteousness.
Radiant.
Prepared.
And the Bridegroom comes.

No more delay.
No more distance.
No more waiting.

“History is not moving toward chaos…
it is moving toward a wedding.”
So the question is not just:
Do you believe in God?
The deeper question is:
Are you living like the Bride?

Are you preparing…
or just attending?

Are you devoted…
or just involved?

Are you waiting with anticipation…
or distracted by everything else?
Because the Church is not just gathering every Sunday.
She is being prepared every day.
And the Bridegroom is coming.

Engagement Question:
If the Church is the Bride of Christ… what is one thing in your life that needs to shift from distraction to devotion?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t fall when he faced the king.
paragraphs:
He didn’t fall when he faced the king.
He fell when he trusted the wrong voice.
Let that sink in.

The man in 1 Kings 13 stood in front of power and did not tremble. He confronted the altar at Bethel. He spoke the word of the Lord with fire in his bones. And God confirmed it—the altar split, the ashes poured out. Even the king’s hand withered and was restored at the prophet’s word.

Public victory.
Undeniable power.
Heaven-backed authority.
But the story does not end at the altar.
It follows him… to the road.
Because the greatest battles are not always fought in front of crowds. They are fought in quiet moments, when no one is clapping, when no one is watching, when obedience becomes deeply personal.

God gave him a command—clear, specific, non-negotiable:
Do not eat bread.
Do not drink water.
Do not return the same way.
No confusion. No gray area.
And he obeyed… at first.
But then came a voice.

Not a pagan.
Not a king.
Not a false idol priest.
A prophet.

An older voice.
A familiar voice.
A spiritual voice.
“An angel spoke to me,” the old prophet said. “Come back with me.”
And here is where everything breaks.
Because when God has already spoken clearly, any voice that contradicts Him—no matter how spiritual it sounds—is not from Him.

The young prophet listened.
He sat.
He ate.
He drank.
And in that moment, partial obedience became full disobedience.
Let me speak plain, kapatid:

You can be right in your assignment and still be wrong in your response.
You can carry God’s power and still fall to subtle deception.
You can win in public and lose in private.
That’s the warning.

We often guard ourselves against obvious sin.
But we don’t always guard ourselves against spiritual-sounding compromise.
That’s more dangerous.

Because it feels safe.
It feels justified.
It feels… godly.

But truth is not measured by how it feels.
Truth is measured by what God has already said.
The tragedy deepens.
After the meal, the real word of the Lord comes—and this time, it’s judgment.
“You have disobeyed the command of the Lord…”
And on the road, a lion meets him.

And here’s the chilling part:
The lion kills him—but does not eat him.
The donkey stands beside the body.
The lion stands beside the donkey.

No chaos.
No randomness.
Just precision.
A divine sign.

This was not an accident.
This was accountability.
God was marking something for every generation to see:
Half obedience is still rebellion.
Feel the weight of that.

Not delayed obedience.
Not almost obedience.
Not “I meant well.”
Obedience.
Because God is not just concerned with what we start—He is concerned with how we finish.
And maybe this is where it hits you.

Because some of you reading this…
You started strong.

You were on fire.
Clear convictions.
Sharp discernment.
But somewhere along the way, another voice crept in.

A relationship.
A leader.
A trend.
A whisper that said, “It’s okay now.”
And slowly… you adjusted what God never changed.
Listen carefully:
God does not contradict Himself to accommodate us.

If He said it, He meant it.
If He commanded it, it still stands.
But don’t miss the Gospel here.
Because this story is not just a warning—it is a mirror that drives us to Christ.
Where this prophet failed, Jesus did not.

In the wilderness, Jesus also heard a voice.
A persuasive voice.
A spiritual voice that even quoted Scripture.
But Jesus did not bend.
He answered, “It is written.”

Again.
And again.
And again.
Where one prophet was deceived by a false word, Jesus stood anchored in the true Word.

And where disobedience brought death in 1 Kings 13…
Jesus stepped into death to pay for our disobedience.
That’s our hope.
Because if you’re honest—you’ve listened to the wrong voice too.
We all have.

But grace is not the permission to stay compromised.
Grace is the power to come back and obey.
So here’s the call:

Return to what God already said.
Silence the voices that dilute truth.
Test every word by Scripture.
And obey—not halfway, not selectively—but fully.

Even when it’s quiet.
Even when it’s inconvenient.
Even when no one sees.
Because the road after the victory still matters.
And you don’t have to end your story in tragedy.
In Christ, you can finish well.
“Trust in the Lord with all your heart… and He will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

So choose the straight path again.
Choose the narrow road again.
Choose obedience again.

Sit with it.
Pray.
Repent if needed.

Because this generation doesn’t just need powerful voices—
it needs faithful ones.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He called it urgency.
paragraphs:
He called it urgency.
God called it disobedience.
Pause.
Because this is where it gets uncomfortable.

You can look spiritual…
and still be out of alignment with God.

Saul wasn’t chasing idols.
He wasn’t bowing to false gods.
He was standing beside an altar.
Sacrificing.
Praying.
Doing something that looked right.
But heaven was not impressed.
And that should shake us.
Here’s the tension:

What if the thing you’re doing “for God”…
is actually a cover for not trusting Him?
What if your urgency is just fear in disguise?

What if your “I had no choice”
is really
“I didn’t want to wait”?
Let’s go there.
Because Saul’s story is not ancient history.
It’s a mirror.

The army was slipping away.
Fear was spreading like wildfire.
The enemy was gathering.
Pressure was rising.
Samuel said, “Wait.”
But waiting started to feel like losing.
So Saul stepped in.
Took control.
Grabbed the priestly role that wasn’t his.
And lit the fire.
1 Samuel 13:13–14
“You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God… For then the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever. But now your kingdom shall not continue…”
Read that again.

He didn’t commit murder.
He didn’t deny God publicly.
He simply refused to obey fully.
And God called it foolish.
Here’s the hard truth:
Partial obedience is still disobedience.
Delayed trust is still distrust.

And religious activity
can still be rebellion
when the heart refuses surrender.
Let’s talk about us.
Because this hits close.

You prayed…
but you also manipulated.

You said “God, I trust You”…
but still forced the outcome.

You posted Scripture…
but hid compromise in private.

You rushed decisions,
crossed lines,
justified shortcuts—
because waiting felt like dying.
That’s Saul’s spirit.

When pressure rises,
obedience feels negotiable.

When silence stretches,
control feels necessary.

When fear gets loud,
faith gets quiet.
And here’s the deeper layer:
This is not just failure.
This is pride.
The belief that:
“I know better than God in this moment.”
“I can fix this faster.”
“I cannot afford to wait.”
But Scripture cuts through that illusion.
Proverbs 3:5–6
“Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make straight your paths.”
Not some ways.
All.

Even the urgent ones.
Especially the urgent ones.
Now feel the weight of this:

Saul lost a kingdom
not because he was weak—
but because he refused to trust God under pressure.
And if we’re honest…
So have we.
Moments we rushed.
Decisions we forced.
Boundaries we broke.
Silence we couldn’t endure.
And now?
There’s shame.
Regret.
That quiet voice saying:
“You messed it up.”
Because this is where grace breaks in.
Jesus steps into Saul’s failure.

Where Saul grabbed control—
Jesus surrendered control.

Where Saul disobeyed under pressure—
Jesus obeyed under pressure so intense
He sweat blood in Luke 22:42:
“Father, if You are willing, remove this cup from Me. Nevertheless, not My will, but Yours, be done.”
Feel that.
Jesus had every reason to avoid the cross.
Every reason to take control.
But He chose obedience.
Fully.
Perfectly.
For you.
And because He did—
Your failure is not final.

Your impulsive decisions
are not the end of your story.

Your “unlawful sacrifices”
do not have the last word.
Romans 5:8
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after you fixed it.
Not after you learned patience.
While you were still choosing control.
This is the Gospel:

You sinned.
You rushed.
You disobeyed.

But Jesus obeyed in your place,
died for your sin,
and rose again to give you new life.
So what now?
Don’t hide.
Don’t justify.
Don’t rename disobedience as “strategy.”
Repent.
Turn.
Lay down control.
Release the outcome.
Trust God again—
even if it feels slow.
Because God is not late.
He is never late.

The delay you hate
may be the protection you don’t see.

The waiting you resist
may be forming the faith you need.
You don’t need to fix everything.
You need to surrender everything.
Right now.
Yes, you.
The one who rushed.
The one who forced it.
The one who regrets it.
Jesus is not pushing you away.
He is calling you back.
Come with honesty.
Come with your failure.
Come with your impatience.
And watch what grace does.
Psalm 51:17
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.”
God is not looking for perfect performance.
He is looking for surrendered hearts.
So breathe.
Let go.
Return.
If this hit you deep…
If this stirred something in you…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She corrected him… but God corrected her.
paragraphs: She corrected him… but God corrected her.
Pause.

Because this wasn’t rebellion in the streets—
this was rebellion in the family.

She had history with God.
She had influence.
She had a voice.
But something shifted.
And almost no one saw it coming.
The sin that doesn’t look like sin

It didn’t start with shouting.
It started with comparison.

A quiet question.
A subtle irritation.
A creeping thought:
“Why him… and not me?”
Miriam didn’t deny God.
She just… repositioned herself.
“Has the Lord indeed spoken only through Moses? Has He not spoken through us also?” — Numbers 12:2
That sounds spiritual.
That sounds reasonable.
But heaven heard something deeper.
Pride.
Pride wears holy language
Let’s be honest.

Not all sin looks dark.
Some of it wears church clothes.

You can quote Scripture
and still compete in your heart.

You can serve publicly
and secretly crave recognition.

You can worship loudly
and quietly resent someone God is using.

Miriam wasn’t outside the camp.
She was leading inside it.

And still—
her heart drifted.
The dangerous shift
Here’s the tension:
Miriam wasn’t wrong that God spoke through her.
She was a prophetess (Exodus 15:20).

But truth became twisted
when it turned into entitlement.

Because calling is a gift—
not a weapon.

And when God assigns roles,
He doesn’t consult our ego.
Heaven steps in
No debate.
No vote.
No committee.
God came down.
“And the Lord came down in a pillar of cloud… and called Aaron and Miriam.” — Numbers 12:5
Imagine that moment.

The air shifts.
The camp goes silent.
Presence becomes heavy.

And then—
one piercing question:
“Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?” — Numbers 12:8

Not “Why were you frustrated?”
Not “Why were you misunderstood?”
Why were you not afraid?
Because pride numbs reverence.
It makes us casual about what God takes seriously.
Meanwhile… Moses
He didn’t defend himself.

He didn’t clap back.
He didn’t correct the narrative.
“Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men…” — Numbers 12:3

While Miriam elevated herself,
Moses lowered himself.
And heaven noticed.
Then it happened
Sudden.
Visible.
Unavoidable.
“When the cloud removed… behold, Miriam was leprous, like snow.” — Numbers 12:10

The one who spoke out
was now set apart.

The one who challenged authority
now faced divine authority.

Leprosy in Scripture wasn’t just sickness—
it was separation.

Isolation.
Exposure.
Public consequence.
Let this land

Jealousy said,
“You deserve more.”

God revealed,
“You’ve misunderstood everything.”

Pride said,
“Step up.”

God responded,
“Step out.”
But here’s the part that breaks you
Moses prayed for her.

The man she criticized
became her intercessor.
“O God, please heal her—please.” — Numbers 12:13

No bitterness.
No revenge.
Just mercy.
The Gospel is hiding here
Because this is not just Miriam’s story.
This is ours.
We’ve all had moments—

Where someone else’s blessing
felt like our rejection.

Where someone else’s elevation
felt like our demotion.

Where we smiled in public
but wrestled in private.

Comparison.
Resentment.
Silent pride.
But Moses is only a shadow
Because there is a greater Mediator.
Jesus Christ.

Where Miriam spoke against Moses,
we have spoken against God—in thought, word, and action.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
We didn’t just slip.
We rebelled.
We elevated ourselves.
We chose our will over His.
And the result?
Spiritual separation.

Not just leprosy of the skin—
but sin in the soul.
But Jesus stepped in
Not just to pray.
To pay.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
On the cross, Jesus took the isolation we deserved.

The shame.
The exposure.
The judgment.

He became what we were—
so we could become what we are not.
“He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us…” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
That’s not religion.
That’s rescue.
Grace didn’t ignore Miriam
And it won’t ignore you.

She was shut out—
yes.
But she was also restored.
“Let her be shut outside the camp seven days, and after that she may be brought in again.” — Numbers 12:14
Judgment was real.
But it wasn’t the end.
So here’s the question
What’s hiding in your heart?

Comparison?
Quiet resentment?
Unspoken pride?
God isn’t just listening to your words.
He’s weighing your motives.
And here’s the invitation
Come clean.

Not later.
Now.
Repent—not just of actions, but attitudes.
Lay down the need to be seen.
Surrender the need to compete.
Let Jesus cleanse what you can’t fix.
Because grace is not for the perfect—
It’s for the honest.
Say it if you’re ready
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You thought having less meant God abandoned you.
paragraphs: You thought having less meant God abandoned you.
But what if it’s proof He’s about to move?
Because Gideon didn’t lose soldiers…
God removed his excuses.
And that changes everything.
Thirty-two thousand men.
That’s what Gideon started with in Book of Judges 7.

A number that feels safe.
Strong.
Respectable.
Then God speaks:
“Too many.”
Too many… for victory?
Read that again.
Because heaven doesn’t measure strength the way we do.

God cuts it down to 10,000.
Still too many.
Then 300.
Three hundred men against an army described as “thick as locusts” (Judges 7:12).
That’s not strategy.
That’s surrender.
And if you’re honest…
You hate that kind of math.

You pray for increase—
God allows reduction.

You ask for clarity—
God gives you less control.

You want security—
God strips your backup plan.
Why?
Because deep down, there’s a quiet addiction we don’t confess:

We want God’s promises…
without needing God.
That’s the hidden pride.

Not loud.
Not obvious.
But deadly.
Let me ask you something:

What are you holding onto
that makes you feel “safe”…
but keeps you from full surrender?
And here’s the harder one:

If God removed it today—
would your faith collapse?
Some of us don’t trust God’s power.

We trust our preparation.
Our connections.
Our reputation.
And we call that “wisdom.”
But Scripture cuts deeper.
God says in Judges 7:2 that if Israel won with a large army, they would boast against Him, saying, “My own hand has saved me.”
That’s the real enemy.
Not Midian.
Self-glory.
Here’s the AHA moment:
God will reduce your resources if your heart is starting to worship them.
Not to punish you—
But to protect you.
Because this is where it gets uncomfortable.
Some people are asking God for breakthrough…
While secretly building a life that doesn’t require Him.
You sing “I surrender all”—
But your decisions whisper, “I got this.”
That’s not faith.
That’s performance dressed like devotion.
SPIRITUAL MIRROR:
If your life still works without prayer, you’re not walking in dependence—you’re walking in control.
And this is why Gideon’s story matters.
Because the victory didn’t come through swords.
It came through obedience.

Torches.
Clay jars.
Trumpets.
Weapons that make no sense—unless God is the strategy.
And when they broke the jars and lifted the light…
God caused confusion in the enemy camp.
They turned on each other.
Victory—without human explanation.
Because when God moves, He removes your ability to take credit.
But don’t miss this.
Gideon’s story is not just history.
It’s prophecy of a greater “reduction.”
At the cross of Jesus Christ.
Everything looked like loss.

Followers scattered.
Hope crushed.
The Savior nailed and bleeding.
Reduced.
But in that moment—
God was doing His greatest work.
Because Isaiah 53:5 says He was pierced for our transgressions… crushed for our iniquities… and by His wounds, we are healed.
Sin was the real enemy.
Not Midian.
And Jesus didn’t come with an army.
He came with a cross.
Here’s the Gospel, clear and unfiltered:
You and I are not just weak—we are sinners.

We’ve trusted ourselves more than God.
Chosen control over surrender.
Pride over obedience.
And sin separates us from God.
But Jesus stepped in.

Lived the life we couldn’t live.
Died the death we deserved.
Rose again to give us new life.
Not by our strength.
Not by our numbers.
By His grace alone.
Ephesians 2:8 says we are saved by grace through faith—not by works, so no one can boast.
Do you see it?
God reduces…
So grace can be revealed.
CONVICTION LINE:

Some people don’t want God to be glorified—
they just want God to be useful.
But real faith says:

“Even if You strip it all away…
I still trust You.”
IDENTITY SHIFT:
You are not called to be impressive.
You are called to be dependent.
You are not the source.
You are the vessel.
And maybe that’s why things feel smaller right now.

The circle.
The opportunities.
The resources.
It’s not rejection.
It’s refinement.
God is setting the stage for a victory that cannot be explained by your résumé.
Only by His presence.
So here’s the invitation.
Lay it down.

The backup plan.
The silent pride.
The need to be in control.
Repent.
Not just of sin you hate—
But of the independence you secretly love.
And come to Jesus.
Because the same God who reduced Gideon’s army…

Is the same God who can rebuild your life
on grace that never fails.
If this hit your heart, don’t ignore it.
Not hype. Formation.
And the next message might be the one that confirms what He’s already whispering to you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He waited his whole life… for a moment most people would have missed.
paragraphs: He waited his whole life… for a moment most people would have missed.

No spotlight.
No thunder.
No royal procession.
Just a baby.
And yet—everything in eternity was wrapped in that Child.

Luke 2 doesn’t shout. It whispers.
And only those who are listening… hear God.

Simeon was not famous.
Not powerful.
Not trending.
But heaven knew his name.

Because while others performed religion,
he carried expectation.
The Holy Spirit had told him:
“You will not see death before you have seen the Lord’s Christ.” (Luke 2:26)
Think about that kind of promise.

Not vague.
Not symbolic.
Personal.
Specific.
God tied Simeon’s death… to the arrival of salvation.
So every day Simeon lived with tension.

Is it today?
Is it now?
Will I finally see Him?
Years passed.

Dreams delay.
Bodies age.
Prayers stretch thin.
But God does not forget what He speaks.

And on an ordinary day—
with ordinary footsteps echoing in the temple—
destiny walked in unnoticed.

Mary.
Joseph.
And Jesus.
No halo.
No visible crown.
No announcement.
Just a poor couple carrying a Child wrapped in humility.

But the Spirit said,
“That’s Him.”
And Simeon moved.
Listen—this is where many miss God.
Because heaven’s greatest moves often look… small.

Too simple.
Too quiet.
Too ordinary.
But Simeon didn’t need spectacle.
He had revelation.
He takes the Child into his arms.
Pause there.
An old man… holding the One who holds the universe together.
Wrinkled hands… carrying eternal glory in fragile flesh.
And he says:

“Lord, now You are letting Your servant depart in peace…
for my eyes have seen Your salvation.” (Luke 2:29–30)

Not a path to salvation.
Not instructions for salvation.
Your salvation.
A Person.
Jesus.
This is where many still stumble today.

We want formulas.
Steps.
Systems.
But God didn’t send a method.
He sent His Son.

You don’t earn salvation.
You receive Him.
But then—
The moment shifts.
Because the Gospel is not just comfort.
It is confrontation.
Simeon blesses them… then looks at Mary and says:

“This Child is appointed for the fall and rising of many…
and for a sign that is opposed…
and a sword will pierce through your own soul also.” (Luke 2:34–35)
That’s heavy.

This baby—
soft skin, quiet breath, tiny fingers—
would divide humanity.

Some would rise because of Him.
Others would fall because of Him.

Same Jesus.
Different response.
Because Jesus doesn’t leave hearts neutral.
He reveals them.
He exposes what we truly love.

Pride or surrender.
Control or trust.
Sin or repentance.

And Mary—blessed, chosen, favored Mary—
would feel the cost.
A sword.

Not literal steel—
but the piercing agony of watching her Son rejected, beaten, crucified.

The Child she cradled…
would one day hang on a cross.
This is the part we don’t put in soft nativity scenes.
But it’s the truth.
The manger was never the destination.
It was the doorway.
And here’s the question that refuses to leave:
What will you do with Jesus?
You cannot admire Him from a distance forever.

He is not just a symbol.
Not just a teacher.
Not just inspiration.
He is salvation.
And Simeon shows us the only right response:

Receive Him.
Trust Him.
Rest in Him.
Maybe you’ve been waiting.

Waiting for clarity.
Waiting for breakthrough.
Waiting for God to show up.
Simeon’s story speaks to you:
God keeps His promises.

Not always fast.
Not always loud.
But always faithful.

And when He moves—
it may not look how you expected.

It may come wrapped in simplicity.
Hidden in humility.
But don’t miss it.
Don’t let familiarity blind you to glory.
And maybe this is the deeper layer:

Some of you want peace…
without surrender.

You want comfort…
without repentance.

You want Jesus…
without the cross.
But Simeon’s prophecy stands:

Jesus will either be your rising…
or your falling.
There is no middle ground.
Here’s the hope:

The same Child Simeon held
grew up to carry your sin.

The same Jesus who was received in the temple
was rejected outside the city.

He was pierced—
so your soul doesn’t have to be destroyed by sin.

He died—
so you could live.

He rose—
so your story doesn’t end in shame.
So come.

Not with perfection.
Not with performance.
But with surrender.
Take Him like Simeon did.
Hold nothing back.
And say:
“Lord… my eyes have seen Your salvation.”
Because in the end, this is not just Simeon’s story.
It’s yours.

A life of waiting.
A moment of encounter.
A decision that defines everything.
Receive Him.
Before the waiting turns into regret.
Before the opportunity passes unnoticed.
Before the moment is gone.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t inherit revival.
paragraphs:
He didn’t inherit revival.
He inherited ruin.

A throne at eight years old.
A nation already drifting.
A temple already decaying.
And the most dangerous part?
Everyone got used to it.

That is how spiritual collapse happens.
Not with a loud explosion.
But with quiet tolerance.

Dust settles.
Standards lower.
Conviction softens.
And what once broke your heart…
But then came Josiah.

Not the strongest king.
Not the oldest.
Not the most experienced.
But he had something rare:
A heart that still cared.

At sixteen, he began to seek the Lord (2 Chronicles 34:3).
At twenty, he started tearing down idols.
And at twenty-six… he faced what others ignored.
The temple of God was in ruins.

Not abandoned.
Not destroyed.
Just… neglected.

Still standing.
But no longer sacred in the hearts of the people.
Let that sink in.
Because many of us are living like that temple.

Functioning.
Smiling.
Posting.
But inside?
Cracks.

Prayer life collapsing quietly.
Sin hiding in familiar corners.
Convictions buried under convenience.
The Word of God… unopened, but never far.
And here’s the truth most people avoid:
Neglect can destroy what rebellion never could.

Josiah didn’t decorate the damage.
He didn’t rename the ruin.
He repaired it.

Stone by stone.
Room by room.
Costly.
Intentional.
Uncomfortable.
And in the middle of that restoration…
They found it.
Buried under years of dust.
Forgotten, but not gone.
The Book of the Law. (2 Kings 22:8)
Pause there.

The Word of God was always in the house.
But the people had lost their hunger for it.
And when it was finally read to Josiah…

He didn’t argue.
He didn’t justify.
He didn’t explain it away.
He broke.
“When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his robes.” (2 Kings 22:11)

That is not weakness.
That is awakening.
Because real encounters with God’s Word will always confront you before they comfort you.

They will expose before they embrace.
They will cut before they heal.
And Josiah felt it.

Not just personal conviction…
but national weight.

Generational drift.
Inherited compromise.
A people who had forgotten their God.
And instead of protecting his image…
He humbled himself.
Listen to what God said about him:
“Because your heart was responsive and you humbled yourself before the Lord… I have heard you.” (2 Kings 22:19)
That is the doorway.

Not perfection.
Not performance.
A responsive heart.

A heart that still trembles at truth.
A heart that refuses to normalize what God calls sin.
A heart willing to be undone so it can be remade.
But don’t miss this—
Josiah could repair a building.

He could restore order.
Reinstate worship.
Lead a nation back to covenant.
But he could not fix the deepest ruin of all:
The human heart.
Because the real broken temple is not made of stone.

It’s you.
It’s me.
And no amount of effort, discipline, or religion can fully restore what sin has corrupted.
That’s where Jesus enters the story.

Not as another reformer.
Not as a better king.
As the Savior.

Where Josiah tore his robes…
Jesus had His body torn.

Where Josiah responded to the Word…
Jesus is the Word made flesh (John 1:14).

Where Josiah led people back to the law…
Jesus fulfilled the law and carried its judgment on the cross.
This is the Gospel:

We were the ruined temple.
We were the neglected place.
We were the ones who buried truth under sin.
And instead of abandoning us…
Christ came to rebuild.

Through His blood, forgiveness flows.
Through His resurrection, new life begins.
Through His Spirit, dead hearts awaken again.
He doesn’t patch your life.
He transforms it.
He doesn’t just clean the outside.
He restores the inside.
So now the question is not historical.
It’s personal.
What have you learned to ignore?

That hidden habit?
That secret compromise?
That cold prayer life?
That Bible collecting dust?
That calling you keep postponing?
Don’t wait until everything collapses.
Don’t wait for public consequences.
Be like Josiah.

Return to the Word.
Respond with humility.
Let conviction lead you—not into shame—but into surrender.
Because here is the hope that changes everything:
God is not looking for perfect people.
He is looking for responsive hearts.
And if you come to Him today—honest, broken, willing—
He will not reject you.
He will receive you.
He will forgive you.
He will rebuild what you thought was too far gone.
This is your moment.

Not tomorrow.
Not someday.
Now.

Open the Word again.
Fall on your knees again.
Call on the name of Jesus again.
And watch what He restores.

Because what shame tried to bury…
grace is ready to resurrect.

From neglected to renewed.
From broken to rebuilt.
From silence to surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Your face is glowing… but your life is hiding something.
paragraphs: Your face is glowing… but your life is hiding something.
Read that again.

Because it’s possible to look like Moses…
and live like the crowd around the golden calf.

You can carry the tablets…
and still carry secret sin.

You can speak “God is good”…
while your private life whispers something else.
And here’s the tension—
What happens when glory touches a life that still has shadows?
Exodus 34 is not soft.
It is holy collision.

Moses walks down the mountain after meeting God—
and his face is shining so intensely that people back away.
Not inspired.
Afraid.
Why?
Because glory exposes.

Light doesn’t negotiate with darkness.
It reveals it.
And don’t miss this—
This moment comes right after one of Israel’s darkest failures.
The golden calf.
Idolatry.
Spiritual betrayal.
They traded the living God for something they could control.
Sound familiar?
We don’t melt gold today.
But we melt time.
We melt attention.
We melt affection.
Into things that replace God.
Careers.
Relationships.
Secret habits.
Hidden screens.
Private compromises.
And still—
We show up “shining.”
Church on Sunday.
Quotes on Instagram.
“Blessed” in the bio.
But deep down—
You know.
There’s a gap.
Here’s the truth that hits like thunder:
God is not impressed by reflected light that hides unrepented sin.
Listen to what God declares about Himself:
“The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness…” — Exodus 34:6
This is not just poetry.
This is identity.

God reveals His glory not just in power—
but in mercy.
But don’t twist it.
Mercy is not permission.
It’s invitation.
Some scholars interpret this moment as the clearest self-revelation of God in the Old Testament—where His justice and mercy meet without contradiction.
He sees sin fully.
And still chooses to make a way.
That’s where the story turns.
Because Moses’ glow…
Was temporary.
The apostle Paul later explains:
“The Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end…” — 2 Corinthians 3:7
It faded.
Even glory reflected from God…
could not last.
Let that settle.

You can have moments with God…
and still fade back into old patterns.

You can cry at the altar…
and still return to the same chains.
So what’s missing?
Not more effort.
A new heart.
This is where Jesus steps in—
Not as a better Moses.
But as the fulfillment Moses was pointing to.
Moses reflected glory.
Jesus is the glory.
“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen His glory…” — John 1:14
Moses covered his face with a veil.
Jesus tore the veil open.
“And the curtain of the temple was torn in two…” — Matthew 27:51
Moses brought tablets of stone.
Jesus writes on hearts.
“I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you…” — Ezekiel 36:26
Here’s the Gospel—
Clear.
Undeniable.
Unavoidable.
You are not just someone who needs improvement.
You are someone who needs redemption.
Sin is not just mistakes.
It’s rebellion.
It’s choosing self over God.
And no amount of “glow” can cover that.
But Jesus didn’t come to expose you and leave you there.
He came to save you.
On the cross—
Your hidden sin wasn’t hidden anymore.
It was nailed.
Public.
Exposed.
Judged.
“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree…” — 1 Peter 2:24
And then—
Grace exploded.
Not earned.
Not deserved.
Given.
This is the shift:

From covering your sin…
to confessing it.

From performing light…
to becoming transformed by it.
Paul says:
“And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image…” — 2 Corinthians 3:18
Not fading.
Transforming.
Not hiding.
Beholding.
This is not behavior management.
This is heart resurrection.
So let me ask you—
Where are you still wearing a “veil”?
Where are you managing appearance instead of surrendering reality?

Where are you glowing…
but not growing?
God is not asking you to shine harder.
He’s calling you to come closer.
Because real transformation doesn’t come from trying.
It comes from turning.
Repentance.
Honest.
Raw.
Unfiltered.
And here’s the hope—
You don’t have to clean yourself before coming to Him.
You come as you are—
and He makes you new.
No more pretending.
No more double life.
No more borrowed glow.
Just grace.
Just Jesus.
Right now—
This moment—
You can respond.
Whisper it if you have to:
“Jesus… no more hiding.”
Let Him into the places you’ve locked.
The habits you’ve justified.
The shame you’ve buried.
Because the same God who made Moses’ face shine…
is ready to transform your entire life.
Not temporarily.
Eternally.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He waited so long… it almost felt like God forgot.
paragraphs: He waited so long… it almost felt like God forgot.
And that’s where the shame crept in.

Not loud.
Not obvious.
But quiet… dangerous… accusing.
“Maybe the promise wasn’t really for you.”

You won’t say it out loud.
But deep inside?
You’ve thought it.

You’ve prayed.
You’ve believed.
You’ve held on longer than most people would.
And still… nothing.
So now you’re smiling in public—but wrestling in private.

Still serving—but slowly doubting.
Still posting faith—but carrying silent disappointment.
That’s where Abraham was.

Not the hero version we like to quote.
Not the “father of faith” highlight reel.
But the waiting version.
The tired version.
The version where his body was aging, Sarah’s womb was silent, and the promise of God felt… delayed.
And here’s the uncomfortable truth:

Waiting didn’t just test his patience.
It exposed his unbelief.

Because when the promise delays…
we start producing alternatives.
Abraham didn’t just wait.
He tried to help God.
Genesis 16 shows it clearly—he slept with Hagar to produce what God had already promised.
That wasn’t just a mistake.
That was a moment of shame.
A moment where faith slipped… and flesh took over.
And if we’re honest?
We’ve done the same.
We don’t wait anymore—we force.
We don’t trust—we control.
We don’t surrender—we strategize outside of God’s will.
We create Ishmaels in seasons meant for Isaac.
And afterward?
We carry the weight of it.

The regret.
The “I should’ve trusted God.”
The quiet guilt no one else sees.
But here’s the turning point.
Here’s where everything shifts.
Genesis 21:1 says:
“And the Lord visited Sarah as he had said, and the Lord did unto Sarah as he had spoken.”
Read that again.

As He had said.
As He had spoken.

Not as Abraham performed.
Not as Sarah believed perfectly.
Not as their faith remained flawless.
But as God said.
This is where shame breaks.
Because the promise was never sustained by Abraham’s perfection.
It was sustained by God’s faithfulness.
Let that sink in.
You didn’t disqualify yourself as easily as you think.

Yes—you stumbled.
Yes—you doubted.
Yes—you tried to fix things your own way.
But God did not cancel His word over your life.
Romans 3:3–4 says:
“Will their unfaithfulness nullify God’s faithfulness? Not at all! Let God be true, and every human being a liar.”
Your failure is real.
But it is not final.
And Abraham’s story doesn’t end with shame.
It ends with fulfillment.
Isaac was born.
Not because Abraham got it right.
But because God never gets it wrong.
And here’s the deeper revelation—
Isaac wasn’t just a miracle baby.
He was a shadow.
A preview.
A whisper of something greater.
Because just like Abraham waited for a promised son…
Humanity waited for Jesus.
And just like Isaac came when it seemed impossible…
Christ came in the fullness of time.
Galatians 4:4 says:
“But when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son…”

Not early.
Not late.
Perfect timing.
And Jesus didn’t just come to fulfill a promise.
He came to deal with your shame.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when you got your act together.
Not when your faith was strong.
Not when you stopped making mistakes.
While you were still broken.
That’s the Gospel.

Sin is real.
Failure is real.
Shame is real.
But grace is greater.
Through Jesus—

Your sin is forgiven.
Your shame is covered.
Your failure is not the end of your story.
Isaiah 61:7 declares:
“Instead of your shame you will receive a double portion… and everlasting joy will be yours.”
That’s not motivational.
That’s redemption.
So hear this clearly:
Stop disqualifying yourself from what God already promised.
Stop letting your past speak louder than His word.
Stop believing that delay means rejection.
Because if God fulfilled His word to Abraham…
If God sent Jesus right on time…
Then He is not confused about your life.
He is not late.
He is not absent.
And He has not changed His mind about you.
But here’s the invitation—
Don’t just admire Abraham’s story.
Step into surrender.
Repent where you forced what God told you to wait for.
Release the shame you’ve been hiding behind your smile.
Come back to Jesus—not with performance, but with honesty.
Because the same God who gave Isaac…
Is the same God who gave His Son.
And Jesus didn’t come just to inspire you.
He came to save you.
To restore you.
To rewrite you.
Right now—this moment—He’s calling you back.
Not to perfection.
But to Himself.
Sit with it.
Respond to it.
Let it confront you—and heal you.
And if this stirred something deep in you…
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t just fall to his knees…
paragraphs:
He didn’t just fall to his knees…
he realized heaven was watching.
And suddenly—everything he thought was “normal”… felt filthy.

Because sin doesn’t feel heavy…
until you see it in the light of God.

Ezra 9 doesn’t begin with shouting.
It begins with silence…
then trembling…
then a man collapsing under the weight of something most people had learned to ignore.

Israel wasn’t clueless.
They weren’t pagans.
They were people who knew Scripture…
but slowly made peace with what God had already spoken against.

Intermarriage wasn’t just cultural blending.
It was spiritual compromise.
It was the quiet erosion of holiness.
And nobody panicked.
Nobody wept.
Nobody stopped.

Until one man saw it…
and couldn’t unsee it.
“I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to You…” (Ezra 9:6)
Read that again.

A priest—
a leader—
ashamed to even look up.

Not because he personally committed every sin…
but because he understood something deeper:

Sin is never just personal.
It’s relational.
It grieves God.
And here’s the part that cuts—

We don’t cry over sin anymore.
We manage it.

We rename it.
We justify it.
But heaven hasn’t changed its mind.
God still calls sin… sin.
And according to Isaiah 59:2, “your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God.” Not distance. Separation.

That’s not poetic language.
That’s reality.
So let me ask you—
When was the last time you felt grieved over something you tolerated?

Not embarrassed.
Not exposed.
Grieved.

Or have we become so used to compromise…
that conviction feels uncomfortable instead of holy?
Here’s the hidden struggle nobody posts about:
Delayed obedience.

You know what God said.
You even agreed with it.
But you told yourself, “Later.”
And later became a lifestyle.
Or maybe it’s quieter than that—

You still pray.
Still worship.
Still show up.

But there’s a corner of your life…
you’ve silently told God not to touch.

No announcement.
No rebellion out loud.
Just quiet resistance.
And you’ve learned how to function with it.
That’s where Ezra 9 hits different.

Because Ezra didn’t say,
“Well, at least we’re not as bad as before.”
No.

He tore his clothes.
He pulled his hair.
He sat in shock.
Why?

Because when you truly see sin…
you stop negotiating with it.
Here’s the AHA moment:

The problem isn’t that we sin.
The problem is we’ve stopped being shocked by it.
That’s the danger.

Not failure.
Familiarity.
And here’s the mirror—
If your sin doesn’t bother you anymore… something deeper is already broken.

This isn’t about guilt.
This is about awakening.

Because there are people who know Bible verses…
but no longer feel the weight of God’s holiness.
And that’s more dangerous than ignorance.
Jesus said in Luke 5:32, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

Not improvement.
Not behavior management.
Repentance.
Turning.
Breaking agreement with sin.
But here’s where grace steps in—

Ezra fell in shame…
but Jesus stepped in to carry it.

Where Ezra said, “I can’t lift my face,”
Hebrews 4:16 invites us to “approach the throne of grace with confidence.”
How?
Because of Christ.

Because on the cross, Jesus didn’t just feel sorrow over sin—
He absorbed its penalty.
2 Corinthians 5:21 says, “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us…”
Read that slowly.
He became what you’re hiding.
So you wouldn’t have to hide anymore.
This is the Gospel:

Yes, your sin is serious.
Yes, it separates.
Yes, it deserves judgment.
But Jesus took your place.

Not to excuse sin—
but to destroy its power.

Not to make you comfortable in compromise—
but to call you back to holiness.
Here’s the conviction:
You cannot carry both your sin and your Savior at the same time.
One has to go.
And here’s your identity—

You are not someone managing sin.
You are someone called to be made new.

Not slightly improved.
Not externally adjusted.
Transformed.

If you feel something right now…
that’s not shame crushing you.
That’s mercy calling you.

Because conviction is not rejection.
It’s invitation.
So come back.
Not halfway.
Fully.

Name the sin.
Drop the excuses.
Turn your heart.
Because 1 John 1:9 promises, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us…”

Not shame you.
Cleanse you.

And the same God Ezra was afraid to look at…
is the same God who, through Jesus, is now calling you closer.
Let that sink in.
You don’t have to stay stuck in what you’ve normalized.
You can start again.
Right now.
If this hit your heart—don’t ignore it.
Not noise. Real nourishment.)
Stay close.
Because the next message might be the one that pulls you all the way back.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: David was not on a throne when Shimei cursed him.
paragraphs: David was not on a throne when Shimei cursed him.
He was walking in humiliation.

Dust on his robe.
Tears in his heart.
The king of Israel… leaving Jerusalem like a defeated man.

His own son, Absalom, had taken the throne.
His own people were turning against him.
The palace was behind him, and the wilderness was ahead.
And that is when Shimei appeared.
He came out from the hillside along the road, shouting curses at the king. Stones in his hands. Rage in his voice.
The Bible says:

“Shimei… came out, cursing continually as he came. And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David.”
— 2 Samuel 16:5–6
Imagine the moment.
Shimei standing above the road, yelling accusations.
David walking below, silent.
The king who once killed Goliath… now being mocked by a man throwing rocks.
David’s warriors were furious.
Abishai, one of his mighty men, said what many people would have said:

“Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head.”
— 2 Samuel 16:9
But David stopped him.
He refused revenge.
Instead, David said something remarkable:

“Let him curse, because the Lord has said to him, ‘Curse David.’ Perhaps the Lord will look on my affliction and repay me with good for his cursing today.”
— 2 Samuel 16:11–12
So David kept walking.

The stones kept flying.
The curses kept coming.
But David kept walking.
And here is the part Shimei did not understand.
David’s weakness was temporary.
God’s calling on David was not.
The rebellion of Absalom did not last.
The same king who walked out of Jerusalem in shame would later return to the city in restoration.
And when the tide turned… Shimei suddenly changed his tone.
The Bible tells us that Shimei hurried to meet David when he returned and fell before him, begging for mercy.

“Do not hold me guilty… I know that I have sinned.”
— 2 Samuel 19:19–20
The man who once cursed the king was now pleading for grace.
And David gave it.
He spared Shimei’s life.
In that moment, mercy covered a man who deserved judgment.
But the story of Shimei teaches something deeper that many people miss.
Mercy can delay consequences.
But mercy does not always erase them.
Years later, when Solomon became king, he gave Shimei a clear command:

Stay in Jerusalem.
Do not cross the Kidron Valley.
If you leave, you will die.
For a time, Shimei obeyed.
But eventually, he broke the command.
He crossed the boundary.
And when Solomon heard what he had done, the judgment that had once been delayed finally came.

“You know in your heart all the harm you did to my father David.”
— 1 Kings 2:44
Shimei had once escaped death.
But he never escaped the weight of his actions.
And that brings us to the lesson.
Shimei represents something we still see today.
People who attack others when they look weak.
People who throw stones when someone is in their lowest moment.
People who assume a season of struggle means a person’s story is over.
But the truth is this:
Temporary weakness does not mean permanent defeat.
David was not finished when he walked that road.
God was still writing his story.
And that is why the Bible warns us about the power of our words.

Because the people we mock today
may be the people God restores tomorrow.

The leader we criticize today
may be the leader God lifts again tomorrow.

The person we attack in their wilderness
may return stronger than we ever expected.
Shimei thought the crown was gone.
But the crown was only waiting.
And here is another lesson hidden inside this story:
David had the power to destroy Shimei immediately.
But he chose restraint.
He chose humility.
He chose to trust God with the outcome.
Sometimes the greatest strength is not proving someone wrong.
Sometimes the greatest strength is simply continuing to walk the road God gave you.
Even while stones are being thrown.
So before we rush to judge someone in their lowest moment, we should remember Shimei.
Because every story in the Bible reminds us of this truth:
God is not finished when people think He is.

And the throne that looks empty today
may be restored tomorrow.
So be careful who you throw stones at.
Because God may still be writing their story.

And sometimes the loudest curses spoken in someone’s wilderness
become the quietest regrets when their restoration arrives.

Scripture:
2 Samuel 16:5–13
2 Samuel 19:16–23
1 Kings 2:36–46

Reflection Question:
