Have you ever seen someone judged during a season of weakness—only for God to restore them later?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Two mothers.
paragraphs:
Two mothers.
One child.
One truth that could not be faked.
And a sword that almost fell.
Pause.

Because this is not just a story about wisdom.
This is a story about what love is willing to lose… to save what matters most.
The courtroom was raw with tension. No lawyers. No witnesses. No evidence. Just two women standing before a young king, both claiming the same baby.

One was telling the truth.
The other was not.

But here’s the problem—
truth doesn’t always shout.
Sometimes it hides behind tears.
Sometimes it gets drowned by louder voices.
So what do you do when facts are unclear… but hearts are exposed?
King Solomon didn’t ask for more testimony.
He asked for a sword.
“Divide the living child in two.”
Can you feel that moment?

The air tightening.
The silence cracking.
The shock burning through the room.

Because suddenly—this wasn’t about arguments anymore.
This was about love under pressure.
One woman didn’t flinch.
Cold. Detached. Almost relieved.
“If I can’t have the child, neither can she.”
But the real mother…
She broke.

No pride.
No ego.
No need to win.
Just one desperate cry:
“Please, my lord, give her the child. Just don’t kill him.”

And in that moment—
truth screamed louder than words ever could.
Solomon didn’t need more evidence.
Because real love revealed itself.

Real love doesn’t cling when clinging destroys.
Real love doesn’t compete when life is at stake.
Real love would rather be misunderstood than watch something innocent die.
And just like that, the king declared:
“Give her the living child. She is the mother.” (1 Kings 3:27)
Because this story is not just about two women.
It’s about you.
It’s about me.
It’s about the moments when life puts a “sword” to the things we claim to love.

Your reputation.
Your relationships.
Your control.
Your hidden idols.

And suddenly God allows pressure—not to destroy you…
but to reveal you.
Scripture says in Hebrews 4:12 that the Word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword—discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
Did you catch that?
God doesn’t just hear what you say.
He sees what you’re made of.

When pressure hits…
when your pride is challenged…
when your comfort is threatened…
your response reveals your reality.
But here’s the Gospel turn—don’t miss this.
Because if we’re honest?
We are not the noble mother in this story.

We’ve all had moments where our love was selfish.
Where our desires overruled truth.
Where we clung instead of surrendered.
We have all, in some way, stood on the wrong side of the sword.
Yet God did not divide us.
He didn’t expose us just to condemn us.
He sent His Son.
Jesus Christ—the greater and wiser King than Solomon—didn’t raise a sword to test love.
He took the sword Himself.
At the cross, there was no courtroom debate.
There was a verdict.
And it should have been ours.
But Jesus stepped forward.

Not to argue.
Not to defend Himself.
But to lay down His life so that we could live.

Isaiah 53:5 says,
“He was pierced for our transgressions… by His wounds we are healed.”
Do you see it now?
Solomon revealed the true mother by threatening the child.
Jesus revealed the true heart of God by becoming the sacrifice.
One exposed love.
The other fulfilled it.
So here’s the question that lingers—
When the sword comes close to your life…
When God asks you to surrender something you’re holding tightly…
When following Christ costs you comfort, pride, or control…
What will your love choose?
Possession?
Or sacrifice?
Because real love still looks like this:

Choosing forgiveness when revenge feels justified.
Choosing surrender when control feels safer.
Choosing obedience when compromise feels easier.
That kind of love doesn’t come from human strength.
It comes from a heart transformed by Jesus.
Today, if you feel exposed…
If you see the cracks in your love…
If you realize you’ve been clinging to things more than trusting God…
Don’t run.
Come to Christ.
The King who sees your heart is the same Savior who died for it.

No pretending needed.
No performance required.
Just surrender.
Because in the end—
The Gospel is not about proving you are the true one.
It’s about trusting the One who already proved His love for you on the cross.
Let this sink deep:

Real love sacrifices.
Jesus already did.
Now He invites you to follow.
If this pierced your heart, don’t keep it to yourself.
Start a conversation that points back to truth.

Because someone out there is still standing in that courtroom…
still holding on…
still not realizing—
love is revealed when it’s willing to let go.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He laughed…
paragraphs:
He laughed…
but heaven had already chosen where he would fall.

Goliath didn’t just step onto the battlefield—he owned it.
Nine feet of intimidation. Bronze armor catching the sun. A voice that echoed like thunder across the valley.
And for forty days, no one answered him.

Not because Israel had no soldiers.
But because fear had already won inside them.
Let that sink in.

Before Goliath ever lifted a spear…
he had already conquered hearts.

That’s what pride does.
It doesn’t just make noise—it paralyzes others and deceives the one who carries it.

He cursed.
He mocked.
He belittled the people of God.
“Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?” (1 Samuel 17:43)
But here’s the tension—don’t miss this:
Goliath thought he was fighting David.
He wasn’t.
He was standing against the living God.
And that is the fatal mistake of every proud heart.

Because pride always miscalculates the battlefield.
It measures strength by what is seen…
and ignores the God who is unseen.
Then comes David.

No armor.
No sword.
No reputation.

Just a sling.
Five smooth stones.
And a heart anchored in God.
And suddenly… the entire story shifts.

David doesn’t respond to Goliath’s size.
He responds to Goliath’s defiance.
“You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts…” (1 Samuel 17:45)
That line… that line is everything.

Because the battle was never about size.
It was about allegiance.

Goliath trusted in weapons.
David trusted in God.

Goliath stood in pride.
David stood in covenant.

Goliath spoke from arrogance.
David spoke from authority.
And then—one stone.

Not five.
Not ten.
One.
Because God doesn’t need multiple attempts when He decides the outcome.

The stone flies.
Cuts through the air.
Finds the only exposed place.
The forehead.
And just like that…
The giant falls.
But hear me—Goliath didn’t fall because David was skilled.
He fell because God was dishonored.
“Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)
That wasn’t just a proverb.
That was a prophecy… and Goliath fulfilled it.
Now pause.
Because this is where it gets personal.
Goliath is not just a character in Scripture.
He is a mirror.

He is every moment we think we are untouchable.
Every time we rely on our own strength.
Every quiet thought that says, “I’ve got this—I don’t need God.”
That’s pride.

And pride doesn’t always shout.
Sometimes it whispers.

It shows up in success without gratitude.
In sin without repentance.
In confidence without surrender.

And just like Goliath, it stands tall…
until it doesn’t.
Because no one outgrows the need for God.
No one.

Not the strongest.
Not the smartest.
Not the most successful.
We are all one breath away from collapse without Him.

But here—this is the turn.
This is where grace steps in.
Because the story of David and Goliath points to a greater battlefield.

A greater Giant.
A deeper enemy.
Sin.

Not just the things we do…
but the pride inside us that resists God.
And here’s the truth: we were never meant to defeat that giant on our own.
So God sent a better David.
Jesus Christ.

Where Goliath stood in arrogance, Jesus stood in humility.
Where Goliath cursed, Jesus forgave.
Where Goliath defied God, Jesus obeyed Him—even to death.
Philippians 2 tells us that Jesus “humbled Himself… even to the point of death on a cross.”
And at that cross—everything changed.

Sin was struck.
Death was defeated.
The true Giant fell.
Not by a stone…
But by nails.
Not through pride…
But through surrender.
And three days later, Jesus rose—proving that the greatest enemy has already been conquered.
So what does that mean for you?
It means you don’t have to live like Goliath—loud, proud, and destined to fall.
You can live like David—dependent, surrendered, and covered by God’s power.
Better yet—you can belong to Christ, where the battle for your soul has already been won.
So lay it down.

The pride.
The self-reliance.
The hidden sin you keep excusing.
Come to Jesus.

Not as a giant.
But as a child who needs saving.
Because grace is not given to the strong.
It is given to the humble.

And the same God who brought down Goliath…
is ready to lift you up.
If you’ll bow.

Before the fall, Goliath was full of himself.
After the cross, the believer is full of Christ.
This is your moment.

Choose humility.
Choose surrender.
Choose Jesus.
And watch every giant in your life lose its power.
Someone out there is fighting a giant in silence.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You keep asking God for order…
paragraphs:
You keep asking God for order…
but you resist His authority.
Pause.
Because this is where most people get it wrong.

You love the idea of “divine alignment.”
You post about “God’s timing.”
You pray for breakthrough.
But deep inside?
You still want control.
You want the blessing… without the government.
And that tension is exposing something.
🔥 Here’s the open loop you can’t ignore:
Why does God repeat the number 12… again… and again… and again?
Why not 10?
Why not 7?
Why 12—when He builds His people, His leadership, even heaven itself?
This is not coincidence.
This is revelation.
⚔️ ESCALATION — The Hidden Struggle
Let’s be honest.
We don’t struggle with believing in God.
We struggle with submitting to Him.

We want a Savior…
but not a King.

We want comfort…
but not correction.

We want grace…
but not governance.
And that’s where pride hides.
Quiet.
Respectable.
Religious.
But still rebellion.

You can go to church
and still resist God’s authority.

You can quote Scripture
and still live self-ruled.

You can say “Lord, Lord”…
and still sit on the throne of your own life.
That’s the tension.
That’s the war.
📖 SCRIPTURE ANCHOR — God Reveals His Pattern
Throughout Scripture, God establishes 12 as a number of divine government.
1. 12 Tribes of Israel — Structure of God’s People
“All these are the twelve tribes of Israel…” — Genesis 49:28
God didn’t build a scattered crowd.
He formed a governed nation.
Order. Identity. Authority.
2. 12 Apostles — Structure of the Church
“He called his twelve disciples to him and gave them authority…” — Matthew 10:1
Jesus didn’t choose randomly.
He was reestablishing God’s government—this time through grace.

Twelve men.
Carrying Kingdom authority.
3. 12 Gates + 12 Foundations — Structure of Eternity
“It had a great, high wall with twelve gates… The wall of the city had twelve foundations…” — Revelation 21:12–14
Even heaven is not chaotic.
It is perfectly governed.
Perfectly ordered.
Perfectly aligned under God.
4. And then this…
“For to us a child is born… and the government shall be upon His shoulder…” — Isaiah 9:6
Catch that.
Not just peace.
Not just salvation.
Government.
⚠️ Some scholars interpret…
Some scholars interpret the number 12 symbolically—as completeness in leadership or divine administration.
Others see it as a consistent pattern of God organizing His people under authority.
But across interpretations, one truth stands:

God is a God of order, not chaos.
(1 Corinthians 14:33)
💔 THE REAL PROBLEM
Here’s the uncomfortable truth:
We don’t reject God loudly.
We resist Him quietly.
Through:
delayed obedience
hidden sin
selective surrender
“I’ll follow… but on my terms”
That’s not submission.
That’s negotiation.
And God does not negotiate His throne.
✝️ GOSPEL TURN — Where Grace Breaks In
This is where it gets real.
Because if God is truly King…
Then we are all guilty of rebellion.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
Every one of us has stepped out from under His authority.
We chose self over surrender.
Control over trust.
Sin over obedience.
But here’s the shock of grace:
God didn’t crush the rebels.
He came for them.
Jesus Christ stepped into our chaos.
Lived in perfect submission to the Father.
“Not my will, but Yours be done.” — Luke 22:42
Then He took our rebellion… to the cross.
Every act of pride.
Every hidden sin.
Every moment we said, “My will over Yours.”
Nailed.
Paid for.
Finished.
“Christ died for our sins… He was buried… He was raised on the third day.” — 1 Corinthians 15:3–4
And now?
The King we resisted…
is the Savior inviting us back.
Not just to be forgiven.
But to be restored under His loving rule.
🔥 THIS CHANGES EVERYTHING
The number 12 is not about math.
It’s about a message:
God is establishing His Kingdom.
And the question is no longer:
“Do you believe in God?”
The real question is:
Is He Lord over your life?
Because you can admire Jesus…
and still not follow Him.
You can sing about Him…
and still not surrender to Him.
You can know about His government…
and still live in your own.
❤️ RESOLUTION — The Invitation
Right now.
Not later.
Not when life is cleaner.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.
Lay it down.

The control.
The pride.
The hidden sin.
Come under the authority of Christ.
Not as a prisoner—

but as a son.
as a daughter.
Because His rule is not harsh.
It is healing.
His authority is not crushing.
It is restoring.
If you’re ready to surrender fully—not halfway, not selectively—
And if this message opened your eyes…
Come back to it.
Live it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The journey should have taken weeks.
paragraphs: The journey should have taken weeks.
From Egypt to the Promised Land was not a distance that required forty years.
In fact, Deuteronomy 1:2 tells us the journey from Mount Sinai to Kadesh Barnea was about eleven days.
Eleven days.
Yet Israel wandered in the wilderness for forty years.
Why?
Because the greatest delays in life are rarely caused by distance.
They are caused by disbelief.
God had already done the impossible for Israel.

He shattered the power of Pharaoh through the plagues.
He opened the Red Sea and let them walk through on dry ground.
He fed them with manna from heaven.
He brought water from a rock.
Every step of their journey was surrounded by miracles.
But when they finally arrived at the border of the land God promised, everything changed.
In Numbers 13, Moses sent twelve spies into the land of Canaan.
For forty days they explored the land God had promised to Abraham generations earlier.
When they returned, they all agreed on one thing:
The land was good.
It flowed with milk and honey.
The fruit was so large that it had to be carried on a pole between two men.
But ten of the spies saw something else.
They saw giants.
They saw fortified cities.
They saw enemies that looked stronger than them.
And suddenly the miracles of the past felt smaller than the problems in front of them.
Only two men — Joshua and Caleb — saw the situation differently.
They didn't deny the giants.
They simply believed God was bigger.
Joshua and Caleb said:
"The Lord will give us the land."
But the people chose to believe the majority.
Fear spread like wildfire through the camp.
The Bible says the people wept all night.
They even began saying something shocking:

"We should choose a leader and go back to Egypt."
(Numbers 14:4)
Imagine that moment.

After slavery.
After deliverance.
After miracles.
They wanted to go back.
Not because Egypt was better.
But because fear made the future look impossible.
That moment changed the course of their destiny.
God declared that the generation that refused to trust Him would not enter the Promised Land.
Instead, they would wander in the wilderness until that generation passed away.
The forty years corresponded to the forty days the spies explored the land (Numbers 14:34).
One day of exploration became one year of wandering.
The wilderness was never supposed to be their destination.
It became their consequence.
And here is the deeper lesson.
Israel didn't wander because God abandoned them.
God still provided manna.
God still guided them with the pillar of cloud and fire.
God still protected them.
But they lost something priceless:
the chance to step into the promise sooner.
Unbelief didn't remove God's promise.
It delayed their participation in it.
This story still speaks today.
Many people think the biggest obstacles in life are external.
Lack of resources.
Opposition.
Circumstances.
But sometimes the greatest obstacle is something invisible.
Fear.
Fear of failure.
Fear of stepping out.
Fear of trusting God when the giants look real.
Israel stood on the edge of their miracle and said:
"We can't do this."
But Joshua and Caleb stood in the same place and said:
"God can."
Same land.
Same giants.
Different faith.
Sometimes the difference between entering the promise and wandering in circles is the voice you believe.
The voice of fear will always magnify the giants.
The voice of faith remembers the Red Sea.

Fear asks:
"What if we fail?"

Faith asks:
"What if God is faithful like He has always been?"
And here is something powerful to remember.
Even though that generation wandered, God's promise did not die.
A new generation rose.
Joshua eventually led the people into the Promised Land.
Because what God promises may be delayed by people—but it is never cancelled by fear.
So the story of the wilderness is not just about ancient history.
It is about a question every generation must answer:
When you stand at the edge of God's promise…
Will you focus on the giants?
Or will you remember the God who already split the sea?
Sometimes the distance between where you are and where God is leading you is not measured in miles.
It is measured in trust.
Israel's journey could have taken eleven days.
But unbelief turned it into forty years.
May we learn from their story.
Because the wilderness was never meant to be home.

“Your children will be shepherds here for forty years, suffering for your unfaithfulness… forty years—one year for each of the forty days you explored the land.”
— Numbers 14:33–34
Reflection Question:
What “giants” in your life are tempting you to doubt what God has already promised?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She wasn’t supposed to care.
paragraphs: She wasn’t supposed to care.

Not about him.
Not about them.
Not about the cries echoing through a river that had become a silent graveyard.
But one moment… one sound… one trembling breath from a woven basket—and everything changed.
A princess stepped into the water.
And history shifted.
The Nile was no longer just a river. It was a command.
A dark decree from a throne intoxicated with power: “Every Hebrew boy must die.” (Exodus 1:22)

No debate.
No mercy.
No exceptions.
This was state-approved destruction.
And she was raised in that house.
Pharaoh’s daughter.

Royal blood.
Privileged.
Protected.
Conditioned to obey the system that fed her.
But grace has a way of interrupting systems.
She saw the basket.
Small. Fragile. Floating between life and death.
She opened it.
And there he was.
A baby.
Crying.
Not a threat. Not a statistic. Not an enemy.
A child.
Scripture says it simply—but don’t miss the weight of it:
“She had compassion on him.” (Exodus 2:6)
Pause there.
Because compassion is dangerous when cruelty is legal.
She knew exactly what he was.
“A Hebrew boy.”
That means this wasn’t confusion.
This was a decision.
A line drawn in her own soul:
Will I align with power… or with mercy?
And in that sacred tension—
She chose mercy.
Feel the risk.
This was not a quiet adoption story.
This was defiance wrapped in tenderness.
Every heartbeat of that child in her arms was a contradiction to her father’s command.
Every breath he took was evidence that she refused to let evil define her obedience.

She didn’t protest publicly.
She didn’t start a movement.
She simply refused to let a baby die.
And sometimes, that’s where revival begins.
Here’s the twist that only God can write:
The very house that ordered death…
…became the place of preservation.
She named him Moses—“drawn out of the water” (Exodus 2:10).
But what she didn’t know?
She wasn’t just rescuing a child.
She was protecting a deliverer.
Let this sink in:
The future liberator of Israel was raised in Pharaoh’s palace.
Fed by Pharaoh’s resources.
Educated in Pharaoh’s system.
All because one woman refused to let compassion be silenced.
Some of you feel like you’re surrounded by systems that oppose your faith.

Workplaces.
Families.
Cultures.
Voices that normalize compromise.
You feel the pressure to blend in. Stay quiet. Don’t risk it.
But listen—
God does not need perfect environments to protect His purposes.

He can place courage inside unlikely people.
He can plant mercy in hostile places.
He can preserve destiny in the middle of danger.
You are not trapped.
You are positioned.
But this story doesn’t stop with Moses.
It points forward.
Because Moses is a shadow.
A whisper of a greater rescue.
Another Child would be born under a murderous decree.
In the days of King Herod, boys were slaughtered out of fear (Matthew 2:16).
Another Deliverer had to be hidden. Protected. Preserved.
But this time—
He wouldn’t just be saved from death.
He would walk straight into it.
Jesus Christ.
Not drawn out of water—
But lifted up on a cross.
Not rescued from death—
But choosing it.
Why?
Because we were the ones floating helpless.
We were the ones marked by sin.
We were the ones under a sentence we could not escape.
And grace came for us.

Not because we deserved it.
Not because we were innocent.
But because God is merciful.
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Pharaoh’s daughter reached into the river and pulled a baby out.
Jesus stepped into our death and pulled sinners out.
That is the Gospel.
So now the question turns to you.
Where is God asking you to show compassion?
What “basket” have you been trained to ignore?
What voice have you been taught to silence?
Because sometimes the most powerful act of faith is not loud.
It’s a quiet refusal:
“I will not agree with what destroys life.”
You don’t need a throne to change history.
You need a heart that responds when God moves.
You need the courage to choose mercy when fear is easier.
You need Jesus.
If you’ve been living numb…
If you’ve been blending in…
If you’ve been ignoring what God is stirring—
This is your moment.
Turn back to Him.
Receive His grace.
Let Him reshape your heart.
Because the same God who preserved Moses…
The same God who sent Jesus…
Is still writing stories today.
Including yours.

Drop a 🔥 if you choose mercy over fear.
And never forget:
One act of compassion can carry the weight of destiny.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She wasn’t fighting her sister.
paragraphs: She wasn’t fighting her sister.
She was fighting what she saw in the mirror.
And it was losing her.

Two women.
One house.
One man.

But beneath it all—
one silent war.

Rachel had beauty.
Leah had children.

Rachel had Jacob’s love.
Leah had God’s favor in her womb.
And somehow… both felt empty.
This is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because this isn’t just their story.
It’s ours.

You can be loved…
and still feel lacking.

You can be fruitful…
and still feel forgotten.

You can win in public…
and bleed in private.
Rachel’s cry wasn’t just emotional.
It was desperate.
“Give me children, or I die!” — Genesis 30:1
That is not poetry.
That is pressure.
That is identity collapsing under comparison.
And Leah?
She wasn’t celebrating her sons.
She was naming her pain.

“Now my husband will love me…” (Genesis 29:32)
“Because the Lord heard that I am unloved…” (Genesis 29:33)
“Now this time my husband will become attached to me…” (Genesis 29:34)

Every child…
a silent plea.

Every blessing…
a cry for approval.
This is the trap of comparison.
It doesn’t matter what you have.
It convinces you it’s not enough.
Rachel envied Leah’s fruit.
Leah envied Rachel’s love.
Different lives.
Same ache.
And here’s the truth most people won’t say out loud:

Comparison is not just insecurity.
It’s a spiritual issue.
It reveals where we are trying to find identity outside of God.
James didn’t soften it.
“For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.” — James 3:16
Jealousy doesn’t stay quiet.
It corrodes.
It distorts.
It turns blessings into burdens.
And some of you are there right now.

Scrolling.
Smiling.
Comparing.

Her life.
Her body.
Her calling.
Her relationship.
Her timing.
And quietly asking:
“Why not me?”
That question…
can either lead you to God—
or pull you deeper into resentment.
But watch the shift.
It’s subtle.
But it changes everything.
Leah stops chasing Jacob’s approval.
And says:
“This time I will praise the Lord.” — Genesis 29:35
That line breaks the cycle.
For the first time—
her identity is no longer anchored in a man’s affection…
but in God’s presence.
And Rachel?
God did not forget her.
“Then God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb.” — Genesis 30:22
Not because she competed better.
Not because she earned it.
Because God is merciful.
Let this sink in:
God met both women in their brokenness.
The unloved one.
The barren one.
He didn’t choose based on performance.
He moved based on grace.
But the story doesn’t end with them.
It points forward.
From Leah came Judah.
And from Judah—
came Jesus Christ.
The Savior who steps into comparison, envy, and hidden shame—
and breaks it at the root.
Because here’s the deeper issue:
Comparison is a symptom.
Sin is the disease.
We don’t just compare because we’re insecure.
We compare because we’ve built identity on things that cannot save us.

Beauty.
Validation.
Success.
Approval.
And all of it eventually fails.
That’s why we need more than self-confidence.
We need a Savior.
Jesus didn’t come for perfect people.
He came for people exhausted from trying to prove they are enough.
At the cross—
every false identity is exposed.
And every broken heart is invited.

“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
This is the Gospel:
You don’t need to compete for worth.
Jesus already paid for it.
You don’t need to outshine someone else to be seen.
God already sees you in Christ.
You don’t need to prove your value.
The cross already declared it.
And the resurrection?
It means your story is not stuck in comparison.
It can be rewritten in grace.
So what now?
Stop measuring your life against someone else’s timeline.
Stop rehearsing their blessings as evidence of your lack.
Stop feeding the silent war.
Bring it to Jesus.
The envy.
The insecurity.
The ache.
The question you’re afraid to say out loud.
Because healing begins where honesty meets grace.
Repent.
Not just of comparison—
but of building your identity on anything other than Christ.
Receive His forgiveness.
Rest in His finished work.
Walk in a new identity.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17
You are not Leah.
You are not Rachel.
You are not your lack.
You are not your delay.
If you are in Christ—
you are already chosen.
Already seen.
Already loved.
No competition needed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re not just struggling.
paragraphs:
You’re not just struggling.
You’re being exposed.
And that scares you… because you know it’s true.
Something is shifting.

The sin you used to hide…
is starting to feel heavier.

The silence you used to enjoy…
now feels loud.

And the excuses?
They’re not working anymore.

You keep telling yourself,
“I’m just tired.”

But deep down you know—
this is not exhaustion.
This is conviction.

And conviction feels like breaking
before it feels like breakthrough.
Let’s be honest.
Some of us are not under attack…
We are under exposure.

Not because God wants to shame you—
but because He refuses to leave you chained.

You smile in public…
but fight secret battles in private.

You lift your hands in worship…
but lower your standards in hidden places.
You say, “God understands…”

But what you really mean is,
“I don’t want to surrender this yet.”
That tension you feel?
That discomfort?
That inner war?
That’s not God abandoning you.
That’s God pressing on the wound you keep covering.
Because healing doesn’t start with denial.
It starts with truth.
“For the word of God is alive and active… it judges the thoughts and attitudes of the heart.” — Hebrews 4:12
God’s Word doesn’t just comfort.
It cuts.

Not to destroy you—
but to remove what is destroying you.
Some scholars interpret this passage as describing Scripture like a surgeon’s blade—precise, intentional, life-saving.
It goes deeper than behavior.
It reaches motive.
Desire.
Intent.
And suddenly…
You’re not as okay as you thought.
Here’s the part we avoid:
Conviction is not condemnation.

But if you ignore conviction long enough…
you will live like you’re condemned.
Because unrepented sin doesn’t stay silent.
It grows.
It hardens.
It deceives.
“Whoever conceals their sins does not prosper, but the one who confesses and renounces them finds mercy.” — Proverbs 28:13
Not hides.
Not manages.
Not explains away.
Confesses. Renounces.
That’s where mercy meets you.
Not in your perfection—
But in your honesty.
And this is where everything changes.
Because your breakthrough is not when life gets easier…
It’s when your heart gets honest before God.
Let me say it clearly:
You don’t need a better strategy.
You need a Savior.
Because the real issue is not your habits.
It’s your heart.
And no amount of discipline can save a soul.
Only Jesus can.
Here is the Gospel:
You and I have sinned.

Not just outwardly—
but inwardly.
We’ve chosen ourselves over God.
We’ve justified what He called sin.
We’ve delayed what He called obedience.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
That includes the hidden parts.
The secret compromises.
The thoughts no one sees.
But God did not leave you there.
He didn’t wait for you to clean yourself up.
He stepped in.

Jesus Christ lived the life you could not live.
He died the death you deserved.
And He rose again so you could have new life.
“But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Not when you fixed yourself.
Not when you improved.
While you were still in it.
That shame you carry?
He already paid for it.
That sin you’re hiding?
He already sees it.
And still—
He invites you.
But grace is not permission to stay the same.
Grace is power to become new.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us… and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
Not partially.
Not temporarily.
Fully. Completely.
So here’s the question:

What are you still holding on to
that Jesus already died to free you from?

What are you protecting
that is slowly destroying you?

What are you postponing
that God is calling you to surrender today?
This is your moment.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.
Drop the mask.
Name the sin.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
Because your breakthrough is not waiting on the other side of better circumstances…
It’s waiting on the other side of repentance.
And hear me—
There is no sin too dark.
No past too broken.
No pattern too strong.
That the blood of Jesus cannot redeem.
But you must come.
Humble.
Honest.
Hungry.
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” — James 4:6

Breakthrough begins
where pride ends.
So if this is you—
This is not just a post.
This is a call.

Your breaking point
may become your birth point.
If you let Jesus in.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t wake up evil.
paragraphs: He didn’t wake up evil.
He became it… one choice at a time.
And that’s what should terrify you.

Because the red horse isn’t just coming for nations—
it rides through hearts.
You see the sword.
You see the rage.
You see the blood.
But you don’t see where it started.

Not on a battlefield.
Not in a war room.
Not even in politics.
It started… quietly.

A wound.
An offense.
A pride that refused to bow.
And suddenly, peace didn’t stand a chance.
We think we’re far from this man.
We say, “I would never become that.”
But let’s be honest.

How many times have you replayed an argument in your head—
wanting to win, not reconcile?

How many times have you let anger simmer…
until it felt justified?

How many times have you smiled outside,
but inside… you were already at war?
Jesus said it plainly:
“Anyone who is angry with a brother or sister will be subject to judgment.” — Matthew 5:22
Not murder.
Anger.
That’s how deep this goes.
The red horse in Revelation isn’t just about global chaos.
It’s about the removal of peace.
“Its rider was given power to take peace from the earth and to make people kill each other…” — Revelation 6:4

Some scholars interpret this as literal warfare across nations.
Others see it also as the unraveling of human relationships—
violence breaking out because sin is no longer restrained.
But either way, the root is the same:
A heart that no longer submits to God.
And here’s the uncomfortable truth:
You don’t need a sword to carry the spirit of the red horse.
You just need:
Unforgiveness.
Pride.
Bitterness you refuse to release.
Because war doesn’t always look like bloodshed.

Sometimes it looks like silence.
Cold shoulders.
Sharp words.
Secret hatred.
And God sees all of it.
“The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure.” — Jeremiah 17:9

That means you can convince yourself you’re right—
while your soul is slowly hardening.
But here’s where everything shifts.
Because while the red horse takes peace away…
Jesus gives it back.
Not by force.
Not by domination.
But by sacrifice.

When Jesus stood before His accusers,
He had every right to call down angels.
Every right to destroy His enemies.
Every right to end the war with power.
But He didn’t.
He chose the cross.
“He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth…” — Isaiah 53:7
“The punishment that brought us peace was on Him…” — Isaiah 53:5
Let that sink in.

The peace you keep losing in your relationships…
the peace your heart keeps craving…
the peace the world cannot manufacture…
It was purchased.
In blood.
Not the blood of others.
His blood.
This is the Gospel.
You are not just a victim of chaos.
You are a participant in sin.
We all are.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
But God didn’t leave you there.
“But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
Jesus took your anger.
Your pride.
Your hidden wars.
And He carried them to the cross.
Then He did what no rider, no king, no system could ever do.
He rose again.
“Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” — Romans 5:1
Peace.
Not temporary.
Not fragile.
Eternal peace with God.
So now the question isn’t:
“Is the red horse real?”
The question is:
What are you doing with the war inside you?
Are you feeding it?
Justifying it?
Hiding it?
Or are you ready to surrender it?

Because you cannot hold onto anger
and expect to walk in peace.

You cannot cling to pride
and expect to experience grace.

You cannot keep fighting everyone around you
and claim to follow the Prince of Peace.
“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.” — Matthew 5:9
This is your moment.
Not tomorrow.
Not when things calm down.
Now.
Lay down the sword.
Release the offense.
Confess the pride.
Turn to Jesus.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just and will forgive us…” — 1 John 1:9
He’s not waiting to condemn you.
He’s ready to restore you.
You don’t have to be ruled by rage.
You don’t have to keep losing peace.
You don’t have to become what you fear.
In Christ, you can become new.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation…” — 2 Corinthians 5:17
So choose.
War…
or peace.
Self…
or surrender.
The red horse…
or the cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GET UP AND EAT.
paragraphs: GET UP AND EAT.

Four words.
But they came from heaven to a man who wanted to die.
Let that sink in.
The prophet Elijah—fire-calling, nation-shaking, idol-destroying Elijah—collapsed under a desert tree and whispered something many believers are afraid to admit:

“It is enough now, O LORD, take away my life.”
— 1 Kings 19:4

Not a pagan.
Not a rebel.
A prophet.
The man who just stood on Mount Carmel and watched God send fire from heaven now sat in the wilderness asking God to end his life.
Why?
Because exhaustion changes how everything looks.

Victory can be loud.
But burnout is quiet.

You can preach with fire on Sunday
and cry alone on Tuesday.

You can stand bold before crowds
and feel completely empty when the noise fades.
And Elijah had reached that point.

The threat from Jezebel echoed in his mind.
Fear chased him into the desert.
Loneliness wrapped around his heart.

And suddenly the prophet who once faced 450 prophets of Baal…
felt like he couldn’t face tomorrow.
He lay down under a broom tree and fell asleep.
And here is where the story turns.
God did not thunder from heaven.

He did not say,
“Elijah, why are you weak?”

He did not say,
“Get over it.”
He sent an angel.
The angel touched him.
Touched him.
That small detail carries enormous mercy.
The touch of heaven to a broken servant.
Then the angel spoke four simple words:
“Get up and eat.”
That’s it.

Not a sermon.
Not a lecture.
Bread.
Water.
Rest.
Elijah woke up to find bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water beside his head.
Provision was already waiting for him before he even opened his eyes.
Read that again.

Before Elijah recovered his faith…
God had already prepared his strength.
This is the tenderness of the Lord.
Sometimes we think God only meets us in our strength.
But Scripture shows something deeper.
God meets us in our collapse.

When our prayers feel weak.
When our courage runs dry.
When our minds spiral into dark places.
God does not abandon His servants under the broom tree.
He feeds them.
He restores them.
He whispers life back into tired bones.
And Elijah didn’t just eat once.
The angel came again.

Another touch.
Another meal.
Another act of mercy.
Because the journey ahead was too great for him.
Listen carefully.
This is not just Elijah’s story.
This is the story of every believer who has ever been exhausted by life, ministry, family battles, spiritual warfare, depression, or disappointment.
You may look strong to everyone else.
But God sees the hidden fatigue.
The quiet tears.
The prayers you can barely form.
The moments when you wonder if you can keep going.
And into that moment God speaks the same words:
“Get up and eat.”
But the story of Scripture doesn’t stop with bread in the wilderness.
That moment in 1 Kings points forward to something greater.
Centuries later, another voice would say something shocking:

“I am the bread of life.”
— John 6:35
Jesus didn’t just offer food.
He became the food our starving souls needed.
Because our deepest exhaustion isn’t just physical.
It’s spiritual.

Sin drains us.
Shame weighs us down.
Guilt crushes our hearts.
We run from God like Elijah ran into the desert.
But instead of abandoning us, God came after us in Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Jesus carried our sin, our shame, our despair, and every moment we collapsed under the weight of life.
Then He rose again—so the weary could rise too.
That means this:
Your burnout is not the end of your story.
Your fear is not your final chapter.
Your breakdown is not your burial.
God still feeds weary prophets.
God still restores exhausted hearts.
God still whispers hope into caves and deserts.

And maybe today…
you are under your own broom tree.
Tired.
Drained.
Emotionally empty.
Spiritually numb.
If that’s you, hear the mercy of heaven:
Get up and eat.
Come back to Christ.
Open the Word again.
Pray even if your words feel small.
Rest in the grace that Jesus already finished on the cross.

Because the God who fed Elijah
still sustains His people today.
And the journey ahead may feel impossible…
but God always provides strength for the road He calls you to walk.
So take a breath.
Receive the grace.
And rise again.
Because the God who met Elijah in the wilderness is the same God meeting you right now.
And He is not finished with your story.

Someone out there is sitting under their broom tree tonight…
and they need to hear these four words from heaven:
GET UP AND EAT.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The wall looked permanent.
paragraphs: The wall looked permanent.

Stone stacked on stone.
Thick. Ancient. Intimidating.
The kind of wall that whispers to every enemy outside it:
“You will never get in.”
That was Jericho.
A fortress city. Military stronghold. Gates sealed. Warriors ready. Towers watching the horizon. To human eyes, Jericho was untouchable.
And standing outside those walls?
Former slaves.
A wandering nation with no siege towers, no battering rams, no elite war machines.
Just a promise from God.
And sometimes the biggest battle is not against the wall…
It’s against the doubt inside your chest.
Because when God gave the battle plan, it didn’t sound like war.

March around the city.
Once a day.
For six days.

No shouting.
No attacking.
No breaking the gates.
Just walking.
Can you imagine what Jericho’s soldiers thought as they watched Israel circle the city in silence?

Mockery.
Confusion.
Arrogant laughter from the towers.
“Is that all they’ve got?”
But heaven was not confused.

Every silent step was an act of faith.
Every lap around the wall was obedience.
Every quiet march was a declaration:
God said this city will fall.
Then came the seventh day.

Seven marches.
Seven trumpets.
One command.
“Shout.”
And when the people lifted their voices in faith…
The earth trembled.
Stone cracked.
Dust exploded into the sky.
The walls of Jericho—walls that looked invincible for generations—collapsed in a moment.
Not because Israel was strong.
But because God had already spoken.
Let that sink deep into your spirit.
The walls didn’t fall because the people shouted.
They shouted because God had already won.
And maybe that’s exactly where you are right now.
Standing in front of a wall.

A wall of addiction.
A wall of fear.
A wall of financial pressure.
A wall of broken relationships.
A wall of shame you’ve been hiding behind for years.
From where you stand, it looks permanent.
Immovable.
Unbreakable.
But the story of Jericho whispers a dangerous truth to every wall you face:
If God has spoken, the wall is already living on borrowed time.
But here is the deeper scandal hidden in the story.
While Jericho was collapsing…
One house was still standing.
Inside that house lived a woman with a past.
Her name was Rahab.

She wasn’t a soldier.
She wasn’t an Israelite.
She wasn’t “religious.”
She was a prostitute in a doomed city.
But she believed.
She believed the God of Israel was real.
So she tied a scarlet cord in her window—the sign of the promise that when judgment came, mercy would find her house.
And when the walls crashed down around the city…
That house remained.
Grace stood where destruction fell.
Rahab and her family were rescued.
And if you follow the story far enough…
You’ll discover something breathtaking.
Rahab becomes part of the lineage of Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
A woman with a scandalous past in a collapsing city becomes part of the family line of the Savior of the world.
Because that’s what God does.
He rescues people the world writes off.
He rewrites stories shame tried to erase.
And that scarlet cord hanging in Rahab’s window?
It points forward to another scarlet thread.
The blood of Jesus.
Because the greatest wall humanity ever faced wasn’t Jericho.
It was the wall of sin separating us from God.

A wall built by pride.
Rebellion.
Secrets.
Failures.
The quiet things we hope no one ever discovers.
No amount of effort could break it.
No religion could climb it.
No good deeds could dismantle it.
So Jesus came.
He stepped into our broken world.
He carried our sin to the cross.
And when He rose from the grave, the greatest wall in history collapsed forever.
Forgiveness opened.
Grace poured out.
And anyone—no matter their past—can walk free.
That means the wall in front of you today is not the end of your story.

Your addiction is not the final chapter.
Your failure is not the final sentence.
Your shame is not the final word.
Because the same God who brought down Jericho is still in the business of collapsing impossible walls.
Sometimes the breakthrough happens suddenly.
Sometimes it comes after six long days of marching.
But obedience is never wasted.
Faith is never invisible to heaven.
And God never forgets His promises.
So if you’re staring at a wall today…
Don’t run.
Don’t surrender.
Don’t believe the lie that it will stand forever.
Keep walking.
Keep trusting.
Keep believing.
And when God says shout…
Shout with faith.
Because the wall may look loud…
But God is greater.

Someone staring at a wall.
Someone fighting a silent battle.
Someone who thinks their story is already over.
Tell them this:

Walls fall.
Grace wins.
Jesus saves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You can look holy… and still be completely fake.
paragraphs: You can look holy… and still be completely fake.
Let that sit.
Because this isn’t about “them.”
This might be about you.
You sing the songs.
You know the verses.
You lift your hands at the right moment.
But there’s something you’re avoiding.
Something hidden.
Something untouched.
And you’re hoping no one notices.
Here’s the tension:

What if your devotion is real on the outside…
but counterfeit in the eyes of God?
What if the mask has become your identity?
What if you’ve learned how to perform Christianity…
but never actually surrendered to Christ?
Let’s go deeper.
Because this is where it gets uncomfortable.
Counterfeit Christianity thrives in silence.
It smiles in public…
…but negotiates with sin in private.
It says “Lord, Lord” in church…
…but says “later” when conviction comes.
It posts Scriptures…
…but avoids obedience.
And here’s the scariest part:
You can do all of that…
and still feel “okay.”
No trembling.
No brokenness.
No urgency to repent.
Just… normal.
But Jesus shattered that illusion.
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of My Father who is in heaven.” — Matthew 7:21
Read that again.
Slowly.
Jesus is not impressed with words.
He’s after surrender.
Some scholars interpret this passage as a direct warning against false assurance—people who genuinely believe they are saved, but have never truly submitted their lives to Christ.
That should wake us up.
Not to fear…
…but to honesty.
Because if we’re real for a moment—
We’ve all worn the mask.
We’ve all hidden something.
We’ve all delayed obedience.
We’ve all tried to manage sin instead of killing it.
That secret habit.
That hidden compromise.
That pride dressed up as “confidence.”
That bitterness you keep justifying.
That private life that doesn’t match your public faith.
You know it.
God sees it.
And still…
He calls you.
Here’s the truth we don’t like to say out loud:

Counterfeit faith doesn’t reject Jesus outright…
it resists His authority quietly.
It wants the cross…
but not the cost.
It wants grace…
but not repentance.
It wants salvation…
but not surrender.
But Scripture cuts through the noise:
“Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves.” — 2 Corinthians 13:5
This is not condemnation.
This is invitation.
Because God is not trying to expose you to shame you.
He’s exposing you to save you.
Now here comes the turning point.
Don’t miss this.
Jesus did not come for the polished.
He came for the honest.
He did not die for the image you project.
He died for the sin you hide.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when you fixed yourself.
Not when you cleaned up your act.
While you were still in it.
On that cross—
Jesus saw every hidden motive.
Every secret compromise.
Every double life.
Every moment you chose yourself over Him.
And He stayed.
This is the Gospel:
You are more sinful than you admit…
but more loved than you can comprehend—
because of Jesus Christ alone.
But grace is not permission.
Grace is power.
Titus 2:11–12 says:
“For the grace of God has appeared… training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives.”
Real grace transforms.
Real grace convicts.
Real grace leads to repentance.
So if your version of Christianity never challenges your sin…
never confronts your pride…
never calls you to surrender—
that’s not freedom.
That’s deception.
But here’s the hope:
You don’t have to stay there.
You don’t have to keep pretending.
You don’t have to keep performing.
You don’t have to keep living divided.
You can come clean.
Right now.
Not with a perfect prayer.
But with a surrendered heart.
Say it honestly:
“Jesus, I don’t want a fake faith anymore. Expose what’s false in me. Break what needs breaking. Lead me into truth.”
Because saving faith doesn’t hide.
It runs to Christ.
And when you come to Him—
Not polished.
Not pretending.
But real—
He doesn’t reject you.
He restores you.
1 John 1:9 gives us this promise:
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some.
All.
This is your moment.
Not to scroll.
But to respond.
If this pierced your heart…
Don’t ignore it.
That conviction?
That’s mercy knocking.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She was loved…
paragraphs: She was loved…
…but still breaking inside.
And that tension is where many believers quietly live.

You can be surrounded by love—
and still feel unseen.

You can be prayed for—
and still feel unanswered.

You can be held—
and still feel hollow.

So what do you do when love is real…
but your pain is deeper than what people can reach?
Stay with me.
Because Hannah’s story is not just about barrenness.
It’s about the silent shame that follows you even into places of worship.
Hannah had a good man.
Elkanah loved her. He chose her. He tried to comfort her.
But every year, the same wound reopened.

No child.
No answer.
No relief.
And worse—
Peninnah made sure Hannah never forgot it.

Mocked.
Provoked.
Humiliated.
Year after year.
Until the Bible says she wept and would not eat (1 Samuel 1:7).
That’s not just sadness.
That’s soul-level exhaustion.
And here’s where it gets real—
Some of you know this feeling.

The kind of pain that doesn’t scream…
it leaks.

Quiet tears.
Forced smiles.
Worship songs sung with a cracking voice.

You love God—
but you’re tired.

You believe—
but something inside you is breaking.
And when Elkanah speaks, it almost sounds right:
“Am I not more to you than ten sons?” (1 Samuel 1:8)
It’s loving.
But it misses the depth.
Because human love—even sincere love—has limits.
And this is where shame creeps in.

“Why am I still hurting?”
“Why can’t I just be grateful?”
“What’s wrong with me?”
That voice…
It’s not from God.
Let’s anchor this in Scripture.

“She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly.”
— 1 Samuel 1:10
Hannah didn’t fake strength.
She didn’t perform faith.
She brought her real self to God.

Raw.
Ugly.
Unfiltered.
And then she says something powerful:

“I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD.”
— 1 Samuel 1:15
Not presenting.
Not pretending.
Pouring.
Some scholars interpret this as a picture of complete emotional surrender—not just prayer, but the emptying of the heart before God without restraint.
And here’s the revelation:

God did not reject her for her brokenness.
He met her in it.
But let’s go deeper.
Because Hannah’s story is not just about emotional pain.
It points to something bigger.
Our deepest problem is not just unanswered prayers.
It’s a broken relationship with God because of sin.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
That means—
Even if your external situation changes…
Without Christ, the deepest emptiness remains.
And here’s the Gospel turn.
Jesus didn’t come just to fix your circumstances.
He came to redeem your soul.
Isaiah 53:3 says:
“He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.”
Do you see it?
Jesus understands sorrow—not from a distance, but from experience.

Rejected.
Mocked.
Misunderstood.
Sound familiar?
But He didn’t stop there.
On the cross, Jesus took not only our pain—
but our sin.

“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree…”
— 1 Peter 2:24
That’s the turning point.
Because the greatest barrier wasn’t your situation—
it was separation from God.
And through Jesus—
forgiveness is offered.
Grace is extended.
A new life is possible.
Not because you cleaned yourself up…
but because He gave Himself up.
So what does that mean for you right now?
It means you don’t have to hide your pain.
You don’t have to pretend you're okay.
You don’t have to earn God’s attention.
You can come—
as you are.

Broken.
Confused.
Tired.
And pour it out.
Not to people who may not fully understand…
but to a Savior who already does.
Hebrews 4:15–16 says:
“For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses… Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace…”
Confidence.
Not because you’re strong—
but because Jesus is enough.
Here’s the resolution.
Hannah walked into that temple empty…
but she walked out different before her situation even changed.
Why?
Because she encountered God.
And sometimes—
God doesn’t immediately change your situation.
He changes your posture.
Your heart.
Your peace.
So let me ask you directly:
What are you still carrying…
that you haven’t fully poured out to God?
What pain have you dressed up in “I’m okay”?
What prayer have you stopped praying because it hurts too much?
Bring it back.
Bring it all back.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
If this spoke to you—
Let that be your declaration.
You don’t know who needs this reminder.
And if this stirred something in you…
You are not alone in your pain.
And you are not beyond His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lesson I Learned From Abigail
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From Abigail
There was a moment in Scripture when 400 armed men were marching toward a massacre.

Swords were drawn.
Anger was rising.
And destruction was only minutes away.
All because of one foolish man.
His name was Nabal.
David and his men had spent months protecting Nabal’s shepherds and flocks in the wilderness. They were like a living security wall around his servants.
So when David politely asked for kindness in return, it should have been simple.
But Nabal responded with arrogance.
He insulted David.
He mocked him.
And in doing so, he ignited something dangerous.
David turned to his men and said:
“Strap on your swords.”
Four hundred warriors began marching toward Nabal’s household.
And if nothing changed, that entire household would be wiped out before morning.
But someone heard what was happening.
Her name was Abigail.
And the Bible describes her with two words that reveal everything about her character.
She was beautiful and discerning. (1 Samuel 25:3)
But what she did next proves that her wisdom was far more powerful than her beauty.
Because when Abigail heard what her husband had done, she didn’t panic.
She acted.
She quickly gathered food — bread, wine, sheep, raisins, and figs — and sent servants ahead to meet David.
Then she rode out herself.
Right into the path of a furious warrior with 400 soldiers behind him.
Imagine that moment.
Dust rising from marching feet.
Swords hanging from belts.
Anger burning in David’s chest.
And then a woman appears on the road.
She steps down from her donkey.
And she bows.
Not because she was guilty.
But because she was wise.
And with humility and courage, she began to speak.
She acknowledged the wrong.
She appealed to David’s future.
She reminded him that he was destined to be king.
And she gently warned him that shedding innocent blood would stain his destiny.
In other words…
She stopped a moment of rage with a moment of wisdom.
And something remarkable happened.
David listened.
The man who had just prepared for violence suddenly paused.
And then he said something that reveals how powerful wisdom can be.
He said:

“Praise be to the Lord… who has sent you today to meet me. May you be blessed for your good judgment and for keeping me from bloodshed.”
— 1 Samuel 25:32–33
Think about that.
A single wise voice stopped 400 swords.
One sensible woman prevented a massacre.
And an entire household was saved because someone chose wisdom when everyone else chose pride.
There is a powerful lesson here.
Because life is full of “Nabal moments.”
Moments when pride speaks too quickly.
Moments when anger escalates too far.
Moments when destruction feels inevitable.
But sometimes God places an Abigail in the middle of chaos.
Someone who knows how to calm the storm.
Someone who knows how to speak wisely when emotions are running high.
Someone who understands that wisdom is stronger than rage.
Abigail teaches us something many people overlook.
Not every hero in the Bible carries a weapon.
Some carry discernment.
Some carry humility.
Some carry the courage to step into conflict and stop destruction before it begins.
And sometimes the most powerful people in a crisis are not the loudest ones.
They are the wisest ones.
Because wisdom sees what anger cannot.
Wisdom protects what pride would destroy.
Wisdom preserves futures that foolishness would ruin.
And Abigail reminds us of something else.
Beauty may open doors.
But discernment protects destinies.
Her story shows us that wisdom is not passive.
Wisdom moves quickly when danger appears.
Wisdom takes responsibility even when the mistake wasn’t yours.
Wisdom steps between anger and destruction and says, “There is a better way.”
And because of that wisdom, God used Abigail to change the course of a violent moment in history.
One woman.
One decision.
One moment of courage.
And an entire disaster was stopped.
Sometimes we look for heroes in the middle of battle.
But the Bible reminds us that some of the greatest victories happen before the battle ever begins.
Because someone was wise enough to stop it.
And that is the lesson Abigail leaves behind.
Memorable Lines From This Story
“Some battles are not won with swords, but with wisdom.”
“Pride creates disasters that wisdom must repair.”
“One wise voice can stop a thousand foolish decisions.”
“Discernment is often the quiet hero in moments of crisis.”
“Beauty may open doors, but wisdom protects destinies.”
Now I’m curious…
Have you ever seen one wise decision prevent a huge conflict?
Or have you experienced a moment where someone’s wisdom stopped a situation from getting worse?

Share your story below.
Let’s learn from each other.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He should have been the next king.
paragraphs: He should have been the next king.

That was the expectation.
That was the bloodline.
That was the crown with his name already written on it.
Jonathan.
But the moment David walked into the story, everything shifted.

Songs started rising in the streets:
“Saul has slain his thousands… and David his tens of thousands.” (1 Samuel 18:7)

And with every lyric, Saul’s heart darkened.
Jealousy turned into suspicion.
Suspicion turned into violence.
A spear flew.

Not at an enemy.
At David.
And in that charged, dangerous, tension-filled palace—where loyalty was measured by silence—one man refused to play along.
Jonathan.
Pause.
Because this is where most people get it wrong.

Jonathan had every reason to turn on David.
Every reason to protect his future.
Every reason to stay quiet and let destiny remove his competition.
But instead…
He stepped in.

Scripture says:
“Jonathan… delighted much in David.” (1 Samuel 19:1)

Not tolerated.
Not endured.
Delighted.

This wasn’t political strategy.
This was covenant love.

Jonathan saw something others refused to see—
God’s hand on David.
And when you truly see God moving in someone else, you have a decision to make:

Compete…
Or protect.
Jonathan chose protection.

He spoke up when it was dangerous.
He defended David before a king consumed by rage:
“Let not the king sin against his servant David… because he has not sinned against you.” (1 Samuel 19:4)

That’s bold.
That’s costly.
That’s rare.
Because most people?
They stay silent when truth gets uncomfortable.
But Jonathan didn’t stop there.

When Saul’s hatred hardened again, Jonathan risked everything to warn David.
Signals were sent.
Arrows were shot.
Tears were shed.
“And they kissed one another and wept… until David exceeded.” (1 Samuel 20:41)
Feel that.

This is not shallow friendship.
This is love under pressure.
Jonathan knew something most people fear to admit:
David was the future king.
Not him.
Let that sink in.

The crown he could have fought for…
He surrendered.

The throne he could have protected…
He released.
Why?
Because honoring God’s will mattered more than securing his own position.
That’s the kind of loyalty heaven recognizes.
That’s the kind of humility hell hates.
But don’t romanticize this too quickly.
Jonathan’s story also exposes us.
Because if we’re honest…
We’ve all had moments where someone else’s rise made us uncomfortable.

Moments where we questioned instead of celebrated.
Withheld instead of defended.
Stayed silent when we should have spoken.
Jealousy doesn’t always shout.

Sometimes it whispers:
“Why not me?”
And if left unchecked, it slowly turns admiration into resistance.
Saul became that warning.
Jonathan became the contrast.
One fought against God’s choice.
One surrendered to it.
So where do you stand?
But here’s the deeper truth—the one that breaks through the story like light through a storm.
Jonathan is not the hero we ultimately need.
He’s a shadow.
A glimpse.
A signpost pointing forward.
Because Jonathan could only protect David temporarily.

He couldn’t stop death.
He couldn’t erase sin.
He couldn’t carry the weight of judgment.
But Jesus…
Jesus didn’t just stand between a spear and a man.
He stood between a holy God and a sinful world.
Let that hit you.
We were not David in this story.
We were closer to Saul—resistant, prideful, threatened by God’s authority.
Yet instead of destroying us…
Christ stepped in.
Not with a warning.
With a cross.
“God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

He absorbed the wrath.
He took the blow.
He carried the punishment.

Not because we deserved protection—
But because He is love.
Jonathan risked his position.
Jesus gave His life.
Jonathan defended a friend.
Jesus died for His enemies.
That is the Gospel.
And that changes everything.

Because now the question isn’t just:
“Will you be like Jonathan?”
The real question is:
Will you surrender to Jesus?

Will you lay down your pride…
your jealousy…
your need to be seen, chosen, elevated—
And trust the King who chose the cross for you?
Because here’s the invitation:
Repent.
Turn from the Saul within—the insecurity, the comparison, the silent resistance to God’s will.
And receive the grace of Christ—the One who protects, restores, and redefines your identity.
Then rise.

Become the kind of person who defends what God is doing in others.
Who celebrates without competition.
Who stands in truth even when it costs.
Because the world has enough Sauls.
God is still raising Jonathans.

And through Jesus—
He’s still transforming hearts.
Sit with it.
Pray.
You don’t have to fight for a crown God didn’t give you.
You just have to be faithful where He placed you.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Lot was called righteous.
paragraphs: Lot was called righteous.

Not lukewarm.
Not compromised in belief.
Not an unbeliever.
Righteous.
And yet… he chose to live in Sodom.
That tension should unsettle you.
Because it means a man can belong to God, feel conviction in his soul, and still build his life too close to what is destroying everything around him.
Scripture says his righteous soul was “vexed” by what he saw and heard every day (2 Peter 2:7–8).

That means Lot was not comfortable with sin.
He was troubled by it.
But he still stayed.
And that is the warning.
Because many people today think that conviction is protection.
They assume that as long as they still feel bothered by sin, they are safe.
But Lot proves something deeper:

You can be grieved by sin…
and still be positioned where sin is shaping your environment.
Lot didn’t fall in a moment.
He drifted in stages.
Genesis tells us he first looked toward the well-watered plains.
Then he pitched his tent near Sodom.
Then he lived in Sodom.
Then he sat in the gate — a place of influence, agreement, and leadership.
That progression is not random.
It is the anatomy of compromise.

It starts with what you allow your eyes to admire.
It continues with where you choose to place yourself.
And it ends with what you eventually normalize.
“Compromise rarely begins with rebellion. It begins with proximity.”
Lot never announced, “I want to become like Sodom.”
He just kept moving closer to it.
And here is the danger:

What you stay around long enough…
you start adjusting to.

At first, it grieves you.
Then it becomes familiar.
Then it becomes normal.
And eventually, it stops sounding as serious as it once did.
That’s why one of the most heartbreaking moments in Lot’s story is not the fire.
It’s the laughter.
When Lot warned his sons-in-law about the coming judgment, the Bible says they thought he was joking (Genesis 19:14).
Let that sink in.

A man who knew God
A man who felt conviction
A man who saw the danger clearly
…had lived in compromise so long that his urgency sounded like a joke to his own family.
That is terrifying.

Because it means you can be right spiritually…
but lose credibility relationally.

You can carry truth…
but raise people who no longer recognize its weight.
Environment matters more than most people admit.
What surrounds your life will eventually seep into your house.

Not always through rebellion…
but through slow exposure.

“Some people are not destroyed because they love evil.
They are destroyed because they stayed too close to it.”
Lot was not destroyed by passion for sin.
He was weakened by proximity to it.
And some of the hardest consequences in his story weren’t about him escaping.
They were about what was lost along the way.

His influence.
His family’s sensitivity.
His clarity.
His legacy.
Yes, God delivered him.
But the escape was messy, urgent, and painful.
That alone should speak loudly:

You can be saved…
and still suffer loss because of where you chose to stay.
This is where the message gets uncomfortable.
Because many believers today are living in the same tension as Lot.

They are grieved… but settled.
Convicted… but comfortable.
Aware… but unmoving.

They know certain environments are draining them.
They know certain influences are shaping their thinking.
They know certain spaces are weakening their spiritual life.
But like Lot… they stay.

Because it’s convenient.
Because it’s profitable.
Because it looks good from a distance.
But what looks like opportunity can hide spiritual danger.
“Do not use inner conviction as permission for outer compromise.”

Conviction is not meant to comfort you while you stay.
It is meant to guide you when it’s time to move.
There comes a point where the most spiritual decision you can make is not to endure an environment…
…but to leave it.

To step away from what keeps dulling your sensitivity.
To distance yourself from what keeps normalizing what God calls dangerous.
To protect your household from what slowly reshapes values.
Because sometimes the issue is not your heart.
It’s your proximity.
Lot’s life leaves us with a sobering truth:
You don’t have to love darkness for darkness to affect you.
You only have to live close enough to it.
And the question every believer must wrestle with is this:

Are you relying on your conviction…
while ignoring your location?
Because being troubled by sin is not the same as being positioned wisely.
And in the end, Lot escaped…
But barely.

Engagement Question:
What is one environment, influence, or habit that believers today often stay too close to—even when they know it’s affecting them spiritually?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They anointed his head…
paragraphs:
They anointed his head…
but no one prepared him for the cave.

Oil was still fresh on David’s skin—
yet dirt filled his nails.

Promise above him.
Pressure around him.
Silence within him.
And this is where most people break.

Because we love the prophecy…
but we panic in the process.

David was chosen in 1 Samuel 16—set apart, called, marked by God.
But by 1 Samuel 22, he’s not sitting on a throne.
He’s hiding in a cave.
Let that sink in.

God can speak something over your life—
and still lead you through seasons that feel like the exact opposite.

David wasn’t just hiding from Saul.
He was hiding with questions.

“Lord… did I hear You wrong?”
“Why does obedience feel like punishment?”
“Why am I running when I was called to reign?”

Be honest.
You’ve prayed those too.

Because the wilderness doesn’t just test your strength—
it exposes your theology.

Do you only trust God when life is clear?
Or will you trust Him when life contradicts what He promised?
David had every reason to become bitter.

Rejected by the king.
Hunted like prey.
Surrounded not by warriors—but by the distressed, the indebted, the discontented (1 Samuel 22:2).
This was not the kingdom he imagined.
But here’s the tension—don’t miss this:

The cave was not a detour.
It was development.

God was not delaying David.
God was discipling David.
Because a crown without character is a curse.
In the cave, David learned restraint.

Twice, he had the chance to kill Saul (1 Samuel 24, 1 Samuel 26).
Twice, he refused.
Why?
Because David understood something deeper than ambition:
You don’t have to force what God has already promised.
That’s the word for someone reading this.

You’re tired of waiting.
Tired of being overlooked.
Tired of being hidden.

And the temptation is rising—
to manipulate, to shortcut, to compromise.
But hear me:
If you have to sin to get it, it’s not from God.

David chose integrity over immediacy.
Obedience over opportunity.
Reverence over revenge.
That is what made him a man after God’s own heart (Acts 13:22).

Not perfection—
but surrender.
And in that cave, something powerful happened.

David didn’t just survive.
He started writing.
Many scholars interpret that several Psalms—like Psalm 57 and Psalm 142—were born in the cave.

Songs in the dark.
Worship in hiding.
Faith with no audience.
“Be merciful to me, O God… for in You my soul takes refuge” (Psalm 57:1).
Do you see it?

David didn’t wait for the palace to worship.
He turned the cave into an altar.
And that changes everything.
Because your environment does not define your devotion.

You can be in the darkest season of your life—
and still burn with holy fire.
Now here’s where the Gospel crashes into David’s story.

David hid in a cave to escape death.
Jesus stepped into the wilderness to defeat it.

Where David ran from a king,
Jesus stood before rulers and remained silent.

Where David spared his enemy,
Jesus died for His.

This is not just history—
this is salvation.

Because the greatest cave is not made of stone—
it’s the grave.
And Jesus went there.
For you.

For your sin.
Your compromise.
Your impatience.
Your moments when you tried to “play Saul” instead of trust God.
He carried it all to the cross.
“Christ died for our sins… He was buried… He was raised on the third day” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

And when He walked out of that grave—
He proved something eternal:
No cave is final when Jesus is involved.

So if you’re in a hidden season right now—
this is not your ending.
This is your formation.

God is doing surgery in secret.
Building strength where no one sees.
Purifying motives.
Breaking pride.
Deepening dependence.

The world may not clap for this season—
but heaven is invested in it.
Stay.

Stay faithful.
Stay clean.
Stay surrendered.

Because the same God who met David in the cave
is the same God who meets you right now.

And He’s not just preparing a place for you—
He’s preparing you for the place.
Don’t rush the process.

The throne is coming.
But first—
the cave.

And when you finally step into what God promised,
you’ll carry something far greater than success:
You’ll carry a heart that knows Him.

Someone you know is in a cave right now.
Share this with them.
Pray for them.

And if you’re the one hiding—
come back to Jesus.

Not just for answers.
For surrender.
Because the wilderness is not where God abandons you.
It’s where He introduces Himself in ways the palace never could.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t just betray Jesus…
paragraphs:
He didn’t just betray Jesus…
he exposed what he loved more.
And that’s the part we don’t want to face.
Because this isn’t just Judas’ story.
It’s ours.
He walked with Jesus.

Close enough to hear His heartbeat in the quiet moments.
Close enough to see miracles before the crowd even realized what happened.
Close enough to carry the money bag… and hide what no one else saw.
And still—
he sold Him.
For silver.
Not overnight.
Not suddenly.
But slowly… secretly… silently.

A heart drifting.
A desire growing.
A compromise repeating.
Until one day—
thirty pieces of silver felt worth it.
Let’s be honest.

No one wakes up and says,
“I’m going to betray Jesus today.”
It starts smaller.
Hidden.
Respectable.

You still show up.
You still worship.
You still say the right words.
But inside—
there’s something else you love more.

Money.
Approval.
Pleasure.
Control.
Comfort.
And it whispers,
“Just this once.”
Secret sin always sounds soft… before it becomes loud.
Judas didn’t fall at the moment of the kiss.
He fell long before that—
when he stopped guarding his heart.

📖 John 12:4–6
“But Judas Iscariot… said, ‘Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?’ He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief… and he used to help himself to what was put into it.”
Read that again.
He was already stealing.
Already hiding.
Already pretending.
And no one noticed.
But Jesus did.
This is the danger of secret sin → grace misunderstood.
You think,

“It’s small.”
“It’s private.”
“It doesn’t matter.”
But sin grows in the dark.

And what you tolerate in secret…
will one day speak in public.

📖 Luke 16:10
“One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.”
Judas didn’t jump to betrayal.
He trained for it.
Let that sink in.
Because the real issue wasn’t just money.
It was misplaced love.

📖 Matthew 6:21
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
His treasure wasn’t Jesus.
So when the moment came—
his heart followed the silver.
And here’s the confrontation:
What are you loving… more than Jesus right now?
Don’t answer quickly.
Sit in it.

Because whatever you refuse to surrender—
you are at risk of choosing over Him.
But don’t stop at Judas.
Look at Peter.
Peter denied Jesus too.
Three times.
Publicly.
Loudly.
So what’s the difference?
Judas felt regret.
Peter ran to repentance.

📖 2 Corinthians 7:10
“For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.”
Judas felt bad.
Peter turned back.
That’s the dividing line.
Not perfection.
Not performance.
But where you run after you fall.
🔥 Here’s the Gospel.
Lean in.
Because this is where everything changes.
Jesus knew Judas would betray Him.
Knew it.
Felt it.
Watched it unfold in real time.
And still—
He washed his feet.

📖 John 13:2–5 (paraphrased context)
Jesus, knowing what Judas would do, still knelt… still served… still loved.
Let that wreck you.
Jesus wasn’t surprised by betrayal.
And He isn’t surprised by your hidden struggles either.
You think your secret sin disqualifies you?
Jesus already saw it—
and still went to the cross.

📖 Romans 5:8
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after you fixed yourself.
Not after you cleaned up.
While you were still in it.
That’s grace.
Not permission to keep sinning—
but power to come out of hiding.
Because the cross doesn’t just forgive sin.
It exposes it—
and then destroys its power.
Judas ran from Jesus.
Peter ran to Him.
And today—
you get to choose.
You don’t have to keep pretending.
You don’t have to keep hiding.
You don’t have to keep negotiating your obedience.
Drop the silver.
Let go of the secret.
Come back to Jesus.

📖 1 John 1:9
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not “maybe.”
Not “if you’re good enough.”
He is faithful.
So here’s the invitation:
What if today—
you stopped managing your sin…
and started surrendering it?
What if the thing you’ve been hiding…
became the place where grace meets you?
Jesus is not asking for perfection.
He’s asking for your heart.
All of it.
No more divided love.
No more secret altars.
No more thirty pieces of silver.
Just surrender.
If this is you—
Respond.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They believed the lie.
paragraphs:
They believed the lie.
And the innocent man paid the price.
Pause.

Because this isn’t just Joseph’s story.
This is what it feels like when your name gets dragged through the mud…
…even when your heart stayed clean.
You did the right thing.

You said no.
You walked away.
You resisted what others secretly entertain.
And somehow…
You became the villain.
Let’s not sanitize it.
Joseph didn’t just face temptation—he ran from it.
Genesis says:
“How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?” — Genesis 39:9

He wasn’t just avoiding scandal.
He was protecting his relationship with God.
But righteousness didn’t reward him immediately.
It cost him.

His reputation.
His position.
His comfort.
His freedom.

One moment he was trusted.
The next—he was chained.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Because deep inside, many of us carry this silent belief:
“If I obey God… things should go well.”
But Joseph’s life confronts that lie head-on.

Obedience is not a contract for comfort.
It is a commitment to Christ—no matter the cost.
Let’s go deeper.
Potiphar’s wife didn’t just accuse Joseph.
She reversed the narrative.

She made purity look like perversion.
She made integrity look like guilt.
Sound familiar?

That’s what sin does.
It twists truth.
It weaponizes lies.
It distorts reality until righteousness looks wrong.
And some of you…
You’re living inside that distortion right now.

Misunderstood.
Misjudged.
Misrepresented.
And it hurts.

Not just the situation…
But the injustice of it.
But watch this.
Right in the middle of Joseph’s lowest moment—Scripture drops a quiet, explosive truth:
