author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY TORE THE ROOF OPEN.
paragraphs: THEY TORE THE ROOF OPEN.

Dust fell first.
Then silence.
Inside the house, the air was thick with bodies and breath. Every corner packed. Every doorway blocked. People leaned over shoulders just to glimpse the Teacher.
And outside?
Four men refused to leave.

Their friend could not walk.
Could not stand.
Could not push through the crowd.
But they carried him anyway.
The Desperate Climb (Mark 2:1–4)
The doorway was jammed.

No space.
No path.
No chance.
Most people would have turned back.
But faith is stubborn.
So the four men did something reckless… something disruptive… something unforgettable.
They climbed the roof.

Clay tiles scraped under their hands.
Their friend lay on the mat beside them — helpless, silent, trusting.
Then they started tearing.

Tile.
Mud.
Wood.
Rip.
Crack.
Dust rained down into the crowded room below.

People shouted.
Someone probably yelled, “HEY! What are you doing?!”
But the hole kept getting bigger.

Until sunlight poured into the room…
and a man on a mat began descending slowly from the ceiling.
Right in front of Jesus.
The Moment That Shocked Everyone (Mark 2:5)
The room held its breath.
The man expected healing.
The crowd expected a miracle.
But Jesus saw something deeper.
Scripture says:
“When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’” — Mark 2:5
Not your legs are healed.
Not get up yet.

First…
your sins are forgiven.
Because the deepest paralysis in the room was not in the man’s legs.
It was in the human heart.
Sin is the real disease.
And Jesus came to cure it.
The Grace That Broke the Ceiling
The religious leaders were furious.
“Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
Exactly.
That was the point.
Jesus wasn’t just a healer.
He was God in flesh standing in the dust-filled room.
So He asked them:
“Which is easier—to say ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say ‘Get up and walk’?”
Then He turned to the man on the mat.
The Command That Changed Everything
“I tell you, get up. Take your mat. Go home.” (Mark 2:11)
Strength rushed into lifeless legs.

Bones aligned.
Muscles fired.
Nerves woke up.
The man stood.
Then he picked up the mat that once carried him…
…and walked out through the stunned crowd.
Mark writes:
The Roof Was Never the Real Miracle
Yes, the roof was torn open.
But something far greater happened.
Grace broke through a human life.

A paralyzed man walked.
A condemned soul was forgiven.
And four stubborn friends became heroes of faith.
Because sometimes the miracle happens…
when someone refuses to give up on you.
The Gospel Hidden in the Ceiling
Friend, this story whispers something powerful:
We are all that man on the mat.

Unable to fix ourselves.
Unable to stand before God on our own strength.
But Jesus sees deeper than our visible problems.

He came first to forgive…
then to restore.
And the cross proved it.
When Jesus died and rose again, He tore open something far bigger than a roof.
He tore open the barrier between sinners and God.
So anyone who comes to Him in faith can walk free.
Because someone in your life might still be lying on a mat…
waiting for friends who refuse to quit.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE WAS JUST PASSING BY.
paragraphs: HE WAS JUST PASSING BY.

No plan.
No warning.
No idea his name would echo through eternity.
Mark tells it in one line:
“A certain man from Cyrene, Simon, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was passing by on his way in from the country, and they forced him to carry the cross.” — Gospel of Mark 15:21
Passing by.
That’s it.

Simon wasn’t a disciple.
He wasn’t a volunteer.
He wasn’t part of the crowd screaming for blood.
He was just walking into the city.
Then Rome grabbed him.

A soldier’s hand on his shoulder.
A command barked in a language that meant you don’t argue.
“Carry it.”
And suddenly Simon’s hands were on the wood meant for Jesus.
The Weight of Someone Else’s Sentence
Picture it.

The beam rough against his skin.
Splinters biting into his palms.
The smell of sweat, blood, and dust in the Jerusalem air.
And beside him—
Jesus.

Bruised.
Bleeding.
Barely standing.
Simon didn’t know the full story yet.
But he felt the weight.
Not just wood.

Judgment.
Sin.
History itself.
The cross pressed into his shoulder while the Son of God staggered beside him.
And the road to Golgotha suddenly had two men carrying one cross.
Here’s the twist.
Simon thought Rome forced him.
But heaven was writing a different script.
Because Jesus had already said:
“Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me.” — Gospel of Mark 8:34
Simon didn’t volunteer.
Yet he became the first man in history to literally do it.
And something changed that day.
Mark drops a small detail like a quiet thunderclap:
Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus.
Why mention them?
Many scholars believe the early church knew these men personally.
Which means this moment didn’t end on the road to Golgotha.
It followed Simon home.

Around the dinner table.
Into the hearts of his sons.
Into the story of the church.
A man who met Jesus under the weight of the cross raised sons who followed Him.
Listen closely.
Sometimes you think you’re just passing through life.

Just another day.
Just another crowd.
Just another moment.
Then suddenly—
God interrupts your path with a cross.

Pain.
Responsibility.
A burden you didn’t choose.
And you think:
Why me?

But what if the place where the cross touches your shoulder
is the place where you finally walk beside Jesus?
Because here’s the Gospel.
Simon carried the wood.
Jesus carried the sin.
Simon helped for a moment.
Jesus finished the work forever.

At Golgotha, Christ took the full weight—
your rebellion,
your shame,
your hidden failures—
and nailed them to the cross.
Not partially.
Completely.
And three days later, death lost the argument.
So if today you feel like life forced something onto your shoulders…
Look again.
You may not just be passing by.
You might be walking closer to Jesus than you ever have.
🔥 Friend, the cross you carry might be the place you meet the Savior.
And if you’ve never trusted Him—
Today is the day.

Lay your sin down.
Trust the One who carried it all the way to the grave—and walked out alive.
Because Jesus doesn’t just change history.
He rewrites lives.
✝️ We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Your future spiritual strength is being built by today’s habits.
paragraphs: Your future spiritual strength is being built by today’s habits.
Most people want strong faith.

They want unshakable peace.
They want courage when trials come.
They want wisdom in difficult decisions.
They want endurance when life becomes painful.
But many people overlook the quiet place where spiritual strength is actually built.
It’s not built in a single emotional moment.
It’s built in daily habits.

Faith is not forged in comfort.
It is formed in consistent obedience.
The believer who stands strong tomorrow is the believer who chooses discipline today.

The prayer whispered when no one sees.
The Bible opened when your mind feels tired.
The decision to obey God when temptation whispers louder than truth.
These moments may feel small.
But heaven sees them.
Every time you choose righteousness over compromise, something inside you grows stronger.
Every time you choose prayer instead of distraction, your spiritual muscles develop.
Every time you choose patience instead of anger, your heart becomes more like Christ.
The world celebrates dramatic moments.
But God builds strong disciples through daily faithfulness.
You may not feel the change immediately.

You may still struggle.
You may still fall sometimes.
You may still feel weak.
But do not mistake slow growth for no growth.
Seeds grow underground before they ever break through the soil.
God is working in the hidden places of your life.
Every time you open Scripture, your mind is being renewed.
Every time you pray, your heart is being aligned with heaven.
Every time you resist temptation, your spirit is becoming stronger.
Spiritual strength is not an accident.
It is the result of repeated obedience.
And this is exactly why the Bible gives us this powerful encouragement:

“Let us not grow weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.”
— Galatians 6:9
This verse is not just encouragement.
It is a spiritual law.
What you repeatedly sow into your life will eventually produce a harvest.
If you sow distraction, you reap confusion.
If you sow compromise, you reap weakness.
But if you sow prayer, truth, and obedience…
You reap strength.
You reap peace.
You reap spiritual authority.
The strongest believers you know did not become strong overnight.
They became strong through thousands of small decisions.

Choosing faith when fear whispered.
Choosing truth when culture pressured them.
Choosing prayer when life felt overwhelming.
Your daily habits are shaping your future faith.
The quiet moments matter more than you think.

The chapter you read today.
The prayer you whisper tonight.
The discipline you practice tomorrow morning.
These are the bricks God is using to build a strong spiritual life.
So if you feel tired…
Do not quit.
If you feel unnoticed…
Do not stop.
If you feel like your effort isn’t producing anything yet…
Keep going.
Because the harvest always comes after the sowing season.
And God promises that faithfulness will never be wasted.
Your future spiritual strength is already being built.

One habit at a time.
One prayer at a time.
One act of obedience at a time.
Keep building.
God is preparing you for more than you can see.
🙏 If you need prayer, comment PRAYER and we will pray for you.
📤 Share this reminder with someone who needs strength today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “JESUS MARVELED.”
paragraphs: “JESUS MARVELED.”
At a Roman soldier.

Not a prophet.
Not a priest.
Not one of the Twelve.

A man in uniform.
A man trained to kill.
A representative of the empire crushing Israel’s neck.

And Jesus…
marveled.
Why?
Stay with me.
In Gospel of Matthew 8, a centurion approaches Jesus. A commander over a hundred soldiers. Authority in his voice. Steel in his spine.
But when he speaks, it isn’t command.
It’s compassion.
“Lord, my servant lies paralyzed at home, suffering terribly.”

Did you catch it?
A Roman officer… pleading for a servant.

Not demanding.
Not threatening.
Pleading.
Jesus answers, “I will come and heal him.”
And this is where heaven leans in.
The centurion replies:
“Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. But only say the word, and my servant will be healed.”
Stop.

A Gentile soldier saying he’s unworthy.
While Israel’s religious elite argued about worthiness every day.
He continues:
“For I too am a man under authority…”
Under.
That’s the word.

He understood something many church people still miss:
Authority flows from submission.
He saw in Jesus not just a healer… but a King.
He recognized divine authority wrapped in dusty sandals.
And Scripture says Jesus marveled.

There are only two times in the Gospels where Jesus marvels.
One at unbelief (Mark 6:6).
Here — at faith.
“Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith.”
Can you feel the tension?

The outsiders are leaning in.
The insiders are missing it.
A pagan soldier sees what the covenant people overlook.
And then the promise explodes:
“Many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham…”
That’s the Gospel breaking through the border wall.
This is bigger than one healing.
This is about access.

The centurion didn’t ask for a touch.
He didn’t demand a sign.
He didn’t negotiate terms.
He trusted the Word.
“Only say the word.”
And Jesus did.
And at that very hour, the servant was healed.
Let me speak to you straight.

You don’t need proximity.
You need faith.

You don’t need perfect pedigree.
You need surrender.

You don’t need to clean up your résumé.
You need to recognize authority.

Some of you feel too far.
Too pagan.
Too stained by your past.
But this Roman soldier stepped across every cultural line and said, “Lord… I am not worthy.”
That’s where real faith begins.

Not hype.
Not performance.
Humble trust in the authority of Christ.
And here’s the scandal of grace:
The One with all authority became the Servant who went to a cross.
The King who commands armies allowed nails to command His hands.
Why?
Because we were the paralyzed ones.

Sin had us pinned.
Shame had us shackled.
Death had us scheduled.
And Jesus didn’t just say a word from a distance.
He came near.

He bore our sin.
He took our judgment.
He rose in authority over death itself.
Now the invitation stands:
Believe the Word.
Trust the King.
Submit to His authority — and you will find life under it.

Faith is not loud.
It is surrendered.

And when heaven marvels…
it’s not at talent.
It’s at trust.
Will Jesus marvel at your faith?

Bow the knee.
Trust His Word.
Receive His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE WAS READING ALONE.
paragraphs: HE WAS READING ALONE.

Scroll open.
Chariot moving.
Heart searching.
And heaven refused to let him stay that way.
In Acts of the Apostles 8, a powerful man from Ethiopia rides through the desert. Not a peasant. Not a drifter. This is the treasurer of a queen. Wealthy. Educated. Influential.
Yet spiritually?
Hungry.
He had just left worship in Jerusalem. He owned a scroll of the prophet Isaiah—expensive, rare, sacred.
But understanding?
Missing.
Let me say something that might sting:

You can sit in church.
Hold the Bible.
Read the verses out loud.
And still be alone in your soul.

The desert around him was quiet.
The desert inside him was louder.
“Like a sheep led to the slaughter…” he read.
He didn’t know he was reading about Jesus.
And here’s the tension — he had access to Scripture but not yet access to salvation. Religion was near him. Revelation was not.
So God moves.

Not with thunder.
Not with angels blazing across the sky.
He sends one obedient man.
Philip the Evangelist.
“Go to the desert road,” the Spirit said.
Desert roads don’t trend. Desert roads don’t impress. But revival rides there.
Philip runs beside a moving chariot — dust in his lungs, sun burning his skin — and asks one piercing question:
“Do you understand what you’re reading?”
That question split history.
The official answers with aching honesty:
“How can I… unless someone guides me?”
There it is.

Power without peace.
Knowledge without new birth.
Position without pardon.

Some scholars interpret the official’s status as a eunuch to mean he would have been limited in temple participation under Deuteronomic law. If so, imagine the ache — close to worship, yet not fully welcomed.
And now he’s reading Isaiah 53 — the prophecy of the Suffering Servant.

Wounded.
Pierced.
Silent before His accusers.
Philip opens his mouth.
And starting with that Scripture, he tells him the good news about Jesus.
This is the pivot.

The Lamb in Isaiah is not a metaphor.
He is the Messiah.
Jesus Christ — crucified for sin, risen for sinners.
The Ethiopian wasn’t just confused.
He was condemned — like all of us.

“For all have sinned…” (Romans 3:23)
Sin is not ignorance. It’s rebellion.
Not weakness. Treason against a holy God.
But grace chased a chariot that day.
They pass water.
Water in a desert.
The official says, “Look — here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?”
Hear the cry beneath the question:
Is there still room for me?
And the Gospel answers —
Yes.
Because the cross tore down every barrier sin erected.

No race excluded.
No past too stained.
No outsider too far.

He believed.
He was baptized.
He went on his way rejoicing.
Alone no more.
The Spirit carried Philip away, but the Savior stayed.
Listen to me carefully.

You might be reading alone right now.
Scrolling.
Curious.
Restless.

Religion can inform you.
Only Christ can transform you.

Jesus lived the life you failed to live.
Died the death you deserved to die.
Rose to give you the life you could never earn.
Repent. Turn from sin. Trust in Him alone.
And the desert inside you will bloom.
Because heaven still sends messengers to lonely chariots.
And maybe this post is running beside yours.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IT LOOKED LIKE DEFEAT.”
paragraphs: “IT LOOKED LIKE DEFEAT.”
But it wasn’t.

The sky went dark.
The crowds mocked.
His back was torn open.
His face—swollen, blood-streaked, dust clinging to wet skin.
And heaven was silent.

It looked like Rome had won.
It looked like hell had triumphed.
It looked like God had lost control.
But watch closely.
Because in Gospel of John 19, when Jesus hangs between earth and sky, when His chest strains for one more breath, when His body trembles under the weight of your sin and mine—
He does not whisper, “I am finished.”
He declares, “It is finished.” (John 19:30)
That word in Greek—Tetelestai.

Paid.
In full.
The Cross Was Not a Tragedy. It Was a Transaction.

Set: Golgotha, jagged rock under a bruised sky.
Wardrobe: Torn linen. Skin marked by lashes.
Lighting: Crimson-gold sunset slashed by cold blue shadow.
Camera: Close. Intimate. Breath-level.
FX: Dust in the air. Wind lifting strands of hair.
Mood: Tension before victory.
Symbol Layer: The Lamb becoming the payment.
The world saw a broken man.
The Father saw a finished mission.

Every lie you ever told.
Every lustful thought you tried to bury.
Every secret addiction.
Every moment you chose darkness over light.
Placed on Him.
“For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin…” (2 Corinthians 5:21)
Brother, sister—this was not accidental suffering. This was substitution.

Some scholars interpret “It is finished” as a cry of relief.
Others emphasize it as a legal declaration stamped across the debt of humanity.
Both bow before this truth:
The price was fully paid.

Not partially.
Not pending.
Not waiting for your good behavior.
Finished.
The Silence Was Not Abandonment. It Was Fulfillment.
The same chapter says Jesus fulfilled Scripture even in thirst (John 19:28). Nothing random. Nothing wasted. Every drop of blood moving history toward redemption.

Sin demanded death.
Holiness required justice.
Love demanded a way.
So Jesus became the way.
He bowed His head—not because life was taken from Him—but because He gave it.

No one forced the cross on Christ.
He embraced it.
For you.
And Here Is the Pivot
What looked like defeat was the demolition of hell’s claim on your soul.
The enemy thought the grave would seal the story.
But Sunday was coming.
And when Jesus said, “It is finished,” He meant:

Your shame—finished.
Your record of debt—finished.
The accusation over your name—finished.

You don’t fight for victory.
You fight from it.
So What Do You Do With a Finished Work?

You repent.
You believe.
You receive.
You stop trying to add your own nails to a cross that already carried enough.

If you’re exhausted from pretending…
If you’re tired of hiding…
If you feel like your failures define you—
Hear the Gospel clearly:
Jesus Christ, fully God and fully man, died in your place, bearing your sin. He truly died. He was buried. And on the third day He rose again, proving the payment was accepted.

Salvation is not earned.
It is received by grace through faith in Him alone.

This is not self-improvement.
This is resurrection.
Look at the cross again.
It looked like defeat.
But it was your freedom.

And if the Son has finished the work—
Why are you still carrying what He already buried?
Come to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHO WILL ROLL THE STONE?
paragraphs: WHO WILL ROLL THE STONE?
That was their question in the dark.

Before sunrise.
Before hope.
Before answers.

Three women walking toward a sealed grave.
Arms full of spices.
Hearts full of grief.
And one heavy thought pounding in rhythm with their steps:
“Who will roll the stone away?” — Gospel of Mark 16:3
Pause there.

They weren’t doubting Jesus.
They were drowning in logistics.

The stone wasn’t symbolic to them yet.
It was physical. Cold. Massive. Sealed.
Roman-certified final.
And here’s the open loop:
They went anyway.
The Weight of That Stone
Picture it.

Dawn light—ice blue against a crimson horizon.
Mist clinging to olive trees.
Their sandals scraping gravel.

Close-up: trembling hands gripping burial spices.
Tear-streaked cheeks catching the first gold rays.
Grief sitting heavy on their chests like wet cloth.
They had watched Him die.

The cross wasn’t poetic. It was brutal.
The nails were real. The blood was real.
The silence after was worse.
Now they walk toward what looks like the end.
And their question is ours.
Who will move what I cannot move?

The diagnosis.
The addiction relapse.
The broken marriage.
The shame nobody knows about.
The calling that feels buried.
That stone.
The Shock
“But when they looked up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large.” (Mark 16:4)
Very large.
God makes sure we know.

It wasn’t small faith that moved it.
It wasn’t their strength.
It wasn’t their strategy.
It was already done.
Before they arrived.
Let that sink in.
They were worrying about something Heaven had already handled.
The Angelic Interruption

Inside, a young man in white.
Brilliant. Still. Unshaken.
“Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen. He is not here.” (Mark 16:6)

Crucified.
Risen.
The Gospel in one breath.

Sin did its worst.
Jesus did better.

Death sealed the tomb.
God split it open.
Here’s the pivot.
The stone was never just about access to a body.
It was about access to life.

The resurrection is not metaphor.
It is the decisive victory of Christ over sin and death (see also 1 Corinthians 15).
Some scholars interpret Mark’s shorter ending (16:8) as intentionally abrupt—leaving the reader in trembling awe, forced to decide what they will do with the risen Christ.

Will you run in fear?
Or will you run with fire?
The Deeper Stone
Listen carefully.
The greatest stone wasn’t in front of the tomb.
It was in front of our hearts.

Sin.
Rebellion.
Guilt we try to perfume with good works.

But the same power that rolled that grave open
tears the veil
breaks the chains
and calls dead souls to breathe again.
Jesus didn’t rise to inspire you.
He rose to save you.

You cannot move the stone of your sin.
You cannot resurrect your own righteousness.
You cannot negotiate with death.
But Christ already walked out.

Repent.
Turn from sin.
Trust in the risen Lord alone.

The stone has been rolled away.
Not so Jesus could get out.
But so you could come in.
Now I ask you:
What stone feels impossible right now?
Type it. Name it. Drag it into the light.
Because we tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WE WILL NOT BOW.”
paragraphs: “WE WILL NOT BOW.”

The music was loud.
The pressure was louder.

Three young men.
One blazing furnace.
And a king who believed he was god.
Lean in. Because this isn’t just ancient history. This is your Monday morning.
🔥 Book of Daniel 3 — The Furnace That Tested Allegiance

King Nebuchadnezzar II builds a golden image—ninety feet high.
Ego plated in gold.
Power demanding worship.

The decree goes out:
When the music plays… bow.
Everyone does.
Except three.

Shadrach.
Meshach.
Abednego.

No hashtags.
No applause.
Just conviction.
They’re reported. Dragged. Threatened.
“Bow—or burn.”
And here’s the line that shakes history:

“If we are thrown into the blazing furnace, the God we serve is able to deliver us…
But even if He does not… we will not serve your gods.” (Daniel 3:17–18)
Did you catch that?

Faith isn’t bargaining.
Faith is allegiance.
🔥 The Heat Was Turned Up Seven Times

Nebuchadnezzar loses it. Orders the furnace hotter than ever.
Soldiers bind the men—hands tied, robes on, bodies exposed to the blaze.
The fire is so fierce it kills the soldiers who throw them in.

Shame.
Public spectacle.
Execution-level pressure.
But when the king looks into the flames…
He blinks.
“I see four men walking around in the fire, unbound and unharmed… and the fourth looks like a son of the gods.”
Some scholars interpret this fourth figure as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ. Others see an angelic deliverer sent by God.
But hear me clearly:
They were not alone in the fire.
And neither are you.
🌊 The Pivot — From Fire to Glory

The ropes burn.
The men don’t.

Not a hair singed.
Not a garment scorched.
Not even the smell of smoke.
The very thing meant to destroy them became the place of divine revelation.
Listen to me.
Your furnace might be exposing who you really serve.

Comfort?
Approval?
Secret sin?
Cultural applause?
Or Christ?
The Gospel in the Flames

We love courage stories. They spread fast.
But here’s the deeper truth:
You and I have bowed before.

We’ve bowed to lust.
To pride.
To fear.
To reputation.
And the wages of sin is not just embarrassment.
It’s death.
But there was Another who stood before the ultimate furnace.

Not Babylon’s fire—
but God’s wrath against sin.

Jesus Christ did not bow to Satan in the wilderness.
He did not bow to the crowd.
He did not bow to the cross to escape it.
He stepped into the fire for us.

On the cross, He absorbed what we deserved.
Three days later, He walked out—unharmed by the grave.

That’s not motivational courage.
That’s substitutionary redemption.
Close the Loop
They said, “We will not bow.”

Because they already had bowed—
in secret.
In prayer.
Before the true King.
That’s where courage is born.

Not in public defiance.
But in private surrender.

If you’re in the fire right now—
don’t measure God by the heat.
Measure Him by the Cross.

Repent where you’ve bowed to false gods.
Turn from secret compromises.
Trust Christ alone to save you.
And stand.

Even if the music plays.
Even if the crowd kneels.
Even if the furnace roars.
Because when you belong to Jesus—

The fire doesn’t define you.
His presence does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY SANG AT MIDNIGHT.
paragraphs: THEY SANG AT MIDNIGHT.

Not when the doors opened.
Not when the pain stopped.
Not when justice came.
Midnight.

The hour when faith feels foolish.
When prayers sound like echoes.
When your back still bleeds.
Let me take you inside the cell.
🔥 Acts of the Apostles 16 — The Prison That Couldn’t Silence Praise

They were stripped.
Beaten publicly.
Humiliated before a city.
Paul and Silas weren’t criminals. They cast a demon out of a slave girl. Freedom broke somebody’s business model. Profit screamed louder than truth.
So they were flogged—backs torn open, skin welted, blood drying against rough stone.
Then the jailer fastened their feet in stocks. Maximum security. No movement. No comfort.
Midnight.
And here’s the line that wrecks me:
“About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.” (Acts 16:25)
They didn’t whisper.
They sang.

Not denial.
Not delusion.
Defiant worship.

Family, this is the tension:
Most of us praise after the breakthrough.
They praised before it.
Why?
Because their joy wasn’t chained to circumstances. It was anchored to Christ.
Remember — this is the same Paul who met Jesus on the road to Damascus. The same Paul who once hunted Christians and now bleeds for Christ. He knew something:
If Jesus conquered death, a prison cell is just a waiting room.
And the other prisoners were listening.

Your midnight song is never private.
Someone in the dark is borrowing your faith.
Then suddenly—
An earthquake.
Not a tremor. A divine interruption. Foundations shook. Doors flew open. Chains fell.
But watch this.
They didn’t run.
Freedom opened the door… and they stayed.
Why? Because the real miracle wasn’t escape. It was salvation.
The jailer, trembling, thinking his life was over, was about to fall on his sword. Shame. Failure. Fear.
Paul shouts into the dark:
“Do not harm yourself! We are all here!”
Grace in the shadows.
The jailer falls before them and asks the only question that matters:
“Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
And Paul answers with Gospel clarity:
“Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.” (Acts 16:31)
There it is.

Not earn it.
Not fix yourself first.
Not escape your mess.
Believe.

That night, the jailer washed their wounds.
And they washed his soul with the Word.
He and his whole household were baptized.
The prison became a church.
Listen to me carefully:

Sometimes God allows the beating
so He can position you for someone’s salvation.
Sometimes your midnight is somebody else’s dawn.

You thought the chains were punishment.
They were placement.

You thought the silence meant abandonment.
Heaven was preparing an earthquake.
And maybe you’re in your midnight right now.

Marriage strained.
Body tired.
Secret shame whispering.
Sing anyway.

Not because it doesn’t hurt.
But because Jesus is still Lord at 12:00 AM.

Christ sang toward the cross.
Christ endured the darkest hour.
Christ stepped into our ultimate prison — sin and death — and shattered it from the inside.

The empty tomb is proof:
Midnight never gets the final word.
Brother, sister — what is your song in the dark?
Lift it.
Somebody is listening.
And heaven still shakes foundations.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There are battles in life that make you feel like you're losing.
paragraphs: There are battles in life that make you feel like you're losing.

The pressure keeps coming.
The prayers feel unanswered.
The weight on your shoulders feels heavier every day.
Some mornings you wake up already tired of fighting.

Tired of the anxiety.
Tired of the doubts.
Tired of feeling like you’re constantly trying to hold everything together.
And if you're honest… sometimes it feels like you're fighting for survival.
But God wants to remind you of something powerful today.
You are not fighting for victory.
You are fighting from victory.
That changes everything.
Because the outcome of your story was already decided the moment Jesus stepped out of the grave.
The enemy wants you to believe the battle determines your identity.
But the truth is — Christ already secured your victory.
The cross was not defeat.
The empty tomb was not a maybe.
It was the declaration that darkness does not get the final word.
Scripture tells us in Romans 8:37:
"In all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us."
Not barely surviving.
Not barely holding on.
More than conquerors.
Think about that for a moment.
A conqueror wins the battle.
But God says through Christ, you are more than a conqueror.
That means the victory you walk in today is not based on your strength.

Not your discipline.
Not your willpower.
Not your ability to hold everything together.
Your victory is rooted in the love of Christ.

The same Christ who defeated sin.
The same Christ who crushed the power of death.
The same Christ who walked out of the tomb in victory.
And if you belong to Him…
That victory belongs to you too.
Yes, the battle may still be loud.
Yes, the storm may still be raging.
Yes, the enemy may still whisper lies into your mind.
But the truth remains unshaken:
Your identity is not defeated.
You are not abandoned.
You are not forgotten.
You are not the mistakes from your past.
You are not the shame that tries to follow you.
You are not the fear that tries to control you.
Through Christ, you are:

Chosen.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
Strengthened.
Protected.
You are a warrior of faith.
Not because you never struggle.
Not because you never feel weak.
But because the power of God is with you in the fight.
Even when you feel tired, heaven is still fighting for you.
Even when you feel overwhelmed, God is still holding you.
Even when you feel like you’re losing, the victory of Christ still stands.
So if today feels like a battlefield…
Remember this truth:
You are not fighting for victory.
You are fighting from victory.
Stand firm.
Keep praying.
Keep trusting.
Keep believing.
Because the same God who raised Jesus from the dead is still working in your story.
And He is not finished with you.
Your story is not over.
Your faith is not wasted.
Your battle is not meaningless.
Through Christ, victory is already written over your life.
🔥 If this message spoke to your heart today, declare it in faith.
❤️ Share this so someone fighting a silent battle can be reminded that they are more than a conqueror through Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE ROOM FILLED WITH FIRE.
paragraphs: THE ROOM FILLED WITH FIRE.

No choir.
No stage lights.
No cathedral ceiling.

Just a room…
and a promise waiting to explode.
They were hiding.

Doors shut.
Hearts pounding.

Fishermen.
Tax collectors.
Women who once wept at a cross.

Jesus had ascended.
The sky had closed.
And now they were left with His last command:
“Wait for the promise of the Father.” — Acts 1:4
So they waited.

Not knowing how it would come.
Not knowing when.
Only knowing Who had spoken.
Then it happened.
Suddenly.

Not politely.
Not quietly.
A sound like a violent rushing wind.
The kind that shakes walls.
The kind that makes people stop breathing.
And the whole house filled with it.
Fire appeared.
Not burning the building…
But resting on people.
Tongues of flame above ordinary heads.

Fishermen.
Widows.
Former doubters.
God’s presence had moved from temples… into hearts.
The room filled with fire.
And the Church was born.
But understand this:
Pentecost was not about spectacle.
It was about salvation going public.

The Spirit filled them.
And suddenly they spoke in languages they had never learned.
Pilgrims from everywhere heard the message:

Parthians.
Medes.
Egyptians.
Romans.
And every one of them heard the same thing:
“We hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues.” — Acts 2:11
Heaven had crossed the language barrier.
The Gospel was no longer confined to one nation.
The mission had begun.
Then Peter stood up.
Yes—that Peter.
The one who denied Jesus three times.
The one who once trembled before a servant girl.
Now filled with the Spirit…
He thundered before thousands.

He preached Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ exalted.
And he did not soften the truth.

“You crucified Him…
but God raised Him.” — Acts 2:23–24
The crowd felt it.
The Word pierced them.
Conviction burned deeper than the fire above their heads.
They cried out:
“Brothers… what shall we do?”
Peter answered with the Gospel.

Clear.
Direct.
Hope-filled.
“Repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.” — Acts 2:38
Repent.
Turn.
Receive the One you rejected.
And that day—
3,000 souls stepped out of darkness into life.
The Church did not begin with strategy.

Not branding.
Not marketing.
It began with repentance and the power of the Holy Spirit.

Fire in hearts.
Truth on lips.
Jesus at the center.
And here is the quiet thunder of Pentecost:
The same Spirit who filled that room…
is the Spirit who calls to you today.
You don’t need a burning building.
You need a surrendered heart.
Because the greatest miracle of Pentecost was not the wind.
Not the languages.
Not even the flames.
It was this:
Sinners became family.
Through Jesus Christ.
Friend…
If your heart feels cold, ashamed, or distant—
Pentecost still whispers hope.

Repent.
Turn to Christ.
Receive the Spirit He promised.
The fire of God does not come to destroy you.
It comes to make you new.
The room filled with fire.
And the world has never been the same.
Because when Jesus sends His Spirit…
the Church rises.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY ACTUALLY LISTENED.
paragraphs: THEY ACTUALLY LISTENED.

Not to a celebrity.
Not to a king.
Not to a polished preacher with a perfect past.
To a runaway prophet who smelled like fish and failure.
And that’s where the tension begins.

Because if God can use a man who ran from Him…
what does that say about us who are still running?
In Book of Jonah 3, the word of the Lord comes to Jonah again.
Again.
That word should wreck you.

God did not cancel him.
God recommissioned him.
Jonah walks into Nineveh—a violent empire capital. Blood on their hands. Idols in their temples. Pride in their bones. Historians describe Assyria as ruthless. Cruel. Inventive in torture.
And God sends one reluctant preacher with one sentence:
“Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”

No worship team.
No miracles.
No altar call.
Just judgment.
Forty days.

Tick.
Tock.
Now here’s the shock.
They believed God.
Read that again.
“They believed God.” (Jonah 3:5)

Not Jonah.
God.

From the greatest to the least, they fasted. Sackcloth scratched against royal skin. Ashes smeared across proud foreheads. Even the king stepped down from his throne, removed his robe, and sat in dust.

Power in ashes.
Authority on its knees.
Who does that?

A pagan empire trembles.
While Israel often shrugged.
Let that sink in.
But don’t romanticize it.
Their repentance was desperate. The king says, “Who knows? God may turn and relent…” (Jonah 3:9)

No presumption.
No entitlement.
Just raw mercy-seeking.
And here’s the pivot.
“When God saw what they did… God relented of the disaster.” (Jonah 3:10)
Grace interrupted judgment.

Not because they earned it.
Not because sackcloth saves.

Repentance doesn’t purchase mercy.
It throws itself on it.

Some scholars interpret this passage as describing God’s “relenting” in human language—an anthropomorphic expression—because Scripture also teaches that God does not change in His character (cf. Numbers 23:19). What changed was Nineveh. And when sinners turn, they meet the mercy God already delights to give.
Listen carefully:

Nineveh’s story is not about behavior modification.
It’s about a holy God responding to humble repentance.
But here’s the deeper Gospel thread.
Nineveh got 40 days.
We got the Cross.
Jesus Himself referenced this moment (Matthew 12:41). He said the men of Nineveh would rise up in judgment against a generation that saw something greater than Jonah—and still refused to repent.

Jonah preached impending destruction.
Jesus absorbed it.

Jonah warned of overthrow.
Jesus was overthrown on a cross.

Nineveh hoped God might relent.
At Calvary, mercy was secured in blood.
This is the scandal of grace:

The wicked city repents.
The rebellious prophet is used.
The holy God forgives.
And today?
He is still saying “again.”

Again to the addict.
Again to the hypocrite.
Again to the secret sinner who thinks it’s too late.

You think your past disqualifies you?
Jonah ran.

You think your city is too corrupt?
Nineveh was worse.

You think judgment is final?
Look at the empty tomb.

Repentance is not humiliation.
It is alignment with mercy.
And Christ is the mercy.
Turn. Not tomorrow. Not when you feel cleaner. Now.
Because if Nineveh listened…
what’s stopping you?
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SPIRIT SAID NO.
paragraphs: THE SPIRIT SAID NO.

Not the devil.
Not delay.
Not distraction.
The Spirit.

Paul was ready. Bags packed. Heart burning. Gospel blazing in his bones.
Asia was waiting. Or so he thought.
But in Acts of the Apostles 16, the unthinkable happens:
“They were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.” (Acts 16:6)
Forbidden.
Let that sit on your chest for a second.

The man who wrote half the New Testament…
Shut down.
Blocked.
Redirected.
Why would God stop a good thing?
The Closed Door
Paul tries Bithynia.
No.
He pivots. Adjusts strategy.
No again.
Scripture says, “the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.” (Acts 16:7)
This wasn’t a scheduling conflict.
This was divine interruption.

And here’s the tension:
Sometimes the most painful “no” in your life isn’t demonic attack.
It’s divine protection.

You prayed.
You fasted.
You obeyed.
And the door slammed anyway.

Rejection email.
Breakup text.
Visa denied.
Opportunity evaporated.
You called it loss.
He called it direction.
The Night Vision
Then it happens.
In Troas, at night, Paul sees a vision — a man of Macedonia pleading, “Come over and help us.” (Acts 16:9)
God wasn’t closing a door to punish Paul.
He was closing Asia to open Europe.
Closed doors are often God’s scalpel — precise, intentional, protective.

Because if Paul had gone east,
Philippi wouldn’t have heard.

And if Philippi never heard,
Lydia never would’ve believed.
The jailer never would’ve cried, “What must I do to be saved?”
Europe’s spiritual history shifts.
One “no” unlocked a continent.
Let’s Get Honest
You’re grieving a closed door right now.

A relationship.
A ministry role.
A dream.

And secretly you’re asking:
“God… why block me when I’m trying to serve You?”
Because He sees what you don’t.
Because obedience matters more than momentum.
Because sometimes the Spirit says no to protect you from:

• burnout
• compromise
• hidden danger
• wrong timing
• smaller impact
And because His mission is bigger than your map.
The Gospel Pivot
Let’s go deeper.
Jesus Himself experienced a closed door.

In the garden, He prayed,
“Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from Me.” (Matthew 26:39)
He asked for another way.
He received a “no.”
But that “no” became your salvation.

The cross looked like rejection.
It was redemption.

The tomb looked sealed.
It became victory.
Closed doors in Christ are never the end of the story.
They are the corridor to resurrection.
Hear Me Carefully
The Spirit’s “no” is not abandonment.
It is alignment.

Paul didn’t argue.
He didn’t sulk.
He didn’t force the door.
He listened.
And because he listened, the Gospel crossed borders.
What if your frustration is actually protection?

What if the door you’re pounding on
is the one that would have crushed you?
Brother, sister—
Trust the closed door.

If you are walking in obedience,
submitted to Scripture,
anchored in Christ—
His “no” is mercy.
And mercy sometimes feels like rejection before it feels like rescue.
Today, surrender your Asia.
Ask God for your Macedonia.

And when He redirects you—
follow.

Because from scandal to grace—
Jesus rewrites everything.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most people misunderstand what God is actually trying to do in their lives.
paragraphs: Most people misunderstand what God is actually trying to do in their lives.
We often think the goal of following God is happiness.

Comfort.
Ease.
A life without problems.
But the truth of Scripture tells a very different story.
God doesn’t just want you happy.
He wants you holy.
That might not be the message people want to hear in a culture that constantly says:

“Follow your heart.”
“Do what makes you happy.”
“Live your truth.”
But the Bible calls us to something deeper than temporary feelings.
It calls us to transformation.
Happiness is based on circumstances.
Holiness is based on character.
Happiness can disappear the moment life gets hard.
Holiness grows stronger in the middle of the fire.
Many people approach God like He exists to make their lives easier.

They pray for problems to disappear.
They pray for comfort.
They pray for blessings.
But God is often doing something much greater than removing your problems.
Sometimes He is removing the sin, the pride, the idols, the selfishness, and the old life that is keeping you from becoming the person He created you to be.
The truth is this:
God cares more about who you are becoming than how comfortable you feel today.
Scripture makes this clear.
1 Peter 1:16 says:
“Be ye holy; for I am holy.”
That is the calling.
Not just to feel good.
Not just to be successful.
But to become more like Christ.
Holiness means surrender.
It means choosing obedience even when it’s difficult.
It means walking away from things the world celebrates.
It means loving righteousness more than temporary pleasure.
And that’s where many people struggle.
Because holiness requires death to self.
It requires humility.
It requires repentance.
It requires choosing God’s will over our own desires.
But here’s the powerful truth:
Holiness is not about perfection.
It’s about direction.
It’s about a heart that says:
“God, change me.”
“God, refine me.”
“God, make me more like You.”
And when that happens, something incredible begins to take place.
God begins to transform your heart.
Your desires change.
Your priorities shift.
Your perspective becomes eternal instead of temporary.
You stop chasing the things that once controlled you.
And you start pursuing the things that actually matter.

Peace.
Truth.
Righteousness.
Faith.
Love.
Hebrews 12:14 gives a sobering reminder:
“Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord.”
Holiness is not just a suggestion.
It is the path of those who truly belong to God.
But here is the amazing part.
When we pursue holiness, something unexpected happens.
We often discover a deeper joy than the world’s version of happiness could ever give.
Because true joy is not based on circumstances.
It comes from walking with God.
It comes from knowing you are living for something eternal.
It comes from being transformed by His grace.
So the real question is this:
Are you chasing happiness…
Or are you pursuing holiness?
Because one fades.
And the other lasts forever.

Happiness fades.
Holiness lasts forever.
Look up: Hebrews 12:14
🔥 Let’s talk honestly:
Do you think modern Christianity focuses more on happiness than holiness?
I’m curious what you think.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WASN’T ISRAELITE.
paragraphs: SHE WASN’T ISRAELITE.
Yet heaven carved her name into eternity.
And if you don’t feel the tension in that, you’re not reading the Bible close enough.
Let me show you why this should shake you.
🌾 Ruth the Outsider Who Became Royal
She was from Moab.
Moab.
A nation born from scandal (Genesis 19). A people who seduced Israel into idolatry (Numbers 25). Enemies. Outsiders. Not covenant blood.
And her name?
Ruth.
When famine hit Bethlehem, an Israelite family ran to Moab. Elimelech. Naomi. Two sons. (Book of Ruth 1)
The sons married Moabite women.
One of them was Ruth.
Then death came like winter.

Elimelech — gone.
Both sons — gone.
Three widows.
No provider. No protection. No future.
Naomi decides to go back to Bethlehem. She tells her daughters-in-law to stay in Moab.
One leaves.
Ruth doesn’t.
And here is the line that split history:
“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.” (Ruth 1:16)
That’s not romance.
That’s repentance.
That’s conversion.
That’s a Moabite woman turning her back on idols and walking into covenant with Yahweh.
🔥 The Risk No One Talks About
She followed Naomi into a land where she would always be “the foreigner.”

Accent different.
Skin tone different.
History different.
She gleaned in fields — the scraps. The leftovers. The mercy edges of the harvest (Ruth 2).
And that’s where grace found her.
Not in a palace.
In a field.
She meets Boaz — a kinsman-redeemer. A man of standing. A man of covenant mercy.
Some scholars interpret the threshing floor scene (Ruth 3) as culturally symbolic language of seeking covenant covering, not seduction. The text presents Ruth as righteous, bold, and honorable.
Don’t miss that.
The Bible doesn’t glamorize scandal.
It magnifies redemption.
Boaz redeems her. Marries her. Restores her name.
And then—
The scandal explodes into glory.
Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of King David (Ruth 4:17).

Yes. That David.
David
And through David’s line comes—
Jesus.
Jesus Christ is born into a genealogy that includes a Moabite widow.
Let that sink in.
The Messiah’s bloodline carries Gentile mercy.
🌊 The Gospel Hidden in Her Story
You and I?
We weren’t Israelites either.
We were outsiders to the covenants of promise (Ephesians 2:12).
Foreign.
Spiritually Moab.
But Christ is our true and better Boaz.
He didn’t just toss us leftovers.
He redeemed us with His own blood.
He didn’t marry us because we were worthy.
He covered us because He is merciful.
Ruth walked away from Moab and clung to Naomi.
We walk away from sin and cling to Christ.
That’s the turn.

From shame to lineage.
From foreigner to family.
From scraps to inheritance.
“Grace Gleans the Outsider.”
💔 Maybe That’s You
You feel disqualified.

Wrong background.
Wrong family.
Wrong past.
Listen to me carefully.
Ruth’s passport said Moab.
Heaven’s record said redeemed.
The Gospel does not ask where you were born.
It asks who you cling to.
Cling to Christ.

Turn from your idols.
Trust the Redeemer.
Step into covenant mercy.
Because the same God who wrote a Moabite widow into the story of salvation is still writing stories today.
Including yours.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY THREW HER DOWN.
paragraphs: THEY THREW HER DOWN.

Dust exploded around her face.
Hands shaking.
Hair tangled.
Breath broken.
A circle of men closed in.
Stones already in their fists.
And the law on their lips.

She wasn’t arrested quietly.
She was dragged.

Pulled from the shadows of her secret.
Thrown into the blazing sunlight of public shame.
“Teacher,” they said, their voices sharp with accusation.

“This woman was caught in adultery.
The Law of Moses commands us to stone such women.
What do You say?”
But this was never about justice.
It was a trap.

If Jesus said “Stone her,” He would destroy His reputation for mercy.
If He said “Let her go,” they could accuse Him of rejecting the law of God.
So they waited.

Stones ready.
Crowd leaning forward.
And the woman?
She didn’t even look up.
Because when your sin is exposed, the ground feels safer than people’s eyes.
Then Jesus did something strange.
He stooped down.

No speech.
No debate.
No defense.
Just a finger moving through dust.
Writing.
The mob grew restless.
“Answer us!”
They demanded a verdict.
So Jesus stood.
And with one sentence… He shattered the circle.

“Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone.”
(John 8:7)
Silence.
Not the peaceful kind.
The kind that cuts.
One stone dropped.
Then another.
Older men first.
Because the longer you live, the more you know your own sins.
Soon the courtyard was empty.
No accusations.
No stones.
Just Jesus.
And the woman they threw down.
Jesus looked at her.
Not with disgust.
Not with cold religious distance.
But with the eyes of the only truly sinless man who ever lived.

“Woman… where are they?
Has no one condemned you?”
Her voice trembled.
“No one, Lord.”
Then came the words that still echo through history.

“Neither do I condemn you.
Go, and from now on sin no more.”
(John 8:11)
Do you see the Gospel here?
Jesus didn’t pretend her sin was harmless.
Adultery is sin.
But He also refused to let shame have the final word.
The law exposed her guilt.
Grace offered her a new life.
And here’s the deeper mystery.
Those stones?
They were real.
And someone would pay the price for sin.
Just not her.
A few chapters later, Jesus Himself would stand in another courtyard.
Not as the judge.
But as the condemned.
And the punishment the law demanded…
would fall on Him at the cross.
So the guilty could walk free.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be that woman.

A secret exposed.
A mistake replaying in your mind.
A label people won’t let you forget.
But hear this clearly:
Jesus is not standing with a stone.
He is standing with nail-scarred hands.

Ready to forgive.
Ready to restore.
Ready to say:
“You are not finished.”
Because somewhere out there is a person who thinks their shame is the end of their story.
And they need to hear this truth:
Jesus still bends down in the dust for sinners.
And when He stands up…
grace stands with Him.
✝️ We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ISRAEL NEEDED A JUDGE.
paragraphs: ISRAEL NEEDED A JUDGE.
God raised a woman.

Not a warrior king.
Not a battle-hardened general.
Not a priest from the temple courts.
A woman… sitting under a tree.
And the nation came to her.
The land was choking under oppression.

For twenty years the iron grip of Jabin, king of Canaan crushed Israel.
Nine hundred iron chariots.
Armies led by the ruthless commander Sisera.

Villages emptied.
Roads abandoned.
Fear everywhere.
Israel was silent.
Until God spoke.

And when He did—
He didn’t raise the expected.
He raised Deborah.

A prophet.
A judge.
A woman who heard the voice of God while sitting beneath a palm tree.
“The Israelites came to her to have their disputes decided.” — Judges 4:5
Pause there.
In a world dominated by swords and men of war, God lifted a woman whose greatest weapon was the Word of the Lord.
Then came the moment.
Deborah summoned Barak.
“Has not the Lord, the God of Israel, commanded you?” (Judges 4:6)
She gave the battle plan.

Not from strategy manuals.
Not from military intelligence.
From God.
But Barak hesitated.
“If you go with me, I will go… but if you don’t go with me, I won’t go.”
Fear still lingered in Israel.
Even in its warriors.
Deborah answered with calm fire:
“I will go with you. But the honor will not be yours, for the Lord will deliver Sisera into the hands of a woman.” (Judges 4:9)
And God did exactly that.

The mighty general Sisera—
the terror of Israel—
did not fall to a sword on the battlefield.

He fell in a quiet tent…
through the hands of Jael, another woman God positioned in the story.
The tyrant collapsed.
The oppressor ended.
The impossible victory belonged to the Lord.
Here’s the deeper truth.
Deborah was never the hero.
God was.
He raises leaders from unexpected places.

A shepherd boy.
A stuttering prophet.
A fisherman.
A persecutor turned apostle.

And yes—
a woman under a palm tree.
Because the power of God does not rest on status.
It rests on obedience.
But Judges also whispers a warning.
Israel needed a judge because sin had returned.
The cycle was always the same:

Rebellion.
Oppression.
Crying out.
Rescue.

Again.
And again.
And again.
Human judges could win battles.
But they could not change the human heart.
Israel didn’t just need Deborah.
Israel needed a greater Deliverer.
Centuries later, God raised another unlikely Savior.
Not from a palace.
From a manger.
Jesus Christ.

The final Judge.
The true Deliverer.
The One who defeats not just armies—but sin, death, and Satan.

Where Deborah brought victory for a season,
Jesus brings eternal redemption.
The cross is the battlefield where the real enemy fell.
And the empty tomb is the final victory song.
So here’s the question:
Is your life still trapped in the cycle?

Sin.
Bondage.
Temporary rescue.
Again and again.
Jesus breaks the cycle.
Completely.
If you come to Him.

Repent.
Believe.
Follow the true Judge and King.
Because when Christ writes the ending…
Oppression does not get the final word.
Grace does.
🔥 We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Most people want clarity before they move.
paragraphs: Most people want clarity before they move.
But many times, God lets you move before you see.

In Gospel of Luke chapter 24, two disciples were walking the long road to Emmaus. Their hearts were heavy. Everything they believed had just been shaken. The one they followed… the one they thought would change everything… had been crucified.

They were confused.
They were disappointed.
They were trying to make sense of it all.
And while they were walking, someone joined them.
It was Jesus.
But they didn’t recognize Him.
Think about that for a moment.
They were literally walking beside the answer, and they still couldn’t see it.
Not because Jesus wasn’t there.
But because their understanding had not caught up yet.
And that is where many people find themselves today.

Walking.
Questioning.
Trying to understand why things happened the way they did.

You prayed for direction.
You asked for clarity.
You wanted the whole plan revealed before you took the next step.
But sometimes heaven works differently.
Sometimes God allows the road to teach you before the revelation comes.
The disciples didn’t stop walking because they were confused.
They kept going.

They talked.
They wrestled with their thoughts.
They listened.
And slowly, something started happening.

Jesus began explaining the scriptures to them.
Piece by piece.
Story by story.
Their understanding wasn’t forced.
It grew.
Not instantly.
But gradually.
Then something powerful happened later that evening.
When they sat down to eat, Jesus broke the bread.
And suddenly…
Their eyes opened.
Everything made sense.

The journey.
The conversation.
The scriptures.
And they said something that still echoes today:
“Did not our hearts burn within us while He talked with us on the road?”
Here is the lesson many people miss.
Their eyes didn’t open at the beginning of the journey.
They opened after the walk.
This is where faith and discipline meet.
Because discipline often means continuing the walk even when you don’t fully understand the road yet.
Showing up.
Praying when the answers are quiet.
Working when the results are slow.
Trusting when the picture is incomplete.
The world teaches people to move only when they are certain.
But faith sometimes asks you to move while certainty is still forming.
That doesn’t mean blind rushing.
It means steady walking.
Consistency.
Patience.
Trust built step by step.
Some of the clearest moments in life don’t appear at the beginning of a journey.
They appear after the road has shaped you.
After the questions have refined you.
After the waiting has deepened your perspective.
Eyes open slowly.
Not because God is distant.
But because some understanding can only be carried by a heart that has walked far enough to hold it.
So if you’re in a season where things don’t fully make sense yet…
Keep walking.
Keep learning.
Keep showing up.
Clarity has a way of meeting people on the road, not just at the destination.
And one day, you may look back and realize something powerful:
God was walking beside you the whole time.
You just hadn’t recognized Him yet.
One day, this reminder might be exactly what you need on the road.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT.
paragraphs: MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT.

Paul begged God to remove it.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And heaven answered with something shocking.
Not deliverance.
Grace.
Listen closely, friend.
In Second Epistle to the Corinthians chapter 12, the apostle Paul the Apostle opens a window into a secret pain he carried like a splinter under the skin.
He calls it:
“a thorn in the flesh.”

We’re never told exactly what it was.
Some scholars interpret it as a physical illness.
Others believe it could have been relentless persecution, spiritual harassment, or even chronic weakness.
But Paul describes it this way:

“A messenger of Satan to torment me.”
— 2 Corinthians 12:7
Let that sink in.

This is the same Paul who saw miracles.
The same man who planted churches across the Roman world.
And yet…
He limped.
The Prayer That Wasn’t Answered
Three times Paul cried out.
“Lord, take it away.”

Imagine the nights.
The frustration.
The question:
Why won’t You heal this?
Then came the voice of Christ.
Not the answer Paul expected.

“My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is made perfect in weakness.”
— 2 Corinthians 12:9
Read that again.
God did not remove the thorn.
He transformed the weakness.
The Divine Paradox
The world worships strength.
Jesus glorifies surrender.
Paul suddenly understood the secret most believers miss:
Weakness is not disqualification.
Weakness is the stage where Christ shows His power.
So Paul makes a radical declaration:
“Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.”
Not tolerate.
Boast.
Why?
Because every crack in the vessel becomes a window for God’s glory.
The Thorn You Carry
Some of you reading this know exactly what this feels like.
The prayer you’ve prayed for years.
The struggle that hasn’t left.
The weakness you wish God would erase.
But what if the thorn isn’t punishment?

What if it’s protection from pride…
or a platform for grace?
Paul says earlier in the passage that the thorn kept him from becoming conceited because of the incredible revelations he had received.
God sometimes allows a thorn so our soul stays close to Him.
The Gospel Hidden in the Thorn
Look to the cross.
Jesus Christ Himself carried what looked like defeat.

Nails.
Thorns.
Shame.
Yet that very weakness became the doorway of salvation for the world.
Sin was crushed not by earthly strength—
but by sacrificial love.
And through His death and resurrection, grace flows to sinners who repent and trust Him.

That same grace that held Paul…
holds you.
The Final Word
Your thorn does not mean God abandoned you.
It may mean He’s doing something deeper than healing.
Something eternal.
Because when human strength collapses…
Christ stands tallest.
And His whisper still echoes through history:
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
If this message reached you tonight, take a moment.
Bring your thorn to Jesus.

Confess.
Surrender.
Trust the Savior who turns weakness into glory.
Because in Christ,
your worst wound can become the place where grace shines brightest.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE BROKE THE JAR.
paragraphs: SHE BROKE THE JAR.

Not by accident.
Not by clumsiness.
She broke it on purpose.
Because some worship cannot stay sealed.
Picture the room in Bethany.

Dinner is on the table.
Laughter in the air.
The smell of roasted food.
And sitting there like any other guest…
Jesus.
The same Jesus who just raised her brother from the grave.
The same Jesus who called “Lazarus, come out.” (John 11:43)
Everyone is eating.
But Mary of Bethany is remembering.

Remembering the tomb.
Remembering the grief.
Remembering the miracle.
And suddenly—
She stands.

No speech.
No announcement.
Just a jar.

An alabaster jar of pure nard.
Perfume worth a year’s wages. (John 12:5)

One moment of devotion…
that cost everything.
Then she does the unthinkable.
She breaks the jar.
The fragrance explodes into the room.

Thick.
Sweet.
Overwhelming.
John writes:
— John 12:3
But Mary isn’t done.
She kneels.
She pours the perfume on Jesus’ feet.
Then something even more shocking—
She loosens her hair.
In that culture, a woman never did that in public.
But Mary doesn’t care about reputation anymore.
She wipes His feet with her hair.
Worship.
Raw.
Costly.
Unfiltered.
And immediately…
The criticism comes.
Judas speaks up.

“Why wasn’t this perfume sold and the money given to the poor?”
— John 12:5
Translation:
This is wasteful.
This is excessive.
This is embarrassing.
But John exposes the truth.

“He did not say this because he cared about the poor but because he was a thief.”
— John 12:6
Religious logic hates extravagant worship.
But Jesus?
Jesus defends her.

“Leave her alone.”
— John 12:7
In Greek, it carries the force of “Stop bothering her.”
Then Jesus reveals something chilling.

“It was intended that she should save this perfume for the day of my burial.”
— John 12:7
Mary understood something the disciples missed.
The cross was coming.

So before the nails…
before the thorns…
before the tomb…
She anointed Him.
And here’s the part that grips me.
Mary didn’t pour some perfume.
She poured all of it.
Because once the jar is broken…
You can’t take it back.
That’s worship.
Not polite religion.
Not calculated devotion.
Total surrender.
Let me ask you something.
What jar are you still protecting?

Your reputation?
Your comfort?
Your secret sin?
Your control?
Mary broke hers.
Because she knew this:
Jesus is worth more than the perfume.

More than approval.
More than dignity.
More than money.
More than everything.
And here’s the Gospel.
In just a few days…
Jesus would be broken too.
Not a jar.
His body.
Broken on a cross for sinners like us.

“This is my body, which is for you.”
— 1 Corinthians 11:24
Mary poured perfume on His feet.
Jesus would pour His blood for the world.
That’s the scandal of grace.
So today…
Break the jar.
Pour out the worship.
Give Jesus the devotion you’ve been holding back.
Because the fragrance of a surrendered life?
It still fills the house.
And heaven never calls it waste.
Someone out there thinks their devotion is too messy, too costly, too late.
Let them know:
Jesus still welcomes broken jars.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE ANGEL CALLED HIM MIGHTY.”
paragraphs: “THE ANGEL CALLED HIM MIGHTY.”
While he was hiding.

Not preaching.
Not leading.
Not conquering.
Hiding.
In a winepress.
Let’s step into Book of Judges 6.

Israel was crushed under Midian.
Seven years of fear.
Seven years of crops stolen.
Seven years of hiding in caves like hunted animals.
And there he is—Gideon.
Threshing wheat in a winepress.
Winepresses were carved low into rock. Tight. Sunken. Defensive. You don’t thresh wheat there. You thresh on a hilltop where wind separates grain from chaff.
But Gideon? He’s underground.
Because fear will shrink your calling.
Then the Angel of the Lord appears.
“The Lord is with you, mighty warrior.” (Judges 6:12)
Mighty.
Warrior.
To a man hiding.
Here’s the open wound in this story:

Gideon doesn’t feel mighty.
He feels forgotten.
“My clan is the weakest… and I am the least.” (Judges 6:15)
You ever said that in your own words?

“I’m not that gifted.”
“I’m the least in my family.”
“I messed up too much.”
“I’m just trying to survive.”
Listen carefully.
Heaven called him what he could not see in himself.
Not because he was brave.
Because God was with him.
Midway pivot. Watch this.

God does not deny Gideon’s fear.
He confronts it with presence.
“I will be with you.” (Judges 6:16)
That’s the difference.
Your weakness + His presence = courage born in secret.
Some scholars interpret the “Angel of the Lord” here as a theophany—an appearance of God Himself. Others see it as a high-ranking angelic messenger. Either way, the authority is divine.
And that changes everything.
But here’s where it gets personal.
Before Gideon fights Midian, he has to tear down his father’s altar to Baal.
Private obedience.
Before public victory.
He does it at night.
Still afraid.
And God still uses him.
Did you catch that?
God did not wait for Gideon to become fearless.
He moved while Gideon was trembling.
This is the Gospel thread running beneath the soil.
We were hiding too.

Hiding in shame.
Hiding in sin.
Hiding in our own winepress of self-protection.
And heaven spoke over us.

Not “failure.”
Not “coward.”
Not “least.”
But through Jesus Christ—

“Beloved.”
“Redeemed.”
“Chosen.”
At the cross, Jesus was publicly shamed so you could stop hiding privately.
At the resurrection, He proved that fear does not get the final word.
Sin does not get the final word.
Your insecurity does not get the final word.
Christ does.
Maybe you’re reading this from your own winepress.

Quiet.
Small.
Afraid to be seen.
Hear me, beloved.
God sees you in hiding.
And He is not mocking your fear.
He is calling your destiny.
Not because you’re strong.
But because He is with you.

Repent of unbelief.
Step out of hiding.
Trust the Savior who steps into winepresses to rescue cowards and turn them into warriors.
Jesus does not recruit the brave.
He creates them.
If this is you, pray:
“Lord, I feel least. But if You are with me, that is enough. Tear down my idols. Build courage in me. I trust Christ alone.”
And step forward.
Even if it’s at night.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DO YOU LOVE ME?”
paragraphs: “DO YOU LOVE ME?”
The fire was already burning.

Not the fire of Pentecost.
Not yet.
This one crackled on a lonely shoreline in Gospel of John 21 — charcoal and smoke twisting into the morning air. The same smell as the courtyard.
The night he failed.
Peter had gone back to fishing. Back to nets. Back to muscle memory. Because when shame screams loud enough, you return to what doesn’t ask questions.
But Jesus was waiting on the shore.
And He was cooking breakfast.
Peter hears it.
“Children, do you have any fish?”
They don’t recognize Him. Not at first. The mist hangs low over the water. The sea is steel-blue. Their skin is wet with sweat and salt. Nets cutting into calloused hands. Empty.
“Cast the net on the right side.”
Obedience feels small. Almost foolish.
Then—
Overflow.
Fish thrashing silver in the rising sun. Water exploding in droplets. Nets straining. Hearts racing.
John whispers, “It is the Lord.”
And Peter?
He doesn’t wait for the boat.
He dives.
Why would a man who denied Jesus three times swim toward Him?
Because shame had one more round to lose.
On the shore: charcoal fire. Bread. Fish. Mercy in human form.
Jesus doesn’t start with the denial.
He starts with a question.
“Simon, son of John… do you love Me more than these?”
Not once.
Three times.
The same number as the denials.

Some scholars interpret the shift in Greek words for love (agape and phileo) as significant — others see it as stylistic. But the weight is undeniable. Jesus meets Peter exactly at the depth of his failure.
Three wounds.
Three restorations.

Each question peeling back pride. Each answer trembling.
“Yes, Lord… You know.”
By the third time, Peter is grieved.
Good.
Not condemned.
Grieved.
Because godly sorrow is the doorway to restoration.

And then Jesus says it — not “Try harder.”
Not “Don’t mess up again.”
“Feed My sheep.”
Failure did not disqualify Peter.
It prepared him.
Let this sink deep.

The same mouth that cursed and denied would preach at Pentecost.
The same hands that warmed by a coward’s fire would heal the lame.
The same heart that broke in shame would blaze in boldness.
Grace after failure always wins.
But only if you turn back to the shore.
Maybe you’ve denied Him too.

Not with words — but with silence.
With compromise.
With secret sin that smells like smoke.
And today Jesus stands on your shoreline.
Not with a lecture.
With breakfast.
And one piercing question:
Do you love Me?

Not “Are you perfect?”
Not “Did you get it right?”
Do you love Me?

Because love leads to repentance.
Repentance leads to restoration.
Restoration leads to purpose.
Peter’s story is not about a fisherman.
It’s about a Savior.

Jesus Christ died for deniers. He rose for failures. He restores the ashamed. At the cross, your worst moment met His greatest mercy. And in the resurrection, He calls you again — not to earn love, but to walk in it.
Turn back.
Answer Him.
And feed His sheep.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HE BOUGHT A TICKET IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION.”
paragraphs: “HE BOUGHT A TICKET IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION.”
Not because he didn’t hear God.
Because he did.
And he hated what he heard.
🎬 JONAH RUNS — Jonah 1

God said,
“Go to Nineveh.”
Jonah booked Tarshish.

Opposite direction.
Different port.
Different future.

He didn’t mishear the voice of God.
He resisted it.

Nineveh was violent. Cruel. Israel’s enemy.
And God wanted to show them mercy.
Jonah didn’t struggle with fear.
He struggled with grace.

Some scholars interpret Jonah’s flight as nationalism — he didn’t want Israel’s enemies forgiven. Others see it as prophetic pride — a fear that if Nineveh repented, his warning would look false. Either way, the root was the same:
He did not want God to be that merciful.
And before we judge him…
How many of us have bought tickets in the opposite direction?
God whispers, “Forgive.”
We book resentment.
God says, “Apologize.”
We purchase silence.
God says, “Speak truth.”
We board compromise.
The ship sailed.
The wind rose.
Because you can run from assignment…
But you can’t outrun presence.
“Then the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea…” (Jonah 1:4)
Notice that.
It wasn’t random weather.
It was mercy in the form of a storm.

The pagan sailors panicked.
Jonah slept.
Isn’t that wild?

The unbelievers prayed.
The prophet snored.
Sin will exhaust you so deeply that you can sleep in the middle of chaos you created.
But God wouldn’t let him drown quietly.

They cast lots.
The finger pointed.
Jonah finally said it:
“I fear the LORD…” (Jonah 1:9)

He feared God.
But he fled Him.
That’s the tension some of you live in right now.
You love God.
But you’re avoiding the hard obedience.
And the storm keeps knocking.
Listen carefully.
The storm was not punishment alone.
It was pursuit.

Because the same God who sent the wind
prepared the fish.
Judgment and mercy, woven together.
Here’s the Gospel.
Jonah said, “Throw me into the sea.”
And the sea grew calm.
An innocent substitute, calming the storm.
Centuries later, another man would stand in a different storm — not running from sinners, but running toward them.
Jesus Christ didn’t board a ship to escape enemies.
He climbed a cross to save them.
Where Jonah resisted mercy, Jesus embodied it.
Where Jonah slept in rebellion, Jesus wept in surrender.
Where Jonah was thrown into the sea for his own disobedience, Jesus was cast into death for ours.
Three days in the deep.
Then resurrection.
You see it?
Jonah 1 isn’t just about a runaway prophet.
It’s about a relentless God.
You may have bought a ticket in the opposite direction.
But grace is faster than ships.
Grace rides the storm.
Grace prepares the fish.
Grace will interrupt your escape to restore your calling.
So let me ask you, heart to heart:
What “Tarshish” are you heading toward?
What obedience are you postponing?
You don’t have to keep running.
Repentance is simply turning around.
The same God who sends the wind also provides the way back.
And His name is Jesus.
Come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I WON’T LET GO.”
paragraphs: “I WON’T LET GO.”

Midnight.
Alone.
No worship band. No spotlight. No filter.
Just a man… and God.
In Genesis 32, Jacob is on the edge of everything he fears. His past is catching up. His brother Esau is coming—with 400 men. The liar. The manipulator. The heel-grabber.
And now?
He’s about to be grabbed.
But not by Esau.
By God.
Scripture says, “A Man wrestled with him till the breaking of day.” (Genesis 32:24)

Not a dream.
Not a metaphor.
A collision.
Midnight faith always costs something.

Jacob had spent his life wrestling people—
his brother in the womb,
his father with deception,
his uncle with schemes.
But this night?
He wrestles God.
Why would God wrestle a man?

Some scholars interpret this “Man” as a theophany—an appearance of God in human form. Others see it as an angelic messenger. But Jacob’s conclusion is clear: “I have seen God face to face.” (Genesis 32:30)
This wasn’t just a fight.
It was mercy in disguise.
Because sometimes God will step into the ring not to destroy you—
—but to break what’s destroying you.
And just when Jacob thinks he’s holding his ground…
The Man touches his hip.
One touch.
Socket out of joint.
Strength gone.
Swagger shattered.
And that’s when Jacob says the line that splits the night open:
“I will not let You go unless You bless me.”
Listen carefully.

He’s limping.
He’s losing.
He’s wounded.
And he still won’t let go.
That’s not arrogance.
That’s desperation.
That’s midnight faith.

He doesn’t demand comfort.
He doesn’t ask for safety.
He asks for blessing.
Why?
Because deep down Jacob knows what every sinner eventually learns—
If God lets go of me… I’m finished.
And here’s the scandal.
The blessing doesn’t come because Jacob wins.
The blessing comes because he clings.
God changes his name.
Not “Deceiver.”
But “Israel” — one who strives with God.
His identity shifts before his situation does.
He limps into the sunrise.

New name.
New walk.
Same grace.
Beloved, the Gospel is hidden in this midnight fight.
You and I wrestle not because we’re strong—
—but because we’re scared.
We cling not because we deserve—
—but because we need mercy.
At the cross, Jesus did what Jacob could not.

Where Jacob wrestled for blessing,
Christ was wounded to secure it.

Where Jacob limped away alive,
Jesus was pierced so we could rise forgiven.

Sin dislocates us.
Pride deforms us.
Fear hunts us.
But grace?
Grace wrestles us until we surrender.
And when we cling to Christ by faith—
He does not let go.

Midnight might bruise you.
It might expose you.
It might strip your confidence.
But if you hold onto Jesus—
morning is coming.
So tonight, if you’re in the dark…
If your past is marching toward you…
If your hip is out and your pride is broken…
Say it with Jacob.
“I won’t let go.”
Not because you’re strong.
But because He is.

Repent.
Cling.
Trust the wounded Savior who fought for you on the cross and rose again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: NO MORE TEARS.
paragraphs: NO MORE TEARS.

Not someday maybe.
Not wishful thinking.
A promise.
But before that promise arrives, the Bible shows us something unsettling.
This world… is passing away.

The cities we build.
The graves we visit.
The tears we hide at night.
All of it.
Gone.
In Book of Revelation 21, the apostle John the Apostle sees a vision so breathtaking it almost feels impossible.

And yet it is Scripture.
And Scripture does not exaggerate.
Listen carefully.

“He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain.”
— Revelation 21:4
Pause there.
Every tear.

Not just the visible ones.
The hidden ones too.

The tears you wiped before anyone noticed.
The tears you cried over betrayal.
Over regret.
Over the sins that still haunt your memory.
God sees them all.
And in the new creation—
He personally wipes them away.
But here is the tension most people miss.
Revelation 21 begins with a cosmic reset.

“Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.”
— Revelation 21:1
Not repaired.
Replaced.

The broken system of sin, death, decay—
the world infected since Book of Genesis 3—
will finally be undone.

No funerals.
No hospitals.
No addiction chains.
No secret shame.
Even the sea—the ancient biblical symbol of chaos and evil—
gone.
And then something even more shocking appears.
A city.
The New Jerusalem.
A holy city descending from heaven like a bride walking down the aisle.

Beautiful.
Radiant.
Prepared by God Himself.
And the voice from the throne declares:

“Look! God’s dwelling place is now among the people.”
— Revelation 21:3
Do you hear that?
Heaven is not just where we go.
It is where God comes to dwell with us forever.
No temple needed.
Because Jesus Himself is the center of everything.
But the chapter also whispers a warning.
This future belongs only to those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life.
The Lamb is Jesus Christ.

The One who bled on the cross.
The One who carried our sin.
The One who rose from the grave.
The new world is not earned by good behavior.
It is entered by grace.
Grace received through repentance and faith in Jesus.
So let me speak to the person reading this quietly tonight.
You feel tired of this broken world.

The anxiety.
The guilt.
The endless cycle.
Listen.
The story does not end with tears.
The final chapter of the Bible is not disaster.
It is restoration.

A new sky.
A new earth.
A new beginning.
And the King Himself wiping the tears from your face.
Friend,

If you belong to Jesus,
your future is not darkness.
Your future is Revelation 21.

No graves.
No regret.
No more tears.
Only the presence of God.
Forever.
Because the world needs to hear this:
The end of the Bible is not destruction.
It is home.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “NOT MANY WERE WISE.”
paragraphs: “NOT MANY WERE WISE.”

That’s not an insult.
It’s an indictment.
Paul looks at the church in Corinth — a city drunk on philosophy, status, influence — and says:
“Not many of you were wise according to worldly standards. Not many were powerful. Not many were of noble birth.” (1 Corinthians 1:26)
Pause.
Feel that.

God didn’t build His Church with influencers.
He built it with interruptions.
