And here’s the open loop you don’t want to ignore:

If God chooses the weak…
why do we spend our lives trying to look strong?

Corinth was a flex culture.
Pedigree mattered. Eloquence mattered. Platform mattered.
But Heaven had a different metric.
“God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong.” (1 Corinthians 1:27)
Chosen.

Not tolerated.
Not barely accepted.
Chosen.
Let me talk to the one who feels disqualified.

The addict who relapsed.
The leader who failed privately.
The student who thinks they’re not smart enough.
The believer who whispers, “I should be further by now.”
Listen to your pastor’s heart:
God builds with broken tools.

Not because He enjoys dysfunction.
But because when cracked hands hold holy fire, no one mistakes the Source.
The cross itself looked like weakness.

A beaten body.
Sweat and blood mingled.
Breath collapsing under Roman brutality.
Nails through nerve and tendon.
Weak.
Or so they thought.
But what looked like defeat was divine strategy.
“For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” (1 Corinthians 1:18)
Here is the scandal:

Your weakness is not your disqualification.
Your pride is.

The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up and then come.”
It says, “Boast only in the Lord.” (1 Corinthians 1:31)
Some scholars interpret Paul’s language as a direct confrontation against Greek rhetorical elitism — but the Spirit’s message still stands: God refuses to share His glory with human ego.

So He chooses the overlooked.
The unimpressive.
The trembling.
Why?
“So that no human being might boast in the presence of God.” (1 Corinthians 1:29)

This is not about celebrating weakness.
It’s about exposing false strength.
Because in Christ —

Your insecurity becomes dependence.
Your failure becomes repentance.
Your repentance becomes restoration.
And your restoration becomes a testimony that silences the wise.
And here’s the Gospel anchor:
“Because of Him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption.” (1 Corinthians 1:30)

Not self-made wisdom.
Not earned righteousness.
Not self-help redemption.
Jesus.

Sin made you weak.
Grace makes you His.
So stop hiding the cracks.

Bring them to the Cross.
Lay them down.
Repent where pride has ruled.
Receive where shame has shouted.

God is not looking for polished vessels.
He is looking for surrendered ones.
And if you feel like a broken tool in the Builder’s hand…
You are exactly the kind He uses.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IT IS WRITTEN.”
paragraphs: “IT IS WRITTEN.”

Not shouted.
Not argued.
Not negotiated.
Just spoken.
And hell stepped back.

The desert was silent.
Forty days.
No bread.
No comfort.
No applause.
Only hunger.
And that’s when the devil came.

Because temptation rarely attacks when you’re strong.
It waits for the moment your body is weak…
your mind is tired…
your soul is lonely.
Then the whisper begins.

“If You are the Son of God… turn these stones into bread.”
— Gospel of Matthew 4:3
It sounded reasonable.
After all, Jesus was starving.
But the trap was deeper than hunger.

The enemy wasn’t just asking Jesus to eat.
He was tempting Him to act without trusting the Father.
To satisfy legitimate needs in illegitimate ways.
And Jesus answered with four words that shook the wilderness:
“IT IS WRITTEN.”

“Man shall not live by bread alone,
but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.”
— Deuteronomy 8:3
The devil tried again.
This time from the pinnacle of the temple.
“Throw Yourself down… the angels will catch You.”
A dare disguised as faith.
But Jesus saw through it.
Again the sword came out:
“IT IS WRITTEN.”

“You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.”
— Deuteronomy 6:16
The third attack was the boldest.
From a high mountain the devil showed Him all the kingdoms of the world.

Power.
Glory.
Authority.
One shortcut.
“All these I will give You… if You bow down and worship me.”

No cross.
No suffering.
No nails.
Just compromise.
And Jesus answered one final time:
“IT IS WRITTEN.”

“You shall worship the Lord your God and Him only shall you serve.”
— Deuteronomy 6:13
And the devil left.
Not because Jesus was louder.
But because truth carries authority that lies cannot survive.
Here is the Gospel hidden in that desert.

The first Adam faced temptation in a garden…
and he fell.

The second Adam—Jesus—faced temptation in a wilderness…
and He stood.

Where humanity failed,
Christ was faithful.
He resisted every temptation so He could become the spotless Savior who would later carry our sins to the cross.
Your victory over sin doesn’t start with your strength.
It starts with His obedience.

Because the One who said “It is written” in the wilderness
would later say “It is finished” on the cross.
And that changed everything.
Maybe today the enemy is whispering to you.

A secret sin.
A compromise.
A shortcut.
Remember the weapon Jesus used.

Not emotion.
Not willpower.
Scripture.
When lies come…
Speak truth.
When temptation rises…
Stand on the Word.
When darkness whispers…
Declare what heaven has already written.

Because the same Word that defeated the devil in the wilderness
is the Word that can guard your heart today.

And the Savior who resisted Satan
is the Savior who now lives to strengthen you.
So when temptation comes, say it with holy defiance:

IT.
IS.
WRITTEN.
Because some battles are won with fists…
But the greatest victories are won with the Word of God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What if your ambition is the very thing God is slowing down?
paragraphs: What if your ambition is the very thing God is slowing down?
They weren’t building a tower.
They were building a reputation.

Genesis 11 opens like a success story.
One language.
One vision.
One unstoppable movement.
“Come, let us build ourselves a city… and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves.” (Genesis 11:4)
Pause.
Make a name.

That’s not architecture.
That’s ego with blueprints.

They had unity.
They had innovation.
They had brick instead of stone.
Bitumen instead of mortar.
Progress. Technology. Strategy.
But beneath the scaffolding?
Fear.
“…lest we be scattered over the face of the whole earth.”

God had already commanded humanity in Genesis 1:28 and 9:1 to fill the earth.
They said, “No. We’ll stay. We’ll rise. We’ll control our destiny.”
This wasn’t about height.
It was about control.
And here’s the tension we don’t like to admit:

Sometimes what looks like momentum…
is rebellion in disguise.

They weren’t shaking their fists at heaven.
They were just building something impressive without God at the center.
Ambition is not sin.
But ambition without surrender becomes idolatry.
And God came down.

Notice the irony.
They tried to reach heaven.
God had to “come down” just to see it.

He confuses their language.
Not out of insecurity.
Not because He’s threatened.
But because mercy sometimes sounds like interruption.

What if Babel was judgment…
and protection at the same time?
If God had allowed unified rebellion to scale unchecked, the depth of human pride would have hardened beyond repair.
So He scattered them.
He disrupted them.
He slowed them down.
Let me ask you again—

What if your stalled project…
your delayed promotion…
your closed door…
is not punishment?
What if it’s protection?
Babel is the story of humanity trying to ascend without repentance.
But the Gospel is the story of God descending in grace.
At Babel, languages were confused.
In Acts 2, at Pentecost, languages were understood.
The Spirit did not erase diversity—He redeemed it.
At Babel, people said, “Let us make a name for ourselves.”
In Philippians 2:9, God gives Jesus “the name that is above every name.”
Do you see it?

Humanity tried to climb up.
Christ chose to come down.

We build towers to reach God.
God sent His Son to reach us.
The cross is the anti-Babel.

Not bricks stacked in pride—
but a Savior lifted in humility.
Your name will never save you.
Your platform will never redeem you.
Your ambition will never justify you.
Only Jesus.
And here is the hope:

You don’t have to make a name for yourself—
because in Christ, you are already known.

Already loved.
Already secured.
So if God is slowing something down in your life…
Ask Him:
“Lord, is this Babel in my heart?”

And if it is—
repent.

Not in shame.
But in freedom.

Because the same God who scattered in Genesis
gathers in Christ.

He doesn’t crush ambition.
He crucifies pride.
Then He resurrects purpose.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Sometimes the battle you’re fighting isn’t visible.
paragraphs: Sometimes the battle you’re fighting isn’t visible.

No one sees the pressure on your mind.
No one sees the spiritual weight on your heart.
No one sees the silent prayers you whisper when everything feels like it’s falling apart.
But heaven sees it.

There are seasons when life feels like a storm that won’t stop.
Fear hits from one side.
Doubt attacks from another.
Temptation whispers.
Discouragement tries to drain your strength.
And suddenly it feels like you're surrounded.
You may not see it with your physical eyes, but Scripture reminds us of something powerful:
Some battles are spiritual.
Ephesians 6:12 says we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against spiritual forces.

That means the anxiety that comes out of nowhere…
The wave of doubt that suddenly hits your faith…
The pressure that tries to make you quit…
Sometimes it’s more than coincidence.
But here’s the truth the enemy hopes you forget:
God never sends His people into battle defenseless.
You are not standing in that storm alone.
The Bible tells us to take up the shield of faith, because that shield has the power to extinguish every flaming arrow of the enemy.
Think about that.
Every arrow.

Not some.
Not most.
Every single one.
Faith is not pretending the storm isn’t real.
Faith is standing in the middle of the storm and saying:
“God is still greater.”
Faith is kneeling in prayer when fear tells you to run.
Faith is trusting God when circumstances look impossible.
Faith is believing that what God is doing behind the scenes is greater than what you can see in front of you.
And sometimes the strongest position you can take in spiritual warfare is not fighting harder…
It’s kneeling deeper.
Because when you kneel before God, you stand against the enemy.

There is power in prayer.
There is power in surrender.
There is power in faith.
Storms may rage around you, but they cannot destroy what God is protecting.
The enemy may attack your mind, your confidence, your peace, or your future…
But he cannot break a believer who is covered by the presence of God.
And the truth is this:
Many of the greatest victories in your life will happen in battles nobody else saw.

The prayers nobody heard.
The tears nobody noticed.
The nights you kept believing even when it was hard.
Those are the moments when God builds warriors.
So if you feel like you’re under attack right now…
If you feel overwhelmed…
If it feels like darkness is pressing in from every direction…
Remember this:
The battle is real.
But so is your shield.
And the God who stands with you is stronger than any storm that stands against you.
Scripture says:

"Take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one."
— Ephesians 6:16
🛡️ “My shield is faith.”
You never know who needs this reminder today.
God is still fighting for His people. ✝️🔥
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PERHAPS THE LORD WILL ACT.
paragraphs: PERHAPS THE LORD WILL ACT.

Two words that don’t sound like certainty.
Two words that don’t look like victory.
Perhaps.
Faith sometimes begins there.

Not with thunder.
Not with guarantees.
But with a trembling step forward.

Saul was sitting under a pomegranate tree.
Six hundred soldiers.
Swords scarce.
Fear everywhere.
Across the valley stood the Philistine outpost—armed, trained, waiting.
Then Jonathan looked at his armor-bearer and whispered:

“Come, let’s go over to the outpost of those uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will act for us. Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.”
—1 Samuel 14:6
Did you hear that?
Not “God told me the outcome.”
Not “Victory is guaranteed.”
Just:
Perhaps.
Here’s the scandal of faith most people miss.

Jonathan had no army.
No strategy briefing.
No prophetic confirmation.
Just a conviction about who God is.
“Nothing can hinder the LORD.”
That sentence changed everything.
Because when you know God’s character, you can move even when you don’t know God’s plan.
The climb was brutal.

Sharp cliffs.
Hands scraping rock.
Enemy soldiers watching from above.
The Philistines mocked them.
“Come up here, and we’ll teach you a lesson.”
Jonathan turned to his armor-bearer.
That was the sign.
And they climbed.
Two men.
Against an outpost.
Madness.
Unless the Lord is involved.
Steel clashed.
The first twenty Philistines fell.
Panic spread through the camp.
Then something only God could do happened.
The ground shook.
The army trembled.
Confusion exploded among the Philistines.
What began with two men became a divine rout.
Because God stepped into the “perhaps.”
Listen carefully.
Faith is not reckless bravado.
Faith is moving because you know God is able, even when you don’t know if He will act the way you hope.
Jonathan’s faith did not demand a miracle.
It trusted God enough to risk obedience.
Some of you are standing at your own cliff today.

A calling that terrifies you.
A ministry that feels impossible.
A battle against sin that looks unwinnable.
You’re waiting for perfect certainty.
But sometimes heaven whispers only one word:
Perhaps.
And that’s enough.
Because the power was never in Jonathan.
The power was in the Lord who saves “by many or by few.”
But the greatest battle was still ahead.
Centuries later, another Son of Israel walked toward a hill.

No army.
No sword.
Just wood on His back.
At the cross, Jesus faced a far greater enemy—sin, death, and hell itself.
And where we deserved defeat, He secured victory.
Three days later the stone rolled away.
Not “perhaps.”
It is finished.
So today you can move with courage.
Not because outcomes are guaranteed.
But because the God who raised Jesus from the dead is still able to act.
Take the step.
Climb the cliff.
Trust the Lord.
Even if your prayer begins with a trembling whisper:
“Perhaps the Lord will act.”
And sometimes…
that’s exactly where miracles begin.
🔥 We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE WASN’T EVEN INVITED.
paragraphs: HE WASN’T EVEN INVITED.

Not to the sacrifice.
Not to the lineup.
Not even to be considered.
Seven brothers stood tall in front of the prophet.

Strong shoulders.
Warrior posture.
The kind of men who looked like kings.
And yet… heaven stayed silent.
The old prophet Samuel had come to Bethlehem with a trembling horn of oil.
God had rejected Saul.
A new king was coming.
And Jesse proudly presented his sons one by one.
First came Eliab.
Tall. Commanding. Royal-looking.
Samuel’s heart whispered, “Surely this is the Lord’s anointed.”
But heaven interrupted.

“Do not consider his appearance or his height…
The Lord does not look at the things people look at.
People look at the outward appearance,
but the Lord looks at the heart.”
— Book of 1 Samuel 16:7

One brother.
Two brothers.
Three.
Seven passed.
Seven rejections.
The oil in Samuel’s horn remained still.
No king.
Samuel frowned.
“Are these all your sons?”
Jesse hesitated.
“Well… there is the youngest.”
The one nobody called.
The one nobody expected.
The one in the fields.
Out there, beyond the house, a boy wrestled with wind and wilderness.
His name was David.

Sun-browned skin.
Dust on his feet.
A shepherd’s sling hanging from his belt.
No crown.
Just sheep.
But the quiet fields had been training him for a throne.

Loneliness had shaped his prayers.
Danger had sharpened his courage.
Hidden obedience had shaped his heart.
God was watching the whole time.
“Bring him,” Samuel said.
And when the shepherd boy walked in—
Something shifted.
The Spirit spoke.

“Rise and anoint him; this is the one.”
— **Book of 1 Samuel 16:12
Oil poured down David’s head.
Not because he looked like a king.
But because God saw a heart after His own.
And from that moment, the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him.
The forgotten boy became the chosen king.
Listen carefully, friend.
Heaven’s invitation does not depend on human recognition.
Some of you feel like David right now.

Overlooked.
Left out.
Uninvited.
Others are standing in the spotlight while you’re still in the field.
But God sees fields.
God sees hidden faithfulness.
God sees the prayers whispered when nobody is clapping.

And when God calls your name—
no door closed by man can stop the oil of heaven.
But here is the deeper truth.
David points us to a greater King.
Another man born in Bethlehem.
Another one people underestimated.
Another one rejected by men but chosen by God.
His name is Jesus Christ.
The world crowned Him with thorns.
But God crowned Him with glory through the cross.

And through His death and resurrection, the forgotten, the sinful, the rejected—
can be forgiven and made new.
That is the Gospel.
Not the impressive.
The redeemed.
If you feel unseen tonight…
Stay faithful in the field.
Because sometimes the greatest anointing in history begins with a boy…
who wasn’t even invited.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE STARTED STRONG.
paragraphs: HE STARTED STRONG.

One step out of the boat.
Wind screaming.
Waves clawing at his knees.

And for a moment—
he was doing the impossible.

Open loop? Here it is:
How do you go from walking on water…
to choking on it?
Let’s talk about Gospel of Matthew 14:22–33.
The storm wasn’t gentle. It was violent. The Sea of Galilee can turn from glass to chaos in minutes. The disciples were seasoned fishermen—and still afraid.
Then they saw Him.
A figure on the water.
They thought it was a ghost.
But it was Jesus.
And Peter—oh Peter—did what most of us post about but rarely practice.
He said, “Lord, if it’s You, command me to come.”
That’s bold faith.
And Jesus answered with one word:
“Come.”

No life jacket.
No safety net.
Just a voice.
Peter swung his legs over the boat. Wet wood under his toes. Wind tearing at his robe. Heart pounding against his ribs.
And he walked.
On water.
Don’t miss that. Before he sank, he walked. He experienced supernatural obedience.
But here’s the turn.
“When he saw the wind, he was afraid…”
He shifted his focus.

Eyes off Christ.
Eyes on chaos.
And immediately—he began to sink.

Not when he stepped out.
Not when the storm hit.
When he looked away.
That’s us.

We start strong.
New year devotion streak.
Bold prayer.
Clean break from that secret sin.
Then the wind picks up. Bills stack. Temptation whispers. Old habits knock.
And fear floods the lungs.
But here’s the Gospel pivot.
Peter didn’t drown in silence.
He cried, “Lord, save me!”
Three words.

No theology degree.
No polished prayer.
Just desperation.
And the text says immediately Jesus reached out His hand.
Immediately.

Not after a lecture.
Not after shame.
Immediately.

Some scholars interpret this moment as a rebuke of “little faith.” Others see it as training—Jesus stretching Peter’s trust beyond the boat. But both agree on this: Peter was saved by Jesus’ grip, not by his balance.
Hear me.

You are not sustained by how strong you start.
You are sustained by Who holds you when you falter.

Peter sank because he feared.
We sink because of sin.
And sin is deeper than water. It separates us from a holy God. No human effort can walk across that gap.
That’s why Jesus didn’t just stretch out His hand on the sea.
He stretched out His hands on a cross.

At Gospel of Matthew 14, He saves a drowning disciple.
At Calvary, He saves a drowning world.

The storm didn’t disqualify Peter.
The sinking didn’t cancel his calling.
This same Peter would preach at Pentecost. This same Peter would write letters soaked in hope. Failure was not his final chapter—Jesus was.
So if you started strong… and now you’re sinking—
Cry out.

Not eloquently.
Honestly.
“Lord, save me.”
And watch the hand of Christ cut through the wind.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: NOT KINGS. SHEPHERDS.
paragraphs: NOT KINGS. SHEPHERDS.

Not priests.
Not scholars.
Not men with crowns or influence.
Shepherds.

Men who smelled like sheep.
Night-shift laborers.
The kind of people polite society ignored.
And yet…

When heaven tore open to announce the birth of the Messiah—
God chose them.
The Night the Sky Exploded with Glory
Luke writes it simply, but the moment was thunder.
“And there were shepherds living out in the fields nearby, keeping watch over their flocks at night.” — Luke 2:8

Ordinary night.
Cold wind.
Crickets singing.
Then suddenly—
“An angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them.” — Luke 2:9

Light.
Blinding.
Holy.
These hardened field workers fell into terror.
But heaven spoke the words every sinner longs to hear:
“Do not be afraid. I bring you good news that will cause great joy for all the people.” — Luke 2:10
Then the announcement that split history:
“Today in the town of David a Savior has been born to you; he is the Messiah, the Lord.” — Luke 2:11
To you.

Not to Caesar.
Not to Herod.
Not to the powerful.
To shepherds.
Why Shepherds?
Because God loves to shame human pride.

Kings expected the Messiah.
Religious elites debated the Messiah.

But heaven bypassed the palace…
and went straight to the pasture.

Shepherds were rough men.
Dusty. Poor. Often distrusted.
Yet they were the first humans invited to see the Lamb of God.
Do you see the poetry?
Shepherds… meeting the True Shepherd.
Then the Sky Opened
One angel spoke.
Then heaven could not stay quiet.
“Suddenly a great company of the heavenly host appeared… praising God.” — Luke 2:13
The night field became a cathedral.
“Glory to God in the highest heaven, and on earth peace to those on whom his favor rests.” — Luke 2:14
Not silence.
Singing.
The birth of Jesus was so world-shaking that heaven itself broke into worship.
The Shepherds Ran

No debate.
No committee meeting.
“Let’s go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened.” — Luke 2:15
They ran through the dark hills.
And there He was.
Not in a palace.

A feeding trough.
A crying infant.
The Savior of the world wrapped in cloth.
The Gospel Hidden in the Field
God didn’t send angels to kings first.
He sent them to sinners who knew they were small.
That’s the doorway to Christ.

Not pride.
Not status.
Not religious achievement.
Just this confession:
“Lord… I need a Savior.”
And that’s exactly who Jesus came for.
“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” — Luke 19:10
Here’s the question the shepherds leave us:
Will you stay in the field…
or will you go see Jesus?
Because the invitation of Christmas is still echoing across the centuries:
A Savior has been born… for you.
Run to Him.
✝️ We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE WAS ANGRY.
paragraphs: HE WAS ANGRY.

Not tired.
Not confused.
Angry.
And that one moment of anger cost Moses the Promised Land.
Let that sink in.

Forty years of leadership pressure.
Forty years of complaints.
Forty years of people saying:
“Why did you bring us here to die?”
Now it’s Numbers 20.

No water.
Again.
The crowd gathers. Voices rising. Accusations flying.
“You and Aaron brought us into this wilderness to kill us!”
Imagine the weight on Moses’ chest.
A leader carrying the thirst, fear, and rebellion of an entire nation.
God gives a simple instruction:
“Speak to the rock.”

Not shout.
Not strike.
Not perform.
Just speak.
Because the miracle wasn’t about Moses’ strength.
It was about God’s holiness.
But anger does something dangerous to leaders.
It distorts obedience.
Moses walks before the people, staff in hand, voice shaking.
“Listen, you rebels… must we bring you water from this rock?”
Then—
CRACK.
He strikes the rock.
CRACK.
Again.
Water gushes out.
The people drink.
The miracle still happens.
But heaven goes quiet.
Then comes one of the most heartbreaking lines in Scripture.
Because you did not trust Me enough to honor Me as holy before Israel…
you will not bring this community into the land.
(Numbers 20:12)
Think about it.

The man who faced Pharaoh.
The man who split the Red Sea.
The man who spoke with God face to face.
Stopped…
right at the border.
Why?
Because leadership anger can turn God’s glory into a personal performance.
And God will not share His glory.
But here is the Gospel thread hidden in the rock.
In 1 Corinthians 10:4, Paul reveals something stunning:
“The Rock was Christ.”
The rock in the wilderness was a shadow.
A preview.
Jesus would be the true Rock struck for our salvation.
But notice the difference.
The rock in Numbers was struck once.
After that, it was only to be spoken to.
Because Christ would be struck once for all.
Hebrews 10:10 says Jesus’ sacrifice happened once for all time.
No more striking.
Only coming.
Only asking.
Only grace.
Maybe you’re a leader under pressure.

A parent.
A pastor.
A manager.
A servant carrying too many voices in your ear.
And lately…
anger has been closer than prayer.
Listen carefully.
Your worst moment does not cancel God’s redemption.
Yes, Moses missed the Promised Land.
But in Matthew 17, something stunning happens.
On the Mount of Transfiguration, standing beside Jesus in glory…
is Moses.
The man who struck the rock…
standing with the Rock Himself.
Grace writes the final chapter.
So today—
Before anger swings the staff again…
Speak to the Rock.
Call on Christ.
Because the water still flows.
And mercy is still deeper than your worst moment.
Someone you know is one moment away from striking the rock.
And they need to remember:
Jesus is still the Rock.
And His grace still flows.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I DON’T KNOW HIM.”
paragraphs: “I DON’T KNOW HIM.”

Three words.
Sharp as a knife.
Spoken beside a fire that was warming the hands of a man whose heart was freezing.
Simon Peter — the loudest voice of loyalty hours earlier — now whispers denial in the dark.
And heaven heard it.
The courtyard smelled like smoke and fear.

The torches flickered.
Soldiers laughed somewhere in the shadows.
The trial of Jesus Christ was unfolding inside the house of Caiaphas.
Outside?
A fisherman was fighting a different trial.
Fear.
Just hours earlier, Peter had made a promise recorded in Gospel of Luke 22.
“Lord, I am ready to go with you to prison and to death.”
Bold words.
But Jesus had already spoken the prophecy:
“Before the rooster crows today, you will deny three times that you know me.”
Peter probably thought, Impossible.
Then the questions started.
A servant girl squinted through the firelight.
“You were with Him.”
Peter’s pulse spiked.
“Woman… I don’t know Him.”
One denial.
Another voice pressed closer.
“You are one of them.”
Peter’s throat tightened.
“Man, I am not!”
Two denials.
An hour passed.
A man insisted, pointing.
“Surely this fellow was with Him!”
Peter snapped back:
“I DON’T KNOW WHAT YOU’RE TALKING ABOUT!”
Three denials.
And then—
A sound cut through the cold air.
A rooster crowed.
At that moment, Jesus Christ turned and looked at Peter.
Not anger.
Not disgust.
A look that pierced deeper than judgment.
Luke writes something devastating:
Peter remembered.
The prophecy.
The warning.
The love.
And the rock broke.
Scripture says:
“He went outside and wept bitterly.”
Not polite tears.
Not a quiet sniffle.
Bitter weeping.
The sound of a heart collapsing under the weight of its own failure.
Listen carefully.
Peter did not just make a mistake.
He denied the One he swore to die for.

Publicly.
Repeatedly.
Loudly.
And yet…
This is not the end of Peter’s story.
Because the Gospel does something scandalous with failure.
After the resurrection, on another shoreline fire, Jesus Christ will ask Peter three times:
“Do you love Me?”

Three denials.
Three restorations.
Grace does not erase the past.
It redeems it.

The man who said, “I don’t know Him”…
will later stand in Jerusalem and preach Christ so boldly that thousands believe.
That is the mercy of the cross.
Maybe you know this moment.
You didn’t deny Jesus with words.

But with silence.
With compromise.
With secret sin.
You warmed your hands at the wrong fire.
So did Peter.
And Jesus still restored him.
Hear this clearly:
Failure is not final when Christ is involved.

The same Savior Peter denied
went to the cross to forgive deniers like us.
That is the Gospel.

Sin exposed.
Grace extended.
Redemption secured by the blood of Jesus.
If Peter’s story proves anything, it’s this:
Your worst moment does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BIRDS BROUGHT FOOD.
paragraphs: BIRDS BROUGHT FOOD.

Not angels.
Not a king.
Not a miracle basket dropped from heaven.
Birds.

In 1 Kings 17, Elijah was hiding by the brook Cherith because the land was under judgment. Drought. Fear. Silence. And right there—when everything looked dry, dangerous, and uncertain—God commanded ravens to feed His servant.
Pause there.
Ravens were not the kind of creatures you would expect to carry provision. They were wild. Unclean. Unpredictable.
But when God decides to provide, He does not need your preferred method.

He can send help through a place you never planned for.
Through a person you never noticed.
Through a door that did not even exist yesterday.
That is the scandal of God’s provision: He is not limited by what makes sense to us.

Elijah did not survive because the economy improved.
He did not survive because the weather changed.
He survived because the word of the Lord held him up.

Morning and evening, the ravens came.
Again and again, the brook flowed.
Again and again, God proved this truth:

What God orders, He covers.
Where God guides, He provides.
And maybe that is where you are right now.

Dry season.
Tight budget.
Heavy heart.
No clear answers.
You have been waiting for God to provide in one specific way. But heaven is not nervous. The Lord is not pacing. He is not short on ideas.
He can use ravens.

He can use the unlikely.
He can use the overlooked.
He can use what religion would dismiss and what logic would reject—so long as His purpose stands.
But the deeper miracle in 1 Kings 17 is not just food in Elijah’s hands.
It is this: God Himself had not forgotten him.
That is the Gospel heartbeat.
Because our greatest hunger was never merely financial, emotional, or physical. Our deepest need was reconciliation with God. And the Father did not send ravens for that—He sent His Son.

Jesus is the better provision.
Better than bread by a brook.
Better than survival in a famine.
Better than temporary relief.

At the cross, Christ carried what our sin deserved. In His resurrection, He opened the storehouse of grace for all who repent and believe. So now we do not just ask, “Will God feed me?” We rest in the greater promise: in Christ, God has already moved toward me with mercy.
So lift your eyes.

The same God who fed Elijah in secret still knows how to sustain His people today.
And the same Savior who died for sinners still welcomes the weary, the ashamed, and the afraid.

Your brook may be small.
Your season may be hard.
But your God is still creative.

Birds brought food.
And grace still comes from places only God could arrange.

Come back to Jesus.
Trust His Word.
Wait without panic.
Obey without fear.
Because when God speaks life over His children, even ravens become servants of mercy.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE HERO WAS THE OUTSIDER.
paragraphs: THE HERO WAS THE OUTSIDER.

Not the priest.
Not the worship leader.
Not the theologian with clean hands and cleaner reputation.
The hero… was the one they hated.
And Jesus did that on purpose.
A lawyer stood up in Gospel of Luke 10 and asked a holy question with an unholy motive:
“Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”

He knew the Law.
He quoted it perfectly.
“Love the Lord your God… and your neighbor as yourself.”
But then he tightened the trap:
“And who is my neighbor?”

Translation?
Who can I safely ignore and still feel righteous?
Watch what Jesus does.
He tells a story.
A man is walking the dangerous road from Jerusalem to Jericho. Robbed. Stripped. Beaten. Left half-dead.

Blood in the dust.
Breath barely moving.
No applause. No audience.
A priest comes.
He sees him.
Crosses the road.
A Levite comes.
He looks.
Keeps walking.

Religion had eyes.
But no mercy.
Then Jesus drops the scandal.
“A Samaritan came where he was…”

And if you felt the tension in that room — you’d understand. Jews and Samaritans despised each other. Generations of bitterness. The Samaritan was the theological mutt. The outsider. The one you don’t invite to dinner.
And yet…
He stops.
He kneels.
He touches the broken skin.

Oil.
Wine.
Bandages.
He lifts the man’s limp body onto his own animal. Pays for his recovery. Promises to return.

No hashtag.
No spotlight.
Just mercy.
Here’s the open wound in this story:

The religious experts knew the Bible…
But the outsider lived it.
And now the twist.
Jesus doesn’t say, “Be nicer.”
He asks, “Which one proved to be a neighbor?”
The lawyer answers quietly, “The one who showed mercy.”
And Jesus says, “Go and do likewise.”
Now lean in.
You and I are not first the Samaritan in this story.
We are the man in the ditch.

Sin robbed us.
Stripped us.
Left us spiritually dying on the roadside.

Religion walked by.
Good intentions passed us.
But then Jesus came.

The true Outsider.
Rejected. Despised. (Isaiah 53)
He didn’t cross the road.
He crossed heaven.

He bound our wounds at the cross.
Paid our debt in full.
Promised to return.

Some scholars interpret this parable purely as an ethical teaching about neighbor-love. And it absolutely calls us to radical mercy. But the greater arc of Scripture shows us something deeper: every command flows from redemption already given.
We love because He first loved us.
So yes — go and do likewise.

Cross the street.
Interrupt your schedule.
Touch what others avoid.
But don’t do it to earn eternal life.
Do it because the Outsider saved you.
So here’s the question that will start a comment war in the best way:
If Jesus told this story today…
Who would be the Samaritan?

The immigrant?
The addict?
The political enemy?
The person your church quietly avoids?
Let’s talk.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.”
paragraphs: “FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.”

The nails were still tearing His flesh…
And mercy was already flowing.

Not after the pain.
Not when the soldiers apologized.
Not when the crowd changed their minds.
Right there.

In the middle of the blood.
In the middle of the mockery.
In the middle of the cross.
“Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” — Luke 23:34
This is the scandal of grace.

The men who hammered the spikes into His wrists…
The soldiers gambling for His clothes…
The leaders sneering, “He saved others; let Him save Himself.”
Jesus did not answer with fire.
He answered with forgiveness.
Pause and feel the weight of that moment.

Every breath on the cross was torture.
Every word cost Him oxygen.
Every sentence was agony.
And the first recorded sentence from His bleeding lips was not judgment.
It was mercy.
Not “Father, destroy them.”
But:
“Father, forgive them.”
Why?
Because the cross was not just an execution.
It was a rescue mission.

The same people shouting for His death…
were the very people He came to save.
And here is the terrifying truth.
It was not only their sin that nailed Him there.
It was ours.

Our pride.
Our hidden lust.
Our lies.
Our anger.
Our quiet rebellion against God.
The cross exposes us.
But it also saves us.
Because while humanity was doing its worst…
Jesus was doing His best.

He was absorbing the punishment sin deserved.
He was standing in the place of the guilty.
He was opening the door of mercy.

Some scholars interpret that Jesus’ prayer may have been specifically for those who did not fully understand the magnitude of what they were doing. But Luke’s Gospel shows something even greater: forgiveness flowing outward, reaching anyone who will turn to Him.
Just look at what happens next in Luke 23.
A criminal hanging beside Him says:
“Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.”
And Jesus answers:
“Today you will be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43)
Do you see it?
The cross becomes the place where a dying criminal becomes a forgiven man.
Because Jesus was not only forgiving His killers.
He was purchasing forgiveness for the world.
For you.
For me.
For anyone willing to turn and trust Him.

No sin too dirty.
No past too heavy.
No shame too deep.
The cross says:
Mercy is still possible.
Right now.

If your heart is heavy today…
If guilt whispers that you are too far gone…
Listen again to the voice from the cross.
“Father, forgive them.”
That prayer is still echoing through history.
And the invitation still stands.

Turn to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust the One who bled for you.
Because the cross proves one unstoppable truth:
God’s mercy is louder than our worst mistakes.
And Jesus is still saving sinners.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE HAD HOURS LEFT.
paragraphs: HE HAD HOURS LEFT.

Not years.
Not months.
Hours.

A man nailed to wood.
Lungs collapsing.
Blood drying in the Jerusalem sun.
And eternity breathing down his neck.
You know his name?
You don’t.
Because shame tried to erase it.
⚔️ The Scene — Gospel of Luke 23:39–43

Two criminals.
One Savior.
One thief spits venom.
“Are You not the Christ? Save Yourself and us!”

Pain made him sarcastic.
Death made him bitter.

But the other thief…
Something shifted.
He rebukes his partner in crime:
“We are receiving the due reward of our deeds… but this Man has done nothing wrong.”
Feel that.

No excuses.
No blame-shifting.
No self-justification.
Just raw confession.
“We deserve this.”
Brother, that is the doorway to mercy.
The Open Loop
Why would a dying criminal defend Jesus?

What did he see…
that the religious leaders missed?
The Pivot
He turns his head — as far as nails will allow — and whispers:
“Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.”

Not “get me down.”
Not “prove Yourself.”
Just… remember me.

That’s faith stripped of pride.
Faith with no bargaining chip.
Faith when there is no future left to fix your past.
And Jesus answers with words that explode through history:
“Truly, I say to you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.”
Today.

No probation.
No religious performance.
No delayed processing.
Grace outran the clock.
🔥 What This Means (Don’t Miss This)
He couldn’t:
Be baptized.
Return stolen goods.
Join a synagogue.
Serve in ministry.
Live a “better life.”
He had nothing to offer.

Except repentance.
And trust.
Some scholars interpret this passage as a powerful demonstration that salvation is by grace through faith apart from works — consistent with the whole testimony of Scripture.
And right there — nailed between justice and mercy — we see the Gospel.

Sin? Real.
Judgment? Just.
Grace? Greater.

Jesus did not excuse his crime.
He absorbed his condemnation.

That cross wasn’t symbolic.
It was substitution.
Christ dying for sinners.

For thieves.
For rebels.
For secret addicts.
For religious pretenders.
For you.
The Tension You Feel Right Now
You think you’ve gone too far.

Too dirty.
Too compromised.
Too late.
But hear me as a shepherd of souls:

If mercy reached a man with minutes left,
what makes you think it can’t reach you with breath still in your lungs?
Late mercy still saves.
But don’t gamble on last-minute repentance.
He had hours left.
You don’t know if you do.
Look at the Two Crosses Beside Jesus

Same proximity.
Different response.

One died mocking the Savior.
One died trusting Him.

Both broken.
Only one redeemed.
The difference?

Repentance.
Faith.
Christ.
Jesus is not waiting for your cleanup.
He is waiting for your surrender.
Turn your head toward Him.
Whisper His name.
“Remember me.”
And the Savior who forgave a dying thief will forgive you.
Today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHO SINNED?
paragraphs: WHO SINNED?
That was the question echoing in the dust.

A man sat beside the road—
eyes open…
but never seeing.

Born blind.
Born into whispers.
Born into blame.
People didn’t see a man.
They saw a theological problem.

“Rabbi,” the disciples asked Jesus,
“who sinned—this man or his parents—that he was born blind?”
— Gospel of John 9:2
Translation:
Someone must be guilty.

Because suffering makes us uncomfortable.
We want a culprit.

A mistake.
A curse.
A scandal.
But Jesus flipped the question.
Not Who sinned?
But What if God is about to move?

“Neither this man nor his parents sinned,” Jesus said,
“but this happened so that the works of God might be displayed in him.”
— Gospel of John 9:3
Pause there.
The man’s blindness was not the final sentence.
It was the stage.
Then Jesus did something strange.
He spat on the ground.

Mud.
Dust.
Clay in His hands.
The same hands that once formed Adam from the earth.
Jesus pressed the mud onto blind eyes.
“Go wash in the Pool of Siloam.”
The man obeyed.
And for the first time in his life—
Light.

Colors.
Faces.
Sky.
The world exploded into sight.
But here’s the twist nobody expected.
The miracle didn’t end the controversy.
It started one.
The religious leaders interrogated him.
“How were your eyes opened?”
They weren’t celebrating the miracle.
They were defending their system.

And the healed man—
once a silent beggar—
became a bold witness.

“I was blind,” he said.
“Now I see.”
That sentence has echoed through centuries.
Because it’s more than eyesight.
It’s the Gospel.
Every one of us starts the same way.
Not physically blind.
But spiritually.
The Bible says sin darkens the heart.

We stumble through life guessing…
groping…
blaming…
Until Jesus touches our eyes.
Christ is not just a teacher.
He is the Light of the World.
That’s exactly what Jesus said earlier in the same chapter.

“I am the light of the world.”
— Gospel of John 9:5
When His light enters your life, something radical happens.
You begin to see:

• Your sin clearly
• God’s holiness clearly
• And the cross of Christ clearly
Because the greatest blindness is not in the eyes.
It’s in the heart.
And the greatest miracle is not restored vision.
It’s redemption.
Jesus went to the cross so blind sinners like us could finally see.

Forgiven.
Washed.
Made new.
Friend, maybe people have labeled you.

Your past.
Your mistakes.
Your family.

Maybe the world keeps asking,
“Who sinned?”
But Jesus asks a different question:
“Do you want to see?”
And if you come to Him—
Really come—
Your story can become the same as that once-blind man.
“I was blind.
But now I see.”
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE LEFT THE TABLE.
paragraphs: HE LEFT THE TABLE.

Coins still clinked.
Ink still wet on the ledger.
Power still in his pocket.
And then—
Two words split his world.
“Follow Me.”
In Gospel of Matthew 9, a man named Matthew is sitting at a tax booth. Not just working. Thriving.

Tax collectors weren’t misunderstood introverts.
They were collaborators.
Agents of Rome.
Profiting off their own people.

Dirty money.
Clean robes.
Empty soul.
And Jesus walks straight to the table.

No debate.
No lecture.
No résumé review.
Just this:
“Follow Me.”
Pause there.
Why Matthew?

Why not a synagogue leader?
Why not a polished rabbi-in-training?

Because grace doesn’t knock on the door of the worthy.
It invades the booth of the compromised.

Some scholars interpret Matthew’s immediate response as a sign that Jesus had prior interactions with him. Maybe.
But Scripture says this clearly:
“He rose and followed Him.” (Matthew 9:9)
He rose.

From comfort.
From income.
From identity.
He left the table.
And here’s the scandal.

Jesus doesn’t just call Matthew.
He goes to Matthew’s house.
Sits at Matthew’s table.
Eats with Matthew’s friends.

Tax collectors.
Sinners.
Outcasts.

Religious leaders whisper,
“Why does your Teacher eat with them?”
Because mercy tastes better than self-righteousness.

Jesus answers:
“I desire mercy, not sacrifice… For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” (Matthew 9:13)
That’s the Gospel in one sentence.

Not the polished.
Not the impressive.
Sinners.
You.
Me.
Let me speak to the one gripping your own “table” right now.

The relationship that feeds your ego.
The habit that funds your comfort.
The identity built on compromise.
Following Jesus will disrupt you.
It will cost you.
But what you leave is nothing compared to Who you gain.

Matthew left coins.
He gained Christ.

He left a booth.
He received a calling.

He left a corrupt ledger.
He wrote a Gospel.
From scandal to Scripture.
From greed to grace.
Here’s the open loop I promised you:
Matthew’s name means “Gift of God.”
The man who once extracted money became a gift to the Church.
That’s what Jesus does.

He doesn’t just forgive your past.
He repurposes it.
He rewrites it.
He redeems it.
Listen to me carefully.
Jesus is still walking past tables today.
Still locking eyes.
Still speaking.
“Follow Me.”

Not when you clean up.
Not when you feel worthy.
Now.

Repent.
Rise.
Release the table.
And follow.

Because the One calling you is on His way to a cross—
where He will leave heaven’s glory,
stretch out His hands,
and pay your debt in full.
That’s the greater exchange.

Your sin.
For His righteousness.

Your shame.
For His name.

And if He can turn a tax collector into an evangelist—
He can turn your mess into a message.
Come.
Leave the table.
Follow the Savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN THESE BONES LIVE?
paragraphs: CAN THESE BONES LIVE?
That wasn’t a poetic question.
It was a confrontation.

The valley was not quiet. It was loud with silence.
Sun-bleached skulls. Rib cages split open. Femurs scattered like abandoned swords.
No pulse.
No breath.
No future.
And God walks His prophet right into it.
In Book of Ezekiel 37, the Spirit sets Ezekiel down in the middle of death and asks one question:
“Son of man… can these bones live?”
Pause.

God already knew the answer.
The question wasn’t for information.
It was for revelation.
Ezekiel looks at irreversible loss… and answers carefully:
“O Lord GOD, You know.”

That’s faith under pressure. Not hype. Not denial.
Just surrender.
Let me talk to you straight.
Some of you are standing in a valley right now.

A marriage that feels picked clean.
A calling that dried up.
A prayer that’s been buried so long you stopped visiting the grave.

Dry.
Very dry.
And heaven is asking you the same question.
Can these bones live?
Here’s the tension.

God doesn’t tell Ezekiel to organize the bones.
He doesn’t say, “Strategize. Improve. Network.”
He says:
“Prophesy.”
Speak My Word into what looks impossible.
When Ezekiel obeys, something wild happens.
A rattling.

Bone to bone.
Sinew wrapping structure.
Flesh covering framework.
Skin sealing the miracle.
But they were still not alive.
Structure without Spirit is still a corpse.
Then God commands him again:
“Prophesy to the breath.”
The Hebrew word there is ruach — wind, breath, Spirit.
And when the breath enters?

They stand up.
An exceedingly great army.
From graveyard to army in one chapter.

That’s not self-help.
That’s resurrection power.
Some scholars interpret this vision as primarily about Israel’s national restoration from exile. And yes — historically, that is true. God was promising to bring His people back from Babylon.
But don’t miss the greater echo.
This is the Gospel in shadow form.
Because centuries later, another Son of Man would stand in a valley of death.
His own.
And on the third day, breath would re-enter a pierced body.
Jesus Christ walked out of His grave so your dry bones wouldn’t stay dry.
The same Spirit that raised Christ from the dead is the same Spirit that steps into your valley.
Not to decorate it.
To resurrect it.
What feels dead in your life?

Your purity?
Your courage?
Your first love for God?
Your dream to serve Him?
Bring it into the valley. Don’t hide it.
Then do what Ezekiel did.
Open your mouth.

Speak God’s Word over what shame tried to silence.
Invite the Spirit into what fear declared finished.

Because if Jesus conquered the grave,
your situation is not beyond redemption.

Not the addiction.
Not the betrayal.
Not the wasted years.
What valley are you standing in?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: I’M NOT GOOD ENOUGH.
paragraphs: I’M NOT GOOD ENOUGH.
The deliverer of Israel had a speech issue.
You think your weakness disqualifies you?
Let me take you to a desert.

Sand in the wind.
A bush on fire — but not burning.
And a shepherd with trembling lips.
In Book of Exodus 4, Moses finally says what he’s been thinking all along:
“Lord… I’m not eloquent. I am slow of speech and tongue.”
Translation?

I can’t do this.
I’m not built for this.
Send someone else.

The man who would stand before Pharaoh…
The man who would stretch out his hand over the Red Sea…
The man whose face would shine with glory…
He stuttered.
Or at least he believed he did.
And here’s the open wound we don’t like to touch:

God had already called him.
Already chosen him.
Already promised, “I will be with you.”
But Moses was still arguing.
Why?
Because insecurity feels safer than obedience.
Listen carefully.

Moses wasn’t just doubting his speech.
He was doubting the One who made his mouth.
And then God answers with thunder wrapped in tenderness:
“Who made man’s mouth? … Is it not I, the Lord?”
Feel that.

Your weakness?
Not a surprise to God.
Not an oversight.
Not a flaw in His design.
It’s the stage.

We love polished leaders.
God loves surrendered ones.
Here’s the tension — and don’t miss this.

Moses’ insecurity didn’t disqualify him.
But his refusal almost did.
“Please send someone else.”

That wasn’t humility anymore.
That was resistance.
Some scholars interpret Moses’ “slow of speech” as a literal speech impediment. Others see it as lack of confidence or rhetorical training. Either way, the point stands:

God knew.
And He still called him.
Let me come close.
What excuse are you hiding behind?

“I’m too broken.”
“I’m not educated.”
“I failed before.”
“I don’t speak well.”
“I’m not spiritual enough.”

Beloved… that’s not humility.
That’s fear dressed in logic.

The Gospel doesn’t begin with your adequacy.
It begins with your surrender.

Moses needed Aaron.
Yes.
But you know what Moses needed more?
Presence.
And that’s what you and I have in fullness through Jesus Christ.

Where Moses had a staff,
we have a cross.

Where Moses had a burning bush,
we have an empty tomb.
The greater Deliverer has already come.

Gospel of Matthew 28:20 —
“I am with you always.”

Same promise.
Greater covenant.

Your insecurity is loud.
But Christ is louder.

Your weakness is real.
But His grace is stronger.
You are not good enough.
And that’s the point.
Because the story was never about your strength.
It’s about a holy God who uses trembling vessels to display unstoppable glory.
Stop negotiating with your calling.

Repent of hiding.
Lay down the excuse.
Say yes — even with shaking hands.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Moses Argues With God
paragraphs: Moses Argues With God
(Exodus 4)
Fire danced in the desert.

Not wildfire.
Not lightning.
Not a mirage bending in the heat.

A bush… burning.
But not consumed.
And standing barefoot before that holy flame was a fugitive shepherd with forty years of failure hanging on his shoulders.
His name was Moses.
God had just handed him the assignment of a lifetime:

“Go back to Egypt.
Face Pharaoh.
Lead My people out of slavery.”

A nation’s deliverance…
resting on the shoulders of a man who once ran for his life.
And Moses did something that many of us secretly do when God calls.
He argued.
First excuse.

“What if they don’t believe me?”
(Exodus 4:1)
God answers with miracles in Moses’ own hands — a staff becoming a serpent, a hand turning leprous then clean.
But Moses isn’t done.
Second excuse.

“I’m not eloquent.”
(Exodus 4:10)
In other words:

“I’m not the speaking type.”
“I’m awkward.”
“I don’t have the voice.”
God replies with thunderous tenderness:

“Who made man’s mouth? … Is it not I, the Lord?”
(Exodus 4:11)
The Creator of vocal cords does not need perfect speakers.
He needs surrendered hearts.
Then Moses finally says the thing he was trying to say all along.
The raw confession.
The desperate plea.

“Please, Lord… send someone else.”
(Exodus 4:13)
There it is.
Not inability.
Reluctance.
Fear.
And here is the mystery of grace.
God does not cancel Moses.

He corrects him…
provides Aaron as help…
and still sends him.
The mission stands.
Because God's calling is not based on your confidence.
It is based on His covenant.
Listen carefully, friend.
Moses felt unqualified.
Yet through that trembling shepherd, God would split a sea, shake an empire, and birth a nation.
The greatest leaders in Scripture did not start with confidence.
They started with obedience.
But the story whispers something even deeper.
Moses needed a spokesman.
Centuries later, another Deliverer would come who needed none.
Jesus Christ — the greater Moses — would stand before rulers, speak with perfect authority, and deliver His people not from Pharaoh…
…but from sin and death.

At the cross, the Son of God did not say,
“Send someone else.”
He said:
“Father… Your will be done.”

And because He obeyed,
our failure can be forgiven.
Our hesitation can become surrender.
Our fear can become calling.
So if God is stirring something in your heart right now…

A ministry.
A step of faith.
A calling that terrifies you.
Remember this:
God does not call the qualified.
He qualifies the called.

Engagement Question:
Have you ever felt unqualified for something God asked you to do?
Tell your story below. Someone may need the courage hidden inside it.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ALMOST OBEDIENCE.
paragraphs: ALMOST OBEDIENCE.

Two words.
One ruined crown.
Lean in.

Because 1 Samuel 15 is not just Saul’s story.
It’s ours.
God gave King Saul a clear command through Samuel:

Destroy Amalek.
All of it.
No leftovers.
No trophies.
No mercy masquerading as wisdom.
(1 Samuel 15:3)
It was severe. It was uncomfortable. It was absolute.
And Saul… obeyed.
Almost.

He crushed the Amalekite army.
He won the battle.
He looked powerful. Victorious. Anointed.

But he spared King Agag.
And he kept the best sheep.
Why?
Because partial obedience still lets you keep something.

Something shiny.
Something profitable.
Something that feeds your image.
Saul built a monument to himself (v.12).
Let that sink in.

Before he built an altar to God—
he built a statue for Saul.
When Samuel confronted him, Saul said the most dangerous sentence in the Bible:
“I have obeyed the Lord.”
He believed it.
That’s the terror.
He renamed rebellion as righteousness.

He blamed the people.
He spiritualized the compromise.
“The sheep? Oh… sacrifices for the Lord!”

Religious language.
Rotten heart.
And then Samuel thundered the line that splits the soul:
“To obey is better than sacrifice.” (1 Samuel 15:22)
Almost obedience is disobedience.
Almost surrender is rebellion in slow motion.
Here’s the part we don’t preach enough:
God rejected Saul as king.

Not for murder.
Not for immorality.
But for selective obedience.

The Spirit departed.
The crown slipped.
The insecurity began to rot him from the inside.
Secret compromise always becomes public collapse.
But pause.

Before you close the app and feel condemned—
remember this:
Saul’s story ends in tragedy.
Yours doesn’t have to.

Because where Saul lost a kingdom through disobedience,
Jesus won an eternal kingdom through perfect obedience.

Where Saul spared what God said destroy,
Jesus destroyed what we could never defeat—sin, death, hell.
On another hill, another King faced a hard command.
And He didn’t say “almost.”

He said,
“Not My will, but Yours be done.”

Perfect obedience.
To the point of death.
For rebels like us.
This is the Gospel.

We are not saved by our flawless obedience.
We are saved by Christ’s.

But grace does not excuse compromise.
It empowers surrender.
So let me ask you plainly—
What “Agag” are you keeping alive?
What “best sheep” are you justifying?

Delayed forgiveness?
Secret lust?
Hidden pride?
Half-truth integrity?
Almost obedience feels safe.
Until it costs you everything.

Today, don’t defend it.
Don’t rename it.
Don’t spiritualize it.
Bring it to Jesus.

Repentance is not humiliation.
It’s freedom.

The King who rejected Saul
offers mercy to you.

Bow fully.
Surrender completely.
Trust wholly.
Because Jesus doesn’t demand almost.
He deserves all.

If this cut you… good.
If this freed you… even better.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HE TRIED TO RETURN THE MONEY.”
paragraphs: “HE TRIED TO RETURN THE MONEY.”

Thirty pieces of silver.
Cold.
Heavy.
Loud in his trembling hands.
But the sound that haunted him wasn’t the coins.

It was the rooster.
The silence.
The look on Jesus’ face.
In Gospel of Matthew 27, Judas does something shocking. He confesses.
“I have sinned,” he says. “For I have betrayed innocent blood.” (Matthew 27:4)
Let that sink in.

He knew Jesus was innocent.
He knew he was guilty.
He felt regret burning through his chest like acid.
And he tried to undo it.

He ran back to the religious leaders.
Coins clutched in sweating fists.
Eyes wild.
Voice cracking.
“I don’t want this anymore.”
But religion without repentance has no mercy.
“What is that to us?” they answered. “See to it yourself.”
That’s the coldest line in the chapter.

They wanted his betrayal.
They didn’t want his brokenness.
So Judas threw the money into the temple.
The silver hit the floor like thunder.

But hear me, beloved—
throwing away the money didn’t wash away the sin.
And here’s the tragedy.

Judas had regret.
But he didn’t run to Jesus.
He ran from Him.
There is a difference between remorse and repentance.

Remorse says, “I feel bad.”
Repentance says, “Jesus, save me.”
The Greek word used for Judas’ regret implies deep anguish. Some scholars interpret it as emotional remorse rather than true repentance that turns toward God.
And that difference changes eternity.

Peter denied Jesus three times.
Judas betrayed Him with a kiss.
Both failed.

One wept and ran back to Christ.
One isolated himself in despair.

The enemy loves that space.
The space between guilt and grace.
Judas believed his sin was bigger than the Savior.
And that is the lie hell whispers to every one of us.

“Too far.”
“Too dirty.”
“Too late.”
But look at the cross rising in the same chapter.

While Judas is drowning in regret,
Jesus is walking toward crucifixion.

For betrayers.
For deniers.
For religious hypocrites.
For you.

The silver could not purchase forgiveness.
But the blood of Christ could.
Listen carefully.
If Judas had fallen at Jesus’ feet instead of collapsing under shame, the story could have been different. The cross was sufficient even for him.
That’s how powerful the Gospel is.

Sin is real.
Betrayal is real.
Consequences are real.
But grace is more real.

Regret that runs away becomes despair.
Regret that runs to Jesus becomes redemption.
So what are you holding right now?

A secret?
A compromise?
Thirty pieces of silver in another form?
Don’t just throw it down.
Turn around.
Run to the One you betrayed.
Because the same chapter that records Judas’ regret records Christ’s sacrifice.
And the cross is bigger than your worst decision.
Always.
Come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE CHOSE THE BETTER LAND.
paragraphs: HE CHOSE THE BETTER LAND.

Green fields.
Shimmering rivers.
Endless opportunity.

Short-term gain.
Long-term regret.
Brother, lean in.
In Book of Genesis 13, a quiet decision becomes a generational disaster.
Abram and Lot stand on a ridge. The land can’t hold both their flocks. Strife is rising. So Abram—father in faith—offers his nephew first choice.
Grace gave Lot the microphone.
And Lot lifted his eyes.
He saw the Jordan Valley — “well watered everywhere… like the garden of the Lord” (Genesis 13:10).
It looked like Eden.
But it was leaning toward Sodom.
The text whispers something chilling:
“Lot chose for himself…”
For himself.

Not “What honors God?”
Not “What protects my family?”
Not “What preserves righteousness?”
Just — what prospers me.
The grass was greener.
So he moved closer.
Closer.
Closer.
Verse 12 says he pitched his tents near Sodom.
Not in it.
Near it.

Compromise rarely begins with a headline sin.
It begins with proximity.

You don’t fall overnight.
You drift.

And the next chapter? War.
The next chapters? Wickedness.
By Genesis 19, Lot is inside Sodom, sitting at the gate — a civic leader in a corrupt city.

Short-term gain.
Long-term grief.

Some scholars interpret Lot as a believer whose soul was “tormented” by Sodom’s sin (see 2 Peter 2:7–8). If so, hear this: even the redeemed can live in self-inflicted misery when they prioritize prosperity over presence.
Lot got the valley.
Abram got the promise.
After Lot separated, God told Abram:
“Lift up your eyes…” (Genesis 13:14)
Notice the contrast.

Lot lifted his eyes to see land.
Abram lifted his eyes to hear God.

One chose by sight.
The other walked by faith.
And here is the scandal of grace:

Abram, the wronged one, becomes the blessed one.
Lot, the chooser, becomes the captive.
Sin always overpromises.
It sparkles like the Jordan at sunrise — cool blue waters, golden light dancing on the surface — but beneath it is a current pulling you toward Sodom.
Brother. Sister.
Where have you pitched your tent?

Near what?
Close to what?
Flirting with what?
The Gospel does not shame you. It calls you home.
Jesus Christ did not choose the “better land.” He chose the cross.

He stepped into our Sodom.
He absorbed our compromise.
He bore the fire meant for us.
On that hill called Calvary, He reversed Lot’s story.

Where we chose for ourselves,
He chose to save.

Where we drifted toward sin,
He moved toward us in mercy.
Repentance is not losing land.
It is gaining life.

Turn the tent.
Move away from Sodom.
Lift your eyes again — not to the valley, but to the Savior.
Because in Christ, even compromised believers can be restored.
This is not the end of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JUST ONE LAST MEAL.
paragraphs: JUST ONE LAST MEAL.
That’s what she said.

Not tomorrow’s meal.
Not next week’s.
The last one.

A widow in Zarephath, scraping dust from the bottom of a jar.
A handful of flour.
A few drops of oil.
Enough for one small cake.
Enough for one final goodbye.
Her plan was simple and devastating:

Cook it.
Feed her son.
Wait to die.

The famine was not just outside her door—it was inside her hope.
This was the world of First Book of Kings, chapter 17.
Drought everywhere.
No rain.
No harvest.
No rescue.

And then—
God sends a prophet.

Not to a palace.
Not to the rich.
To a starving widow.
Elijah the Prophet walks into her story and says something that sounds almost cruel:
“Do not fear… but first make me a small cake from it.” (1 Kings 17:13)
First.

Before your son eats.
Before your hunger ends.
Before your future changes.
Give.
Imagine the tension in that moment.

Her ribs showing through tired skin.
Dust clinging to her hands.
A child waiting behind her.
And God asks for faith in scarcity.

Not abundance.
Not comfort.
Scarcity.
Because heaven was about to write a different ending.
Elijah continues:
“For thus says the Lord… the jar of flour shall not be spent, and the jug of oil shall not be empty.” (1 Kings 17:14)
Now the real question arrives.

Would she trust a stranger…
with her last meal?
She did.

She baked the bread.
Placed it in Elijah’s hands.
And in that moment—
The famine met faith.
The jar did not run empty.

Morning after morning, the flour remained.
Night after night, the oil still poured.

Not overflowing abundance.
Not luxury.
Just enough.
Enough to live.
Enough to prove something eternal:
God often multiplies what we release in faith.
But the deeper Gospel whisper is even more powerful.
This widow gave her last bread to God’s prophet.
Centuries later, God would give His last and only Son for us.

Where we deserved famine of the soul,
Christ became the bread of life.
Jesus said in Gospel of John 6:35:
“Whoever comes to Me shall not hunger.”
The widow thought the story would end with death.
But God was already preparing daily mercy.
Friend, maybe your jar feels empty tonight.

Empty finances.
Empty strength.
Empty faith.
But the God who filled a widow’s jar in Zarephath is the same God who filled an empty tomb through Jesus Christ.
Scarcity is not the end of your story.
Grace is.
So here is the question the widow answered first:
Will you trust God with what feels like your last?

Because sometimes the miracle begins
the moment we let go.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE CHOSE SIDES.
paragraphs: SHE CHOSE SIDES.

Two men stood on her roof.
The king’s soldiers were pounding on the door.
And the woman hiding them?
A prostitute.

Not a prophet.
Not a priest.
Not a princess.
A woman whose reputation clung to her like the dust of Jericho’s streets.
Yet that night… heaven was watching.

The spies from Israel had slipped into Jericho quietly.
But the city had already heard the rumors.

A sea split in two.
Kings crushed in battle.
A God who fought for His people.
Fear spread through the city like wildfire.
Rahab felt it too.
But while everyone else trembled…
She believed.
When the king’s men came searching, Rahab did the unthinkable.
She hid the spies under stalks of flax on her roof.
Then she faced the soldiers and sent them chasing ghosts into the night.
One choice.
One risk.
One moment where she chose the God she had never seen over the king she lived under.
Later that night she whispered to the spies:

“The LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.”
—Joshua 2:11
Think about that.
A pagan woman in a corrupt city made one of the clearest declarations of faith in the entire Old Testament.
She had heard the stories.
And she believed.
But Rahab didn’t just believe quietly.
She chose sides.
Faith is never neutral.
You cannot hide spies for the people of God and remain loyal to the kingdom of darkness.
The spies gave her a sign.
A scarlet cord.

Tie it in your window, they said.
When judgment comes, anyone inside your house will live.
And when Jericho’s walls collapsed…
Rahab’s house still stood.
Grace hanging from the window.
Red as blood.
But here’s the twist that shakes history.
Rahab didn’t just survive.
She was welcomed into Israel.
She married into the people of God.
And centuries later…
Her name appeared in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Yes.

The prostitute from Jericho became an ancestor of the Savior of the world.
(Matthew 1:5)
This is the Gospel written in advance.

A scarlet cord in a window.
A coming judgment.
A shelter for anyone who believes.
Just like the blood of Jesus.
Maybe your past looks like Jericho.
Maybe your name carries shame.
Maybe people know your worst chapter.
Rahab proves something powerful:

God is not looking for perfect people.
He is looking for people who will choose His side.
When you trust Christ, your past does not disqualify you.
Grace rewrites your lineage.
So today the question is simple.
When the moment comes…
Which side will you choose?
Because one decision of faith can change not only your story—
but generations after you.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DONKEY SAW THE ANGEL.
paragraphs: THE DONKEY SAW THE ANGEL.
Balaam didn’t.

The prophet had the title.
The reputation.
The spiritual résumé.
But the donkey had the vision.

And sometimes…
God lets the animal see what the prophet refuses to see.
The Road to Moab
Balaam was riding toward Moab with a pocket full of opportunity.
The king, Balak, had promised wealth and honor if Balaam would curse Israel.
God had already warned him.
But Balaam kept walking toward the money.
So God placed a sword in the road.
Not metaphorically.
Literally.
The Angel of the Lord stood there—blade drawn, judgment ready.
And only one creature saw Him.
The donkey.
When the Animal Has More Discernment Than the Prophet
Three times the donkey stopped.
Three times Balaam beat the animal.
Three times the angel blocked the path.
And finally…
God did something scandalous.

“Then the LORD opened the donkey’s mouth.”
— Numbers 22:28
The donkey spoke.
Not poetry.
Not prophecy.
A protest.
“Why are you beating me?”
Imagine the moment.

A prophet arguing with his donkey…
while an angel stands there with a sword.
Because sin makes us blind to the obvious.
The Terrifying Reveal
Then God opened Balaam’s eyes.
And suddenly he saw it.
The angel.
The sword.
The judgment he had been riding toward the entire time.
And the angel said something chilling:

“Your way is perverse before Me.”
(Numbers 22:32)
The donkey had actually saved his life.
If the donkey had kept walking…
Balaam would have died on that road.
Sometimes Truth Comes From the Voice You Ignore
Here’s the uncomfortable part.
God sometimes uses the least expected voice to confront us.
A child.
A stranger.
A sermon you didn’t want to hear.
Even a crisis.

Sometimes the voice we mock…
is the one God sent to save us.
Balaam beat the messenger that was protecting him.
We do the same thing when we resist correction.
The Gospel in the Story
This story isn’t just about a talking donkey.
It’s about blind hearts.

The Bible says sin blinds us.
We walk toward danger while insisting we are right.
But grace interrupts the road.
God blocks the path.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes embarrassingly.
But always mercifully.
Because unlike Balaam, there was another man who rode toward death knowingly.
Jesus Christ walked straight toward the cross.
Not blinded.
Not confused.
Willing.
He took the sword of judgment we deserved.
So sinners like us could live.
Final Word
If God could open a donkey’s mouth…
He can open your eyes.
Listen when truth confronts you.
It might be the very thing standing between you and destruction.
And remember:
Grace sometimes sounds like a voice you didn’t expect.
Because Jesus still stops people on dangerous roads.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They didn’t scream “cult.”
paragraphs:
They didn’t scream “cult.”
They whispered, “Submit.”

And slowly…
you stopped hearing God for yourself.
Listen carefully.

Not every voice in a pulpit carries the heart of Christ.
Some carry control dressed as “covering.”
Manipulation baptized as “discipleship.”

And if you’re not discerning—
you will call bondage… loyalty.
⚠️ WARNING SIGNS YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE

1. They replace Christ with themselves
Every decision must pass through them.
Every calling must be approved by them.

You’re no longer following Jesus—
you’re orbiting a personality.
But Scripture says: “There is one mediator… Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5)

2. They weaponize authority
Correction feels like control.
Questions feel like rebellion.

They don’t shepherd your soul—
they silence it.

Some leaders in Scripture “lord it over” others (1 Peter 5:3)—
and God condemns that spirit.

3. They isolate you
“Don’t listen to others.”
“Only we have the truth.”

Slowly, your world shrinks…
until their voice is the only one left.

That’s not spiritual covering.
That’s spiritual captivity.

4. They feed on fear, not faith
“If you leave, you’ll be cursed.”
“If you question, you’ll fall.”
Fear becomes the leash.

But Jesus said,
“You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” (John 8:32)
Not trap you.

5. They stunt your growth
You’ve been there for years…
but you’re still dependent.

No maturity.
No personal conviction.
No deep relationship with God.
Because control thrives on immaturity.
🔥 HERE’S THE HARD TRUTH

A leader who fears your growth
is not protecting you—
they are protecting their control.

And anything that replaces Christ as your source
is an idol… even if it wears a collar.
✝️ THE GOSPEL PIVOT

Jesus does not control you.
He calls you.

He does not silence you.
He restores your voice.

He does not enslave.
He sets free.
“For freedom Christ has set us free…” (Galatians 5:1)
Read that again.

Freedom.
Not fear.
Not control.
Not manipulation.
💔 IF THIS HIT YOU…

Maybe you stayed too long.
Maybe you ignored the red flags.
Maybe you called it “honor” when it was actually fear.
But hear me:

Jesus is not angry at you.
He’s calling you out… not to shame you—
but to restore you.
🙏 WHAT YOU NEED TO DO NOW

• Return to Scripture—not just sermons
• Rebuild your personal prayer life
• Seek godly leaders who point you to Christ, not themselves
• Ask the Holy Spirit for discernment

And if needed…
walk away.

Not from God.
But from what distorted Him.

You were never meant to be controlled.
You were meant to be free in Christ.
If this exposed something… don’t ignore it.

Because sometimes the most dangerous chains
are the ones we call “spiritual.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE STEPPED OUT.
paragraphs: HE STEPPED OUT.

Not onto a dock.
Not onto a plan.
Onto chaos.

The wind was screaming.
The waves were flexing their muscle under a bruised midnight sky.
And in the middle of it all—Jesus.
Let’s step into Gospel of Matthew 14.
🌊 The Moment That Split the Night

They were professional fishermen.
Men who knew water.
Men who respected storms.
But this one?
This one had them shaking.

Then they saw Him.
A silhouette cutting through wind and spray.
Water bending under His feet.
“Lord, if it’s You… tell me to come.”
Pause.

He didn’t ask for the storm to stop.
He asked for permission to step into it.
Jesus said one word.
“Come.”
And Peter… stepped out.
🔥 Fire in His Chest. Water Under His Feet.
For a few breathless seconds, Peter did the impossible.

Wet skin glistening with spray.
Hair whipped by violent wind.
Eyes locked on Jesus.
Faith louder than thunder.
He walked.

Not because he was bold.
Not because he was special.
Because his eyes were fixed.
But then—
He noticed the wind.
He measured the waves.
He calculated the danger.
And the water that once held him… swallowed him.
“Lord, save me!”
Immediately.

Not eventually.
Not after a lecture.
Immediately.
Jesus reached.
💔 The Real Miracle
Some scholars interpret this passage as a lesson on faith under pressure. Others emphasize Christ’s authority over chaos. Both are true.
But don’t miss this:
The greatest miracle wasn’t Peter walking on water.
It was Jesus holding onto a sinking man.
Because walking on water impresses crowds.
But saving drowning hearts reveals the Gospel.
Peter failed.
But he failed toward Jesus.
And that changes everything.
✝️ The Gospel in the Storm
Sin feels like drowning.

Shame pulls at your ankles.
Fear fills your lungs.
Your confidence sinks.
But the Savior still says, “Come.”

And when you falter—
His hand is already extended.
On another stormy day, years later, Peter would deny Jesus three times.
And still—
Grace restored him.
The cross would prove it.

Jesus stepped into deeper waters than Galilee.
He stepped into judgment.
Into wrath.
Into death itself.

So you could step out of condemnation
and onto mercy.
That’s the Gospel.
Not brave men walking on waves.
A merciful Christ who rescues sinking sinners.
⚓ So Let Me Ask You…
What’s your boat?

Comfort?
Reputation?
Addiction?
Control?
That relationship you know God told you to release?
That calling you’re afraid to answer?
What’s keeping you seated when Jesus said, “Come”?
Step out.

Yes, the wind will howl.
Yes, your knees may shake.

But better to sink reaching for Jesus
than stay dry without Him.
And when you cry, “Lord, save me”—
He will.
Immediately.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IT WAS EVERYTHING.
paragraphs: IT WAS EVERYTHING.
Two coins.
That was all she had.

No applause.
No spotlight.
No priest calling attention to her sacrifice.

Just a widow…
and the quiet sound of metal touching metal in the offering box.
In the courts of the temple, wealthy men arrived with confidence.

Long robes.
Heavy purses.
Coins spilling loudly into the treasury.

Clang.
Clang.
Clang.
People noticed.
The noise itself felt impressive.
But then she stepped forward.
A widow.

Invisible to most.
No husband. No security. No inheritance. No safety net.
Just two tiny copper coins.
She held them in her palm.
Two lepta.
Together worth almost nothing.
A whisper of currency.
She could have kept one.
Nobody would know.
Nobody would blame her.
But she didn’t split the sacrifice.
She gave both.
Clink.

And just like that…
her entire life savings was gone.
Across the courtyard, Jesus was watching.
Not the loud gifts.
Not the wealthy donors.
Her.
He called His disciples closer.

“Truly I tell you,” He said,
“this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others.”
— Mark 12:43
More?
How?
Because heaven does not measure gifts by amount.
Heaven measures surrender.
The rich gave from abundance.
She gave from survival.
They gave leftovers.
She gave her life.
Here’s the uncomfortable truth.
God is not impressed by what costs us nothing.
The widow’s offering exposed a deeper reality:
Some people give to be seen.
Others give because God is everything.
She did not know her story would echo across 2,000 years.
She was not trying to inspire sermons.
She was simply trusting the God who sees.
And that is where the Gospel whispers through this moment.
Because one day, another offering would be given.
Not two coins.
A life.
Jesus would step forward to a different altar — the cross.
Not giving from surplus.
Giving everything.

“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich.”
— 2 Corinthians 8:9
The widow gave two coins.
Jesus gave His blood.
And through that sacrifice, sinners like us receive grace we could never afford.
Maybe today you feel like that widow.
Small.
Overlooked.
What you have seems too little.
But heaven is not asking for impressive offerings.
Heaven is asking for your heart.

Your trust.
Your surrender.
Your everything.
And when you place that in God’s hands…
He calls it more than enough.
Someone out there thinks their life is too small to matter.
But the Kingdom of God is built on quiet faithfulness.
Two coins.
A surrendered heart.
And a Savior who gave everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THIS MUST BE THE ONE.
paragraphs: THIS MUST BE THE ONE.

Tall.
Strong.
Kingly.
The kind of man who makes a room go quiet when he walks in.
The prophet Samuel looked at him and felt it immediately.
This must be the king.
But heaven interrupted.
“No.”
Samuel had come to the house of Jesse in Bethlehem with oil in his hand and a mission from God.

Saul had failed.
A new king would rise.
So Jesse brought out his sons.
First came Eliab.

Broad shoulders.
Warrior posture.
Leadership written across his face.
Samuel thought,
“Surely the Lord’s anointed stands before Him.”
But God answered with a line that still shatters human pride:

“Do not consider his appearance or his height…
The Lord does not look at the things people look at.
