People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.”
— First Samuel 16:7
One by one the brothers passed.

No.
No.
No.
Seven impressive men.
Seven divine refusals.
Until Samuel finally asked Jesse:
“Are these all the sons you have?”
Jesse hesitated.
“Well… there is the youngest.”
Not in the house.
Not in the lineup.
Not even considered.
Out in the fields.
Watching sheep.
His name was David.

A shepherd boy.
Dust on his feet.
Probably smelling like the field.
But when he walked in…
God spoke.

“Arise.
Anoint him.”
Think about that moment.
The prophet almost crowned the wrong man.
Not because Samuel was evil.
Because Samuel was human.

We see height.
God sees humility.

We see charisma.
God sees character.

We see the resume.
God sees the heart beating in secret places.
And here is the deeper Gospel thread.
David, the overlooked shepherd, became king.
But centuries later another Son of David would come.

Not tall.
Not royal-looking.
The prophet Isaiah said of Him:

“He had no beauty or majesty to attract us to Him.”
— Book of Isaiah 53:2
That Son of David is Jesus Christ.

Rejected by human eyes.
Chosen by God.
The King we almost would have missed.
Friend, hear this carefully.
God is not searching for the most impressive person in the room.
He is searching for the heart that belongs to Him.

The heart that repents.
The heart that trusts Christ.
The heart that says,
“Lord, I am Yours.”
And when Jesus saves a heart like that—
He turns shepherds into kings.
If this stirred something in you, pause and pray:

“Lord Jesus, look into my heart.
Remove what is false.
Create in me a heart that is fully Yours.”
Because the God who rejected Eliab…
is the same God who lifted David.
And the same Savior who died and rose again is still rewriting stories today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHERE YOU GO, I WILL GO.”
paragraphs: “WHERE YOU GO, I WILL GO.”

Four words.
But they sounded like an earthquake.

A young widow…
Standing at a dusty crossroads…
About to abandon everything she had ever known.

Her language.
Her land.
Her gods.
Her future.
Gone.
This is the moment in Book of Ruth chapter 1 when Ruth the Moabite looked at her broken mother-in-law, Naomi, and made one of the most radical vows ever spoken by a human heart.
Not romantic love.
Covenant love.
Naomi had nothing left.

Her husband dead.
Her sons buried.
Her future empty.
Three graves in a foreign land.
So Naomi told her daughters-in-law the hard truth:

“Go home. Start over. I have nothing to give you.”
(Ruth 1:11–13)
One daughter-in-law kissed Naomi goodbye.
But Ruth?
She gripped Naomi tighter.
Then she spoke words that still thunder across history:

“Do not urge me to leave you…
Where you go I will go.
Where you stay I will stay.
Your people will be my people,
and your God my God.”
— Ruth 1:16
Pause there.
Ruth wasn’t just changing addresses.
She was abandoning Moab — a land of idols — to follow the living God of Yahweh.
She chose faith over familiarity.
She chose God over comfort.
She chose loyalty over survival.
And she had no idea what it would cost.
Or what it would lead to.
Here’s the shock.

This foreign widow…
This outsider…
This immigrant woman with nothing…
Would become the great-grandmother of King David.
And generations later…
Her bloodline would carry the Savior of the world.
Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
A Moabite widow…
woven into the genealogy of the Messiah.
Grace does that.
God writes redemption in places people expect rejection.
Some of you are standing at Ruth’s crossroads right now.
Following Christ might cost you comfort.

Maybe reputation.
Maybe relationships.
Maybe the future you planned.
But the road that looks like loss…
…can become the road that leads straight into the purposes of God.
Ruth walked away from everything.
And walked straight into redemption.
Friend, the Gospel is this:
We were outsiders too.

Foreign to God.
Broken by sin.
Hopeless on our own.
But Jesus came to bring us home.

Through His cross, strangers become family.
Through His grace, the rejected become heirs.

No past is too far.
No story too ruined.
If God can weave Ruth into the story of Christ…
He can rewrite yours too.
🔥 Question for you:

What is God asking you to leave behind
so you can follow Him fully?
Because sometimes the holiest step you’ll ever take…
is walking away from the old life.
Toward God.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE FORGOT HER WATER JAR.
paragraphs: SHE FORGOT HER WATER JAR.

The one thing she came for.
The reason she walked to the well under the burning noon sun—
when no other women would be there.
Her jar.
Her routine.
Her quiet place to hide.
But when she met Jesus…
She forgot it.

Pause there.
Because that jar wasn’t just pottery.
It was her cover.

Five husbands behind her.
A man in her house who wasn’t her husband.
A reputation that whispered through the streets of Samaria like smoke.

So she came at noon.
Alone.

No judgmental eyes.
No whispers.
Just the well.
Then Jesus sat down.
A Jewish rabbi… speaking to her—a Samaritan woman with a scandal attached to her name.
And He didn’t start with condemnation.
He started with thirst.
“Give me a drink.” — John 4:7
But the conversation turned.

From water…
to worship…
to truth.
And then Jesus touched the wound she tried to bury.
“You have had five husbands…” — John 4:18
Not to shame her.
To free her.
Because the One speaking to her already knew everything…
…and stayed anyway.
Then came the moment that changed her life:
“I who speak to you am He.” — John 4:26
The Messiah.
Standing in front of the most unlikely witness in Samaria.
And suddenly the jar didn’t matter anymore.
Scripture says:
“Then the woman left her water jar, went back to the town and said to the people…” — John 4:28
She ran.
The woman who avoided people…
now ran toward them.
“Come see a man who told me everything I ever did!”
That jar stayed by the well.
Because when you meet the Living Water…
you stop carrying the things you once needed to survive.
Listen carefully, friend.
Some of us are still gripping our jars.

Shame.
Secrets.
Old identities.
The labels people gave us.
But Jesus is still sitting at wells today.
Still looking at broken stories.
Still offering living water that satisfies the deepest thirst of the human soul.
The Gospel is this:

We all have a past.
We all carry jars.
But Jesus Christ came to seek sinners, reveal truth, and give new life through His cross and resurrection.
Grace does what shame never could.
It sets you free.
So maybe today is the day you drop the jar.
Leave the shame.
Run with the story.
Because the Savior who knew everything about her…
is the same Savior who died and rose again for you.
And He is still saying:
“Whoever drinks the water I give will never thirst.” — John 4:14
Come to Him.
Drop the jar.
Drink deeply.

—
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BREAKTHROUGH IS CLOSER THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: BREAKTHROUGH IS CLOSER THAN YOU THINK
Have you ever felt like your life was locked behind a door that just wouldn’t open?

A season where you prayed… but nothing changed.
A moment where fear whispered, “This is how it will always be.”
A place where hope felt distant and the walls around you seemed too strong to break.
Maybe your prison doesn’t have iron bars or stone walls.

Maybe it’s the fear of failure.
Maybe it’s anxiety about the future.
Maybe it’s regret from the past.
Maybe it’s a situation that makes you feel trapped, stuck, and powerless.
But here is the truth many people forget:
God specializes in impossible breakthroughs.
In the book of Acts, Paul and Silas were sitting in a real prison. Their hands were chained. Their future looked hopeless. The doors were locked. The guards were watching. Escape was impossible.
Yet instead of surrendering to fear, they chose something powerful.

They prayed.
They worshiped.
They trusted God even in the darkness.
And then something extraordinary happened.

The ground began to shake.
The prison foundations trembled.
The chains fell off.
And every prison door flew open.
Scripture says:

"Suddenly there was such a violent earthquake that the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the prison doors flew open, and everyone’s chains came loose."
— Acts 16:26
Notice the word “suddenly.”
Breakthroughs often happen suddenly.

You can feel stuck for months.
You can struggle for years.
You can pray and wait and wonder if God hears you.
Then in a moment — everything changes.

The door you thought would never open… opens.
The chain you thought would never break… falls.
The situation you thought was permanent… shifts.
God can do in one moment what you couldn’t do in a lifetime.
And sometimes the very place that felt like your prison becomes the place where God reveals His power the most.

Your struggle may feel heavy today.
Your fears may feel overwhelming.
Your situation may look impossible.
But remember this:

No prison is stronger than God.
No chain is stronger than His power.
No darkness can stop His light.
What looks like the end of the road may actually be the moment before your breakthrough.
The door you fear will never open…
God can break it wide open.
Your breakthrough might be closer than you think.

So don’t stop praying.
Don’t stop believing.
Don’t stop trusting God in the middle of the storm.
Because when God decides it’s time to move…
no door can stay closed.
Your share might be the reminder someone needs today that their chains are not permanent and their story is not over. 🙏🔥
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE SLIPPED AWAY.
paragraphs: HE SLIPPED AWAY.

Not from pressure.
Not from people.
Not from purpose.
From applause.
Crowds were exploding around Jesus Christ.

The sick were lining the streets.
Demons were screaming.
Leprosy was vanishing from skin like mist under the morning sun.
Power was everywhere.
But something strange kept happening.

Right when the crowds got bigger…
Right when His name spread louder…
He disappeared.
Scripture whispers the moment:
“But Jesus often withdrew to lonely places and prayed.” — Luke 5:16
Often.

Not occasionally.
Not when convenient.
Often.
Think about the tension.

People were desperate for Him.
Miracles were multiplying.
Momentum was building.
If this were modern ministry, the advice would be clear:

Stay visible.
Keep the crowds.
Build the platform.
But Jesus slipped away.
Because public power is born in private surrender.

Before the miracles…
there was silence.

Before the authority…
there was intimacy.

Before the crowds…
there was a lonely hillside where the Son spoke with the Father.
Imagine the scene.

The night air cool against His skin.
Dust clinging to His robe from a long day of healing.
Stars burning quietly above Judea.
No applause.
No disciples.
Just the Son of God whispering to the Father who sent Him.
Not performing.
Communing.
Here is the scandal most people miss:
The One with all power still prayed.
If anyone could skip prayer, it was Him.
Yet Jesus Christ chose dependence.
Why?
Because the Kingdom doesn’t run on human strength.
It runs on surrender.
And this exposes something in us.

We rush to platforms.
We chase influence.
We want impact.
But we avoid the lonely place.

The quiet room.
The kneeling moment.
The honest prayer where pride dies and the heart becomes small again before God.
But the Gospel begins there.
Not with strong people.
With broken ones.
With sinners who realize they cannot fix themselves.
That is why Jesus came.
He did not come merely to teach prayer.
He came to carry our sin to the cross.
At Golgotha, the sinless Son took the weight of every hidden failure, every secret shame.
Then three days later, the grave lost its grip.
Because grace had the final word.
So when we slip away to pray, we are not climbing toward God.
We are responding to a door Jesus already opened.
Through His blood.
Through His resurrection.
Through His mercy that still reaches the quiet corners of our lives.
Maybe the power you’re asking God for…
is waiting in the prayer you keep postponing.
Slip away.
Close the door.
Whisper His name.
And watch what God does with a heart that chooses the lonely place.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IF YOU REALLY MEAN IT…”
paragraphs: “IF YOU REALLY MEAN IT…”
That was Gideon’s prayer.

Not polished.
Not heroic.
Not the kind you frame on a wall.
It sounded more like this:
“Lord… if You really mean what You said… prove it.”
And heaven did not strike him down for asking.
Israel was crushed under Midian’s boot in Judges 6.

Crops stolen.
Families hiding in caves.
Hope… buried in the dust.
And Gideon?
He wasn’t standing tall with a sword.
He was hiding in a winepress, secretly threshing wheat so the enemy wouldn’t see.
Fear was his shadow.
Then the Angel of the LORD appeared and spoke words that sounded almost ridiculous:
“The LORD is with you, mighty warrior.”
Mighty?
The man was shaking in a pit.
Here is the tension most people miss.
Gideon believed.
But his faith trembled.
So he said the words many believers are too ashamed to say out loud:

“If You will save Israel by my hand as You have said… show me a sign.”
(Judges 6:36)
Not rebellion.
Just a heart trying to trust while fear whispered.
So Gideon laid a fleece on the ground.
First test:

Dew on the fleece.
Dry ground everywhere else.
Morning came.
The fleece was soaked. Gideon wrung out a bowl full of water.
But Gideon still trembled.
So he asked again:
“Lord… don’t be angry… just one more.”
Second test:

Dry fleece.
Wet ground.
And God answered again.
Here’s the beautiful scandal of grace.
God did not reject Gideon for his trembling faith.
He met him inside it.
Because the story of Gideon is not about a confident hero.
It’s about a patient God.
A God who turns fearful farmers into deliverers.
A God who walks gently with people who believe… but still shake.
But here is the deeper truth.
The greatest sign was still coming.
Not a fleece.
A cross.
At the cross, God didn’t just prove His plan.
He proved His love.
“But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
Jesus is the ultimate answer to every trembling prayer that begins with:
“Lord… if You really mean it…”
The empty tomb shouts back:
“I meant it all along.”
So if your faith feels small today…
If fear is whispering louder than courage…
If you are quietly asking God for reassurance—
You are standing exactly where Gideon once stood.
And the same God is still speaking.
Not with anger.
But with invitation.

Trust Me.
Walk with Me.
I will finish what I started.
Because many people don’t need stronger faith.
They just need to know God is patient with trembling hearts.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SILENCE BROKE.
paragraphs: THE SILENCE BROKE.
Four hundred years.

No prophet.
No fresh word.
Heaven… quiet.
And then — an old priest stepped out of the temple unable to speak.
Something was happening.
In Gospel of Luke 1, we meet a couple wrapped in both righteousness and reproach.

Zechariah and Elizabeth.
Faithful. Blameless.
And barren.
Do you know that tension?

Serving God publicly…
while carrying private disappointment.

The years had folded their skin.
The prayers had grown thin from repetition.
“Lord, give us a child.”
Silence.
Until one ordinary day in the temple — incense rising like fragile hope — the angel Gabriel appeared.
Not with suggestion.
With declaration.
“You will have a son.”

Breakthrough does not knock politely.
It interrupts.
But here’s the scandal — Zechariah doubted.
A priest… doubting in the presence of glory.
And heaven answered his unbelief with discipline.
Mute.

Because sometimes God will silence your mouth
so your miracle can grow without your skepticism killing it.
Nine months of quiet.
Nine months of watching Elizabeth’s womb swell with what doubt tried to suffocate.
And when the baby was born, the neighbors assumed tradition would name him Zechariah Jr.
Safe.
Predictable.
But Elizabeth said, “No. His name is John.”
John.
Grace.

They turned to the silent father.
“What do you say?”
He wrote it down.
“His name is John.”
Obedience broke the silence.
And immediately his tongue was loosed.

He didn’t clear his throat.
He prophesied.
Because when God restores your voice, it won’t be small talk — it will be worship.
Let’s not miss the Gospel.

John’s birth was not the destination.
It was the announcement.
John would prepare the way for Jesus.

The barren womb opening was a preview of a greater impossibility —
a virgin womb conceiving.
God was shouting through history:
“I am not done speaking.”
Some scholars interpret the 400 years of silence between Malachi and this moment as divine preparation — a dramatic pause before redemption’s crescendo. And when the silence broke, it wasn’t random.
It was rescue.
Because sin had made humanity spiritually barren.

Righteous rituals.
Empty wombs.
Until Christ.
Jesus would step into our silence — our shame, our doubt, our aging hope — and carry the ultimate breakthrough: forgiveness.
John prepared the way.
Jesus became the Way.
Maybe you feel like you’re living in Luke 1 right now.

Praying.
Waiting.
Hearing nothing.

But silence is not absence.
It is incubation.
And when obedience meets promise, the silence will break.

Repent of unbelief.
Write down what God has spoken.
Trust His timing.

Because the same God who opened Elizabeth’s womb
opened a tomb.
And that is the breakthrough that changes everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHAT CAN YOU GIVE ME?”
paragraphs: “WHAT CAN YOU GIVE ME?”
Silence from heaven can feel like betrayal.
Years earlier, God had spoken a promise over a wandering man named Abraham.

A future.
A nation.
Descendants like stars.
But in Book of Genesis chapter 15, the promise still looked impossible.

No son.
No heir.
No evidence.
Just waiting.
Abraham finally said what many believers whisper but rarely admit:

“Lord God… what can You give me, since I remain childless?”
— Genesis 15:2
Not rebellion.
Honesty.
Faith sometimes asks questions with trembling hands.

Waiting stretches the soul.
Every silent year pulls the promise tighter against doubt.

And Abraham had a reasonable backup plan:
His servant, Eliezer of Damascus.
If God’s promise didn’t arrive… he would make his own solution.
Human logic.
Practical.
Safe.
But heaven interrupted.
God brought Abraham outside.
Into the night.

No temple.
No throne room.
Just sky.
And the Lord said:

“Look toward heaven and count the stars—if you are able to count them.”
— Genesis 15:5
Then came the impossible line:
“So shall your offspring be.”
Stars where Abraham saw emptiness.
Promise where Abraham saw delay.
And then Scripture drops one of the most powerful sentences in the entire Bible:

“Abram believed the Lord, and He credited it to him as righteousness.”
— Genesis 15:6
Not perfection.
Not performance.
Faith.
Centuries later, the apostle Paul the Apostle would point back to this very moment to explain the Gospel.
Righteousness comes by faith.
Not by earning.
Not by human effort.
But by trusting the promise of God fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
Here’s the secret many believers miss:
Waiting is not punishment.
Waiting is where faith learns to breathe.
God was not ignoring Abraham.
God was building a story so large that when the promise finally arrived, the only explanation would be grace.
And when Isaac was born years later, every cry of that baby shouted the same truth:
God keeps His word.
Maybe tonight you’re asking the same question Abraham asked:
“Lord… what can You give me?”

A marriage still barren.
A dream still delayed.
A prayer that feels unanswered.
Hear this, friend.
The God who counted stars for Abraham has not forgotten your name.
At the center of every promise stands the cross of Jesus Christ—where God proved once and for all that He does not abandon those who trust Him.
Your waiting is not wasted.
Your faith is not unseen.
And the same grace that justified Abraham still saves today.

Turn to Christ.
Trust His promise.
And watch how God writes redemption into the places where doubt once lived.
🔥 We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I SAW YOU UNDER THE FIG TREE.”
paragraphs: “I SAW YOU UNDER THE FIG TREE.”

Before Nathanael ever followed Jesus…
Jesus already knew where he had been.
Not just the place.
The moment.
The thoughts.
The hidden prayers whispered where nobody else could hear.
Philip ran to Nathanael breathless:
“We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law—Jesus of Nazareth!” (John 1:45)
Nathanael’s response?
Sharp. Skeptical.
“Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46)
Translation today?

Really? That guy?
That church?
That place?
Some hearts dismiss Jesus before they ever meet Him.
But watch what happens next.
When Nathanael finally walks toward Jesus, the Lord speaks first.
Not with condemnation.
With revelation.
“Here truly is an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” (John 1:47)
Nathanael freezes.
“How do you know me?”
Then Jesus drops the sentence that splits the moment open:

“Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”
— John 1:48
Pause there.
The Bible never tells us what Nathanael was doing under that fig tree.
But Nathanael knew.

And whatever happened there…
Jesus saw it.

The secret place.
The private struggle.
The prayer nobody heard.
Seen.
Some scholars interpret the fig tree as a place where Jewish men often sat to meditate on Scripture.
Maybe Nathanael was praying.
Maybe wrestling with doubt.
Maybe asking God if the Messiah would finally come.
And Jesus answered that prayer before Nathanael even knew it.
That’s the grace shock of the Gospel:
Jesus sees us before we see Him.

Before repentance.
Before faith.
Before we even start looking.
He already knows.

Your doubts.
Your questions.
Your hidden failures.
And still…
He calls.
Nathanael’s response explodes with realization:
“Rabbi, You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” (John 1:49)
One moment of divine seeing.
And the skeptic becomes a believer.
Friend, hear this carefully.
There is no fig tree hidden from Christ.

The quiet addiction.
The secret grief.
The prayer whispered through tears.
He saw it.
And the same Jesus who saw Nathanael now invites you:
“Follow Me.” (John 1:43)
Not because you’re perfect.
But because **His grace is.
The Gospel is this:

Jesus sees the worst in us…
and still goes to the cross for us.
Our sin deserved judgment.
But Jesus Christ took that judgment on the cross, rose from the grave, and now offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who repents and believes in Him.
That includes you.
Even under your fig tree.
Especially there.
Look up.

The One who saw you…
is the One who came to save you.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase. ✝️🔥
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE STORY COMES FULL CIRCLE.
paragraphs: THE STORY COMES FULL CIRCLE.

A garden lost.
A tree guarded by fire.
Humanity locked out.
And at the very end of the Bible…
The gates open again.
🌳 The Tree of Life Restored — Revelation 22
In the first pages of Scripture, something terrible happens.
Humanity reaches for the wrong tree.

Adam and Eve choose rebellion over trust.
The result?
Exile.
“The LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden… and placed cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the Tree of Life.” — Genesis 3:23–24
The message was clear:
Sin cannot live forever.
So God blocked the tree.

Not out of cruelty.
But mercy.
Because eternal life with sin inside us would be eternal ruin.
Then comes the final chapter of the Bible.
And suddenly…
The tree is back.

“Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life… flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb… On each side of the river stood the tree of life, bearing twelve crops of fruit… and the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” — Revelation 22:1–2
Do you see the symmetry?

Genesis:
Humanity driven out.

Revelation:
Humanity welcomed home.

Genesis:
A sword guards the tree.

Revelation:
The Lamb opens the way.
But here is the scandal of grace.
The Tree of Life was restored because another tree stood in between.
The cross.
Jesus hung on wood so we could eat from life again.

The One who created the garden
entered the curse of the garden.

The King of Heaven
became the sacrifice.
And when He rose—
The path to life reopened.
“Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by the gates.” — Revelation 22:14
Not because we earned it.
Because the Lamb paid for it.
One day, Scripture says, the curse will be gone.

No more death.
No more shame.
No more exile.
Just a river flowing from God's throne.
And a tree…
Heavy with life.

The story that began in a garden
ends in a garden-city brighter than the sun.
And every redeemed sinner will finally hear the words humanity has longed for since Eden:
“Welcome home.”
🔥 Friend, the invitation is open right now.
The gates of the New Jerusalem are not entered by perfection.
They are entered by grace through Jesus Christ.

Turn to Him.
Trust the Lamb.
Wash your robes in His mercy.
And one day…
You will stand beneath the Tree of Life.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BUSH WASN’T BURNING UP.
paragraphs: THE BUSH WASN’T BURNING UP.
Flames were everywhere.
But the branches refused to die.
Moses stopped walking.
Shepherd staff in hand. Desert dust on his feet. Forty years of quiet failure behind him. Once a prince of Egypt. Now a fugitive hiding among sheep.
Just another ordinary day in the wilderness.
Until the fire appeared.

Not a wildfire.
Not destruction.
A bush blazing… yet untouched.

No ash.
No collapse.
No smoke choking the sky.
Just fire that refused to consume.
And something in Moses whispered:
“This isn’t normal.”
So he turned aside to look.
That turn changed history.
Because sometimes God hides His voice inside strange moments—moments that interrupt routine, disrupt comfort, and force you to stop walking the same direction.
And when Moses leaned closer, the fire spoke:
“Take off your sandals… for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” (Exodus 3:5)
Imagine the shock.

The same Moses who ran from Egypt in shame.
The same man who buried his past under desert sand.
Now standing barefoot before the presence of God.
The fire didn’t come to destroy him.
It came to call him.
And here’s the mystery of the burning bush:
God often sets ordinary things on fire to wake up sleeping destinies.

A bush.
A desert.
A shepherd’s routine.
That’s all Moses saw.
But heaven saw a deliverer.
Friend, listen carefully.
Sometimes your “burning bush moment” doesn’t look dramatic.

It might be a sermon that won’t leave your mind.
A verse that keeps chasing your heart.
A quiet conviction in the middle of an ordinary day.
God interrupts ordinary days.
But the real miracle?
The fire that doesn’t consume.
Because that’s what grace does.
When God’s holiness touches sinners like us, we should burn up.
But because of Jesus…
We don’t.

At the cross, Christ absorbed the fire of judgment we deserved.
He carried the wrath.
He bore the weight of sin.
So when God calls us now, His fire doesn’t destroy us.
It transforms us.
Moses walked toward a burning bush.
And walked away with a mission that would shake empires.
Maybe today God is lighting something in front of you.

A calling.
A conviction.
A holy interruption.
Don’t ignore it.
Turn aside.
Listen.
Remove the sandals of pride, distraction, and fear.
Because the ground you’re standing on right now…
might be holier than you realize.
And the God who spoke from the fire is still calling people today.

Repent.
Come close.
Follow Jesus.
Because when God lights the fire…
it’s not to burn you.
It’s to send you.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LIGHT STOPPED HIM.
paragraphs: THE LIGHT STOPPED HIM.

Not an argument.
Not a debate.
Not a sermon.
A light.
And the man who hunted Christians collapsed into the dust.
Saul of Tarsus was not confused about what he believed.
He was certain.

Certain the followers of Jesus were dangerous.
Certain their message was blasphemy.
Certain God was on his side.
So he hunted them.

House to house.
City to city.
Dragging believers in chains.
Acts says he was “breathing out threats and murder” (Acts 9:1).
This was not casual opposition.
This was obsession.
Then it happened.

On the road to Damascus—
mid-mission,
mid-rage,
mid-certainty—
Heaven interrupted him.
A light from heaven exploded around him.
Not soft.
Not gentle.
Blinding.
The persecutor hit the ground.
And a voice shattered the silence:

“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?”
(Acts 9:4)
Not them.
Me.

Because every wound Saul gave the church
was a wound against Christ Himself.
Saul trembled.

The man who terrified Christians
now whispered a question every sinner must ask:
“Who are You, Lord?”
And the answer changed history.

“I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.”
(Acts 9:5)

The One he thought was dead
was speaking.

Alive.
Glorious.
Unavoidable.
Here is the scandal of grace:
Jesus did not destroy Saul.
He saved him.
The persecutor became the preacher.
The hunter became the missionary.

The man who tried to erase the church
would soon write letters that built it.
Saul became Paul.
But notice something.
Before Paul could see clearly—
He had to go blind.
Three days in darkness.
Three days confronting the truth.
Three days where the proud Pharisee realized:
He wasn’t fighting for God.
He was fighting against Him.
And maybe that’s where someone reading this is today.
Religious.
Confident.
Certain.
But still resisting Jesus.
Friend, the gospel is not that good people find God.
The gospel is that God confronts sinners and gives them mercy.
Saul deserved judgment.
Instead he received grace.

Because Jesus Christ came into the world
not to crush enemies—
but to save them.
Even the worst of them.
That means your story is not finished.
Your past does not scare Jesus.
Your rebellion does not surprise Him.
Your darkness does not overpower Him.
If Christ could stop Saul on a dusty road—
He can stop you today.
And when His light breaks in,
everything changes.
Repent.
Turn to Jesus Christ.

The One who confronted Saul
is the same Savior who died on the cross
and rose again to forgive sinners.
And when His grace finds you—
You will never be the same.

Because one moment with Jesus
can rewrite an entire life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY DIDN’T ATTACK.
paragraphs: THEY DIDN’T ATTACK.
They walked.

Around a city built for war.
Walls thick enough to race chariots on.
Gates sealed. Soldiers waiting.
And God said:
Walk.

Not charge.
Not climb.
Not break the gate.
Just walk.
Day one — silence.

Dust rising under thousands of feet.
Priests carrying the Ark.
Trumpets breathing slow notes into the desert wind.

No arrows.
No swords swinging.
Just… footsteps.
The people inside Jericho must have laughed.
“Is that their strategy?”

Day two.
The same strange parade.

Day three.
Still walking.

No siege engines.
No battering rams.
Just obedience.
Because sometimes the most dangerous thing you can do in a battle…
is trust God’s instructions when they make no sense.
By day six the soldiers of Israel probably felt the tension burning in their chests.

Warriors trained to fight.
But God told them to wait.
Then came day seven.
Seven laps around the city.
The silence stretched like a drawn bow.
Then Joshua gave the command.
“Shout! For the LORD has given you the city!” (Joshua 6:16)

The trumpets exploded.
The people roared.
And the walls…
collapsed.
Not cracked.
Collapsed.
Because Jericho wasn’t defeated by Israel’s strength.
It fell to God’s power and Israel’s obedience.
Listen carefully.
Most of us want God to bless our plans.
But Jericho teaches a harder truth:
Victory belongs to those who follow God’s plan, even when it looks foolish.
Sometimes faith feels like walking in circles.

Praying again.
Waiting again.
Trusting again.
And the walls don’t move.
Until suddenly…
God moves.
But there’s a deeper layer to this story.

Jericho was under judgment.
Yet one household was saved.
Rahab.

A woman with a stained past who believed the God of Israel was real.
Because grace always finds the one who turns toward God.
Even in the middle of collapsing walls.
That is the Gospel pattern.

Judgment is real.
Sin builds walls around the human heart.
But salvation still hangs from the window — like Rahab’s scarlet cord.
A picture pointing forward.
To the blood of Jesus Christ.
Because when Christ died and rose again, the greatest wall ever built — the wall between sinful humanity and a holy God — came crashing down.
Not by our strength.
By His sacrifice.
So if you feel like you're walking in circles today…
Don’t quit on the sixth lap.
The shout may be closer than you think.
And if your past feels like Rahab’s story…
Grace is still knocking.
Turn to Jesus.

Because He is the God who brings down walls —
and rebuilds lives.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “SPEAK, LORD.”
paragraphs: “SPEAK, LORD.”
Three words.

But the night they were whispered…
a sleeping nation began to wake.
The lamp of God was still burning in the tabernacle.
But Israel’s spiritual fire?
Almost gone.

The priests were corrupt.
The people were drifting.
And the voice of God had grown… rare.
Then heaven chose the most unlikely listener.

Not a prophet.
Not a king.
A boy.
Samuel.

Still young. Still learning.
Sleeping near the Ark where the presence of God dwelt.
Then suddenly—
A voice cut through the darkness.
“Samuel.”
The boy jumped up.
He ran to Eli.
“Here I am. You called me.”
But Eli hadn’t called.
Back to bed.
Again the voice came.
“Samuel.”
Again the boy ran.
Again the confusion.
Until the old priest finally understood something terrifying… and beautiful.
God was speaking.
And the child didn’t yet know His voice.
So Eli whispered instructions that would echo through history:
“When He calls again, say this…
‘Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening.’”
And the voice came again.
“Samuel… Samuel.”
This time the boy didn’t run.
He stayed.
He listened.
And heaven entrusted a child with a message that would reshape a nation.
Because revival doesn’t always start in palaces.
Sometimes it begins in the quiet obedience of a young heart willing to listen.
Here’s the truth many of us forget:
God still calls names in the night.
Not always with thunder.
Sometimes with a whisper inside the soul.
But most people never hear it…
Because they’re too loud.
Too distracted.
Too full.
Samuel heard because he was available.
Because he stayed near the presence of God.
Because when the moment came… he surrendered.
“Speak, LORD.”
Not: “Speak, Lord, I’m busy.”
Not: “Speak, Lord, maybe later.”
Just:
“Your servant is listening.”
And the Gospel reminds us why this still matters.
Centuries later, another voice would call ordinary people by name.
“Follow Me.” — Jesus (Matthew 4:19)
Fishermen listened.
Tax collectors listened.
Sinners listened.
And the world was never the same.

Because the God who called Samuel in the night
is the same God who still calls hearts today.

Through His Word.
Through His Spirit.
Through the voice of Jesus Christ.
The question isn’t whether God still speaks.
The question is—
Are we listening?
Tonight, maybe your prayer is simple.
Three words.
“Speak, Lord.”
And if you’ve wandered far, remember this:

The same Jesus who calls you
also died and rose again to bring you home.
Listen.
Respond.
Follow Him.

Because one listening heart
can still change a nation.
📖 1 Samuel 3
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I AM ONLY A CHILD.”
paragraphs: “I AM ONLY A CHILD.”
That was Jeremiah’s defense.

Not rebellion.
Not unbelief.
Just fear wearing humility’s mask.
God’s voice had just shattered the quiet.

“Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.
Before you were born I set you apart.” — Book of Jeremiah 1:5
Imagine hearing that.
Chosen before your first heartbeat.
Appointed before your first breath.
And Jeremiah’s response?
“I can’t.”

Not because God was unclear.
Not because the mission was vague.
But because the calling was bigger than his confidence.
Jeremiah looks at himself.

Young.
Inexperienced.
Unready.
“I am only a child.”
The Hebrew word na'ar can mean youth, servant, or inexperienced boy.
In other words:
“Lord… I’m not qualified.”
Sound familiar?
We say it differently.

I’m not ready.
Someone else can do it better.
I’m too broken.
Too unknown.
Too late.
But heaven answers Jeremiah with a thunderclap.

“Do not say, ‘I am only a youth.’
You must go to everyone I send you.” — Book of Jeremiah 1:7
Notice something powerful:
God did not argue about Jeremiah’s weakness.
He simply overruled it.
Then comes the moment that changes everything.
The Lord reaches out.
Touches Jeremiah’s mouth.
“I have put my words in your mouth.” — Book of Jeremiah 1:9
Jeremiah thought the problem was his age.
God knew the solution was His presence.
This is the pattern of God.

Moses stutters.
David is the forgotten shepherd.
Peter is impulsive and unstable.
Yet God calls them anyway.
Why?
Because God does not recruit the confident.
He creates the confident by His Spirit.
And centuries later, another young man would face a calling that looked impossible.

A carpenter’s son.
No throne.
No army.
Yet through Him, the world would be saved.
That man is Jesus Christ.
And through His cross, our greatest disqualification—sin—was answered by grace.
The Gospel tells us:
You were not called because you are ready.
You are called because Christ is enough.
So if your heart whispers tonight:

“I’m only a child.”
“I’m only a sinner.”
“I’m only a nobody.”
Listen carefully.
God’s answer has not changed.
“Do not say…”
Because when God calls,
He also touches the mouth, strengthens the heart, and sends the messenger.
🔥 Friend, what excuse have you been offering God?
Lay it down.

The same God who called Jeremiah
is still calling today.
And the invitation is the same:

Repent.
Trust Christ.
Follow the voice that knew you before you were born.

Because Jesus still turns
insecure people into Gospel carriers.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY ARE YOU CRYING OUT?
paragraphs: WHY ARE YOU CRYING OUT?

The sea was in front of them.
Pharaoh was behind them.
And panic was louder than faith.

Israel did what scared people do.
They cried.
They blamed.
They forgot.

Exodus 14 is not just a miracle story.
It is the x-ray of the human heart.
When pressure rises, fear starts preaching.

“Was it because there were no graves in Egypt?”
That’s what they said. Not prayer. Not trust. Panic with a voice.
And then God answers Moses with a question that cuts through the noise:

“Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the Israelites to move on.”
—Exodus 14:15
That line burns.

Because there comes a moment when heaven says:
Enough trembling.
Lift the staff.
Step forward.
Watch Me work.

Moses raised his staff, but the power was never in the wood.
The power was in the God who rules wind, water, armies, and timelines.
One lifted hand.
One command from God.
And the impossible split open.

Fear said, “You’re trapped.”
God said, “Make a path.”

That is what human fear never understands:
when God leads you to the edge, He is not setting you up for destruction.
He is setting the stage for revelation.

Some of you are standing at your own Red Sea right now.
Bills rising.
Family breaking.
Old chains chasing you.
Eyes full of tears.
Heart full of noise.
Hear the Word of the Lord:

Stop letting fear narrate your future.
The same God who brought you out knows how to bring you through.
But don’t miss the deeper miracle.

Israel was not only being rescued from Egypt.
They were being separated from it.
God didn’t just open water.
He closed the door on slavery.
That points us straight to Jesus.

Because humanity had a greater Pharaoh: sin.
A deeper bondage: guilt.
A darker enemy: death.

And at the cross, Jesus stepped into the place we could not survive.
He made a way where there was no way.
Not through a sea of water—
but through judgment, wrath, and the grave.

By His blood, the chains break.
By His resurrection, the path opens.
By His grace, your past does not get the final word.

So yes—cry if you must.
But don’t camp in fear.
Raise what God placed in your hand.
Obey the next instruction.
Move when He says move.

The sea does not decide your story.
God does.
And when He makes a way, no enemy can unmake it.
Jesus still turns trapped people into testimony.

Repent.
Trust Christ.
Walk forward.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FATHER RAN.
paragraphs: THE FATHER RAN.

Not walked.
Not waited.
Ran.
And in the culture of Gospel of Luke 15, dignified men did not run.

They ruled from the porch.
They kept their robes clean.
They let shame walk the long road home.
But this father?

He saw the silhouette of a boy who smelled like pigs…
and grace outran dignity.
The son had rehearsed his speech.
"Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you…"

He had wasted everything.
Inheritance burned on wild nights.
Dreams rotting in a pigpen.
Hunger finally broke him.
Not just for food.
For home.
So he walked back with dirt under his nails and shame in his chest.
Every step expecting rejection.
Every mile imagining the door closed.
But the story turns before he even arrives.
Because Luke 15:20 says:
“While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him.”
He ran.

Robes lifted.
Dignity forgotten.
Dust rising behind mercy.
In that moment the village would have gasped.
A patriarch sprinting like a child.
But the father wasn’t protecting his reputation.
He was protecting his son from shame.
Before the boy could finish the apology—
The father interrupts with grace.

“Bring the best robe.”
“Put a ring on his finger.”
“Sandals on his feet.”
Not servant.
Son.
Not tolerated.
Restored.
Some scholars interpret this moment as more than emotion.

They see a cultural act of public reconciliation—
the father running first so the village could not shame the boy.
Grace didn’t just forgive him.
Grace covered him.
Sound familiar?
Because this story whispers the Gospel.
Humanity ran from God.

We burned the inheritance.
We chased pleasure.
We woke up starving in spiritual pigpens.
Yet the Father did something scandalous.
He ran toward us through Jesus Christ.
The cross is heaven sprinting down the road.

Arms open.
Blood spilled.
Shame broken.
Grace runs faster than guilt.
Faster than regret.
Faster than the lies telling you it’s too late.
Maybe you feel like that boy tonight.

Far away.
Empty pockets.
A rehearsed apology in your throat.
Listen carefully.
The Father is already on the road.
Watching.
Waiting.
Ready to run.

And when you turn back—
you won’t meet a lecture.
You’ll meet embrace.
Because in the Kingdom of God,
grace runs faster than shame.
Someone you know is still walking the road home.
And they need to know:
The Father runs.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHAT ABOUT HIM?”
paragraphs: “WHAT ABOUT HIM?”
Peter had just heard the prophecy of his own death.

Not a gentle death.
Not retirement in peace.

But a road that would stretch his arms and cost him everything.
Jesus had just told him: “You will stretch out your hands…” (John 21:18).
And Peter felt it.

The weight.
The future.
The cross-shaped destiny.
So he did what many of us do when obedience starts to feel heavy.
He looked sideways.
John was walking nearby—the disciple Jesus loved, calm, quiet, close to the Master.
Peter pointed.
“Lord… what about him?” (John 21:21)
Not a theological question.
A comparison question.

Why is my road hard?
Why does his look easier?
Why my suffering?
Why his closeness?
And Jesus gave one of the sharpest, most liberating answers in the entire Gospel.

“If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?
You… follow Me.” (John 21:22)
Translation?

Peter.
Eyes forward.
Comparison is a thief of obedience.
When you stare at someone else’s calling, you start doubting your own.
When you measure your suffering against someone else’s blessing, bitterness grows.
But Jesus shuts the door on comparison.

Not harshly.
Lovingly.
Because the Kingdom of God does not run on competition.
It runs on calling.

John had his story.
Peter had his.

John would write the Gospel.
Peter would shepherd the church.
Both would suffer.
Both would glorify Christ.

Different roads.
Same Savior.
And here’s the deeper grace hiding in the moment.
The man asking the question—Peter—was the same man who once denied Jesus three times.
Failure was his past.
But Jesus had already restored him three times:

“Feed My lambs.”
“Tend My sheep.”
“Feed My sheep.” (John 21:15–17)
The Gospel always moves like this:
Failure → Restoration → Calling.
Not because Peter was strong.
But because Jesus saves sinners and reassigns their future.
Your story might not look like someone else’s.

Your road may feel heavier.
Your timing slower.
Your calling quieter.
But Jesus’ words still echo through every generation:
“What is that to you?”

Not your comparison.
Not your scoreboard.
Not your timeline.
Just this:
Follow Me.
And the beautiful scandal of grace?
The One who calls you to follow already walked the road of suffering first.
He carried the cross.
He died for our sin.
He rose again so that broken disciples—like Peter… like us—could live forgiven and sent.
So today, lift your eyes.
Not sideways.
Upward.
The King is still calling.
Follow Him.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DAUGHTER.”
paragraphs: “DAUGHTER.”

One word.
And a twelve-year shame shattered.

She had no name in the crowd.
Only a condition.

Bleeding.
Weak.
Unclean.
For twelve long years.

According to the law, her body made her untouchable (see Book of Leviticus 15).
Anyone she touched became unclean.

So people stepped back.
Whispers followed her.

Don’t let her near.
Don’t touch that woman.
Imagine the loneliness.

No embrace from family.
No place in worship.
No normal life.
Just isolation.

And worse?
The doctors had taken everything she had.
Mark writes it brutally honest in Gospel of Mark 5:26:
She “suffered much under many physicians… and was no better but rather grew worse.”

Pain.
Poverty.
Shame.

But that day…
Jesus walked through the crowd.
The crowd pressed in.

Bodies everywhere.
Noise everywhere.
Yet in the chaos, she whispered a dangerous hope:

“If I just touch His garment… I will be healed.”
(Gospel of Mark 5:28)
So she pushed forward.

Heart racing.
Hands trembling.
One touch.
Just the edge of His robe.
And suddenly—
Power moved.
Her body changed instantly.
The bleeding stopped.

Twelve years of suffering…
ended in a moment.
But then Jesus stopped walking.
He turned.
“Who touched Me?”

The disciples were confused.
Everyone was touching Him.
But Jesus felt something different.
Faith.
The woman realized she could no longer hide.

Shaking…
terrified…
she fell at His feet and told the truth.
She expected rebuke.

Public shame.
Maybe even condemnation.
Instead…
Jesus spoke a word that rewrote her identity.

“Daughter.”
(Gospel of Mark 5:34)

Not woman.
Not unclean.
Not problem.
Daughter.
In a culture that had pushed her out for twelve years, Jesus pulled her into family.
Grace didn’t just heal her body.
Grace restored her belonging.

“Daughter, your faith has made you well.
Go in peace and be healed of your disease.”
Listen carefully.

Jesus did not say, “You stole healing from Me.”
He said, “Your faith.”

The same Savior who stopped for her…
still stops for the broken today.
Maybe shame has been whispering your identity.

Failure.
Addiction.
Secret sin.
Past mistakes.
But when Jesus speaks over your life, the labels change.
Not condemned.
Not rejected.

Daughter.
Son.
Redeemed.
Because at the cross, Jesus carried the deeper disease—sin.

Through His death and resurrection, He offers the healing no doctor can give:
forgiveness, restoration, new life.
The woman reached for His garment.
Today, you can reach for Him.
And when you do, grace speaks a new name over you.
Daughter.

Because the Savior who healed the bleeding woman
still restores identities today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WASN’T SUPPOSED TO TOUCH HIM.
paragraphs: SHE WASN’T SUPPOSED TO TOUCH HIM.

Twelve years of bleeding.
Twelve years of whispers.
Twelve years of being untouchable.

According to the law, she was unclean.
Anything she touched became unclean.
Anyone she touched became unclean.
So she learned to live in the shadows.

Back rows.
Covered face.
Silent shame.

Doctors took her money.
Hope drained from her body the same way the blood did.
And then she heard a name.
Jesus.
But here was the problem:

The crowd was thick.
And the Law said she shouldn’t touch anyone.
Yet something inside her refused to die.
Faith.

“If I just touch His garment… I will be healed.”
(Mark 5:28)

Not His hand.
Not His face.
Just the edge of His robe.
So she pushed through the crowd.

Every step risky.
Every shoulder brushed a violation.
Every heartbeat louder than the noise around her.
And then—
Her fingers touched the hem.
Instantly.

The bleeding stopped.
Strength returned.
Twelve years of suffering ended in a single second.
But Jesus stopped walking.
“Who touched My clothes?”

The disciples were confused.
The crowd was pressing everywhere.
But Jesus felt something different.
Power had moved.
And the woman froze.

Fear gripped her chest.
If she spoke, the whole crowd would know her secret.
But grace was standing right in front of her.

So she fell at His feet…
and told the whole truth.
Not just about the touch.

About the pain.
The isolation.
The shame.
And Jesus did not rebuke her.
He did not step back.
He did not call her unclean.
He called her something no one had called her in twelve years.
“Daughter.”

“Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace and be healed of your affliction.”
— Mark 5:34
Do you see the Gospel here?
She thought she was stealing a miracle.
But Jesus turned it into a relationship.

Religion said:
“Stay away. You’re unclean.”

Jesus said:
“Come near. You’re family.”
This is what Christ does.

He is not afraid of your shame.
Not afraid of your past.
Not afraid of the thing you hide from the crowd.
You may feel like you’re only reaching for the edge of His robe…
But grace is already reaching for you.
And when Jesus speaks over your life, He doesn’t call you by your failure.
He calls you:

Daughter.
Son.
Redeemed.
Someone in the crowd today is still bleeding in silence.
And they need to know:
One touch of Jesus changes everything.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE RAN THE OTHER WAY.
paragraphs: HE RAN THE OTHER WAY.
Not because he doubted God.
Because he knew God too well.
Jonah understood something terrifying about the heart of the Lord.
Mercy.
And he hated the thought of it falling on them.
Nineveh.

The brutal empire.
The nation of cruelty.
The city that crushed nations and skinned their enemies alive.
Jonah wanted justice.
God wanted repentance.
So the prophet ran.
The Run
Jonah didn’t just walk away.
He ran west when God said east.
He fled toward Tarshish — the edge of the known world.
Scripture says:
“But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.” — Jonah 1:3
Notice the language.
Not from Nineveh.
From the presence of the Lord.
Jonah knew exactly what he was doing.
This wasn’t confusion.
This was resentment dressed as obedience avoidance.
The Real Reason
Years later Jonah finally confessed the truth.
“I knew that You are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.” — Jonah 4:2
Do you see it?
Jonah ran because he knew God might forgive them.
The prophet preferred judgment over mercy.
Because mercy for your enemies feels like injustice.
And sometimes our hearts secretly whisper:
"Lord, save me… but deal harshly with them."
The Storm
But you cannot outrun the voice that made the sea.
So God sent a storm.
Not to destroy Jonah.
To wake him up.
The pagan sailors began praying while the prophet slept below deck.
Imagine that.
The man of God asleep.
The unbelievers crying out to heaven.
Sometimes rebellion makes believers colder than pagans.
The Gospel Hidden in the Storm
Jonah would rather die than see his enemies saved.
But centuries later another prophet came.
Jesus.
He didn’t run from sinners.
He ran toward them.
He walked straight into the storm of God’s justice.
Not because He deserved it.
Because we did.
And on the cross He prayed for His enemies:
“Father, forgive them.”
That includes Nineveh.
That includes Jonah.
That includes us.
The Real Question
The story of Jonah is not about a fish.
It’s about a heart.
Do we love mercy only when it benefits us?
Or do we rejoice when grace reaches people we think don’t deserve it?
Because the Gospel is scandalous.
God saves the guilty.
Friend…
If God only showed mercy to the deserving…
none of us would be here.
But Jesus rewrites stories.
Even the ones that ran the other way.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF YOU ONLY KNEW…
paragraphs: IF YOU ONLY KNEW…
The King was finally entering His city.

Crowds shouting.
Palms waving.
Prophecy unfolding in plain sight.
But suddenly—
He stopped.

And the King…
wept.
In Gospel of Luke 19:41–44, as Jesus Christ approaches Jerusalem, the noise of celebration fades behind a moment that feels almost unbearable.
He looks at the city.
And tears fall.

Not quiet sadness.
Not polite emotion.
This is the grief of rejected love.
“If you, even you, had only known on this day what would bring you peace…” (Luke 19:42)
Pause there.

The Prince of Peace was right in front of them.
Yet their hearts were blind.
The Tragedy of Missing God
Jerusalem knew religion.

They had the temple.
The sacrifices.
The Scriptures.
But when God Himself walked their streets…
They didn’t recognize Him.
Some scholars interpret this moment as one of the most profound expressions of divine compassion in Scripture. The Son of God isn’t cold toward sinners.
He aches over them.
Jesus isn’t angry that people need grace.
He grieves when they refuse it.
Tears Before the Judgment
Jesus foretells destruction:

Enemies surrounding the city.
Walls collapsing.
Children crushed within the ruins.
History records that in AD 70, the Siege of Jerusalem by the Roman Empire devastated the city—exactly as Jesus warned.
But here’s the shocking part:
The prophecy is spoken through tears.
Not rage.
Tears.
The Heart of God
Hear me carefully.
God does not delight in judgment.
The cross proves that.
Before wrath came, Jesus wept.
Before the nails, He warned.
Before the empty tomb, He mourned for the lost.
This is not the cold face of religion.
This is love wounded by rejection.
And the Question Still Echoes
“If you only knew…”
How many today still miss the moment of God’s visitation?

Busy.
Religious.
Distracted.
Yet the same Jesus who cried over Jerusalem still calls today.
Not with condemnation.
With open arms marked by nails.
The Gospel Turn
We are the city.

Blind.
Proud.
Lost in our own peace plans.
But Christ came anyway.

He carried our sin to the cross.
He rose again in victory.
And the tears of Luke 19 lead directly to the redemption of Calvary.
Grace was coming.
Friend…
If you only knew what brings you peace.
His name is Jesus.

Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
Receive the mercy Jerusalem refused.
And you will discover the truth:

The Savior who wept for sinners
also died for them.
And rose again.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HOW WILL THIS BE?”
paragraphs: “HOW WILL THIS BE?”

Not rebellion.
Not unbelief.
Just an honest question from a trembling heart.
Nazareth was quiet that day.

No thunder.
No choir of angels filling the sky.

Just a young woman…
and a message that would fracture human history.
“Greetings, favored one.”
Mary’s world tilted.

She was not a queen.
Not a scholar.
Not a woman of power.
Just a village girl promised to a carpenter.
And then the impossible dropped into the room:

“You will conceive and give birth to a son…
and you will call His name Jesus.”
— Luke 1:31
Pause there.

Mary knew biology.
Mary knew culture.
Mary knew what pregnancy outside marriage meant in her village.

Shame.
Whispers.
Possible stoning.
So she asks the question every honest believer eventually asks:

“How will this be?”
— Luke 1:34
Notice something holy here.
She didn’t say “No.”
She asked how.

Faith is not the absence of questions.
Faith is bringing your questions to God instead of running from Him.
The angel answers:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you…
and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”
— Luke 1:35
Translation:
Mary, this miracle will not come from human strength.
It will come from God Himself.
Because the story of salvation has never depended on human ability.
Not Mary’s.
Not yours.
Not mine.
And then comes the moment that shakes heaven.
A teenage girl, staring at a future she cannot control, whispers the most dangerous prayer on earth:

“Behold, I am the servant of the Lord.
Let it be to me according to your word.”
— Luke 1:38
That sentence carried the weight of redemption.
Because the child in her womb would grow to carry another weight.
A cross.
Jesus would enter the world through Mary’s surrender…
and leave the world carrying our sin.

Your shame.
Your secret battles.
Your past you wish nobody knew.
All nailed to wood.
All buried in a borrowed tomb.
And three days later—
Resurrection.
So if you’re standing in a moment where God’s plan makes no sense…
If obedience feels risky…
If your heart whispers the same words Mary spoke—
“How will this be?”
Hear the quiet answer of heaven:

With God, nothing will be impossible.
— Luke 1:37

Not your restoration.
Not your forgiveness.
Not your new beginning.
Jesus specializes in impossible stories.
He is still rewriting them today.
Including yours.
Because the Gospel still turns questions into miracles.
And remember:
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY KNEW THE LAW.
paragraphs: THEY KNEW THE LAW.
But they missed the Messiah.

They could quote every line of Moses.
They could debate the smallest commandment.
They wore Scripture on their sleeves… literally.
And yet when Jesus Christ stood in front of them—
they didn’t bow.
They challenged Him.
The Most Dangerous Kind of Blindness
In Gospel of Matthew 23, Jesus turns toward the religious elite—the Pharisees.
And what He says is not gentle.
“Woe to you, teachers of the law and Pharisees, you hypocrites!” (Matthew 23:13)
Not once.
Not twice.
Seven times.
Seven thunderclaps of truth.
Why?
Because they had turned God’s law into a stage for their ego.
They loved the appearance of holiness.

Long prayers.
Front-row seats.
Titles like Rabbi.
But inside?
Rot.

Jesus says they were like whitewashed tombs—
beautiful on the outside,
full of death on the inside.
Religion had become their costume.
And pride was the poison in their veins.
The Terrifying Irony
The Pharisees studied the Scriptures that pointed to Jesus.
They memorized the prophecies.
They analyzed every syllable.
Yet when the Messiah stood in the flesh before them…
they rejected Him.
Why?
Because knowledge without humility hardens the heart.

You can master theology
and still miss the Savior.

You can teach Scripture
and still refuse surrender.

You can know about God
without ever knowing Him.
The Gospel Pivot
But listen carefully.
Jesus didn’t expose hypocrisy to destroy people.
He exposed it to rescue them.
Because the Kingdom of God isn’t built on performance.
It’s built on repentance.
Not spotless religion.
But surrendered hearts.
The same Jesus who rebuked the Pharisees would soon walk toward a cross.
There, the perfectly righteous Son of God would carry the sin of the hypocrite… the rebel… the religious fraud… the broken.
All of us.
At the cross, grace shattered the scoreboard of religion.
You don’t earn your way to God.
You come empty.
And Christ fills you with mercy.
The Question That Still Burns
The tragedy of Matthew 23 is not ancient history.
It’s a mirror.

Do we love being seen as righteous…
or being made righteous by Jesus?
Do we polish the outside…
while hiding the inside?
Or do we run to Christ and say:
“Lord… clean all of me.”
Because the same Savior the Pharisees rejected
still stands today with open arms.
And He doesn’t ask for perfect people.
He asks for honest ones.
Someone you know might be chasing religion when what they truly need is Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IF I PERISH…”
paragraphs: “IF I PERISH…”
The words weren’t whispered.
They were walked.

Three days without food.
Three nights with only prayer.
No royal makeup could hide the weight in Queen Esther’s chest.
Because the law was clear.
If anyone entered the king’s inner court without being summoned…
Death.

No trial.
No appeal.
Just the sound of guards moving.
And Esther knew it.
She stood outside the throne room doors—robes heavy, crown steady, heart thundering like war drums.
Behind those doors sat the most powerful man in the empire.
Behind her stood an entire people marked for extermination.
Silence.

One step forward…
and her life might end.
But she said it anyway.

“If I perish… I perish.”
—Esther 4:16
Not reckless courage.
Holy courage.
Because Esther understood something many believers forget:

Faith is not the absence of fear.
Faith is obedience in spite of it.
The doors opened.

Marble floors.
Columns rising like giants.
The throne glowing in royal gold.
Every eye turned.
The queen had entered uninvited.
The court froze.

One movement from the king’s hand…
and Esther would die before she spoke a word.
But then—
The king lifted the golden scepter.
Mercy.
Grace in the middle of danger.
Favor where death should have been.
Esther stepped forward and touched the tip of the scepter.

The girl who once hid her identity
now stood before a throne to save a nation.
But this story whispers something even deeper.
Because one day another person would walk toward a throne knowing death awaited.
Not a palace throne.
A wooden cross.
And unlike Esther, Jesus was not spared.
He didn’t say “If I perish.”
He did perish.

For our sin.
For our rebellion.
For every hidden shame we hope no one sees.
Three days later, the King of Heaven raised Him.
Now the throne of God is no longer a place of terror.

Because of Christ, it is a throne of grace.
(Hebrews 4:16)

So when fear tells you to stay silent…
when obedience feels dangerous…
Remember the queen who walked through those doors.
And remember the Savior who walked to the cross.
Courage is not dying for a cause.
Courage is trusting the King with your life.
Someone you know is standing outside a door today, wondering if they should step forward.
Tell them this:

The God who gave Esther courage
is the same God who still moves scepters today.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: FROM INSIDE THE FISH…
paragraphs: FROM INSIDE THE FISH…

Not from a temple.
Not from a clean place.
Not from a victory moment.
From a stomach.

Dark.
Crushing.
Breath tight with the stench of the deep.
Jonah finally prayed.
Think about that.

The prophet ran from God…
boarded a ship…
triggered a storm…
was thrown into the sea…
—and the prayer didn’t come until rock bottom had teeth.
Inside the fish.

Where seaweed wrapped his head.
Where waves crushed over him.
Where every heartbeat whispered:
You should have obeyed.
Jonah cried:

“In my distress I called to the Lord,
and He answered me.” (Jonah 2:2)
Pause there.

God heard a prayer
from inside a fish.

Not polished.
Not pretty.
Not impressive.
Just desperate.
Jonah confessed:
“I have been banished from Your sight… yet I will look again toward Your holy temple.” (Jonah 2:4)
Here is the turning point.
Not when the fish swallowed him.
When repentance swallowed his pride.
Rock bottom has a strange mercy.
It strips away the lies.

The excuses.
The running.
The illusion that we can outrun the voice of God.
And suddenly the heart whispers what it should have said from the beginning:
“Salvation belongs to the Lord.” (Jonah 2:9)
That line is the Gospel in miniature.
You cannot swim back to God.
You cannot climb out of the deep.
You cannot save yourself.
But God hears from impossible places.

From prison cells.
From hospital beds.
From secret addictions.
From nights filled with regret.
And yes—
even from inside the fish.

Some scholars see Jonah’s three days in the fish as a foreshadowing of Jesus in the grave (Matthew 12:40). The greater Jonah would go deeper than any ocean… into death itself… so sinners could rise into life.
Jonah prayed and God spoke.
And the fish obeyed faster than the prophet ever did.
“Then the Lord commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land.” (Jonah 2:10)
God didn’t just hear him.
He gave him another chance.
That is grace.
Maybe your prayer today comes from a dark place.
A place you’re ashamed to admit.
Listen carefully:
God is not intimidated by the depth of your mess.
Cry out.
Right there.
Right now.
Because the same God who heard Jonah in the belly of the fish still listens for broken voices.
And Jesus is still in the business of bringing people from the deep to dry ground.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “GOD ASKED FOR HIS SON.”
paragraphs: “GOD ASKED FOR HIS SON.”

Not his money.
Not his livestock.
Not his reputation.
His son.
And heaven went silent.
Would you still trust God?
Family, lean in.
The Climb — Book of Genesis 22
God speaks to Abraham:
“Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love…”

Do you feel that?
Heaven names the wound before pressing it.

The promised child.
The miracle laughter.
The future wrapped in flesh.
Some scholars interpret this as the ultimate test of covenant loyalty — not because God delights in pain, but because He exposes what owns our hearts.
And Abraham rose early.

No argument recorded.
No delay.
Just obedience.
Three days up a mountain with a question echoing in his chest.

Isaac turns and asks,
“Father… where is the lamb?”
That question split history in half.
The Tension
Abraham binds the promise.

Rough rope against young wrists.
Wood beneath trembling knees.
Fire in his hand.
Knife in the other.
And heaven still says nothing.
This is the moment most people leave God.

When obedience feels like betrayal.
When the promise looks like it’s bleeding.
When faith smells like smoke.
Would you still trust Him?
The Pivot

At the last second —
“Abraham! Abraham!”
The knife stops mid-air.

A ram caught in the thicket.
Substitute provided.

Jehovah-Jireh.
“The Lord will provide.”
But don’t miss it — this wasn’t just about Isaac.
This mountain was whispering about another Son.

Centuries later, another Father would walk up another hill.
This time there would be no voice stopping the blade.
Jesus Christ carried the wood on His back.

No ram in the thicket.
No substitute for Him.
He was the substitute.

For you.
For me.
Where Abraham was stopped, God the Father was not.
Because redemption demanded blood.
And grace demanded love.
Close the Loop
You ask, “Would I trust God?”
Here’s the deeper question:
Do you trust the God who did not spare His own Son for you?

The test in Genesis 22 was never about cruelty.
It was prophecy soaked in mercy.

Abraham received his son back.
We receive salvation because the Father gave His.

Your Isaac — your dream, relationship, career, reputation —
Place it on the altar.

Not because God wants to destroy it.
But because He wants to prove He is better.

Today, surrender what you’re gripping.
And trust the God who provides the Lamb.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE ENEMY BECAME THE APOSTLE.
paragraphs: THE ENEMY BECAME THE APOSTLE.
Let that hit your chest.

The man breathing threats…
became the man breathing Scripture.

The hunter…
became the herald.

People love transformation arcs.
But this one?

This wasn’t a glow-up.
It was a death.
⚔️ The Road to Damascus — Acts of the Apostles 9

Saul wasn’t confused.
He was convinced.

Trained. Brilliant. Burning with zeal.
He thought he was protecting God.
But he was persecuting Christ.

On that desert road—dust rising, sun brutal, heart hotter than the sand—
a light split the sky.
Not soft.
Not sentimental.
Blinding.
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?” (Acts 9:4)
Not them.
Me.
When you touch Christ’s Church, you touch Christ Himself.

Saul falls. Dust in his mouth. Pride in his throat.
Three days blind.
Three days in darkness.
Three days like a tomb.
🌊 The Pivot — Grace Interrupts Fury
Enter Ananias.

Afraid.
Honest about it.
“Lord… he’s dangerous.”
But Jesus says, “Go. He is a chosen instrument of Mine.” (Acts 9:15)
Chosen.

The terrorist becomes the testimony.
The persecutor becomes the preacher.
Scales fall like dead skin.

Water rushes over him in baptism—
cool against the fire he used to carry.

New name.
New heart.
Same intensity.
Now aimed at Jesus.
🔥 Let’s Tell the Truth
Some of you are still Saul.

Religious.
Passionate.
Dead wrong.

You think you’re defending truth—
but you’ve never surrendered to Truth Himself.

Sin isn’t just bad behavior.
It’s rebellion against a holy God.
And grace isn’t self-improvement.
It’s resurrection.

Saul didn’t rebrand.
He repented.

He didn’t find himself.
He lost himself—and found Christ.

As he would later write in Galatians 2:20,
“I have been crucified with Christ…”
That’s the Gospel.

Jesus lived the life Saul failed to live.
Died the death Saul deserved to die.
Rose again to offer mercy to His enemies.
Yes—His enemies.
Romans 5:10 says we were reconciled to God while we were enemies.
You don’t clean up and come to Jesus.
You collapse.
And He raises you.
🎯 Close the Loop
People love transformation arcs.

Weight loss.
Career comeback.
Reputation restored.
But the greatest story?
When the enemy becomes the apostle.

When the sinner becomes the son.
When the rebel becomes redeemed.
That’s not self-help.
That’s the cross.
And if Jesus can turn a church-hunter into a church-planter—
He can rewrite you.
Right now.

Repent.
Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Receive the mercy you’ve been running from.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ONE LIKE A SON OF MAN.
paragraphs: ONE LIKE A SON OF MAN.
Empires rose like monsters from the sea.
Daniel saw them.

Beasts with iron teeth.
Claws that crushed nations.
Wings that carried pride across the earth.

Babylon.
Persia.
Greece.
Rome.
Power after power.
Each one roaring, devouring, promising eternity.
But every empire in Daniel’s vision had the same ending:
They fell.

Kings boast.
Flags rise.
Statues are built.
Then dust.
Daniel watched the chaos of history unfold like a stormy ocean—kingdoms clawing their way out of the waves.
And then…
Everything changed.
The courtroom of heaven opened.

“The Ancient of Days took His seat…
His clothing white as snow.” (Daniel 7:9)
Fire flowed from His throne.
Books were opened.
Judgment fell.
And the beasts lost their power.
But Daniel saw someone else approaching.
Not another beast.
Not another tyrant.
Not another empire built on blood.
He came with the clouds of heaven.

Human.
Yet more than human.

“I saw in the night visions, and behold, one like a Son of Man came with the clouds of heaven…
And to Him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve Him.” (Daniel 7:13–14)
This kingdom would not collapse.

No invasion.
No corruption.
No fall of Rome moment.
An everlasting dominion.
Centuries later, Jesus walked dusty roads in Galilee and used a title for Himself again and again:
“The Son of Man.”
Not random.
Not poetic.
It was a claim.
The carpenter from Nazareth was saying:
I am the one Daniel saw.
The beasts of history still roar.

Empires still rise.
Governments still promise salvation.
Power still seduces the human heart.
But Daniel’s vision whispers a deeper truth:
History is not controlled by beasts.
History is moving toward a King.

A crucified King.
A risen King.
A returning King.
The Son of Man.
And when His kingdom fully comes, every counterfeit throne will bow.

Not to Rome.
Not to Washington.
Not to Beijing.
To Jesus Christ.
Friend, this is the hope beyond empires:
The kingdom of Christ cannot collapse.

Not your failures.
Not your past.
Not even death itself.

Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
The Son of Man who received the eternal kingdom also went to a cross to rescue rebels like us.
And everyone who belongs to Him will share in that kingdom forever.
So lift your eyes above the beasts of history.
The clouds are not empty.
The King is coming.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IT WAS JUST FIVE LOAVES.”
paragraphs: “IT WAS JUST FIVE LOAVES.”

Not a harvest.
Not a bakery.
Just a boy’s lunch.

Five barley loaves.
Two small fish.
That’s it.

And in front of him?
A crowd that scholars estimate at 15,000–20,000 hungry people.

Men. Women. Children.
An ocean of need.
The disciples did the math first.
“Eight months’ wages wouldn’t buy enough bread for everyone to have a bite.” (John 6:7)
Translation?
Impossible.
But then Andrew noticed something.
A child.

Standing there quietly.
Holding a small meal someone had packed for him that morning.
Imagine the moment.

The boy hears grown men discussing hunger, impossibility, logistics, budgets.
And still… he steps forward.
Not with abundance.
With everything he had.

Five loaves.
Two fish.
Small hands.
Open heart.
And here’s the detail most people miss:
Jesus did not multiply the bread in the boy’s hands.
He multiplied it after it was surrendered.

Jesus took it.
He gave thanks.
Then the miracle began.

Bread breaking.
Fish dividing.
Basket after basket after basket moving through the crowd.
Until Scripture says:
“They all ate and were satisfied.” (John 6:12)
Not a taste.
Satisfied.
And when it was over?
Twelve baskets left.

The lunch that looked laughably small
became overflow in the hands of Christ.
Listen carefully.

God rarely starts with abundance.
He starts with surrender.

Moses had a staff.
David had a sling.
A widow had a jar of oil.

And one unnamed boy
had a lunch.
That’s the Gospel pattern.

You bring what feels small.
Jesus turns it into what only God can do.

Your little faith.
Your broken story.
Your imperfect offering.
Placed in the hands of Christ—
becomes more than enough.
Because the real miracle in John 6 wasn’t the bread.
It was the Bread of Life standing in front of them.
Later Jesus said:
“I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never hunger.” (John 6:35)
The crowd came for food.
But Jesus came to give eternal life.
And that life is given the same way the boy gave his lunch:

Open hands.
Full surrender.
Trust in Jesus.
So here’s the question tonight:
What are you holding that feels too small for God to use?

Your time?
Your talent?
Your faith?
Place it in the hands of Christ.
He is still multiplying surrendered lives.
And He is still feeding hungry souls.
Come to Him.

Because the Bread of Life
is more than enough.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “PUT YOUR HAND HERE.”
paragraphs: “PUT YOUR HAND HERE.”
The room went silent when Jesus said it.

Not to Peter.
Not to John.
To the one disciple everyone whispered about.
Thomas.
The doubter.
The Moment Doubt Met the Wounds
Thomas had drawn a line in the sand.
“Unless I see the nail marks in His hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into His side, I will not believe.” — Gospel of John 20:25
He didn’t whisper it.
He declared it.

Eight days passed.
Eight long days of stubborn unbelief.
Then suddenly—

The locked room.
The trembling disciples.
And Jesus standing there again.
Peace.
And then He turned.
Not to the believers.
To the skeptic.
“Thomas… put your finger here.”
Look at my hands.
“Put your hand into my side.”
Stop doubting.
Believe.
The Scandal of Grace
Jesus did not shame Thomas.
He invited him closer.
Closer than anyone else in that room.

The one who demanded proof
was the one Jesus offered His wounds.
Let that sink in.
The scars were not hidden.
They were the evidence of love.
Thomas touched the place where the spear had torn flesh.
The place where blood and water once flowed.
And in that moment the doubter collapsed into worship.
“My Lord and my God!” — Gospel of John 20:28
Not just teacher.
Not prophet.
God.
The Gospel Hidden in the Scars
Those wounds Thomas touched?
They were for him.

For you.
For me.

The nails.
The spear.
The cross.
All of it because sin demanded justice.
And Jesus took it.
Scripture says:
“He was pierced for our transgressions.” — Book of Isaiah 53:5
The scars of Christ are the receipts of redemption.
Proof that the debt was paid.
And Then Jesus Said Something For Us
Because Thomas saw.
But we… didn’t.
“Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” — Gospel of John 20:29
That blessing travels across centuries.
Across oceans.
Across screens.
Straight to you.
Brother, Sister… Hear the Invitation
Jesus is still saying it.
“Put your hand here.”
Look at the wounds.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.

Doubt can become worship
when it touches the scars of Christ.
If your faith feels shaky…
If questions haunt you…
Come closer.
Jesus is not afraid of honest doubt.
He answers it with nail-scarred hands.
We tell the stories shame tried to erase.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I AM JOSEPH.”
paragraphs: “I AM JOSEPH.”
The room froze.

The most powerful man in Egypt…
just spoke the name they buried.
The brothers felt the blood drain from their faces.
Because they remembered.

The pit.
The rope.
The silver coins.
The screams of a 17-year-old boy they sold like livestock.
And now… that boy stood before them wearing the authority of a kingdom.
Silence.

Heavy.
Terrifying.
Because this was the moment judgment could fall.
But Joseph didn’t call the guards.
He wept.
Loud enough that the palace heard it.
“I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?” — Genesis 45:3
The brothers couldn’t answer.
Not because they forgot how to speak.
Because guilt was choking them.
They expected revenge.
Joseph gave them revelation.
“Do not be distressed or angry with yourselves for selling me here, because it was to save lives that God sent me ahead of you.” — Genesis 45:5
Pause there.
They sold him.
God sent him.

Same event.
Different author.

What looked like betrayal…
was actually God positioning a rescuer.

The pit led to Potiphar.
The prison led to the palace.
The suffering led to salvation.
Joseph wasn’t just surviving.
He was being prepared to feed nations during famine.
Even the brothers who betrayed him.
This is the mystery of providence:
Humans meant evil.
God meant rescue.
But the story doesn’t stop with Joseph.
Joseph is a shadow.
Because centuries later, another Son would be betrayed by His own.
Sold for silver.
Rejected by His brothers.
Crucified between criminals.
Yet through that betrayal…
God saved the world.
Jesus didn’t just forgive His betrayers.
He became the bread that feeds them.
Joseph saved people from famine.
